en: The Essence of Reality (*Tattvasāra*), together with its commentary *Ratnasāriṇī*, [is completed];
my mind yearns for union with the lotus feet of the venerable Viṣṇucitta— what more could be desired beyond this?
If even mine, the speech of Yatīśekhara Bhāratī, were not so, how could this meaning possibly be brought under the control of words? || 1 ||
Oṃ, salutation to Hari, the essence of devotion and the soul of resolve,
who dispels both the Daityas and the disguised Daityas with weapons and scriptures.

The Blessed One, the Guru who grants boons, performs an auspicious rite established by tradition and custom for the sake of completing the intended work without obstacle: "Śrī Viṣṇucitta," and so forth.

(Mama cetaḥ)—[The mind] of Śrī Viṣṇucitta—meaning, of our teacher, whose mind (*citta*) is fixed on Viṣṇu; who, like Bhaṭṭanāthasūri, bears that [teacher’s] name by virtue of his victory over opponents through the determination of the supreme reality (*paratattva*) and so forth, by his service to him, and by his lineage; [the mind] longs for—desires—the union with his lotus feet—that is, for a proper relationship consisting of clasping the hands and bowing the head. The dative case is used according to the rule *spṛher īpsitaḥ*.

Although there is no comprehension of excellence (*prakarpa*) due to the absence of a comparative term in the accusative case, nevertheless, that excellence is understood through the present participle. Here, the intended Vedic scripture is: "He who has supreme devotion for the Lord, and as for the Lord, so for the Guru. Therefore, what is the use of anything else? The meaning is: "By union with the feet of Śrī Viṣṇucitta, I have no other purpose whatsoever. This is because acts such as the salutation of the Lord depend upon the salutation of the Teacher, whereas this [union] is independent of that. For this very reason, there is no dependence even upon that for the attainment of the fruit.

"If not," and so forth: "If my union with the lotus feet of Śrī Viṣṇucitta does not occur"—meaning [the works] such as the *Śrībhāṣya* of Yatīśekhara Bhāratī—[this refers to] their "intention" (*bhāva*), that is, their underlying purpose. The singular number is used with the intention of expressing the lack of contradiction between earlier and later parts; therefore, there is no conflict with the statement that "the *Bhāṣya* is profound in meaning. "Even for me"—even for one like me who is incapable of grasping and retaining [the teachings]—"is made subject to speech" (*vāgvidheya*) by the excellent exposition through the composition of works such as the *Tattvasāra* which I desire to write.

"How" (*katham*) means in what manner; "is he fit" (*arhati*) means he is capable. The meaning is: "In no way whatsoever does he become subject to my word. "Subject to my word" (*vāgvidheya*) means one whose activity and cessation of activity are dependent upon speech—or, more broadly, one who obeys verbal commands. By this, it is indicated that even for someone of dull intellect (*mandadhī*), such as Varadaguru, there is a very clear understanding of the intent of the *Śrībhāṣya*; for according to the maxim: "Whomever one places his hand upon the head, even that person composes verses out of the blue."

In this context, the intended Vedic scripture is: "For him, these meanings that have been declared indeed shine forth. And here, the mention of the subject matter is "Śrī Viṣṇu," the salutation is "Saṅgama," and the benediction is expressed by "spṛhayate" (one who desires). [The work] is composed as a command of speech.

Thus, the purpose (*prayojana*) has been shown. By the words "of Yatiśekhara Bhāratī" and so forth, it is shown that the subject matter (*prameya*) of the work he intends to compose is none other than the very subject matter of the *Bhāṣya*. By the name "Śrī Viṣṇucitta," it is also suggested that the ultimate divinity (*devatā-pāramārthya*) is likewise [the same]. (For this very reason, it is also implied here that the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and so forth are precisely those of the *Bhāṣya*. Just as in the *Bhāṣya* there is a specific sequence between the auspicious invocation concerning the Lord and the one concerning the Teacher, it is suggested here too—following the direction already shown—that the same applies to these two; thus, the style of the work is also revealed to be identical to that.

For this very reason, it is revealed that there is not even a trace of anything here being fabricated by one's own imagination, thereby manifesting its traditional authority. Here, the *siṃhoddhata* meter is employed; and in this work, the variety of meters is intended for the delight of those who are not diligent.

Explaining the incapacity implied by the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "for me too," he describes his own extraordinary benefit through being subject to the speech that constitutes the very essence of the best of ascetics:
"Where on the path of the learned is there such maturity? I swear by Śrī, I consider the ability of a mere gnat like me to be a manifestation of power.
The splendor of the words of the best of ascetics—skillful in the unimpeded destruction of the host of adversaries—is ever awake, bringing fame to me. (2)

This "prauḍhi" (boldness) refers to my own audacity (*prāgalbhya*). "Of the learned" (*viduṣām*) means those distinguished by the constant study of the scriptures; the suffix *kvasu* is used here according to the rule *vido laṭo vā*. "On the path" (*pathe*) means on the way. "Where? (*kva*) implies "nowhere at all. The underlying sense is that this [work] is like something non-existent on the path of the learned. The statement "this is prauḍhi" contains a censure (*kṣepagarbha*). Alternatively, "this prauḍhi" refers to the boldness of the eminent ascetic previously introduced; "of the learned" refers to those dwelling in the world.

"On the path" means "nowhere at all" is [such a thing] seen; the sense is that such maturity is not seen anywhere even among Śaṅkara and others. He confirms this very point by means of an oath: "I swear by the Lord of Śrī. By the qualification "by the Lord of Śrī," it is understood that he swears by Śrī and also by her husband—just as in the expression, "O descendant of Raghu, you are sworn by me and by Sītā herself. But surely...

Fearing that one might suspect your power to be equal to that [of the elephant], he says "maśaka" (mosquito) to show that it is not an illustration of my own power’s maturity, but rather an illustration of a mosquito's power. The meaning is: "I consider the power of a mosquito to be an illustration—a precedent—for the majesty of those like me"; it is my opinion that the power of a mosquito serves as the example for my power. Here too, the act of verification follows by way of the "middle gem" maxim (*madhyamaṇinyāya*).

By this, [the author] indicates that people, observing his own boldness, might lack faith and harbor doubts regarding what he has said (referring to Varadaguru). To the question, "How then is it possible for one such as you to establish your own position and refute the positions of others? he replies with the word "yativara" (the best of ascetics).

"Of the adversaries"—that is, of the opposing disputants; "those groups" who stand as external false views (bāhyakudṛṣṭi), and as the preceding and succeeding portions of false views within the very category of false views themselves—"for their unimpeded destruction," meaning for their total annihilation, [he is] "skilled," that is, proficient. "In me"—in me, who am mostly impotent—"glory-producing," meaning that having himself conquered them, he places upon my head the fame which is the fruit of that victory. The sense is: "Among the Pāṇḍavas, he performs such a service for me alone, just as Kṛṣṇa did."

The words of the best of ascetics are indeed light—illumination. They are metaphorically described as such because they dispel the darkness of ignorance and so forth. Alternatively, the "light" of his words refers to their capacity to overcome others. "It remains ever awake within me" means that even when I am asleep, it remains itself vigilant and protects me, as expressed in the phrase, "He who wakes among those who sleep. "It remains awake within me" means that, remaining hidden within me, it stays watchful for my sake.

This is identified as the style of Sudarśana, which involves concealment regarding the Pāṇḍavas. By stating, "In me resides a splendor that brings fame and is skilled in destroying adversaries," while describing your splendor as something that is eternally favorable to those who are well-disposed toward you yet causes distress to enemies, the similarity between your splendor and that of the Blessed Lord (Viṣṇu) is suggested. This is like the expression "your word is your splendor" or "pride is my lamp. Furthermore, the phrase beginning with "the host of adversaries" is like saying, "in that very place, certain fickle ones become moths."

Therefore, the equality of the words of the best of ascetics with the Vedas, as well as their equality with that which is known through the Vedas, is revealed here. In this verse, the form *śapa* in the phrase "by the Lord of Śrī, [he] cursed" (*śriyaḥ prabhuṇā śapa*) takes the ātmanepada because the root *śap* is used in the sense of reproaching (*upālambhe*). Both this verse and the following verse are composed in the *hariṇīpluta* meter.

Now, it was indeed stated that [this work] brings fame (*kīrtikara*). For fame is the renown of victory; as the venerable Vyāsa said: "There is a distinction between *kīrti* and *yaśas* based on the difference in causes such as generosity and valor. Therefore, raising the objection that if it brings fame, it must also be said to bestow victory, [the author], stating that this too is the case, explains the statement "I consider the flapping of a mosquito" as follows: "Indeed, what loss is ours if we possess only poetic talent? We have no concern for the path of Gautama (Nyāya), nor any acquaintance with the systems of Kaṇāda (Vaiśeṣika) or Kumārila (Mīmāṃsā)."

Even though there are other treatises following the views of the Guru (Bhartṛhari) and others here as well, nevertheless, the labor of the venerable Yatīśvara Gī (Gīrvāṇendra Sarasvatī) bears fruit for us everywhere in victory. || 3 ||

In this world—here in this universe. Of us—of ourselves. By poetry—by the act of composing; for the lexicographers state that *kavana* (the act of composing) is *kavitā*, and one who performs it is a *kavi*. Pride—conceit regarding excellence beyond all limits. "Not indeed"—not at all. The word *khalu* is used here in the sense of negation; its repetition serves to emphasize firmness or to indicate what is well-known. The intended meaning is that there is no need to swear by the Lord of Fortune (*Śrī*) in this matter.

"For it is well known elsewhere that in this world of Viriñci, who else but me is a poet? And he alone knows the essence of Sarasvatī’s speech. As for "us"—meaning those of us who possess diligent study of the Śrībhāṣya—what loss is there? The meaning is: no loss whatsoever.

For poetry has two purposes: as it is said, "If there is good poetry, what is the use of a kingdom?"—this refers to the happiness of attaining a kingdom; and victory over opposing disputants through the use of correct speech, by avoiding the various points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) such as incoherent expression, failure to understand the meaning, or shifting the subject matter during the battle of debate. Since he has attained both of these, the sense is that nothing is lacking for him. Furthermore, he has no acquaintance with the path of Gautama—that is, the science of logic (*nyāyaśāstra*)—nor is there any acquaintance with the system of Kaṇāda (*kāṇāda*). [The word] *gautama*...

The systems of Kaṇāda and the various branches of *anvīkṣikī* [are not known]. In the philosophy of Kumārila—that is, in the treatise of Kumārila, the commentator on the *Jaimini-sūtras*—known as the "Guru-mata" because the teacher (*guru*) is renowned for his application to providing alternative expositions of the very *Jaimini-sūtras*—there too, there is no familiarity. To say more: there is no familiarity even with other sciences such as Sāṅkhya, Yoga, and so forth. Nevertheless—despite the absence of labor in other systems (*tantra*)—"of us" means of ourselves.

The exertion of the venerable Yatīśvara-gī—namely, the diligent application (*pariśrama*) toward the *Śrībhāṣya* and other works—bears fruit as victory everywhere: that is, victory over opposing disputants in all philosophical systems (*sarvatantra*), or victory in all assemblies. The sense is that because it bestows victory, its quality of producing renown (*kīrtikaratva*) is established. The word "venerable" (*śrī*) signifies worthiness of worship; by this, the intended meaning is also the avoidance of the undesirable consequences mentioned in the phrase, "having studied the science of Gautama."

All of this is merely of the nature of a concessionary argument (*abhyupetyavāda*). In reality, however, for one who has mastered the *Śrībhāṣya*, since there is no possibility of any opposing disputant at all, what kind of discussion could there be? Thus he says:
"Where is the possibility of an opposing disputant before that crest-jewel of the assembly of Vaidikas, who exerted supreme effort in the mental fluctuations of the King of Yogis (Rāmānuja)? (4)

He who has exerted supreme effort—either through excessive faith or through an abundance of enjoyment—within the mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*) and the intended meanings (*tātparya*) of the *Bhāratī* of the King of Sages, which takes the form of the *Śrībhāṣya* and other works; [this effort is expressed in the past tense] because the fatigue does not manifest, it remains indirect (*pārokṣya*). Here, one should discern the distinction: effort (*śrama*) toward the *Bhāratī*, supreme effort (*pariśrama*) toward its mental fluctuations, and supreme effort toward those mental fluctuations themselves, as it is said: "One whose inner depths are well-familiarized may pour forth grace."

Of the Vaidikas—those who rely on the inherent excellence of the Veda consisting of two parts; of the assembly—the gathering; of the crest-jewel—the most eminent. "In front of him"—before one who is diligent in the study of the *Śrībhāṣya*—"where is the possibility of opponents?"—the meaning is that their non-existence is certain. Thus, the sense is that statements regarding its bestowing victory and so forth are based on a hypothetical admission (*abhyupetyavāda*). Here, there is the suggestion (*dhvani*) of the figure of speech known as *ākṣepa* (paralipsis). For it is said: "Paralipsis is the denial of what has been stated by oneself, following from deliberation and the like."

The poetic figure *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic indication) is suggested here, as it is appropriate that those who know the *Śrībhāṣya*—which serves as the crest-jewel for Sarasvatī, the presiding deity of the Vedas—should be the crest-jewels of those who study the Vedas;
for it is said that *kāvyaliṅga* is the supporting argument for a point to be established. The meter employed here is *rathoddhatā*.
Thus, this introductory section has been concluded, stating that his own work is rooted in authority and is unshakable by opponents.

Now he begins the treatise, starting with "In the first chapter. This is intended to focus the attention of the student; the ellipsis here is to be supplied as "the prima facie and final positions are stated herein."

For one who has studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*) and the *Śiras*, there arises an initial, superficial conviction (*āpātapratyaya*) regarding the subject matter of the entire Vedic meaning; this constitutes the qualification for the inquiry into the meaning of the entire Veda. In that regard, once the inquiry into ritual action (*karma*) has first been performed according to the sequence of study, there arises an initial conviction regarding the infinite and stable fruit of Brahman—accompanied by the determination that actions dependent on that [Veda] yield unstable and meager results; this constitutes the qualification for the inquiry into the subject matter of the latter portion [of the Veda]. Furthermore, the established position of the Siddhānta is that this "initial conviction" is intended as one whose validity is merely possible (*saṃbhāvitaprāmāṇya*).

In this regard, the Prābhākara, as the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*), objects: the initial acquisition of linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) is not possible through any means other than the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*). For when it is said, "The jar exists," if there is no resulting activity, its status as a communicator of meaning is not recognized. However, after observing the activity of the person being prompted following the use of such words as "Bring the cow," the learner, knowing that activity is preceded by a cognition of something to be done (*kārya*), concludes: "This word communicates an object in the form of a task."

In that regard, having grasped the connection of the word *anuvṛtta* with its recurring meaning and the connection of the word *vyāvṛtta* with its excluded meaning across many applications, one determines the relationship between specific words and specific meanings through the process of insertion and deletion (*āvāpodvāpa*). Thus, the first acquisition of linguistic usage pertains exclusively to the meaning of an action (*kāryārtha*).

Therefore, based on the principle that "whatever is worldly is the same as what is Vedic," the Veda is intent upon action (*kāryapara*). Consequently, since the Vedāntas lack the capacity to reveal an already-established Brahman (*pariniṣpanna-brahma*), their meaning is not established even by superficial cognition (*āpātapratīti*). Thus, due to the absence of a qualified seeker (*adhikārin*), this scripture should not be commenced. This very point he states in the first verse, beginning with "Elsewhere than through worldly usage...

"Elsewhere than through worldly usage, no understanding arises; nor does anyone have a notion of an effect (*kāryadhi*) regarding anything else. How could one act otherwise? And thus it is determined."
Since words are intent upon [prescribing] action, the Veda is authoritative only therein;
how then could it attain validity regarding the perfectly established, supreme Brahman? || 5 ||

From the perspective of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*)—that is, from conventional usage consisting of the activity of speech and engagement by an elder who is the instigator and the one being instigated. Elsewhere...

The meaning is as follows: *vyutpatti* refers to initial acquisition (*ādyavyutpatti*); the apprehension of the word’s power (*śaktigraha*) does not occur—that is, it is not produced [from any other source]. However, subsequent acquisition (*dvitīyādivyutpatti*) is dependent upon that first acquisition of the word’s meaning in terms of an action to be accomplished (*kārya*). Or rather—meaning anyone at all—in a case other than the cognition of an action to be accomplished (*kāryadhiyo’nyatra*), i.e., where there is no object of the cognition of an action to be accomplished, how could one engage in linguistic usage? That is, how could one employ words, and how could one act? The sense is: "not in any way at all. The word *vā* expresses non-necessity; [this applies to] both the person being prompted (*prayojya*) and the prompter (*prayojaka*).

Someone indicates the intended meaning of the word: "itthaṃ" means "this being so. The particle "ca" (and) implies that [the opponent's examples], such as "a son has been born to you," are otherwise established. "Words"—meaning all words—are determined to be intent upon action (*kārya*). Therefore, by the maxim "whatever is worldly [is understood according to its worldly usage]," it is in that very [action]—that is, in what is to be accomplished—that the *śruti*—the collection of eternal words functioning as a means of valid knowledge—is authoritative. [This applies] regarding the "accomplished" (*pariniṣpanna*), which is not of the nature of action, and the "Supreme" (*para*), which is distinct from both the conscious and the unconscious.

Regarding Brahman, however—"in Brahman," but. "Validity"—that is, the capacity to produce cognition. "How could it attain?"—how could it obtain it? By the term "already accomplished" (*pariniṣpanna*), it is stated that there is no validity therein because of the absence of the nature of an effect (*kārya*). By the term "supreme" (*para*), it is stated that there is no validity therein because, unlike the inner self (*pratyagātman*), it lacks agency as a subordinate element of ritual injunctions (*karmavidhi*).

By the word "but" (*tu*)—that is, by the word *punaḥ* meaning "furthermore"—it is stated that because there is no means of ascertaining the reality of the object of meditation, [the Upanishads] do not possess authority as subordinate parts of an injunction for meditation. Therefore, the meaning is that they have no authority whatsoever in that regard.
The reply to this follows.

He begins to state the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "the reply to this" (*atrottaram*). (The phrase "I shall speak" is to be supplied. The meaning is: "In response to this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), I shall state the counter-argument (*uttarapakṣa*)."

There are two types of linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*): accidental acquisition and intentional acquisition. Of these, the former depends upon observing the activities of the person who employs a word and the person who is prompted by it; the latter, however, depends upon the instruction of a father or other teacher. In this regard, the opponent’s view is that there is only accidental acquisition and no intentional acquisition at all. Having conceded that point, [the author] states "yaḥ" and so forth, asserting that even in the case of accidental acquisition, there is indeed acquisition regarding established facts (*siddhārtha*).
When someone who was intent on waking Caitra spoke these words— "The staff standing in the inner chamber has been awakened by the exertion of another; let it be made known"—
another person, hearing this, remained as mute as one who understands the distinction between such actions and their opposite.
Indeed, the child practices the linguistic derivation [of words], thinking, "This is the indicator of this object."

"Of another"—that is, of another person—by "activity," namely by a movement such as the motion of the hand, which is the agent. "Who"—the person who is the object. "In the room"—in one part of the house. He is "informed" [with the command]: "Let the staff be informed for Caitra. The dative case in "for Caitra" (*caitrāya*) is used because it is intended to express that the one to be informed is subordinate to the act of informing. "He"—the person who was informed—"of him"—of Caitra—"in the act of informing"—in the act of informing [Caitra] about the staff standing in the room—"being prepared"—having gone near Caitra.

Regarding the statement: "The speech which has the form 'There is a staff in the room'—he *ūce* (said/uttered). [The substitution of] *vac* for *brū* results in the *ātmanepada* ending due to the triple substitution rule (*bruvo vaciḥ*). Like a mute—one who, like a mute, understands the distinctions in gestures, such as the previously mentioned movements of the hands; the other child—the learner (*vyutpitsu*), distinct from the three persons consisting of the one to be enlightened (*bodhya*) and the enlightener (*bodhaka*). Hearing that—that speech—he, while listening to that sentence 'There is a staff in the room,' [perceives] this: the staff situated in the room."

The etymological derivation of "bodhakam" (the indicator) refers to the apprehension of its capacity to generate verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). "Abhyasyati" means that it makes [the meaning] the object of the initial comprehension, or alternatively, that it repeats it. The particle "khalu" indicates well-known fact. Here, by the phrase "like the triad," it is shown that the knowledge of various specific meanings can occur through gestures and so forth, independently of words.

The sense is this: since, according to the method stated, it is possible to grasp the expressive power (*śakti*) for an established entity even through accidental learning (*yādṛcchika-vyutpatti*), the insistence that linguistic learning (*vyutpatti*) pertains solely to things to be accomplished (*kāryārtha*) is groundless. In the preceding verse and here, the *śārdūlavikrīḍita* meter is employed. || 6 ||

In reality, however, there is indeed an acquisition of linguistic proficiency preceded by conscious intelligence; thus, the apprehension of the expressive power (*śakti*) of words regarding established entities is entirely unimpeded. To this effect, he says: (Verse 7: "By elders such as their fathers, who point with their fingers at the entire object—the mouth of a jar, for instance—and utter various words along with their respective case-endings directed toward the appropriate objects, the children being instructed here repeatedly perceive that the knowledge of those various objects has arisen in themselves from the mere hearing of those words, and thereby they recognize the [expressive] power."

In this world—here in the universe—with a finger, [they] point out—that which has its mouth (the opening) at the front, that is, at the top; such is the description. "That and that" refers to both that which possesses a relation and that which lacks a relation. A *vyadhikaraṇa* (non-co-ordinate) *bahuvrīhi* compound is employed to establish the primacy of that which possesses a relation, and the word "mouth" (*mukha*) is taken in the sense of "above. "Object" (*vastu*) means the "thing" (*karman*). "Pointing out" means "introducing" or "presenting."

"Those words"—namely, relational words denoting "mother" and so forth, as well as non-relational words denoting "pot" and so forth. "Their case-endings as well"—namely, the second and other case-endings that convey specific kārakas (grammatical relations) appropriate to the action. "In their proper domain"—that is, in the objects corresponding to those respective words, which are the objects of the valid cognition of the word-potencies as determined by those respective words; [that is,] in the referents such as mother and pot. "By those speaking"—by those uttering them. "By the elders of former times"—by fathers and others who themselves had been trained in exactly this same manner.

By the first word, "mother," "uncle," and so forth are included. "Being instructed" means having knowledge produced regarding those various objects by those various words. "Children" means infants. "Of that mere word"—that is, of the entire word such as "mother" and so on—"from hearing" means from the act of hearing. "Repeatedly" means regularly. "Arisen" means produced. "The knowledge of those respective objects within themselves"—that is, within their own minds.

"Having observed"—that is, having seen or experienced—the memory whose objects are things such as a mother or a water-jar; by the prefix *pra-*, the non-perception of any other relation between word and object and the ignorance of a person who might establish a convention (*saṃketa*) are intended. "They know"—that is, they ascertain—*śakti* (the expressive power).

The meaning is this: indeed, children are repeatedly instructed by their parents and others—who have set out to make them understand the relationship between words and their referents—by pointing with their fingers to "mother," "father," "uncle," and so forth, as well as to jars and other objects, saying, "Know this one; grasp this. Thus, gradually experiencing the arising of cognition within themselves regarding those respective referents, they come to expect a relationship that sustains the status of the signified and the signifier, much like the relationship between smoke and fire.

Failing to find any other such relation that is both pervasive and non-overreaching, and being unaware of any person who could have established a convention, people determine the relation between word and meaning to be nothing but *śakti* (inherent power).

By the use of the present tense in the phrase "pointing out here" (*atra nirdiśadbhiḥ*) and so forth, it is indicated that as long as children are capable—through the abundance of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) produced by observing the concomitance of the use of words such as "pointing with a finger"—of themselves employing those various words for their respective objects upon seeing the mere object, and of remembering the object upon hearing the mere word, they are thus described. By the term "by the elders of old" (*pūrvavṛddhaiḥ*), the absence of error and the like is indicated. By the term "by fathers and others" (*pitṛādyaiḥ*), their non-negligence is indicated.

(The phrase) "tattad" (this and that) indicates—by means of the expression "ghaṭamukha" (the face of a jar)—that for words possessing correlative relations, the priority of their etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) depends upon the derivation of words lacking such relations. Furthermore, this [priority] is impossible in the case of arbitrary derivation (*yādṛcchika-vyutpatti*), because it does not hold true for one learner with respect to another. By stating "only those words" (*tacchabdamātra*), it is suggested that among the words already learned, there is nothing that lacks denotative power. Alternatively, the word "mātra" (only) is used in a restrictive sense to indicate that the derivation does not occur through anything other than the word itself.

And thus, since it is impossible to deny that linguistic usage is preceded by conscious understanding, and since a superficial comprehension can arise through the determination of the expressive power (*śakti*) regarding established entities, this treatise ought to be commenced; such is the intended meaning. [The meter is] *Sragdharā*. (7)
He introduces the section concerning "origination and so forth" (janmādyadhikaraṇa): "Now, the section concerning origination and so forth.
Now, the section concerning origination and so forth.

In the first section (*adhikaraṇa*), the lack of etymological derivation was resolved; here, the difficulty of comprehension is being resolved. In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is argued that if the state of being the cause (*kāraṇatva*) is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) as a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*), then there would follow a plurality of Brahman due to the diversity of the qualified (*viśeṣya*); whereas if it is the definition as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), then there is an absence of any form belonging to the indicated object. To this, [the reply is: although a contradictory qualifying attribute such as "being divided" (*khaṇḍatādi*) does lead to a difference in the qualified, a non-contradictory qualifying attribute...

Since qualities such as "darkness" do not differentiate the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), there is no contingency of the qualified object being manifold; thus, it is possible for birth and so forth to function as definitions (*lakṣaṇa*) by way of being qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*). Furthermore, since unsurpassed Brahmanhood can constitute the form of the indicated object (*upalakṣya*), it is also possible for them to function as definitions by way of being indicatives (*upalakṣaṇa*). Thus, intending to establish the final position (*siddhānta*) that removes the difficulty of comprehension [which would arise] from the absence of a definition, [the author says: "Because of the absence of a definition..."

With two verses beginning with "bhūtāni" and "asya," [the author] states the reason and purpose for the detailed exposition starting with "acintya" within the sentences of the *Bhāṣya*, which consists of the commentary on the *Sūtra* on "origination and so forth" (*janmādi*) that serves as an explanation of the *Lakṣaṇa-vākya*. This is done by means of the phrases "of this" (*asya*) and "that which belongs to the *Sūtra*" (*sautram*), respectively.
By the words "the elements" and so forth, and by the words "of this" and so forth, which refer to the Sūtra.

When the object was understood through the word "bhūtāni" (the elements), the Lord of All was inferred from the phrase "imāni" (these) by means of the characteristics of the world's birth and so forth;
thereby, the wonderful variety of the world to be created was revealed, and by that, the radiant multitude of qualities of its Creator, Brahman, which serve as the grounds for inquiry, were shown.

In this context, the phrase "in the defining statement beginning with 'from which... refers to the passage starting with *yato vā imāni*. In the sentence beginning with *yato vā*, "upon the comprehension of the reality"—that is, upon the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) concerning the entire range of effects—even when the word "beings" (*bhūtāni*) is present—that is, even when the term "beings" has been uttered (the remainder being that this was said while the word "these" [*imāni*] was being recited; i.e., while the word "these" is being heard)—by means of the characteristics of the world's birth and so forth (by the word "and so forth," its maintenance and dissolution are included), that is, by means of the unique attributes (*asādhāraṇadharmas*), [He is known as] the Lord of All (*akhileśvara*).

The Blessed Lord is described by the words "Lord of the universe" (*patiṃ viśvasya*). By the terms "unnumbered" (*agaṇi*) and "unperceivable" (*alakṣī*), the manifoldness of the world being created—the state of having high and low varieties—is indicated; likewise, its invisibility and lack of cognition are indicated. Alternatively, it is the very manifoldness that is indicated, not its non-appearance. "By that also," and so forth: by that—that is, by the manifoldness of the world—[is inferred] the Brahman who is its creator, the cause of the manifold world.

The "grounds for being an object of inquiry"—that is, the grounds for being investigated due to the necessity of meditation—are the "causes," meaning they are the factors that establish the attainment [of Brahman] as the motive for such inquiry. They are "resplendent" because they appear in the Śrutis without obstruction, as the negative statements are shown to have other purposes through the application of general rules, specific exceptions, general principles, particular counter-exceptions, and the method of initial declarations. These are the "multitudes of qualities," meaning the collections of attributes such as knowledge, power, and so forth. [This is understood from the verb] *abodhyanta* (were made known). The word *adarśi*, which is in the singular, is modified into the plural form to agree with the subject.
The sense is that the qualities are implied by the necessary presumption (*arthāpatti*) arising from the scriptural texts concerning [Brahman's] causality.

Here, by the word *vastu*, it is indicated that the word *bhūta* occurring in the Vedic text refers to that which is connected with the activity of coming into being (*bhavana*), and not merely to living beings. By the use of the term "by characteristics" (*lakṣaṇaiḥ*) as a statement of established fact (*siddhavat-nirdeśa*), both the previously mentioned prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) are also indicated. Since the connection is made with "birth and so forth" (*janmādibhiḥ*) as the characteristics themselves, it is indicated that the aggregate [of these] constitutes the characteristic; thus, the attainment of unsurpassed greatness (*niratiśaya-bṛhattva*) is established. By construing the phrase "variegatedness has indeed been shown," the exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyoga-vyavaccheda*) is understood.

Furthermore, since the qualifier of the intended object (*uddeśya-viśeṣaṇa*) is not intended to be significant according to the logic stated in the section concerning the "cup" (*graha-adhikaraṇa*), there is no possibility of understanding a diversity [of objects] through this word. And as for its exclusion: even when there is a rejection of that which contradicts the enjoining statement—such as the singularity of the cup and so forth—there is no rejection of that which does not contradict it, such as the age of eight years and so forth; this is the case in the present context.

Since the diversity of created things is established by the authoritative scriptures (*prāpakavākya*), there is no abandonment of that [diversity]. As for the phrase "the reasons for being an object of inquiry," it refers to the referent of the second *tat* in the passage "That Brahman, you should seek to understand" (*tad brahma tadvijijñāsasva*), because it has been stated that the meaning of that word (*tacchabdārtha*) is what is under discussion as the object of meditation for one desiring liberation. Therefore, one should consider that there is no contradiction with the statement that "seek to understand" (*vijijñāsasva*) is not an injunction for either inquiry or meditation. The term "of the world" (*jagataḥ*) is stated in accordance with the singular number used in the Sūtra.

And the term "akhileśvara" (Lord of all) is an indication of the conventional meaning through the application of the word "ananta" (infinite) ending in the accusative case, which occurs in the sentence "satyam jñānam anantam brahma" (Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite), forming a single syntactical unit with the defining statement from the Bhṛguvallī. || 8 ||

This [passage] is intended to state the purpose of the word *imāni* (these) in the phrase *yato vā...* and of the word *asya* (of this) from the Sūtra which is rooted in that [phrase]. The meaning is as follows: although the category of effects is already denoted by the word *bhūta* (beings), the word *imāni* refers to the specific forms of that category of effects as established by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the subject (*dharmin*); it does not, however, refer to the world’s being a mere appearance (*ābhāsatā*), because that would be useless for the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*).

The phrase "possessing this supreme variety" (*vaicitryaparam*) is intended to make known that Brahman possesses a pre-eminence of qualities conducive to the production of such effects. This is precisely what the author of the Sūtras intends to convey by using the word "this" (*idam*) in the scriptural passage; it is also the very basis for the extensive commentary in the Bhāṣya beginning with "inconceivable" (*acintya*). Thus he says: "of this" (*asya*). Having introduced the Sūtra term "of this," he then explained the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "inconceivable"; stating the world as it is well-known through its respective means of knowledge, he declares its manifold variety.

Keeping in mind that this statement is both based on the Śrutis and the Sūtras, he first describes the variety regarding the insentient portion with the words "the first term," and then regarding the sentient portion with the words "then it is restricted," and so forth.

"Established by their respective measures"—that is, being perceived at the very moment the substratum (*dharmin*) is perceived; the meaning is that it possesses specific forms established by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehend the substratum. "The world"—the class of effects denoted by the word *bhūta*. "Expressing"—making known through its own power (*śakti*). The syntactical connection is: "expressing [the world] as endowed with forms established by the means of cognition that apprehend the world as a substratum. "Vedic"—residing in such passages as "From which... (*yataḥ...*).

Sautrī: [The commentary] is also based on the Sūtra, "janmādyasya yataḥ" (That from which there is the birth, etc., of this). As for the expression "idamuktiḥ" (the mention of 'this'), the word "tu" (but) should be construed with the sense of "and" (ca), or it may be applied out of its natural order to signify a distinction. The word "tu" expresses a qualification of the subject matter here that excludes the singularity [of the number] found in the case of the soma-vessels (*graha*). The expression "idamuktiḥ"—referring to both "imāni" (these) and "asya" (of this)—is the word "idam. Keeping in mind the Bhāṣya beginning with "inconceivable" (*acintya*), which states that the Sūtra speaks of the manifoldness of this world, [the commentator] took up the Sūtra term "asya" as the subject to be explained and expounded upon it.

In that regard—the commentary [states]: "of that which possesses an inconceivable, manifold, and diverse arrangement; which is mixed with kṣetrajñas from Brahmā down to a blade of grass; and which involves the experience of fruits determined by place, time, and [specific] conditions."

The meaning is: "in the words of the commentary. The preceding word is the phrase *acintyavividhavicitraracanasya* ("of that which has an inconceivable, manifold, and diverse arrangement"). It describes diversity with respect to the non-conscious portion—that is, among the non-conscious elements within one part of the category of effects. Now—meaning immediately thereafter—the phrase beginning with *niyata* (the words *niyatadeśakālaphalabhogabrahmādistambaparyantakṣetrajñamiśrasya*) describes diversity with respect to the conscious portion—that is, among the conscious beings within one part of the category of effects.

Regarding this, the venerable Vyāsa says: "In that regard, he describes the variety of the non-conscious aspect with the words beginning 'inconceivable,' and then he describes the variety of the conscious aspect with the word 'determined. (Verse 9)
He introduces the section concerning the scripture being its source: "Now, [the section] on the scripture being its source.
This is the section on the scripture being its source.

For here, when an objection is raised that "in one part [of the scripture] there is restatement (*anuvāda*), while in another part there is sublation (*bādha*) of the words," a certain reply must be stated. Regarding the doubt that—since the agent is established through inference, there is restatement in that respect; yet, because a mutual difference between the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*) is observed, the status of the efficient cause as the material cause is sublated—the following is said: Insofar as the agent is established by inference, there is a contradiction with the qualifying attribute [of the scriptural statement]; furthermore, since scripture alone is the authority regarding matters that are entirely beyond the senses, and because in cases such as the spider (*ūrṇanābhi*) and so forth, the identity of those two [causes] is observed.

And because both the instrumental cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*) are directly perceived through scripture, there is neither a lack of originality nor a contradiction [with other means of knowledge]. Thus, the establishment of Brahman by means of another authority has been refuted. He states the resolution of that doubt in five verses beginning with "Because of being an effect" (*kāryatvāt*).

[Verse 10]: Because it is an effect, like a jar, the subject under dispute—the earth and so forth—is possessed of an agent; and since all that is an effect possesses parts, that Lord is established as its substratum according to the *ādhāra-siddhānta*.

This would not be tenable in the production of the universe if there were a contradiction between the agent and time, or if there were a calculation of distinctions that deviate from the nature of being an effect. Or rather, [there is a contradiction] because of the cause for enumerating such differences.

In this context, the Naiyāyika, as the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*), establishes the existence of an omniscient creator through inference: "The subject under dispute (*vimataṃ*)—that is, that which is the locus of the controversy—consisting of the earth and so forth (*kṣityādi*), where 'earth' (*kṣitiḥ*) means the ground, and by the word 'and so forth' (*ādi*) mountains and the like are included; the term 'subject under dispute' (*vimatapada*) serves to include various individual instances, or rather, it is intended to exclude those portions already established as being produced by digging, filling, and so on—is possessed of a creator (*sakartṛka*), meaning it has a capable creator who is cognizant of its material cause (*upādāna*); because it is an effect (*kāryatvāt*), that is, because it is produced by an act of volition (*kṛtijanyatvāt*); just like a jar (*ghaṭavat*). Thus, it is "possessed of a creator."

Because of the statement of the grammarians that "the rule regarding the suffixes added at the end of compounds is not universal" (*anitya*), [the absence of the *ka* suffix is justified]. Thus, the fact that the earth and so forth possess an agent has been established by the reason of being an effect (*kāryatva*). Now, he dispels the objection that the reason itself is unestablished (*svarūpāsiddhi*). Regarding the phrase "and it is an effect": that [earth] and so forth is an effect because it possesses parts (*sāvayavatvataḥ*), that is, because it is composed of constituent parts (*avayavārabdhatvāt*), as in the case of a pot; this is to be supplied [to the argument]. By the word "and" (*ca*), other reasons are included: namely, possessing action while being large (*mahattve sati kriyāvattvam*), and possessing form while being large (*mahattve sati mūrtatvam*). [Objection: Granted that the existence of an agent is established, [what follows?]

To the question, "What follows from the proof of God? he says: "That Blessed One. That is, the agent; the Blessed One—the Lord, who possesses eternal knowledge and other attributes—is established. To the question, "Why? he says: "By way of the *ādhāra-siddhānta*," meaning by reason of the *adhikaraṇa-siddhānta* (the established conclusion of the locus), that is, through the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), there is the establishment of eternal knowledge and so forth. The *ādhāra-siddhānta* is a specific category of the term *siddhānta* (established conclusion).

Since it has been stated that "siddhānta" (established conclusion) is fourfold due to the distinction between *sarvatantra* (universal), *pratitantra* (particular), *abhyupagama* (presumptive), and *adhāra* (foundational) siddhāntas, three types of siddhānta are accepted by those who know the Upaniṣads (*trayyantavid*), while for the Vaiśeṣika, there is also a fourth. This is stated in the *Nyāyapariśuddhi*: "It is threefold, through the distinction of *sarvatantra*, *pratitantra*, *abhyupagama*, and *siddhānta*. However, some maintain a fourfold division, saying: "When one thing is being established, another is established as a consequence (*anuṣaṅgasiddha*)."

"Just as the existence of God is established through the proof that the earth and so forth have an agent," and so on. Having thus set forth the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), he begins to refute it with the words "this [is]... and so forth. "This"—the inference of an agent from the state of being an effect in the manner described—"would not be tenable"; it is not fit to be logically consistent. To the question "Why?", he says "since" (*yat*) and so forth: "Since"—that is, because—[in the production of the universe], that is, in the arising of effects such as the earth and so forth.

"Unity of agent and time"—that is, unity of agent in the sense of being created by one [being], and unity of time in the sense of being created at one [time]. "The calculation of the varieties of deviation from 'being an effect'"—the meaning is the determination of the number as two for the varieties of deviation from the reason consisting of "being an effect," namely, the common and the uncommon inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*). The reading *kāryatvam* is also found; in that case, the construction is "being an effect is deviant. There is also the reading *bhedagaṇanāt*, which means "from the observation of the varieties."

And this [contradiction] follows upon the conflict. Alternatively, it refers to the cause—namely, the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*). The "conflict" (*virodha*) consists in its establishing a multiplicity that is not desired. Therefore, the connection with the preceding [text] is: "Consequently, this would not be possible. The meaning is as follows: even if a creator is inferred by means of the state of being an effect, unity is not established, because there is a lack of proof. Nor is the state of being an effect itself the proof, because it cannot withstand logical analysis (*vikalpa*).

Is it merely "being an effect" (*kāryatvamātra*), or is it "being an effect that is not possible for a living being to have created"—which is a property unique to the subject (*pakṣāsādhāraṇa*)—or is it "being a vast effect"? In the first case, there is inconclusiveness due to commonality (*sādhāraṇānaikāntya*). In the second, however, there is inconclusiveness due to uniqueness (*asādhāraṇānaikāntya*). In the third, because we observe long duration and a plurality of agents in vast effects, there is contradictoriness (*viruddhatva*). By the phrase "or rather" (*athavā*), it is indicated that there is inconclusiveness even regarding the third alternative; for we observe vastness in effects even in the absence of a single creator. Thus Vyāsapāda said: "Or rather, there is inconclusiveness. (10)
To the argument that "let there be the establishment of oneness for the sake of parsimony," he says:
"That which is [the claim] that the establishment of the oneness of the creator belongs to those whose minds are eager for the impurity of parsimony— this is not to be respected."
For it is precisely your own pervasiveness that is obstructed; why then do those desiring the attainment of lightness postulate [the world] as having a creator? (11)

"In the lightness of conceptualization" (*kalpanālāghave*) means in the reasoning of parsimony (*lāghavatarka*). "Those whose minds are characterized by longing" (*lālasā*) refers to those Naiyāyikas whose minds possess a great desire for it. "The establishment of the oneness of the agent" (*karturaikyasya siddhiḥ*) means that [the creator] is the object of an inferential cognition regarding an agent, aided by the reasoning of parsimony. "This view" (*yat matam*)—this is not to be respected; it is not to be respected even by those who abide by its own established tenets. For (*hi*), because of that—that is, because of parsimony in general (as indicated by *tat*). Thus, the general category of parsimony is being referred to.

"Tallāghavam" means the very pervasion (*vyāpti*) between being an effect and being produced by an agent. "Ruṇaddhi" means it does not grasp [that pervasion]. "Laghimasaṃpadam" refers to the excellence known as the reasoning of parsimony (*lāghava-tarka*). "Īpsamānaiḥ" means by those desiring to attain it. "Sakartṛkatvaṃ kiṃ kalpyate" means how is it established? The meaning is: just as one gains parsimony by abandoning the burden of multiple agents in favor of a single agent, if parsimony can likewise be gained by abandoning that [single agent] as well, why should it be discarded? It follows the maxim: "By whom is one satisfied with what is better? (i.e., one should always seek the most parsimonious solution).

The point is this: since we observe in some cases that production depends on a triad of causes—namely the inherent (samavāyi), non-inherent (asamavāyi), and instrumental (nimitta)—and since we observe in other cases that production depends on the instrumental cause alone; and since no fixed rule regarding the number of causes is observed for all effects; and because, in view of the number of causes required to produce an effect elsewhere, the intellect naturally favors parsimony and desires the emergence of an effect through fewer causes; and finally, because no agent is perceived in the case of sprouts and the like.

Since the emergence of an effect can be ascertained through those very causes brought about by the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) even without that [intelligent agent], the causal relation between "being an agent" (*kartṛtva*) and "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is not established; consequently, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between being an effect and having an agent is unproven.

Furthermore, because in effects such as jars, it is more consistent with valid cognition to posit multiple causal relations based on the simplicity of the delimiting conditions (*avacchedaka*) such as the genus "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), the principle of the general and the particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣanyāya*) applies only when the entities involved are of equal status. Thus, since the causal relation between "being an agent" and "being an effect" is not established, the aforementioned pervasion is not proven.

And it is stated in the *Nyāyapariśuddhi*: "The same [argument] applies even in proving that [the world] has an omniscient creator as its antecedent; for even without such a creator, the emergence of those various effects is possible through those very same causes when assisted by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). It is also stated in the *Śārīrakasāra*: "By parsimony (*lāghava*), [the world] might be without a creator. By the particle *eva* in the phrase "only pervasion" (*vyāptimeva*), [this is emphasized].

The maxim that "one who desires growth suffers the loss of the root" is indicated here. Furthermore, by the mention of the "attainment of minuteness" (*laghimā-sampat*), the attainment known as *aṇimā* is understood to be included; thus, the refutation of the Pāśupatas is also implied here. For they too establish the Lord through inference. Therefore, it should be noted that the arguments from the Sūtras intended to refute them have been drawn in and presented here in the Bhāṣya as well. || 11 ||

If, following the observation of jars and the like, one were to prove that the earth and other elements possess an agent, it would follow as a logical consequence that they must likewise have an agent who possesses the qualities such as *sattva*, is subject to karma, and possesses a body; furthermore, it would follow as a consequence that the earth and other elements would have to arise and dissolve simultaneously. If...

There is a disregard for what conforms to observation; in that case, one might as well postulate the eternity and other such qualities of the earth and so forth, even though they possess parts. If it is argued that this [eternity] is refuted by the lack of conformity to observation, then the absence of qualities such as existence (sattva) in the Creator is likewise refuted by the lack of conformity to observation; thus, the Lord is not established through inference and the like. He states this point in three verses, both concisely and in detail:

"In the case of the earth and so forth—the subjects (pakṣa)—which consist of many constituent parts and whose bodies are unseen despite effort, if there is a discrepancy with what is observed, then another factor may be postulated; but this is not the case even regarding the Creator."

This [creation], which abandons the path of logic and fails to perceive both simultaneous creation and destruction, is here not the work of anyone; therefore, that Supreme Being is not to be inferred through the apparatus of conceptual construction.

In "kṣmādau" (on earth and so forth)—that is, on the earth, mountains, and so on. In "aṃśini" (in that which possesses parts)—that is, in an object consisting of constituent parts; in the alternative sense, [it refers to] the collection of causes defined by the sprout and so forth.

In the case [of effort]—that is, in the alternative where it consists of effort; in the case of the unseen (adṛṣṭa)—that is, in the alternative where it consists of the unseen; and in the case of the body as well—that is, in the alternative where it consists of the body. There would be a contradiction with what is observed (*dṛṣṭavirūpatā*): namely, in the manner to be explained in the following verse, there would be the qualities of being eternal, having an operation independent of an agent, being independent of knowledge and desire-to-act, and the capacity to produce effects. Through such postulations as its being remote, its being invisible, and so forth, the conformity with observation (*darśanānuguṇya*) is abandoned. "Otherwise" (*aparathā*) means: if the contradiction with what is observed were something to be avoided.

Even regarding the agent—when the agent is sought to be established by the reason of "being an effect"—this very "discrepancy with what is observed" (dṛṣṭavirūpatā) occurs, which is the abandonment of conformity to observation in respect to the portions consisting of the qualities such as *sattva* and so forth. It should not be postulated—it is not to be imagined. Furthermore, for the entire collection of effects, such as the earth and so on, [the creator and destruction] would be deprived of the path of logic—fallen from the track of inference and thus beyond the scope of inference—and would be cognizable solely through scripture (*śruti*). "Simultaneous creation and destruction" refers to creation and dissolution occurring at one and the same time.

"Naikṣitau" means "not seen. If one were to follow what is observed [in the world], it would entail that those two [the creator and the instrument] must occur sequentially; and in the absence of such [sequential observation], it would entail a contradiction with what is observed. "Iha" refers to the subject of God and so forth. "Kalpanāyāḥ" means of inference; "parikaraḥ" means the causal complex (sāmagrī). [The phrase] "that which does not exist"—therefore, the "Other," the universal agent, is "not inferable," meaning he is not established by means of inference. || 12 ||
Having stated it in brief, he explains it in detail with two [verses]: "Eternal earth, etc. and "In accordance with what is observed, etc."—[the meaning is:
although eternal earth and so forth may possess parts, let the operation of other causes be devoid of dependence on an agent; thus, let there be [only] the effort of this [divine] agent.
The intellect and the desire to act do not depend [on a body] for the embodied soul here; nor does the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) require it to bring about its effect.
Therefore, let the embodied soul create the body of the universe—whether visible or invisible—even if it be at a great distance.

Even if it were "possessing parts"—that is, even if it were "composite"—the earth and so forth might still be eternal; this is because they are distinct from things with well-known agents (the remainder of the argument). Alternatively, there may be the lack of a necessary probans (*aprayojakatva*) in the claim that "let there be possession of parts, but let there be no state of being an effect. "Of other causes" refers to the reasons that produce the earth and so forth. "Otherness" here is in relation to the causes of jars and the like. "Activity" may be devoid of dependence on an agent—that is, it may be the producer of an effect independent of an agent.

Let there be causality; let there be no dependence on an agent—this would be an unproving argument [for the existence of God]. This is known from the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*) mentioned in the preceding verse. Regarding this agent: in the effort—that is, in the production of exertion—the intellect and desire—that is, knowledge and will—are not required; that is, let them not be the cause. The remainder is "on account of parsimony. Here—in the inference for God—the sustainer of bodies—that is, the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*)—is capable of bringing about the effect, namely, the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*). Thus, it is said: "he is able," meaning he is competent.

"Let it be"—the meaning is "let there be a counter-argument. It is untenable to claim that merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), being insentient, produce their effects only when presided over by a sentient being, like a bellows; for this would involve a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the Lord’s knowledge, effort, and so forth—this is the sense. "The embodied one" (*dehī*) means the possessor of a body, the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*). "Even though very far away" (*davīyān api*); the suffix *-yasun* is applied to the word *dūra*, resulting in the substitution of *dvā* for *dū*. "The world" (*jagat*) refers to sprouts and the like. "Let him create" means by means of volition (*saṃkalpa*) and so forth; the sense is that its possibility is established just as [a physician] removes poison and the like.

Alternatively, "varṣma" means the body—the body of the creator. "Visible to others" (dṛśyetara) means it may be invisible, like the bodies of piśācas, siddhas, and so forth. The point is that even so, this does not constitute a non-perception of a suitable object (yogyānupalabdhi). || 13 ||
If it is argued that there is no establishment of these [theoretical] constructs here because they lack conformity with what is observed, [we reply that] this would also apply to the agent.
The destruction of the world was seen according to the sequence of its creation; likewise, the arrangement of these two would occur by virtue of perception. (14)

In this context—regarding the previously mentioned subjects such as the eternity of earth and so forth—the meaning is that there is an absence of conformity with observation (*dṛṣṭānuguṇyavirahāt*), that is, an absence of accordance with what is observed, because it contradicts perception. Of these conceptualizations—whether they be inferences (*anumiti*) or logical reasonings (*tarka*)—there is non-establishment (*asiddhi*), meaning either non-arising due to the lack of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth, or invalidity. And if [this were the case], then regarding the agent (*kartṛ*) as well—that is, regarding the agent whom one desires to prove—there would be non-establishment; that is, there would be non-establishment of the inference concerning [attributes] such as being devoid of existence (*sattva*) and the like, or not being subject to karma, and so forth.

Furthermore, the birth—meaning the origination—of the world was seen in succession; this is the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) used in the passive sense of the root *dṛś* (to see). By "the world," objects such as pots and the like are intended. Or else, its destruction—that is, dissolution—was also seen in succession. Regarding these two—the birth and destruction of the world—there would be a "construction," meaning an inference, that they occur in such a manner [of succession]. This is not what we accept; such is the meaning. || 14 ||

He introduces the section on Concordance (*samanvayādhikaraṇa*) with the words: "But that [is established] because of concordance" (*tattu samanvayāt*). Therein, having raised the objection that Brahman—being of an accomplished nature and lacking connection with engagement or withdrawal—cannot be the subject matter of the scripture intended to satisfy the desire for knowledge, it is now demonstrated that Brahman, who is by Himself the supreme human goal and consists of unsurpassed, infinite bliss, can indeed be the subject matter of the scripture. Thus he says: "Alas! How great is the pity for those addicted to the Kaumārilas' view, who, though they have transcended the Prābhākara method, yet prattle that the entire world is bereft of a Lord!"

Since defects in the cause and subverting cognitions are far removed from the Lord, who is the supreme goal of man, why do the declarations of injunctions, mantras, and arthavādas not possess intrinsic validity, just like [the injunctions] themselves? (15)

In the Kaumāriladarśana—that is, in the Bhāṭṭa method—those who are "addicted," meaning those characterized by the exertion of striving to accomplish goals that are difficult to fulfill; "fie" upon them, for they are to be censured. In the Prābhākara method, even those who are "valiant," meaning those whose progress is unhindered; "fie" upon them as well, for they too are to be censured. Why? To this he says: the entire world (*viśvam jagat*) is "destitute of a protector" (*nāthavidhuram*), being without a refuge, while they speak with "incoherent discourse" (*jalpataḥ*), speaking through disconnected speech.

Since the authority of a scripture consists solely in its being directed toward engagement (*pravṛtti*) or withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), and since Brahman does not possess that nature, it cannot be the subject matter propounded by scripture; rather, the Vedāntas attain their authority only as supplements to the injunctions for ritual action (*karma-vidhi*) by propounding the Self as the agent (*kartṛ*) in those rituals—thus they have argued. He refutes this with the word "Fie! (*dhik*).

The reproach expressed by the word "alas" (*hanta*) is this: even though there is mutual contradiction among the various assertions of both these groups regarding the denial of God (*īśvara*), how can there be agreement on that point? For those who, because the momentary destruction of action makes it impossible for it to be the means for attaining future heaven, postulate a *apūrva* (unseen potency), yet do not postulate God—or deny what is heard in scripture—because an insentient thing cannot logically bestow a fruit; or how is it so?

[They argue: "For the sake of establishing a person capable of being enjoined (*niyojya*) who is favorable to the realization of the Self, even that which produces heaven and so forth must be, for us, primarily an object to be accomplished (*kārya*)."

By the phrase "they chatter," it is suggested that those who, according to the manner stated above, first accept a ritual action as having no other purpose, and then claim that its purpose is heaven and so forth in order to justify it, are thereby denying the Lord of the Universe—the foremost of all, the sovereign of all, and the one known through all the Vedāntas.

He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the word "dūre" (at a distance). *Of the defect in the cause*—that is, of the defect in the cause consisting of error, negligence, or deception—and *of the subverting cognition*—that is, of the sublating awareness that "this is not [so]"; these are *dūre*, meaning remote. *Mantras* are those characterized by the definition of being secret counsel (*mantraṇa*) and so forth, or those well-known as such; *arthavādas* are portions that convey existing facts in the form of ancient narratives (*purākalpa*); and *uktis* are Vedic statements of this kind, such as "Truth, Knowledge," and "Being alone, my dear, was this in the beginning."

"According to rule" (*vidhivat*) means "in accordance with the prescribed method. This term connects both to what precedes and what follows. "Inherently the human goal" (*svataḥ pumarthe*) means "even without being a means to a human goal, [they are] already the human goal itself. "In the Lord" (*nāthe*) means "in the one who is the sovereign of the universe. How could they not possess authority? The meaning is that they certainly do possess it.

Just as the statement "there is a treasure in your house" possesses authority because it serves a human purpose, so too the Vedānta, which establishes Brahman as consisting of unsurpassed and infinite bliss, possesses unassailable authority; for even an injunction (vidhi) possesses authority solely by virtue of its being directed toward a human purpose. Nor is there any lack of certainty regarding the reality of its subject matter, since, like an injunction, it is equally eternal, faultless, and non-human in origin.

Because of that certainty, it is stated that [Brahman] is the human goal (*pumartha*) in itself, which implies the exclusion of activity (*pravṛtti*) and cessation (*nivṛtti*). For it is by virtue of being a means to the human goal that those two (activity and cessation) fall within the scope of the scripture; however, their status as objects of the scripture by virtue of being the human goal itself is established through the logic of "how much more so" (*kaimutikanyāya*). Furthermore, Brahman’s status as the subject matter of the scripture is beyond dispute, both as the fruit required by injunctions and as the bestower of the fruit; this is indicated by the two words *nātha* and *pumarthe*. || 15 ||

Thus the four aphorisms have been explained; for they serve to establish the commencement of the treatise (*śāstra*), and "Because of seeing, [the cause] is not that which is not based on scripture" (*īkṣaternāśabdam*) and so forth constitute that treatise. Since the meaning of the section on "seeing" (*īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa*) and other topics has already been made very clear in the commentaries (*bhāṣya*) and other works, these verses are stated here for the sake of clarifying certain points whose meaning was not yet explicit. And therein, in the aphorism concerning the qualities of the section on "seeing"—specifically regarding the phrase "because of contradiction with the initial proposition" (*pratijñāvirodhāt*)—[the author], while rejecting the interpretation of the term *ādeśa* as the subject matter proposed by others, states:
He states his own established position with two verses. Therein, he restates the view expressed by others with the first verse:

"In the *Chāndogya*, some say that in the passage 'O Śvetaketu, you have not asked for the instruction' (*ādeśam aprākṣya*), the prefix *ā-* reveals the meaning of instruction (*upadeśa*); [the root] *śās-* does not denote the act of commanding (*praśāsti*) because it ends in the suffix *ghañ*.
It does not occur in the sense of the agent; rather, when the suffix *ghañ* is added in the sense of the object (*karman*), there is no object here, as the agent is the one who commands."
In the instruction regarding karma, that which is to be taught must be expressed through the language of instruction; this has been stated.

Some say: "The speakers of falsehood say. To the question "What [do they say] here?", he replies with "In the Chāndogya," and so forth. "In the Chāndogya" means in the traditional scripture (*āmnāya*) of the Chāndogas; the suffix *ñya* is applied according to the rule "chandogaukthika... (Pāṇini 4.3.129). In the passage "uta tamādeśamaprākṣyaḥ," the prefix *āṅ* is present, and the word ends in the suffix *ghañ*. The verbal root is *diśati*. "Of the existent" (*sataḥ*) refers to Brahman, which is denoted by the word "existent" (*sat*) in the context of the Sadvidyā. "Instruction" (*upadeśam*) means the making known of that which was previously unknown, having that [Brahman] as its object. "Manifests" (*prakaṭayati*) means "establishes" (*pratipādayati*).

"Praśāstim" means "praśāsanaṃ" (governing). Grammarians state that due to the rule of *bāhulaka* (irregularity), the root *śās* takes the suffix *śasti*, as in the word "rājadaṇḍaḥ" (the king's punishment). For indeed, even the Lord’s act of restraining—expressed as "Yama, the son of Vivasvat, is the King"—is a form of royal punishment (*rājadaṇḍa*). [The Lord] does not manifest [this]. Why? To this he says: "because it ends in *ghañ*. This statement contains the reason within itself. Thus he says: "not in the sense of the agent" (*no kartari*). This is because it is stated that the suffix *ghañ* does not occur in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), but rather in the non-agentive sense; and because it is stated that the suffix *ghañ* is prescribed in the sense of the object (*karman*) and other *kārakas*.

Although the suffix *ghañ* is difficult to obtain when used in the sense of an object (*karman*) that is not a name (*asaṃjñā*), because of the rule stating "when [the action] is a name," nevertheless, due to the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (in various ways), *ghañ* is easily obtained even when it is not a name. For example: *ko bhavatā lābho labdhaḥ* ("What gain was obtained by you?"). Furthermore, the restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding its own denotation (*svābhidheya*) will follow the relationship with the injunction (*vidhi*), as seen in usages such as *ekaḥ pākaḥ puṭapākapratīkāśaḥ* ("One cooking is similar to baking in a crucible"). Here—in the case of your position which resides in the intellect—*sat* refers to Brahman, which is denoted by the word *sat*; *śāstau* means in the teaching; *kartṛ syāt*—"it would be the agent."

The meaning is as follows: [Brahman] is worthy of being the agent, but not the object—meaning it is unworthy of being an object. This is because of the Śruti text: "He rules over nothing whatsoever. Therefore (tat), since the root *diś* with the prefix *ā-* is used in the sense of "instruction" (*upadeśa*), and since the suffix *ghañ* is commonly used in the sense of the object (*karman*), Brahman lacks the status of being the object of instruction (*praśāsana-karma*). Furthermore, because the suffix *ghañ* is not prescribed in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), and because the state of being "to be instructed" (*upadeśyatva*) is logically possible for Brahman, this is the intended meaning.

This—Brahman denoted by the word "Sat"—is what is referred to by the word "instruction" (ādeśa) in the phrase "that instruction"; some say it has been declared as that which is to be taught, and this connects with what precedes.
Refuting this very point, he states his own intended meaning:

"In this regard, we say: [the word] *praśāstiḥ* denotes one who commands; it does not denote instruction, for that is already well-known. Furthermore, there is no occasion here for the unintended consequence of referring to another [teacher]."

This is consistent with the statement regarding the uncommon [usage] even in the case of the suffixes *ghañ*, *ac*, and *karaṇa*; for indeed, the verbal expression of the grammatical factors (*kāraka*) here indicates their optional nature, since there may be a desire to express the agent as the instrument. (17)

(Regarding "atra" and so forth: Here we state [our position]. To this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), we state the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). What is it? To this he says "praśāstim" and so forth. *Āṅmukhaḥ* means preceded by the prefix *āṅ*. *Asau diśiḥ* means the verbal root *diś*. *Praśāstim* means governance, a command. *Vadati* means it expresses or establishes. [The opponent claims: This root *diś*, preceded by *āṅ*, does not express instruction; it does not cause one to understand instruction. Why is that? To this he says: "In the sense of 'teaching' (*śāsti*), it is extremely well-known."

The root *diś* preceded by the prefix *āṅ* is extremely well-known in the sense of "commanding" (*praśāsana*). The author of the Nyāsa states: "The root *diś* preceded by *āṅ* expresses the purpose of the one who commands (*niyoktṛ*), whereas preceded by *upa*, it expresses the purpose of the one being commanded (*niyojya*). This is also the intended meaning based on usages such as "I have been commanded" (*ādiṣṭo’smi*) and "he was commanded by the bull among the Raghus" (*ādiṣṭā raghupuṅgavena*). Regarding the phrase "not indeed in the sense of 'other'": the word *ādeśa* is not commonly known in the sense of "another" (*para*)—that is, its well-known usage is as "instruction" (*upadeśa*). As in the expressions: "This is the *ādeśa*; this is the *upadeśa*."

The sense is that [the two are] mentioned separately. Furthermore, "here"—that is, when [the term *prakṛti*] has the sense of being the "ruler" (*praśāsitṛ*)—there follows the attainment of what was required: for the sake of establishing the promise that through the knowledge of one all is known, it is necessary to state that the material cause (*upādāna*) alone is the efficient cause (*nimitta*), thereby eliminating any other efficient cause; thus, there is the attainment of the required meaning.

Regarding the term *asādhāraṇasya*: by the statement—that is, by the presentation—of the rulership (*praśāsitṛtva*) that is unique to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), this word "instruction" (*ādeśa*) becomes appropriate in the sense of "rulership. The thought is as follows: since the status of being something to be taught (*upadeśyatva*) is established by implication through the very mention of its being an object of inquiry, to state it explicitly would be an unnecessary repetition; furthermore, since the status of being something to be taught is common to the cessation of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra-nivṛtti*), Brahman, and the meditation upon Him (*brahma-tad-upāsanā*), to state it would constitute a common (or redundant) statement. Regarding the suffix *-ghañ*: even when used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), the suffix *-ghañ* is applied.

The term *agaṇi* is formed with the suffix *ghañ*. The sense is that, according to the statement in the *Mahābhāṣya*—"In the rule *upadeśe ’janunāsikaḥ*, even though [the suffix] is not a technical name (*saṃjñā*) by virtue of the rule *halaśca*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) because of the inclusion of the term *bahula*. *Kārakāṇām* means "of the factors of action" (*kārakas*), such as the object (*karman*) and so forth. *Vaivakṣikatvam* means "the state of being dependent upon the speaker's intention," namely, the status of each respective *kāraka*. This was stated by the *śābdikas*—that is, the grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇas*). The sense is that they have stated: "The case-endings denoting *kārakas* become various depending upon the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*). *Nanu* is used here as a particle of emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).

The intention to express the agent as the instrument (*karaṇatayā vivakṣā*) is the desire to convey a cognition whose qualifier is "causality" (*kāraṇatvaprakāraka*). This is indeed possible. The point is that the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) expressed by the term "not when [the agent is] not [intended]" (*akartari*) serves to indicate the ungrammaticality (*asādhutva*) of the suffix *ghañ* when there is an intention to convey a cognition whose qualifier is "agency" (*kartṛtvaprakāraka*).

Regarding this, the venerable Vyāsa says: "In the view that it is an instruction (*upadeśa*), there is a lack of natural fitness for the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*) and a natural fitness for the suffix (*pratyaya*). In the view, however, that it is a command (*praśāsana*), there is a lack of natural fitness for the suffix, whereas there is natural fitness for the meaning of the root—which is the primary element—as well as consistency with the sense of the passage. Therefore, it is proper to accept that the one who commands alone is denoted by the word 'instruction' (*ādeśa*)."

In this case, since both agency (*kartṛtva*) and instrumentality (*karaṇatva*), in the form of being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*), actually reside in the agent itself, the suffix denoting that [instrument] is easily obtained when one intends to express instrumentality alone while not intending to express agency.
