Just as with words like "pot" (*ghaṭa*), where the term is applied according to whether one intends to express potness (*ghaṭatva*), substancehood (*dravyatva*), or other properties, so too—given the principle that "case-endings for grammatical relations (*kāraka-vibhakti*) arise from intention"—there is no possibility of superimposition (*āropa*) here; therefore, there is no need to resort to a figurative meaning (*lakṣaṇā*) of the *ghañ*-suffix as referring to the agent in order to avoid that [superimposition].

The intention to express the agency (*kartṛtva*) of instruments and so forth is not of the nature of a superimposition (*āropa*); for this reason, it has been stated by the systematizers (*tāntrika*) who define independence (*svātantrya*) as "the possession of an activity conducive to that action, which is not dependent upon other factors of action (*kāraka*) mentioned in grammatical co-occurrence with it. Nor should it be argued that such a view contradicts the acceptance of the inherent meaning of the suffixes (*pratyaya*).

Just as, even though both "praśāsana" (ruling) and "upadeśa" (teaching) are used [as meanings for the root], there is natural fitness (*svārasya*) in "praśāsana" due to its greater conventional usage (*prasiddhi-prācurya*), while there is a lack of such fitness in "upadeśa" due to the absence of that usage; so too, although the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of both the object (*karman*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*), there is natural fitness in the sense of the object because of its greater conventional usage, whereas there is a lack of such fitness in the sense of the instrument due to the absence of that usage—and thus there is no fault. Nor should it be argued that the state of being the instrument of ruling is not unique [to the Supreme Self], since it is common to both the Supreme Self and the knowledge thereof.

Nevertheless, with respect to being the object of instruction (*upadeśyatva*), [the term *praśāstṛ*] is unique [to Brahman]; and since it is the agent of the act of commanding while being independent of any other instrument, its status as the instrument of commanding remains unimpaired by its uniqueness. Although the suffix *ghañ* is difficult to obtain in the sense of an object (*karman*)—since it is stated that it occurs in the sense of an action when used in the formation of a technical name (*saṃjñā*) according to the rule *im*—nevertheless, even in the view that it is the object of instruction...

The absence of intrinsic appropriateness (*svārasyābhāva*) is equal [in both cases]; nevertheless, intrinsic and non-intrinsic appropriateness are established without contradiction by the abundance or lack thereof in common usage. Nor should it be argued that, due to the principle of "diversity" (*bāhulaka*), the suffix *ghañ* should be understood as applying only to the agent (*kartṛ*). For the term "diversity" is also applied to the object (*karman*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the context of technical names (*saṃjñā*); however, the author of the Mahābhāṣya does not establish the application of *ghañ* to the agent on the basis of "diversity," as he does for the object and the instrument.

Nor should it be argued that while it is appropriate to intend the agency (*kartṛtva*) of other factors of action (*kāraka*), it is not appropriate to intend the agency of the agent as another factor of action; for it has been stated that in such instances as "you know yourself by yourself" (*ātmānam ātmanā vetsi*) and "you create yourself by yourself" (*sṛjasy ātmānam ātmanā*), there is an intention to express the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) of the agent. Furthermore, in cases such as "the field reaps itself" (*lūyate kedāraḥ svayam*), it is taught that even the reflexive object-agent (*karmakartṛ*) may be intended as the instrument. Moreover, in his commentary on the *Mahābhāṣya* passage, "And indeed, when this [agent] is dispatched, having seen both the action and the non-action," Kaiyaṭa stated that the locative case is used because there is an intention to express the locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) of the agent. (17)
In the section concerning the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), he restates the primacy of the "tail-Brahman" as asserted by others:

"The sixth [case-ending] did not indicate difference; the verse did not speak of it; nor was there ignorance regarding that which was known. Nevertheless, it does not possess the nature of a whole, for another Self is heard of as its [Self]."

Furthermore, the state of being that which is to be purified (the object of knowledge) is expressed by words denoting modification; therefore, "Brahman is the tail" [refers to Brahman], but not the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya). And that [ānandamaya] is described as a sheath (kośa), like the one consisting of food (annamaya), existing on the outside. || 18 ||

"Of this"—that is, of the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*). "By the genitive"—that is, by the genitive in the phrase "its tail. "Otherness"—the state of being other than Brahman. "Was known"—it was understood by the listeners; the sense is that this follows from the natural force of the genitive of distinction (*vyatireka-ṣaṣṭhī*). "This"—this very one consisting of bliss, which was previously mentioned as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) to the state of being other than Brahman.

The verse—“He becomes non-existent indeed”—is a verse concerning Brahman. “Did not state” means he did not set it forth [as the primary subject], but rather the meaning is that he stated that very Brahman which was spoken of as the tail. Regarding “of the known”—of this one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), who is well-known in the world in the form of pleasure, joy, and so on. “State of being unknown” means: ignorance is not the cause [for determining] its existence or non-existence; that is, it does not exist [in that sense]. “Nevertheless”—even if its state of being unknown is established in some way or another.

Of that—of the partless Supreme Self (*paramātman*)—"possessing parts" (*avayavitā*) means the state of having parts such as a head, a tail, and so forth. "Not" (*na*) means that it does not exist. Thus, the meaning is that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), being known as something possessing parts, is not the Supreme Self. Furthermore, another self (*ātmā*) is heard in scripture for that *ānandamaya*: "This very one is his embodied self" (*tasyaiṣa eva śārīra ātmā*). Since no other self is possible even for the Supreme Self, the meaning is that the *ānandamaya*, which possesses another self, is not the Supreme Self.

"Of this"—that is, of the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*). "Its state of being subject to purification is heard"—the meaning is that this is understood from the scriptural statement, "May my [self] consisting of bliss be purified. The word "heard" (*śruta*) is supplied from the preceding context and undergoes a change of gender. Since the state of being subject to purification is untenable in the case of the eternally pure Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the meaning is that the one consisting of bliss, which is perceived as being subject to purification, is not the Supreme Self. "The suffix *mayaṭ* expressing modification"—that is, the suffix *mayaṭ* which conveys the sense of being a modification (*vikāra*) of this one consisting of bliss.

The word *pratyaya* means "form" (*rūpa*). The term *śrutaḥ* ("heard") is supplied [from the context]. The meaning is that because it is impossible for the Supreme Self to be a modification (*vikāra*), that which is heard as a modification is not the Supreme Self. Since this is so, therefore: "the tail would be Brahman"—that is, it becomes fit to be established as the Supreme Self. Alternatively, the construction may be joined by supplying the words: "therefore, the tail would be Brahman, the Supreme Self. However, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) would not be Brahman; the meaning is that it is unfit to be the Supreme Self.

And that [sheath] consisting of bliss—like the one consisting of food—is like the sheaths beginning with the one consisting of food, which are non-souls (aparātman). It is called an "outer sheath" because it serves as a container for the object of the intellect, acting as a means for the intellect to descend toward the reality of Brahman situated within as its tail; so it is heard in scripture.

Regarding this, they say: because the genitive case in the word *tasya* (of him) expresses a relationship and thus implies a distinction; because the subsequent verse concerning Brahman does not have the *ānandamaya* as its subject, it is understood that the Brahman described as the "tail" (*puccha*) is the primary subject; because it is illogical to entertain doubts regarding the existence or non-existence of the *ānandamaya*, who is known in the world through forms such as joy (*priya*), delight (*moda*), and so forth; because it is impossible for the partless Supreme Self to be a possessor of parts (*avayavin*); and because it is impossible for the changeless to be a modification (*vikāra*). Therefore, *tasya eṣa eva...* [is the correct reading].

The summary of the reasons for the doctrine that Brahman is the tail [of the Self] is as follows: because it is untenable for the "Self consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) to be the Supreme Self when another Self—understood from scriptural passages concerning the Self such as "the embodied Self" (śārīra ātmā)—is already established as the Supreme Self; and because it is untenable for the Supreme Self, which is eternally pure, to be subject to purification as taught in the scripture, "May my self consisting of food, my self consisting of vital breath, my self consisting of mind, my self consisting of consciousness, and my self consisting of bliss be purified. Therefore, the "Self consisting of bliss" is not the Supreme Self; rather, Brahman, which is indicated as the tail, alone is the Supreme Self. || 18 ||
This he refutes with the verse beginning "pumliṅga" and so forth:

"And other verses describe the form of the subsequent speech whose primary subject ends in the masculine gender; they do not call it a 'tail,' nor is our own Sūtra [to that effect], nor is there another internal [authority]."

Furthermore, because it is designated as a constituent part starting from the sixth [chapter], due to its being limitless, its conformity, its synonymy, and its expression as having no distinct nature, the "tail-end" argument is refuted. || 19 ||

The word "masculine" (pum̐lliṅga) refers to that which denotes the primary subject under discussion—the word "He" (saḥ) found in the sentence "He desired" (so'kāmayata). By the term "masculine," it is intended that the reference must necessarily be to the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya). By the term "primary" (pradhāna), it is intended that there can be no reference by means of the pronoun "He"—which is common to all the sections and is stated as "this very one is his embodied self" (tasyaiṣa eva śārīra ātmā)—to anything other than the primary subject.

By the word "prakṛta" (the subject under discussion), the intended meaning is that it is impossible for the pronoun in the phrase "from this very Self" (*tasmād vā etasmād ātmanaḥ*)—which refers back to the immediately preceding [subject]—to refer to the distant [subject] denoted by the word "Self" (*ātman*). Thus, the sense is that because the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is perceived as the cause in the passage "He desired" (*so ’kāmayata*), its status as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is established. In this context, by those who are not others...

"By its own parts, which are not distinct from itself"—the "forming" (*rūpaṇa*) refers to the formation of [parts] such as the head and wings; the word "is seen" is to be supplied. And thus, since the *ānandamaya*—which is formed as the whole—is not distinct from Brahman—which is formed as the tail-part—the non-difference of the *ānandamaya* from Brahman is established; this is the meaning of the proof that the *ānandamaya* is the Supreme Brahman. In this context, the "verses" (*ślokāḥ*) refer to the verses situated within those respective sections, beginning with "From food, indeed, creatures [are born]," and so forth.

The meaning is that since they do not say "the tail," but rather "that which possesses a tail," the verse under discussion also refers to the *ānandamaya* as possessing a tail, and not merely to the tail itself. By this, the proponent intends to show that the reason stated by the opponent—that "the verse does not speak of this"—is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*). Furthermore, the phrase "and also represented as such by others" refers merely to a representation as a whole (*avayavin*), not to actual ontological wholeness.

Otherwise, it would follow that Brahman possesses parts; thus, the reason stated—that [Brahman] is "the whole" (avayavin)—is intended to be unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*). Furthermore, the Sūtra—"The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman], because of repetition"—is not [intended] in its primary sense. For us, who maintain that the one consisting of bliss is the Supreme Self, this [interpretation] retains its natural force (*svārasya*); however, if the tail-Brahman were the Supreme Self, it would lack such natural force. This is the meaning: if that were the case, the Sūtra ought to have read, "The tail is Brahman, because of repetition."

In our position, however, by construing the thesis statements either as "the one consisting of bliss is not the other" or as "not that which is non-scriptural," it is established that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Furthermore, the phrase "on account of repetition" (*abhyāsāt*) is natural in meaning when taken as referring to the repetition of the word "bliss" (*ānanda*) found in the proximate context. In your position, on the other hand, it is clear that there is an unnaturalness (*asvārasya*), since you must resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the term *ānandamaya* to mean the Brahman that is the "tail" mentioned in the *ānandamaya* passage.

Furthermore, "there is no other interior [self] beyond it"—the meaning is that, as in the passage beginning "Different from this, indeed, is the other interior self consisting of mind" (manomaya), no other interior self is heard of beyond this one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya). Since the succession of interior selves taught in the text culminates in the one consisting of bliss, it is intended that the one consisting of bliss is the Supreme Self (paramātman).

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the genitive case, and so forth," the following group of factors is intended: the state of being unknown, the hearing of the suffix *mayaṭ*, the state of being a whole (*avayavin*), the state of being something to be purified, the term "Brahman," and the hearing of the "bodily self" (*śārīra-ātman*) in the passage, "Of that, this is indeed the bodily self. In that context, the sequence beginning with "because of the state of being a part" (*aṃśabhāvāt*) serves as the supporting argument. Regarding the genitive in "its tail" (*tasya pucchaṃ*), [it is used] because of the state of being a part—that is, because of being a member (*avayava*). The meaning of the genitive is the relationship between a whole and its parts; this is the intended sense. Furthermore, the non-difference [of the Self from Brahman] has been stated previously by the phrase "not different from others" (*ananyaiḥ*).

The state of being unknown (*ajñātatva*) is due to its being unlimited (*niravadhikatayā*). The sense is that even for that which is known in the form of the beloved and so forth, its state of being unknown is established by virtue of its being undivided bliss (*aparicchinnānandatva*). Furthermore, the hearing of the suffix *mayaṭ* is also [to be understood] as denoting abundance (*prācurya*) because of its being unlimited.

The sense is that the reason based on the mention of a modification (*vikāra*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), because of the application of the suffix *mayaṭ*. It has also been indicated that the reason of "being known" (*jñātatva*) is unestablished due to its being unlimited. "Possessing parts" (*avayavitva*) is due to its being described as having form (*rūpaṇāt*); the meaning is that it is not so in reality. The sense is that the reason of "possessing parts" is unestablished; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of Brahman being a "tail. Nor does the word "tail" (*puccha*) imply a locus (*ādhāra*) by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because that would contradict the context of form (*rūpa*); this is the core point. "Being subject to purification" (*śodhyatva*) is due to its conformity (*ānurūpyāt*).

The meaning is that, just as there is the removal of transmigratory existence in the case where the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is the individual soul (*jīva*), so too, in the case where it is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), there is the cessation of the impurity produced by the soul's transgressions; this constitutes its fitness for purification, which is dependent upon *prapatti* (surrender).

By this, it is intended that the opponent's reason—that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) must be the non-Self because it is subject to purification—is unestablished. Since the word "Brahman" is heard in the context of a synonym—as in "He understood that bliss is Brahman" and "the Self consisting of bliss"—and since the identity of meaning among the terms *ānandamaya*, *ātman*, and *brahman* is determined by such scriptural evidence, the hearing of the word "Brahman" in the verse belonging to the section on the *ānandamaya*—namely, "He becomes non-existent indeed; he is non-existent Brahman"—is not untenable with respect to the *ānandamaya*. This is the meaning.

By this, the non-establishment of the previously stated reason is reinforced. The scriptural hearing of the embodied self (*śārīrātman*) [is established] through the statement that [the Self] has no other self; for, since there is no mention of "another within" in this context of the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), it is understood that the teaching is complete. Thus, the sentence "Of him, this very [Self]" is intended to mean that there is no other self. This is like the expression "The Self, the Lord, is established in his own glory. By this, the non-establishment of the reason—namely, that [the Self] possesses another self—is intended.

Since this is so, therefore: "the reason based on the tail" (*pucchahetu*)—meaning the reasons stated in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the tail being Brahman, which serve as reasons for [concluding] that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is not Brahman; the singular number refers to the genus, and the genitive case indicates distinctness, meaning the reasons stated in such passages [as "He is different from him"]. "Refuted" (*parāstaḥ*) means they have been rendered defective by the powerful reasons establishing the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) and by the fact that their own essential nature is unestablished (*svarūpāsiddhi*). || 19 ||

In the section concerning the "Inner Sun" (*antarāditya*), regarding the subject-matter of the *antarāditya-vidyā*—beginning with the text, "This golden person who is seen within the sun"—it is heard in scripture: "As a lotus flower is reddish-yellow like a monkey's buttocks (*kapyāsa*), so are his eyes. The author of the *Vṛtti* has stated six possible meanings for this passage; he sets them forth in these six verses:

The sun is called "monkey" (*kapi*) because he drinks (*pibati*) the water (*kaṃ*) with his rays; he is also traditionally known as "monkey" (*kapi*) because he shines (*babhasti*). If that [sun] is here [in the passage], then by this [word *kapi*], that [lotus] is [described].
We perceive the "monkey-buttock" [lotus]; because it possesses the beauty of a lotus blossomed by the splendor of the sun, it was reckoned as a comparison for the eye of the Blessed One. (20)

"He drinks *kaṃ* (water) with his rays," thus he is *kapi*, the Sun; the meaning is that the Sun is expressed by the word *kapi* because "he drinks *kaṃ* (water)," as in *kapirādityaḥ*. He cites a Vedic usage beginning with "also" (*api*) and so forth: "He—Āditya—is *kapi*," according to the Śruti: "*Kapi babhasti tejanam*" ("The monkey devours the fuel"). Thus *kapi* is handed down in the tradition (*āmnātaḥ*), meaning it is practiced or studied as *kapi*. The word *api* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*). By this, the entry from the *Nānārtharatnamālā*, "the monkeys are the men born of Arka," is also included.

Here—this being the meaning of the word *kapi*—that which is by this [word], namely *āditya* (the sun); *astaṃ*, meaning "expanded" (*vikasita*). [The suffix] *kta* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) in the root *asu* (to throw). That [is] the action. *Kapyāsaṃ* means that which is denoted by the word *kapyāsa*. *Pratīmaḥ* means we ascertain. It is called *āsa* because it is thrown (*asyate*) or cast; the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the object. According to the statement that words ending in *ghañ* are generally masculine, its neuter gender is used here. He states the meaning:

Regarding the word "divasa" (day): he [the Lord] is described as having "lotuses like the buttocks of a monkey" (*kapyāsaṃ puṇḍarīkam*). By the splendor of the sun-maker—meaning by the rays of the sun—the lotus (*padma*) blooms; for it is stated that the word *padma* may be masculine, as in "the lotus or *nalina* is masculine. Due to its "splendorousness"—that is, on account of its excellence of beauty—it serves as the "analogy" (*upamā*) or standard of comparison for the eyes of the Blessed One, those eyes of the Lord famously known as "Lotus-eyed" (*puṇḍarīkākṣa*). It was "reckoned"—meaning it was made known or indicated.

The construction is: "His two eyes are like the *kapyāsa* lotus. The meaning is that his eyes resemble a white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*) blossomed by the rays of the sun. Here, by the mention of the word "sun" (*āditya*) through the phrase "the monkey is the sun," and by the mention of "on account of its splendor" (*śrīmattvāt*), the statement of the commentator—that [the lotus] is either "thrown by the sun" or "on account of its splendor"—is recalled. By the word "but" (*tu*) in the phrase "the monkey is the sun," the exclusion of the five meanings to be stated hereafter is indicated. || 20 ||
He states another meaning:
"The monkey (kapin) is not capable (nālam), for he drinks the water (kam). That [state] upon which the wise desire his seat (āsana) is that [which is denoted by the compound].
This lotus, brilliant like a monkey’s cheek and noble, is declared to be the eye of the Lord as a visible manifestation. || 21 ||

"Kaṃ" means water; that which drinks [it] is "kapi," which becomes "nāla. Its neuter gender follows from the statement, "nāla is used in the non-feminine [neuter]. This refers to the instrument for drinking water.

The intention is to express its agency. "Of which"—that is, of that which is present in the intellect. "In that stalk" (*nāle*): "therein," the sitting (*āsaḥ*), meaning the instruction, occurs. "That" refers to the action. "The wise ones" (*manīṣiṇaḥ*) means the learned. "They desire the *kapyāsa*"—they seek the meaning of the word *kapyāsa*. [The root] *vaś* is used in the sense of longing; longing is desire. That in which the sitting (*āsa*)—the act of sitting—occurs upon the monkey (*kapi*) stalk is "monkey-sitting" (*kapyāsa*); this is a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* compound. The intention is that the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) to the root *ās*, as it is listed [in the Dhatupatha] with the meaning "sitting" (*upaveśana*).

Alternatively, this is a statement of the resultant meaning: *āste* (he sits) means "sitting" (*āsan*). Because the root *ās* belongs to the *ākṛtigaṇa* class beginning with *pac*, the suffix *ac* is applied, resulting in *āsan*. By the rule of splitting the *yoga* (*saptamīti yogavibhāgāt*), the compound *kapyāsan* is formed. This—

It is described by the word "kapyāsa" (monkey-buttock). For this very reason, it is "ujjvala"—possessing an excellence of splendor; "udāra"—expansive. Vyāsapāda [Śaṅkarācārya] maintains that since the lotus situated on the stalk possesses a greater splendor than even a faded (*apacita*) lotus, that is what is intended here. "Saroja" means a lotus. And this is the meaning of the term *puṇḍarīka* as found in the Śruti. It refers to the Lord—the Blessed One who possesses unconditioned sovereignty, as indicated by His being "Puṇḍarīkākṣa" (Lotus-eyed), for it is said: "That Person, the Pradhāna, whose eyes are beautiful."
The "eye" (*cakṣuḥ*) is the illustration—the metaphor for the two eyes. It is "declared"—stated as a metaphor, with the word "by the Veda" (*śrutyā*) understood as the ellipsis.
Both previously and here [it is said]: "By those [rays] by which the sun shines, Parjanya rains. The nectar of its luster is like something to be drunk from a mouthful.

"Thirsting, the moon has extended its rays like stalks of lotus fiber"—since it is well known that the sun is the drinker of water from the ocean, and because this is consistent with the propriety of the meaning, the suffix *kip* is applied to the root *pā* (to drink) when the word *ka* is used as an upapada, by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*). Indeed, even in other meanings, the application of the suffix *ghañ* to the root *ās* (to sit/eat) is equally characterized by *bāhulaka*; however, the specific distinction here lies in the propriety of the meaning.

Just as the word *tirodhi* ends in the *kip* suffix by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), so too does the word *kapi*; thus, there is no fault. In the *Bhagavadguṇadarpaṇa*, [the author] himself has favored this interpretation: "It protects (*pāti*) or drinks (*pibati*) the bliss of experiencing that [Lord]. [The suffix] *in* is added after all verbal roots. There is elision of the long *ā*. "The word *kapi* is indeclinable"—thus did the venerable Bhaṭṭaparāśara-pāda accept it.

Their intention is as follows: although the suffix *in* prescribed by the rule *sarvadhātubhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 5.2.107] is marked with the *ṅ*-sign (indicating that the preceding vowel is not subject to *guṇa*) by the rule *gāṅkuṭādibhyaḥ*, just as there is *guṇa* in the word *koṭiḥ* due to the principle of *bāhulaka* (irregularity), so too here, even though the suffix is not marked with the *ṅ*-sign, its causing the elision of the *a* (via *al-lopa*) is due to *bāhulaka*. For this very reason, regarding the rule *matvarthācca* [Pāṇini 5.2.121], it is stated that even though the letter *a* is elided due to *bāhulaka*, it is still called a *matvarthīya* (possessive) suffix.

Although the grammarians have written in the rule *kuḍikampyornalopaśca* that the word *kapi* refers to a lion, a monkey, and Madhusūdana—and because of the natural sense of the Śruti and Sūtra passages stating "the vital breath moves forth from Him who causes trembling" (*kampanāt*), which establishes the Supreme Self as the cause of trembling—it is appropriate to say that the word *kapi* applied to the Blessed Lord is based on His quality of being the Causer of Trembling.

Nevertheless, upon carefully considering the consistency of the preceding and following names in the *Sahasranāma-adhyāya*, it is appropriate that the word *kapi* has "the state of being easily swallowed" (*sukhapātitva*) as its cause; for grammarians have no dogmatic insistence on specific etymological methods. This is because it has been stated by them that "means for attaining the goal are not fixed. Such is the intention of the Teachers (*ācārya*). The same applies to the term *kapyāsa*. It should be understood that, by establishing the elision of the suffix *pya*, it is more appropriate to rely solely on the suffix *in* according to the rule *sarvadhātubhya in*.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that since there is no rule restricting words derived by *uṇādi* suffixes to being technical names (*saṃjñā*), the word *kapi*—which occurs thousands of times in the Veda for the Sun and the Blessed Lord, and whose application as a name is possible based on the grounds of 'drinking water' or 'bringing happiness'—is never used for a lotus stalk? Therefore, its derivation via an *uṇādi* sūtra is inconsistent. [Reply: This is not so. Although the term "technical name" (*saṃjñā*) is understood to carry over into the rule *uṇādayo bahulam*, we observe that in certain instances where an *uṇādi* suffix is prescribed, the term "technical name" is mentioned again. Thus, by inference, there is no fault in the fact that *uṇādi*-derived suffixes sometimes function even when they do not denote a technical name. || 21 ||
He states another meaning: "What" (kam), etc. Here, "what" (kam) refers to water; it is that which is the seat or the source of thirst.
That which has been called "kapyāsa" by poets is so named because it arises from deep water.

The lotus, cool, sweet, and glorious, serves as an illustration for the eyes of the illustrious Dāmodara; here, even though the word "api" (also/even) has its form elided, it functions like the particle "iva" (as if). 22.
(Kam, udakam bhavati): According to the lexicon (*kośa*), "kaṃ" means "head" or "water. Here—[it refers to] that whose thirst is for water, or its sitting, its staying; or else, its arising.

That from which something originates is its *utpatti*. *Kapyāsam* means that which is denoted by the word *kapyāsa*. *Kavibhiḥ* means by those of far-reaching vision (*krāntadarśibhiḥ*). *Uditam* means spoken. In the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound *kapyāsam* as "that whose *āsya* (mouth/face) is like that of a monkey (*kapi*)," the sense is that it is a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* (a possessive compound with non-co-referential members). Thus the etymological derivation has been shown. Now, he states the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) beginning with the words "gabhīra... and so forth. *Gabhīrajalodayāt* means due to the arising [of light] in the deepest water; this is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for its persistence (*sthiti*).

"Cool and sweet" (śiśiramadhuraṃ) means cool and beautiful; this is established even by comparison with the object of description. The meaning is that the Lord’s eye removes all the torments of the devotees who are afflicted by the three kinds of suffering. "Glorious" (śrīmat) means possessed of an excellence of splendor; the suffix *matup* is used here in the sense of superlative degree. It is a "lotus" (nalinaṃ). It is the "exemplar" (nidarśanaṃ)—that is, the simile—of the eyes of the Blessed One, who is the refuge of the three worlds (Dāmodara) and who was bound by Yaśodā; specifically, of those two eyes which are reddened by sovereignty and parental affection. It is so.

Now, one might ask: "What is this thing called *pyāsa*? To this, he says: "The [suffix] *lupta*," etc. The prefix *api* is used here. When the verbal root *ās* (to sit) is preceded by the prefix *api*, or when the verbal root *as* (to be) is preceded by the prefixes *api* and *āṅ*, and the suffix *ac* (the *kṛt*-suffix added after roots ending in *a*) is applied according to the rule beginning with *pac-ādi*, the word *apyāsa* signifies either "instruction" (*upadeśa*) or "origination" (*utpatti*). The sense is that the word *pyāsa* is grammatically correct because the letter *a* of the prefix *api* is elided according to the rule: "Vāguri desires the elision [of the *a*] of *api*. By that [prefix] *api* joined with the root *as*, the form *apyāsa* is produced; thus, "origination" is expressed. However, the letter *a* of the word *api* is elided by the grammatical injunction: "Vāguri desires the elision of the *a* of the prefixes *ava* and *api*. This is as in the word *pihita*.

The meaning is that just as there is the elision of the vowel *ā* in the word *pidhāna*, so it is here. The usage of Āpastamba, *abrahmāpy ācāryāt*, is also intended by the word "etc. (*ādi*); [the commentary] *Ujjvalā* explains: "In *abrahmāpi*, the final form is like that of *katanta*; or rather, there is the elision of the vowel *ā* of the prefix *api*."

Even though the word *udakotpatti* (arising from water) is used, the quality of being "deep" (*gambhīra*) is obtained by implication. By the statement regarding the abiding in water that is not agitated (*ananodaka-sthiti*), the exclusion of land-lotuses (*sthalakamala*) results in the obtaining of qualities such as coolness (*śiśiratva*). Here, two meanings for the word *āsa* have been stated: "whose seat" (*yasya āsanam*) or "whose origin" (*yadi vā udbhavaḥ*). In this regard, although it is stated in the *Śrutaprakāśikā* that the verbal root *ās* (to sit), preceded by the prefix *api*, means "water" (*kam jalam*), nevertheless, the Blessed Lord [Rāmānuja] stated in the *Vedārthasaṃgraha*: "from the deep ocean" (*gambhīrāmbhasamudbhuta*). And in the commentary on that [text], the venerable Vyāsa-pāda [Veṅkaṭanātha] said:

It should be understood that the statement of two meanings is intended to convey two alternative views regarding the phrase "water on non-earth" (*asabhūmi*), namely, whether it means "water" or "that which begins with *api*."

If it is argued: "Since the rule *asterbhūḥ* is prescribed under the governing heading *ārdhadhātuke*, mandating that *as-* is replaced by *bhū-* when followed by an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, then in the word *kapyāsam*—where *as-* is followed by the suffix *ghan* or *ac* (of the *pacādi* class)—the replacement *bhū-* would apply, resulting in the form *kapibhāvam* and not the form *kapyāsam*," [we reply]: No. For within the section beginning with *asterbhūḥ*, *bruvo vaciḥ*, and *cakṣiḍaḥ khyāñ*, it must be stated that "it occurs diversely (*bahulam*) in technical names (*saṃjñā*) and Vedic verse (*chandas*)," for the sake of forms such as *anna*, *vadha*, *gātra*, *vicakṣaṇa*, and *ajira*.

In the Vārtika commentary, it is stated that this [rule] applies with reference to all sections: in the word *anna*, there is the absence of *jagdhi*; in *vadhaka*, there is the substitution of *vadha* when the suffix *ṇvul* follows; in *gātra*, there is the substitution of *gā* for *iṇ* when the *uṇādi* suffix *ṣṭran* follows; in *vicakṣaṇa*, there is the absence of *khyāñ*; and in *ajira*, there is the absence of the abstract suffix (*bhāva*).

This is because Kaiyaṭa states in his commentary that "this is said with reference to all topics. Furthermore, in the Vārttika, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "for the sake of *ajira*, etc.," implies that there is no absence of the substitution of *bhū* for the root *as* or the replacement by *vac* for *brū* within those specific contexts; thus, according to the intention of the Teachers, the forms *brāhmaṇo bravaṇāt* and, in the present case, *kapyāsam* are established without obstruction.

And here, regarding the analogy of the Blessed One’s eye—since the word "Blessed One" (*bhagavat*) denotes sovereignty by signifying "the glory of fortune" (*bhaga-śrī*), and since sovereignty is also expressed in the phrase "the illustration of the eye of the Lord" (*īśvarasya cakṣur-nidarśanam*), it is appropriate to intend the meaning of sovereignty even in the term "Dāmodara," according to the rule of "contextual consistency" (*prāyapāṭha-nyāya*). This follows the etymological derivation: "Dāma means the names of the worlds; he who has these within his belly is the god Dāmodara. Furthermore, it should be noted that in this very knowledge (*vidyā*), the lotus-eyed one (*puṇḍarīkākṣa*) is heard to be the lord of all the desires of all the worlds.

Thus, the three meanings accepted as the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) have been stated. Now, three other meanings, determined as the prima facie views (*pūrvapakṣa*), are presented and refuted based on the very nature of the subject matter: "Like the lotus of Kapya" (*kapyāsam*); here, "the lotus of Kapya" refers either to the orb of the sun or to the heart-lotus, the seat for the worship of Hari; and it is not the case that the two eyes of the meditator are like that lotus which is [described as] a *puṇḍarīka*.

The statement "his two eyes" is secondary; even disregarding the lack of expectancy between the two words, there is an ellipsis, and the subsequent mention of that [eye] takes the form of abandoning the status of being co-referential with the word [already present]. || 23 ||

"He who drinks the water is the monkey (kapi)"—that is, the sun; "his āsa" means his seat or locus (*adhikaraṇa*). The suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of a locus because of the rule regarding the frequentative use of suffixes (*bahulagrahaṇāt*). To the question "What is that?", he says: "the solar orb" (*bhānubimba*); the meaning is the disc of the sun. Here, the phrase "lotus" (*puṇḍarīka*) and so forth follows. Thus, just as the solar orb is denoted by the word "monkey's anus" (*kapyāsa*), and the lotus of the heart is intended by the word "lotus"—both being, as it were, the place for the worship of Hari, that is, the station for the meditation upon the Supreme Self—in that same way [it is].

That "the two eyes of the worshipper (*upāsaka*) are the place of worship (*upāsana-sthāna*)"—this is one [proposed] meaning. He says that this is not tenable: "But that is not so" (*iti tu na saḥ*). The meaning is that this is utterly incorrect. Why? To this he says: "Since," and so forth (*yad ityādi*). "Since" (*yat*) means because. "Puṇḍarīka" refers to the word *puṇḍarīka*. "Therein" (*tatra*) means in the previously mentioned lotus of the heart. "Metaphorical" (*gauṇam*) means derived from a similarity of form or a similarity of qualities; [the word *puṇḍarīka*] would be so used—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

Indeed, it has been established in the discussion on "he makes the sacrificial post" (*yūpasya svarūpaṃ karoti*) that even with respect to secondary characteristics (*lakṣaṇā*), figurative application (*gauṇīvṛtti*) is inferior. He states another objection with the words beginning "of that" (*tasya*). The mutual connection of the meanings of the two words "his eyes" (*tasyākṣiṇī*)—which denote a part and its whole—is understood to be free from expectancy for any other word. The implication is that, disregarding this, one accepts a syntactic connection with two supplied words. The word "his" (*tasya*) is connected with the supplied phrase "the place of meditation" (*upāsanasthāna*).

The meaning is that it is accepted that the word "upāsaka" (worshiper), which has been supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhṛta*), is to be construed with the word "eyes" (*akṣiṇī*). The underlying thought is that this involves both abandoning what is heard in the text and imagining what is not heard. He states another objection as well: "There would be [the fault of] supplying an ellipsis," with the word "syāt" (there would be) understood as the remainder. The thought is that when a construction is possible without supplying an ellipsis, the assumption of an ellipsis is a defect. The word "api" (also/even) serves to collect further objections.

To explain: if "of him" (*tasya*) were intended to refer to the lay practitioner (*upāsaka*), it would result in the fallacy of referring to something not under discussion; it would result in a grammatical discordance with the word ending in the genitive case found in the immediately preceding sentence; it would result in a breach of the stylistic method of the section describing the divine limbs; and, because of the scriptural statement that "this which [is] in the right eye" (*yaścāyaṃ dakṣiṇe’kṣiṇī*)—namely, "this which is in the right eye" (*yaścāyaṃ dakṣiṇe’kṣin*)—the right eye is heard of as the locus of meditation, it would result in a contradiction with the dual number in "the two eyes" (*akṣiṇī*).

Since it has been established that "in the inner sun" (*antarāditye*) refers to the location of the solar orb, and likewise for "the two eyes" (*akṣiṇī*), which establishes them as locations, one must consider that because there would be a difference in form due to the difference in location, or a difference in the Vidyā, this would result in a split in the sentence; thus, the word *api* ("also") is to be understood as a conjunctive particle (*samuccāyaka*) including these unstated points. He states another objection: "samāna... [etc.]. *Adhikṛtam* means the topic under discussion (*adhikaraṇam*).

The verbal root *kṛ* preceded by the prefix *adhi* denotes the state of being located upon something (*ādheyatva*). Therefore, in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the suffix *kta* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *kta* is used after roots meaning 'to remain fixed,' 'to move,' or 'to consume,' when the sense is that of a locus. [The two words] are "the same" (*samāna*), meaning non-different (*abhinnam*). Of those two words—namely *kapyaāsam* and *puṇḍarīkam*—which have as their qualificand (*viśeṣya*) the "locus" (*adhikṛtam* = *adhikaraṇam*), the "course" (*gatiḥ*) refers to the attainment of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) which is not set aside due to the absence of particles such as *ca*. Of that [course]:

*Tyaktiḥ*—the abandonment [of the previous name] by resorting to a difference of substratum (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*); the word "it would be" (*syāt*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The sense is that when grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible, a difference of substratum is improper. He states another objection with the words "afterwards" (*ūrdhvam*). Here, the phrase begins with "because of the description of the form" (*rūpakathanāt*). "After the description of the form" means after the name of the subsequent [object] present in the mind. "Utterance" (*uktiḥ*) means the statement; the word "proper" (*ucitā*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. For it is indeed proper to state the form prior to the sentence prescribing the name.

The sense is that if this sentence were intent upon [merely] prescribing a location, there would be a violation of propriety. Herein lies the truth: "the statement following that" means that after this passage beginning with "like a monkey's anus," there is the statement that the eye of the worshipper is the locus for the service of Hari. Therefore, for those who possess the merit of having studied the *Śrutaprakāśikā* on the *Antarāditya-adhikaraṇa*, it is clear that there is no loss of the word "that" (*tat*) referring to the subject matter under discussion.

For in that [previous passage], the knowledge of the upward [eye] has already been stated; therefore, since there is no need to state it here again, this [present passage] is considered redundant. Although the aforementioned objection is indeed established in the *Śrutaprakāśikā*, nevertheless, the intent of the statement "it is stated above" is precisely to point out the redundancy; this is understood from the use of the words "above" (*ūrdhvam*) and "stated" (*ukti*). Thus, the phrase "therefore" (*tasmāt*) does not connect with what precedes as "that is not correct. || 23 ||
Introducing a different point, he refutes it:

Someone says, "The 'monkey's buttocks' (markaṭasya jaghanam) [is used] as an illustration for the 'monkey-buttock' (kapyāsa) of the eyes; how can this be accepted by the Blessed One when another interpretation is possible?"
In this case, grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between the two words is established; why then is it abandoned?
If the word "lotus" qualifies that which resembles it, then for you, the word [“face”] would be used in a figurative sense (gauṇa). // 24 //

A certain person—one unworthy of having his name mentioned, a most wicked man—speaks of "the *kapyāsa* of a monkey," meaning he uses the term *kapyāsa* to refer to something else. He speaks thus because, according to the etymology "that by which one sits (*āsate*) upon it," the word refers to the hindquarters; such is the meaning of what that person says. According to the authority of the lexicon which states that "the *jaghana* is the front part of a woman's hips" or "the region of the waist," the word *jaghana* is here applied to the back.
By the word "jalpati" (speaking), the intended meaning is: "How is it that your tongue does not wither away when you speak what is inexpressible? He refutes this as follows:

By the words "of the eyes," etc.: in another interpretation—namely, in the alternative manner stated in the passage beginning with "the splendor of the sun's rays has blossomed. [The phrase] "only when" refers to the Blessed One, who is the adversary of all that is to be abandoned (*heya*). This is an illustration regarding the eyes; the comparison is the form of a monkey’s back. The meaning is: how can the back of a monkey, an inferior object of comparison, be desired for the divine eyes of the Blessed One, the adversary of all that is to be abandoned? Here—in this sentence—regarding the two words: "kapyāsam" (monkey-back) and "puṇḍarīkam" (lotus).

"Attained" (*prāptam*) means attained by its own nature, without the absence of distinct case endings; and by the absence of words such as "and" (*ca*), it is also not set aside. "Grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇyam*) is the capacity to convey a single object qualified by multiple adjectives. Why is this abandoned? For what reason is it disregarded? The word "that" (*tat*) refers to the word *kapyāsa*. "The lotus" (*padmam*) is that which is denoted by the term *puṇḍarīka*. "If it qualifies" (*viśinaṣṭi cet*) means if it specifies.
The meaning of "that word" (*tacchabdaḥ*) is that, in your view, it would be figurative (*gauṇa*) with respect to something similar to that—namely, something resembling the back of a monkey.

The meaning is as follows: Are both "the back of a monkey" (*markaṭapṛṣṭha*) and "lotus" (*puṇḍarīka*) two separate points of comparison, or is there only one? Not the first, because that would entail abandoning the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) already established by the words themselves; furthermore, when a praiseworthy comparison is possible, it is improper to resort to an inferior comparison. In the second case, it would have to be said: "resembling a lotus that resembles the back of a monkey. In that event, the term *kapyāsa* ("monkey-back") would be used figuratively (*gauṇa*).

The word *tu* (but) is intended to refute another objection. To explain: if it be argued that, following the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) of the word "monkey" (*kapin*) heard first, the word "son" (*āsa*) heard later should be taken in a secondary sense (*gauṇa*), we say no. For this would result in the word "monkey," which provides the qualification for the primary meaning of the word "son," being syntactically disconnected from the sentence; it would result in the fallacy of partial syntactic connection (*ekadeśānvaya*); it would result in the word "monkey" serving merely as an indicator of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*); and it would result in the necessity of resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the word "son."

[Objection: "Is it not the case that, just as in the expression 'feed the maṇḍapa,' where—relative to the etymological meaning (yogartha) consisting of the agent of eating in the pavilion—the conventional-based metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) directed toward the people situated in the pavilion is more powerful; so too here, relative to the etymological connection with 'staying in a reed' (nālasthiti), there is no fault in this conventional-based metaphorical indication directed toward that which resembles the back of a monkey? [Reply: No. Because that rule does not apply here due to the co-occurrence (samabhivyāhāra) with another word whose meaning is etymological (yaugika). For in the expression "feed the maṇḍapa," there is no association with another word whose meaning is etymological.

If it is argued that, according to the maxim "conventional meaning (rūḍhi) sets aside etymological meaning (yoga)," the conventional cognition of a monkey is stronger than the etymological cognition of a lotus-stalk and so forth, we say no. This is because, in this case, the conventional meaning does not even arise; for there exists a mark (liṅga) contrary to the conventional meaning—namely, the presence of the word *āsa* as part of the compound *kapipada-vākya-ananvaya* and so on, which would entail the necessity of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—and there exists a mark favorable to the etymological meaning, namely, the state of being the locus of the white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*). Thus, the conventional sense is not activated here.
Is it not the case that the term *kapyāsa-pada* refers merely to the rump of a monkey? And thus, by construing it as "the *kapyāsa* is like the lotus, even so are the eyes"?

If it is argued that [the term] "like the back of a monkey" and "like a white lotus" are obtainable [in this way], and thus the previously mentioned fault does not apply, but rather there is the merit of including the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*), we say no. For this would entail the collapse of the natural observation that the two words *yathā* and *evaṃ* function as mutual correlative references, as seen in examples such as *yathā vai śyenaḥ* and *yathaiṣikatūlam*. This is because the word *evaṃ* denotes a similarity relative to the meaning of the entire sentence (*vākyārtha*), and therefore does not denote a similarity relative to the meaning of the individual word (*padārtha*).

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that [the face] would be identical to the moon, just as in the case of the expression "the face is like the moon" (candra iva mukham), rather than [the intended comparison] "the face is such as the moon" (candra eva mukham). || 24 ||

Introducing another point, he refutes it: "Someone says that 'daravikasita' means 'slightly bloomed like a monkey's mouth'; let this interpretation apply to the lotuses associated with the examples of the Blessed One’s eyes."
Moreover, that [word] does not exist in its referent, for surely a word is never produced either through its individual parts or through their aggregation.

"Daravikasitam" means slightly blossomed. He explains the meaning of the word "kapyāsa": [he says] "bruvaḥ pañcānām," whereby the substitution of "āha" occurs in the *ṇal* suffix. (It has been stated that the word "āha" functions in the sense of "he spoke"; let it be so). Here, by virtue of the power of the lotus being a qualification for the simile of the eye, and by force of the propriety of the meaning, the conventional power (*rūḍhi-śakti*) of the word "kapyāsa" is understood to refer to something slightly blossomed.

Just as in the world, even when one is unacquainted with a term in a particular context, the understanding of words such as *yūpa*, *āhavanīya*, *sphya*, *kapāla*, *caṣāla*, and *cātvāla*—which denote specific objects—is acquired through their co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with other words in other sentences; or alternatively, just as in the case of the word *prokṣaṇī*, the etymological power (*yogaśakti*) itself is grasped.

Regarding the phrase *īṣadarthe*, it has been stated that the substitution of *ka-* occurs even when the subsequent word begins with a vowel because it is of higher priority; thus, in the case of *īṣadapyāsam*, once the substitution of *ka-* for the word *īṣat* has occurred, we have *kā apyāsam*. Then, either by virtue of the *śakandhvādi* group being an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class), a single substitute (*pararūpa*) is applied, or else, by virtue of the *pṛṣodarādi* group being an *ākṛtigaṇa*, the final letter of the word *kā* is elided. This is the sense in which the formation of the word *kapyāsa* is possible. Here, accepting the appropriateness of the meaning, [the author] refutes it by demonstrating the word's lack of denotative power, starting with the words "But as for the movement... (*gatistu...*).

By the word *tu* (but), there is an exclusion of the two previously mentioned inappropriate meanings. [The qualities] are "conjoined" (*saṃgatā*) with the lotus as the illustrative example of the Lord’s eye; this "course" (*gati*)—that is, this manner—is what is intended. The sense is that a slight expansion [of meaning] is prescribed due to the suitability of the context. Thus, the portion of the argument that is worthy of acceptance has been accepted. Now, he refutes the portion that is to be refuted with the words "even that" (*tadapi*). Even so—that being the case—that [meaning] is not correct; for it is improper to say that the word *kapyāsa* denotes a slight expansion.
The word "ca" (and) is intended to conjoin two corrupted meanings. To the question "Why?", he says: "yataḥ" (because). "Yataḥ" means "yasmāt" (since). "Tatpadam" (that word)—

*Kapyāsapada* (the word *kapyāsa*). In that sense—that is, in the sense of "slightly opened"—[it may be] "by way of its parts" (*avayavaśaḥ*), meaning by means of its constituent parts (*avayavena*); or "by way of its aggregate" (*saṃhatyā*), meaning by means of a collection (*saṅghātena*) or a whole (*samudāyena*). "Somewhere" (*kutracit*) means in a Vedic glossary (*nighaṇṭu*), in a worldly glossary, or in grammar (*vyākaraṇa*). "Was not derived" (*na vyudapadyata*) means it was "unanalyzed" (*avyutpanna*). Derivation by way of parts is "etymological power" (*yoga-śakti*); derivation by way of a whole, however, is "conventional power" (*rūḍhi-śakti*). In the expression "by way of the parts or by way of the whole," the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) has the sense of specification (*vaiśiṣṭya*).

The specific distinction [of the term] consists in the relationship between the locus and the located (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*). Thus, unlike words such as *sphya* and others, it does not possess a conventional power (*rūḍhi-śakti*) based on Vedic lexicons (*nighaṇṭu*) and the like. Since there is another possible explanation, it is improper to resort to the *śakandhu*-class or the *pṛṣodara*-class [analogy], which are used only when no other way out exists; therefore, the sense is that it does not possess an etymological power (*yoga-śakti*) either. The form *vyudapadyata* is the *laṅ* (imperfect) in the active voice (*kartari*). The meaning is: "since it does not arise [from its parts], therefore it is not real (*sat*). The sense is that once the absence of denotative power in a word is established as authoritative, mere appropriateness is of no consequence. || 25 ||

When these six points have been stated, he provides the reason why the first three constitute the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) and the latter three constitute the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):
"When the six points have been set forth, the four who speak like Kapi’s wine are clever, while the three are deep as water"— thus they were accepted by the venerable Rāmānuja.
Those excluded from its acceptance and those other than them are to be abandoned; thus has this classification been declared by me through these six verses for one who knows that [system]. (26)

Regarding "samīriteṣu" (when mentioned): it refers to the six meanings of the word *kapyāsa*. Among these, there are three: *kapi* as the sun; *nālaṃ kapiḥ*; and *kaṃ udakam*—these being the three meanings expressed in the three verses beginning with those words.

Having begun with the phrase "gambhīrāmbhaḥ" (in deep waters), by means of the sentence in the *Vedārthasaṅgraha*: "He whose eyes are as large and stainless as the petals of a white lotus that has blossomed under the rays of the sun, its stalk being well-cleansed and arisen from deep waters," [the author] refers to the positions accepted by the venerable Rāmānuja—that is, the positions accepted by the venerable Bhāṣyakāra (Śaṅkara) as made known by this very statement. Therefore, they are "clever" (*catura*), meaning they are "shining" (*śobhamāna*) because they possess the excellence made known by his acceptance of them.

The other three—those spoken of in the three verses beginning with "Someone says the sun's orb is like the *kapyāsa* flower, slightly blossomed"—are excluded from the acceptance and admission of those venerable commentators (*bhagavad-bhāṣyakāra*). They are thus set aside; that is, they are external to the tradition, their lack of acceptance being made known by the fact that [the commentators] did not mention them. For this very reason, they are to be rejected—that is, they are incorrect, as the defects of not accepting them are thereby made known. By me, who knows this through the power of the instruction of a true teacher and understands the intent of the Commentary (*bhāṣya*), this division has been thus established.

"In this manner"—in the way described; "this"—that which is shown by this verse; "that"—which has come down through the tradition; "division"—the distinction between the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) and the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). It is "stated" by means of six verses. The sense is that the status of being the *siddhānta* is indicated for the former [verses] because they are stated first and are not subject to refutation, while the status of being the *pūrvapakṣa* is indicated for the latter [verses] because they are stated subsequently and are subject to refutation. Thus, the expression "division" is used. This is the intended meaning.

In this context, the expression "divasakaratejovikasitam" (expanded by the splendor of the sun) is stated first for the following reasons: because of the existence of the lexicographical authority stating that "kapayaḥ" means "men born of the Sun"; because of the existence of the usage "kapir babhasti" (the monkey devours); because the primary etymological meaning (*yogārtha*) of being a drinker of water is present; because expansion is an internal quality when compared to the splendor of the Lord’s discus; and because that [expansion] is most beautiful only when dependent upon the rays of the sun.

Even though the individual meanings of the components are present, there is no application of the *kośa* (lexicon) rule because the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*)—which is the only form the individual meaning possesses—is not the same as the status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*), which is the general rule for suffixes denoting the agent (*kartari kṛt*). Furthermore, since the stalk’s position within the lotus bud lacks direct utility in providing the comparison to the eye, its utility lies solely in suggesting the removal of witheredness; therefore, the statement "the monkey becomes a stalk" follows immediately after.

In that very same way, because the presence of water (*salila*) lacks direct utility there—and because one must rely on prefixes whose meaning is not distinct from the verbal root (*dhātu*)—and furthermore, because one must admit the elision of at least some phoneme within the sequential order (*ānupūrvī*) that constitutes the determinant of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*), the phrase "the lotus-like water here" (*kam udakam iha pāyaḥ*) is stated last. For this very reason, we understand the first two [phrases] as expressing what belongs to oneself, as in "they desire the lotus-like," while the final two express what belongs to another, as in "the wise desire what has been spoken by poets."

Therefore, it should be understood that in the *Śrīsūkta* passage beginning with "deep waters" (*gambhīrāmbhaḥ*), just as there is a gradation in a king’s attachment based on the relative proximity of his ministers and others, so too is the relationship of inner and outer (proximate and remote) expressed among the qualifiers such as "rays of the sun" (*ravikara*) through the gradation of proximity to the principal substantive.

And in this context, regarding the modification based on genus (*jāti*) according to the appropriate place, as stated in the ninth chapter, ninth section of the *Śābarabhāṣya* concerning the sacrifice prescribed in the text "One desiring prosperity should offer a *caru* of mung beans for the sake of prosperity," where it says "the sacrificial grasses are *puṇḍarīka* flowers": since it is certain that the word *puṇḍarīka* applies to the red lotus, the word *puṇḍarīka* must be substituted in place of the word *darbha*, and the word *rakta* (red) in place of the word *harita* (green), in the mantra "strew with green *darbha* grasses. This is because the word *puṇḍarīka* is established as denoting the red lotus.

There is no contradiction with such descriptions as "having eyes with red corners" or "having eyes resembling blood. However, in certain instances, such as the phrase "having large eyes like white lotuses" (*puṇḍarīkaviśālākṣau*), the word *puṇḍarīka* is explained as referring to a white water-lily; yet even that is justified by its intended reference to the region of the center of the eye. Thus, because the term is common to both meanings, the Lord himself employed the word *puṇḍarīka* alone in the *Vedārthasaṃgraha*.

It should be understood that here too, in order to indicate that [meaning], general terms such as "this is a lotus," "it is a *nalina*," and "it is possessed of beauty along with a lotus" have been used to suggest it. || 26 ||

In the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa*, the meaning accepted by opponents regarding the term *ādeśa*—which is the subject matter of the statement "due to contradiction with the initial proposition" (*pratijñāvirodhāt*)—is refuted by the passage beginning with "some [think] in the Chāndogya. In the *Ānandamaya-adhikaraṇa*, the primacy of the "tail-Brahman" is refuted, and the status of the *ānandamaya* as the Supreme Self is established by the passage beginning with "the sixth [case-ending indicates] difference," and so forth.

The interpretation accepted by the opponent regarding the scriptural passage concerning the "monkey's seat" (*kapyāsa*), which is the subject matter of the *Antarāditya* section, has been refuted by the passage beginning with "the monkey's seat is the sun" (*kapyāsaṃ bhānuḥ*). Now, in the sūtra that serves as a supporting argument for the *Jyotiḥ* section—namely, "And because the designation of the quarters beginning with 'beings' is appropriate in this way"—the interpretation accepted by us is stated by refuting the meaning asserted by the opponent concerning the subject matter, "Gāyatrī indeed is all this":

"The Gāyatrī named [here] is the Supreme Light meditated upon at the head of the Vedic revelation; its fourfold nature, however, is established through the sixfold divisions consisting of beings, the earth, the body, and the heart."

However, because of the different modes of expression found in the Vedic texts regarding functions such as singing and protecting, the mention of speech and breath is established as being for the sake of another; this is dependent upon the scriptural statements concerning their natural inclinations and their final dissolution. || 27 ||

In this regard, there is this collection of scriptural passages: "Gāyatrī indeed is all this being that exists here, whatever there may be. Gāyatrī is speech; speech indeed sings and protects all this being that exists here. That which is Gāyatrī is indeed this earth, for upon this earth all this being is established; it does not transcend this. That which is the earth is indeed this body within the person, for within this body these vital breaths (prāṇas) are established."

They do not exceed this very thing. That which is the body in the person is indeed this: that which is this heart within the person, for upon it these vital breaths (prāṇas) are established. They do not exceed this very thing. This, then, is the Gāyatrī, four-footed and sixfold.

This is its meaning: "The Gāyatrī, indeed, is all this that has come to be. The word *gāyatrī* refers to Brahman as having four feet; the word *sarvabhūta* (all that has come to be) refers to the Self (*ātman*). That the category of the Self constitutes its foot is stated through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). And wishing to describe the sixfold nature of that very Brahman through singing (*gāna*), protection (*trāṇa*), and so forth, the Śruti declares that it consists of speech (*vāk*) in order to establish those qualities: "Speech, indeed, is the Gāyatrī."

The meaning is that Brahman, which is denoted by the word *gāyatrī*, possesses four feet and is characterized by the form of speech (*vāk*). This is stated beginning with the words, "I am the essence in the waters, O son of Kuntī," up to, "sound in space, and manliness in men. Likewise, there is the statement of the venerable Parāśara: "This is the form of the high-souled Viṣṇu, who bears sound as his body. To the question, "What then is intended by this sixfold nature? he says: "Speech indeed sings and protects all this being. The Supreme Brahman, distinguished by speech, sings of all beings.

It expresses [the truth] and protects by means of enjoining what is beneficial and forbidding what is harmful—this is the meaning. Thus, one quarter has been described as having the two-fold nature of singing (*gāna*) and protecting (*trāṇa*). Following that restatement, he speaks of the second quarter through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*): "That which is Gāyatrī is indeed this very earth. Here, the words *yad* and *tat* refer to the subject under discussion as qualified by the aforementioned characteristics. The meaning is: that Brahman called Gāyatrī, which consists of one quarter in the form of all beings, is indeed this earth.

Regarding how the earth has Brahman as its essence, he says: "For in this... It is precisely because it has Brahman as its essence that it is the support of all beings; for the power to sustain all beings does not belong to the mere physical earth alone—this is the meaning. He states that this status as a support is fixed: "It does not transcend this. The earth, as a class of being, does not go beyond [its nature]. Because it is invariably the support for those whose selves are subject to karma, it is impossible to overstep—this is the meaning. For within the interior of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) composed of earth, the multitude of enjoyers revolves.

Thus, the second foot has been described through its two-fold nature: being the foundation of beings and being that which cannot be transcended by them. Now, he states the third foot: "That which is this earth is indeed this body within this person. The word *puruṣa* refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) as qualified by the body. The meaning is: that *Gāyatrī*—namely, Brahman known as Gāyatrī—which is qualified by the foot consisting of the earth, is the body; that is to say, it is qualified by the foot called the body.

Since the earth and the elements have been designated in grammatical apposition with the *Gāyatrī*, the word "earth" (*pṛthivī*) is capable of signifying Brahman by extension; furthermore, according to the principle of "the pre-eminent being the norm," it is appropriate here as well to designate the other quarters in apposition with it. Therefore, he establishes that the body has Brahman as its self through the fact that it is the substratum of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and cannot transcend them: "For in this [body] these vital breaths are established; they do not exceed this."

He states the fourth foot: "That which is the body in the person is indeed this very thing, namely the heart within this person. The meaning is that the Brahman known as Gāyatrī, characterized by the foot called "body," is precisely this (the heart). As before, he establishes its nature as Brahman: "For in this [heart] these vital breaths are established; they do not go beyond this. The "vital breaths" (prāṇāḥ) refer to the breaths such as prāṇa and apāna, or else the sense organs.

Their establishment in the heart occurs by way of the channels connected to the heart. Thus, the third and fourth feet have been described as having two aspects: being established in the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and being non-transgressible by it. He concludes the stated fourfold nature and sixfold division: "This is that Gāyatrī, four-footed and sixfold. The grammatical connection is: "This [Brahman] is that Gāyatrī, which is four-footed and sixfold. The meaning is that this Brahman is known as Gāyatrī by virtue of its fourfold and sixfold character.

The feminine gender is used here in accordance with the grammatical rule [Pāṇini 6.3.34]. "Indra is the husband of Śacī; he is oppressed by Bala; he is the invincible bull; he is the conqueror in battles"—thus the Gāyatrī is well known as having four feet and being of six types. Its sixfold nature arises from its foot consisting of six syllables. The term "four-footed" (*catuṣpadā*) refers specifically to the foot of the Gāyatrī; for if that foot were not expressive of a word (*pada*), the suffix *ṭāp* prescribed by the rule *ṭābṛci* (Pāṇini 4.1.9) would be untenable.

Therefore, the term "four-footed" (catuṣpadā) qualifies the primary meaning of the word *gāyatrī*—just as the word "deep" (gabhīra) qualifies [the river] in the phrase "in the deep river"—and the term "sixfold" (ṣaḍvidhā) is likewise a qualifier of that [gāyatrī] due to its being mentioned in conjunction with it. Thus, since the four-footedness and sixfold nature are stated regarding the Gāyatrī in relation to Brahman, it is understood that the intention is to convey a similarity between the Gāyatrī and Brahman; he states this very meaning of the Śruti as follows: "The one called Gāyatrī... and so on.

In the *Sāmaśruti-śiras*, that is, the *Chāndogya*: "by the elements, the earth, the body, and the heart"—meaning by the enjoyer-class, the earth, the body, and the heart—"is established" means it culminates. That which has four feet (*pāda*) is "four-footed" (*catuṣpāt*); its state is "four-footedness" (*cātuṣpadyam*). Since [the word] *brāhmaṇa* and others belong to the class of *ākṛti-gaṇas*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied; there is the substitution of *pada* for *pāda*, and in the case of *catuṣpād*, there is the elision of *pāda*, resulting in the elision of the final syllable. Thus, the meaning is "four-footedness. The analysis of the compound is: "that whose culminating four-footedness [is such]."

By means of [the qualities] beginning with "singing" (*gāna*) and "protection" (*trāṇa*)—that is, by means of those whose natures consist of singing, protecting, being the foundation of beings, and not being transgressed; of that—namely, of the four-footedness (*catuṣpāt-tva*); by means of the various modes (*vidhābhiḥ*).

By means of the methods that establish this, the sixfold [Brahman] is realized as being sixfold. "The Supreme Light"—this refers to the Supreme Brahman spoken of in the passage, "Now, that light which is beyond this heaven. "Named Gāyatrī"—it is so called because of its similarity to the well-known Gāyatrī meter by virtue of having four feet and being sixfold. "Was studied"—the meaning is "was recited. The absence of the substitution of *gāṅ* (for the root *i*) occurs due to the rule *vibhāṣā luṅlṛṅoḥ*. Here, there is no superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the concept of Brahman upon the Gāyatrī.

The sense is this: because of the scriptural declaration that one "obtains full and unswerving prosperity," [the meditation] does not result in liberation; nor is it the knowledge of Brahman having the Gāyatrī as its body, according to the logic of the section on ether (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.1.2), for that would render the reasoning regarding the four feet of Brahman purposeless. Therefore, the intended meaning is that the meditation enjoined is simply the contemplation of the similarity between Brahman and the Gāyatrī. In this context, by the word "established" (*siddhyat*), there is an exclusion of the explicit mention of the four feet found in the subsequent mantra: "One foot of His is all beings."

By the word "tu" (but), there is the exclusion of the four-footedness previously stated as "Speech is a foot, Breath is a foot," and also the four-footedness stated as "Fire is a foot, Wind is a foot. Since the conclusion "four-footed" occurs immediately after the mention of the elements, earth, and so forth, it is understood that these elements, earth, and so forth possess the status of being feet; thus, this four-footedness is not explicitly stated, but is established by the force of the final conclusion.

Because of the difference in the mode of expression found in the Śruti—due to the distinct style of the scripture seen in such passages as "That which is Gāyatrī is indeed this [earth]" and "This indeed is that"—and because of the specific stylistic feature consisting of the form "Speech is Gāyatrī, for in her these vital breaths (prāṇas) reside," the mention of speech and the vital breaths is for the sake of another purpose; namely, to establish the nature of singing (gāna), protection (trāṇa), and being the support of the vital breaths, and not for the purpose of establishing the sixfold set of terms beginning with the elements (bhūta).

This—that which was previously stated—is the contemplation of the similarity between Brahman and the Gāyatrī by way of its four-footedness and sixfold nature. "Svarasaṃ" means endowed with the essence characterized by being self-evident; "nigamanaṃ" refers to that [scriptural passage] whose form consists of the conclusion of what has been proclaimed. That scripture is the text beginning with "That very one is four-footed. "Dependent on that" (tadadhīnaṃ) means having that as its authority (tatpramāṇaka).

Here, by means of these two [arguments]—namely, that because of the difference in the modes of expression found in the Vedic texts, [the conclusion] depends on the natural conclusion of the Vedic hearing—it has been demonstrated that the meaning of this Vedic text as stated by the opponent is untenable.

Yādavaprakāśa has indeed stated this meaning of it: the Brāhmaṇa passage, "Gāyatrī is all this," does not have the four-footed nature as its primary purport; rather, it has as its purport the sixfold forms consisting of all beings, speech, earth, body, heart, and breath. Furthermore, the sentence "This very [Gāyatrī] is four-footed and sixfold" is intended to enjoin the four-footed nature by way of restating the sixfold nature. And the four-footed nature is that which is set forth in the wording of the mantra, "A foot of Him... and so on.

This [position] is untenable: because the conclusion (*nigamana*) is naturally understood from both parts in the statement "this [meditation] is four-footed and sixfold," it would follow that one part is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) and the other part is injunctive (*vidhāyaka*), which is inconsistent due to such dissimilarity (*vairūpya*). Furthermore, since speech and breath—unlike singing and protecting—are not the primary subjects to be expounded (as they serve other purposes), the six categories of objects (*padārtha-ṣaṭka*) are not established. || 27 ||
Now begins the section concerning the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmin*).

Regarding the *antaryāmi-brāhmaṇa*, which constitutes the subject matter of this section, there is uncertainty concerning the meaning of the sentence "of whom darkness is the body" (*yasya tamaḥ śarīram*). Since the definition of a body—as that substance which belongs to a conscious being—does not include the property of being a substance, and because there is confusion among the disputants regarding whether darkness is a substance or a non-substance, [the author] says here:
We perceive darkness as a substance that is dense or rarefied, dark-blue and moving; yet no sublation of this perception has ever been observed anywhere by anyone.
Therefore, a cause must be postulated, and verbal testimony (śābda-pramiti) also prevails [as a valid means of knowledge].
For the eye, by virtue of that vision, extends its range even into the lightless. || 28 ||

In the analysis of the compound *bahulaṃ ca tadviralaṃ ca* (and that is both dense and sparse), it is a *samāsa* [compound] like *khañjakubja* and so forth. *Bahulam* means "dense" (*sāndram*), and *viralam* means "with intervals" (*sāntarālam*). Since density and so forth cannot exist in a single individual entity, it follows that it consists of an aggregate of parts; by this, its possession of parts is stated. *Mechakam* means "dark blue" (*nīlam*) and "moving" (*calam*, i.e., possessing motion). The compound is as before. By these two, its possession of qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*kriyā*) is stated. The word *tamaḥ* (darkness) ends in the accusative case, and *nāma* is used in the sense of "well-known."

By this, its manifestation as a positive entity (bhāvarūpa) is stated. We perceive substance; we perceive it through direct perception as "substance-ness," or we infer it: "Darkness is a substance because it possesses parts, like a jar"; "Darkness is a substance because it is the substratum of qualities and actions, like a jar"; "Darkness is not of the nature of the absence of light, because it is perceived as a positive entity, like a jar"; "Darkness is not a quality, because it is perceived as the substratum of qualities, like a jar."

Darkness is not the absence of the perception of form, because it is perceived as a positive entity (*vidhirūpeṇa*), like a jar. By the phrase "like a jar" (*ghaṭavad*), the intended inferences are indicated. Here, by the term "blackish" (*mecaka*), the position that the perception of darkness is actually the perception of the blueness residing in the earthly atoms pervading space is rejected. For if that were the case, the cognition regarding darkness would be simply "blueness. This is the sense.

By the phrase "because it is perceived as having a positive form" (*bhāvarūpeṇa pratīyamānatvāt*), the two positions—that darkness is the absence of contact with light or the absence of the perception of color—are refuted. He dispels the objection regarding the non-establishment of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*) with the words beginning "by anyone" (*kenāpi*). The word "anyone" implies "by a person"; the word "even" (*api*) is understood to include "at any time. "Sublation" (*bādha*) refers to the cognition that negates color and so forth. "Was not seen" (*na dadṛśe*) means "was not perceived"; this is the perfect tense (*liṭ*) of the root *dṛś* used in the passive voice.

The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and sublation" (*bādhaśca*) conjoins the defect of the cause (*kāraṇadoṣa*). Thus, the sense is that because there is an absence of both a defect in the cause and a sublating cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*), the perception of color and so forth in darkness is not of the nature of an error; therefore, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is not unestablished (*asiddha*). No defect is observed that would necessitate the status of the perception of color and so forth in darkness as an error. Furthermore, since the perception of color and so forth in darkness is established by the experience of everyone, to postulate such a defect in every instance is refuted by the principle of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Therefore, the sense is that a defect in the cause is difficult to specify.

[Objection: Is it not the case that darkness is not a substance, because its cause has been defined [as such]? For instance, since darkness possesses color (*rūpa*), the wind and other elements—which lack that color—cannot be its causes.
