Nor can the other elements be its causes, as they are devoid of touch (*sparśa*) and smell (*gandha*). [To this, he replies: "Therefore, a cause must be postulated. The meaning is that, since the perception of color and so forth in darkness is uncontradicted, its status as a substance is established; consequently, a cause for it must be postulated.

For in the world, it is well known that an effect is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the postulation of a cause; however, according to the principle that "an effect clearly ascertained does not deserve to be denied when its cause is being investigated," one must postulate a cause for darkness, which is established by uncontradicted perception. In this regard, because it is a clear substance, darkness is an effect of space (*ākāśa*); its possession of color (*rūpa*), however, is possible due to the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*). Alternatively, Vyāsapāda maintains that darkness is an effect of light (*tejas*) because it possesses color, while the non-perception of touch is due to its transparency.

Light exists in the form of radiance and its power, like a substance of brilliance; whereas earth itself exists in the form of darkness and as the substratum for that [darkness]. Meghanādāri Sūri maintains that shadow is indeed earth. Furthermore, in the *Nyāyasiddhāñjana*, darkness is enumerated among the categories of earth. Therefore, a cause must be postulated.

An objection is raised: "Since darkness is not perceived at the time of perceiving form, its perception might indeed be possible at the time of its non-perception, just as in the case of closing one's eyes; thus, [the existence of] darkness is established by direct perception. To this, he says: "Even valid knowledge derived from scripture prevails. The meaning is that the knowledge consisting of valid cognition (*pramā*) produced by the scriptures serves to dispel the aforementioned doubt. For "victory" (*vijaya*) consists in the refutation of opposing views. What is intended here is such scriptural passages as, "The Blessed Lord created darkness," and so forth.

(The word *api* includes logical reasoning as well. For, since there would be the undesirable consequence that owls and the like [could be suspected of having such vision], because they do not perceive form at the time when we and others do perceive form, and because we and others do not perceive it at the time when they do, the perception of form in the dark is not an error—this is the meaning). Now, one might object: "Darkness is not a substance, because there is no means of apprehending it. Since it is not assisted by light, the eye is not its apprehender."

(If darkness does not persist in the presence of light, it cannot be an object of perception; therefore, the cognition of form [in the dark] is merely an illusion), like the appearance of blue when the eyes are closed—to this he replies with the words beginning "nirālokam" (without light). "Nirālokam" means unaccompanied by light. "Cakṣuḥ" (the eye) is the agent. "Tat" refers to darkness. "Prathayati" means it makes manifest. To the question "Why?", he replies: "By virtue of observation"—that is, because the eye is independent of light when perceiving the absence of form and light for those such as owls and ourselves.

In the view of the opponent, the causal relation is between the state of being a visual perception whose object is distinct from the absence of light and the state of conjunction with light (*ālokasaṃyoga*). In our own view, however, the causal relation is established by substituting "being distinct from darkness" (*tamobhinnatva*) for the place of "being distinct from the absence of light. The implication is that the assumption of the erroneous nature (*bhramatva*) of the cognition of color is an additional burden in the opponent's view. || 28 ||
He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding the topic of "abundance" (*bhūman*):
The Supreme Person named *bhūman* is that which is superior here as the Brahman called "Truth" (*satya*);
for by its power, it is greater than the inferior self called "vital breath" (*prāṇa*), and it is the knower of truth.

One cannot convey [the meaning] that "he who speaks the truth" by means of the word [alone], for it is not possible to understand a different Agnihotra-sacrificer than the one under discussion; moreover, there would be a destruction of the word's aesthetic power (śabdaśrī). || 29 ||

The Chandogas recite: "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else—that is the Infinite (bhūmā). But where one sees something else, hears something else, and understands something else—that is the finite (alpam). Although this word *bhūmā*—derived from the root *bahu* with the suffix *iman*—denotes abundance (*vaipulya*), it nevertheless refers to the substratum of that abundance because it is specified in contrast to the finite (*alpa*). Thus, the meaning is: "the Infinite" means "the vast."

Furthermore, the Self is qualified by the meaning of the word "Bhūman" (the Infinite); for, having begun with "The knower of the Self overcomes sorrow," and having taught the Bhūman, the text concludes with "All this is indeed the Self. In this regard, a doubt arises as to whether this Self characterized by the quality of being the Bhūman is the individual self (*pratyagātman*) or the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the Bhūman is the individual self; because, after the instruction on the vital breath (*prāṇa*) to Nārada who desired to know the Self, no other [entity] is taught thereafter, it is understood that the instruction on the Self reaches its conclusion with the one denoted by the word "prāṇa"—that is, the living individual soul (*jīva*). Moreover, it is logically consistent that the individual self, when liberated from ignorance, is of the nature of bliss.

It should not be said that "he indeed does not speak transcendentally who speaks transcendentally by means of truth" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.16.1) indicates that the one who speaks transcendentally by means of truth is distinct from the speaker of vital breath (*prāṇa*)—due to the particle *tu*—and that, through the understanding that the instruction on the Self is completed in Brahman, whose name is Truth and who is superior to the individual soul (*jīva*) denoted by the word *prāṇa*, the "Fullness" (*bhūman*) is the Supreme Self. For, by the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the aforementioned speaker of vital breath in the phrase "He, indeed, seeing thus," it is rather the speaking of truth that is enjoined as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) for him, as expressed in "But he indeed speaks transcendentally."
Just as in the passage, "He who speaks the truth is indeed an Agnihotrin," the speaking of truth is enjoined for the Agnihotrin under discussion; so it is here.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that the "Plenum" (*bhūman*) is the Supreme Self alone; for it is perceived that "this one, indeed" is distinct from the one who speaks of transcending vital breath (*prāṇātivādin*). Nor does the logic of the sentence "this one, indeed, is a performer of the Agnihotra" apply here. For in that case, since there is no other substance or deity, no other Agnihotra is perceived, and thus, out of necessity, the natural force of the word "indeed" (*tu*) must be set aside. Here, however, since there exists another ground for the designation of "transcending"—namely, the state of transcending which consists in the Supreme Self denoted by the word "Truth" (*satya*), which is distinct from the vital breath that was the ground for the previously mentioned "transcending"—why should the natural force of the word "indeed" be abandoned?

The word *satya* indeed denotes the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), because in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad itself, that Brahman is heard to have the name "Truth" (*satya*). Therefore, since the word *ātman* culminates in the Supreme Self denoted by the word *satya*, the "Abundance" (*bhūman*) is the Supreme Self.

He states this very conclusion with the words beginning "the one called Bhūman," etc. The "Abundance" (*bhūman*), being characterized by unsurpassed bliss, is designated by the word *bhūman* in the Veda as Nārāyaṇa alone, the highest among persons. To the question "Why?", he says: "Because" (*yat*), which means "since."

In this context—that is, in the *Bhūmavidyā*—from that which is called *prāṇa*, meaning from the lower self (*avara-ātman*) to whom the term *prāṇa* is metaphorically applied due to its association with breath; and from the individual soul (*jīva*), which is inferior in comparison to the Supreme Self, as it is seen to be "only the size of the tip of an awl" (Br. 4.2.9)—there is something "greater," that is, more exalted. This is Brahman, designated by the name "Truth" (*satya*). Therefore, since the application of the word "Self" culminates in the Supreme Self, the meaning is that the "Fullness" (*bhūman*) is the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*).

Because the word *puruṣa* is designated in grammatical apposition with the word *satya* in the phrase "the *puruṣa* is truth," the designation "Supreme Person" (*puruṣottama*) indicates the probandum (*sādhya*). The designation "more than" (*adhika*) follows the Sūtra: "On account of the teaching of [him] as being beyond the serene state" (*saṃprasādādadhyupadeśāt*). To the objection that in the passage "But he indeed speaks surpassingly," the speaking of truth is enjoined for one who speaks surpassingly through the vital breath (*prāṇa*), he replies: "By the force of the context," namely, "one who knows the truth."

One who possesses the knowledge of truth (*satyavedana*), which is the cause for transcending speech (*ativāda*) by means of Brahman whose name is Truth (*satyanāmaka*), [is superior] through power (*tubalataḥ*); that is, by power (*tubalena*). He is "superior to him" (*tajjñādhikaḥ*), meaning superior to the one who knows the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Indeed, the word *tu* (but/however) naturally implies a different subject from what was previously mentioned. Therefore, someone other than the one who transcends the vital breath (*prāṇātivādin*)—namely, the one who transcends truth (*satyātivādin*)—is being described in relation to the one who transcends the vital breath.

Furthermore, this excellence is based on the superiority of the truth of this object of knowledge over the vital breath (*prāṇa*) which is its object of knowledge; thus, because the instruction culminates in the teaching of the Self under discussion—denoted by the word "truth"—the meaning is that the "Full" (*bhūman*) is the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*). He states the difference from the sentence "But he indeed is an Agnihotrin" with the words "He who...": the phrase "he who speaks the truth" refers to the sentence "But he indeed is an Agnihotrin who speaks the truth."

The understanding of another Agnihotrin—distinct from the Agnihotrin under discussion—is not capable of being derived from the context (*prakaraṇa*), because there is an absence of a material substance (*dravya*) and a deity (*devatā*). This is the meaning. The word "hi" (for) indicates a reason. Therefore, the "bhaṅga"—meaning the abandonment or violation—of the "śabdaśrī," that is, the natural force of the word "tu" (but), must be tolerated; this is the sense. Just as in that [other] case, since there is no inconsistency in the present instance, it is improper to violate the natural force of the word "tu."

The state of being an "ativādin" (one who speaks beyond) means speaking of a reality that transcends one's own object of worship. This is not possible in the case of the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which possesses limited happiness; rather, it is possible only in the case of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), whose nature is unsurpassed bliss. Therefore, the *bhūman* is indeed the Supreme Self. || 29 ||

In explaining the meaning of the passage beginning with "Now, that which is within this" (*atha yad idam asmin*), which is the subject of the *dahara-adhikaraṇa*, he states the distinction between his own position and the opposing view by pointing out four points of inconsistency in the latter:

(1) the incongruity regarding the force of the pronoun "that" (*yat*); (2) the connection [of the pronoun] with the lotus of the heart (*hṛtpuṇḍarīka*) despite its being separated [from the antecedent]; (3) the disregard for the word "in that" (*tasmin*); and (4) [the resulting lack of syntactic coherence].

Even when there is an interruption by the rule for the expression of desired objects (*kāma*), the two [meanings] reside within its own category; furthermore, when there is a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*) of the word *yat*, there is the state of being treated as a singular (*ekavadbhāva*). || 30 ||

Here is the sequence of the scriptural text: "Now, in this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-palace; within it is a small space (ākāśa); that which is inside it is what one must seek. The meaning of this has been stated by others as follows: "In this city of Brahman"—that is, in the body—"this" refers to the lotus-shaped "small" or minute "palace"; "within this"—inside the palace of the heart-lotus—"the small space" is Brahman; "in that"—within the space of the heart-lotus.

That which is the "small ether" (daharākāśa)—the word being neuter in the general sense—the remainder of the sentence being "it exists"; that is what is to be meditated upon; and the word "that" (tat) as the goal is also neuter in the general sense.

The intended meaning of our own [position] is as follows: that which is this lotus-shaped abode of the heart within the body; in this abode of the heart, the "inner" one—that is, existing within—is the "small space" (*daharākāśa*), which is the Supreme Brahman. Regarding the phrase "in that," etc.: according to the rule *astir bhavatiparaḥ*, the word *asti* (is) is understood; the grammatical connection is "that which exists, within that. The sense is: "that small space which exists"; "that which is within it" refers to that same thing. As for the form *yaśca yacca yad*, it is a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*) of masculine and neuter genders; thus, "that" [refers to both]: both he and that are to be sought (*tadanveṣṭavyam*).

The meaning is that both the small ether (*daharākāśa*) and the collection of qualities existing within it are to be meditated upon. Following the subsequent passage, "Having known the Self and these true [qualities], they depart," one should resort to *ekaśeṣa* (the grammatical retention of one term from a class) for all three items beginning with "that" (*yat*). Due to this *ekaśeṣa*, although the small ether and its qualities are presented by a single word, the small ether connects with the phrase "it exists" (*asti*), while the collection of qualities connects with the phrase "within it" (*tasmin antaḥ*).

This is a case of connection according to suitability, as in expressions such as "the two Puṣpavantau [sun and moon]" or "those which cause the blooming of the lotus and the water-lily by day and night."

He explains the distinction between the naturalness (*svārasya*) and lack of naturalness (*asvārasya*) regarding these two meanings with the words "lack of naturalness," etc.; the remainder of the sentence is "in the passage beginning with *atha yadidam*. Regarding the word *yat*—that is, the word *yat* in the phrase *yad antar*—there is a change of gender: namely, the sublation of the masculine gender that would have resulted from its referring back to the small ether (*daharākāśa*) designated by the masculine noun *ākāśa*. This is one point of lack of naturalness in the opponent's view. In our own view, however, there is no fault, because the neuter gender remains as the residue. Although the neuter gender is scripturally prescribed in both cases;

Nevertheless, the core intention is that the refutation of the inherent masculinity [of the small ether] is more extensive according to the opponent's view. Regarding the phrase "in that": the instrumental case in *anapekṣayā* is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārthe*). It is "separated" by the sentence "small is this [ether] within it. In the lotus of the heart, the connection is with the status of being referred back (*parāmarśitvam*). By the word *anapekṣa*, its uselessness (*vaiyarthyam*) is indicated; and thus, there is the uselessness of the term *tasmin*.

The meaning is that there are two defects: [the word *tad*] would refer to something remote, and [the word *tasmin*] would be redundant. [The sense is: "The small space within this [heart]; that alone is to be sought"—this much would suffice. [In that case, the word *tasmin* would be useless, and it would have to refer to the heart-lotus which is separated by a distance. For us, however, the phrase *tasmin antar* (within that) is meaningful because it serves to set forth the qualities [of the space]. Furthermore, the resort to the grammatical rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retaining only one of two identical words) with the word *yat* is for the purpose of establishing that the small space itself is also an object of meditation (*upāsya*).

The core point is that there is no fault of intervention, because the word "dahara" (small) here refers directly to the "dahara-ākāśa" (the small ether) without any intervening term. Regarding the phrase "etāṃśca satyān" (and these true [qualities]), which is a subsequent reference to what was required for the meaning of the preceding statement—the injunction for the knowledge of desires (*kāma-vedana-vidhi*): "desires" (*kāmāḥ*) are those desirable auspicious qualities, namely freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth; "knowledge of them" (*teṣāṃ vedanam*) is their meditation (*upāsanam*); the "injunction" (*vidhiḥ*) is the establishment of its status as an object of injunction through the inference of being enjoined; the "rejection" (*kṣepaḥ*) of that [objection] is its refutation.

The word *api* (also/even) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*). The intended meaning is that for us [the followers of our own school], since both the qualities (*guṇa*) and the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*) are objects of meditation (*upāsya*), there is no abandonment of them. According to the lexicon (*abhidhānakośa*), "desires" (*kāmāḥ*) refers to longings for desirable objects and [the god] Smara; however, because of the context, the word *kāma*, which primarily denotes the object of desire, here conveys the state of being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth. The syntactical connection is that these four points of lack of elegance belong to the system of Śaṅkara. Regarding the phrase "in our own position" (*svapakṣe*) and so on: the word *yat* (which/that) is an elliptical indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for *tat* (that/it) and other such correlative terms.

When there is *ekaśeṣya*—that is, the state of being a single remainder (*ekaśeṣatva*)—the suffix *ṣyañ* is used in the sense of "being" because it is applied to words such as *brāhmaṇa*. In that context—that is, regarding the word *yad* and others which are accepted as being a single remainder—the fact that they undergo singular treatment (*ekavadbhāvitā*) means they possess the quality of singular treatment necessitated by the rule prescribing singular treatment for the referent. This pair [of points] constitutes the lack of elegance (*akhārasya*) in one's own position; this is the syntactic connection. (It should be understood that since the subsequent word is present, there is no need to supply the word *tat*.)

In this context, regarding the analysis of the compound beginning with "yaśca yacceti," there is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) of the two pronouns *yat* and *tat* by virtue of the rule *tyadādīnām* (Pāṇini 1.2.72). However, in the case of the word *anveṣṭavya*, since the rule *napuṃsakamanapuṃsakenaikavaccāsyānyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 1.2.69) prescribes a singular form (*ekavadbhāva*) when a neuter is joined with a non-neuter, it follows that the pronouns *yat* and *tat*, being in grammatical apposition with the word *dvi* (which is feminine), are established as having the singular number. Furthermore, between the masculine and the neuter, the neuter remains because of its higher priority in the order of application; thus, the neuter gender of *yat* and *tat* is also established.

And this has been favored by the venerable Vyāsa [in the Mahābhāṣya]: "The words beginning with *tyad* are always [retained] by all [the others]. This refers to the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) of the masculine and neuter forms of the word *yad*. By the rule "the neuter [remains] when combined with a non-neuter, and optionally in the singular," there is both the neuter gender and the singular number.

Here, although it is said that "between the masculine and the neuter, the neuter remains due to its posteriority," even without that, pronouns bring about oneness between the subject (*uddiśyamāna*) and the predicate (*pratinirdiśyamāna*), and they adopt the gender of the latter; thus, as it is said, there is freedom of usage (according to the maxim of the "one who eats from a brass vessel").

Since the qualifying term *anveṣṭavya*—which has its gender determined by the rule for neuter nouns (*napuṃsaka-sūtra*) through the formation of a collective compound (*ekaśeṣa*)—is predominant because it refers to the predicate, its very gender is logically appropriate for the pronoun *tat*, which forms a collective compound with the series of pronouns beginning with *tyad* (by the *tyadādi-sūtra*) and serves as the indicator of the subject. Consequently, the pronoun *yat*, being dependent on that [subject], must also have that same gender. With the intention that the neuter gender in all such cases is governed solely by the rule for neuter nouns, the author stated "not neuter" (*ana-puṃsakam*). This is because, regarding the word *anveṣṭavya*, [the neuter gender applies] by virtue of its co-utterance (*sahokti*) with both neuter and non-neuter terms.

It should be understood that the phrase "and the state of being in the singular" was stated with the intention that, because the *napuṃsakasūtra* (Pāṇini 1.2.69) extends the rule of singular number (*ekavadbhāva*) to the meaning [of the compound], the singular ending in the second member (*tatpada*) is established for the sake of achieving singular number even for that which stands in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with it; and by virtue of its dependence on that, the same applies to the first member (*yatpada*) as well. Thus, the laborious interpretation provided here by the author of the *Bhāvaprakāśikā* is not to be respected.

Regarding the statement that "the destruction of demons, the acquisition [of knowledge], ease, and the absence of doubt are the purposes," however, because the *padasaṃskāra* (word-formation) perspective is adopted here, the plurality—induced by the *itaretarayoga-dvandva* (copulative compound) which arises first due to its being *antaranga* (internal)—cannot be sublated by the singular form (*ekavadbhāva*), which is caused by the connection with other words and is thus *bahiraṅga* (external). Consequently, the use of the plural number is justified; for both the *pada-saṃskāra* and *vākya-saṃskāra* perspectives must conform to the actual linguistic usage (*lakṣya*).

In some instances, when those desiring to study grammar have recourse to the view that grammatical refinement applies to the sentence as a whole (*vākyasaṃskārapakṣa*), the purpose [of grammar] is explained; here, the verbal form ending in a *tiṅ* suffix is made singular because it functions as a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇa*). However, other ways of reconciling this statement by the venerable Vyāsa are provided by the Great Teacher (Vedāntadeśika) in his *Pārāśaryavijaya*, and should be consulted therein. || 30 ||
He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding the section on the deities (*devatādhikaraṇa*):
"The worship of the Blessed One is possible even for the inhabitants of heaven who possess exceptionally refined bodies and are subject to the heat of worldly existence."
Now, is it not the case that even hundreds of words from explanatory passages (arthavāda) are here authoritative—just like the words of mantras—being faultless and of non-human origin? (31)

In this regard, deities lack eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) due to the absence of desire and other such prerequisites; and that absence [of desire] exists because they lack consciousness (*caitanya*) and the like. Since the *mantras* and *arthavādas* (as well as *smṛti* and *itihāsa*) are intended for something else, they do not have [the deity's eligibility] as their primary purport (*tātparya*). Furthermore, since it is possible for one devoid of consciousness to be the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*), the deity’s status is not established by the injunction of sacrifice (*yāga-vidhi*), which consists essentially in renunciation (*tyāga*). Nor is its status established by being the locus of the grace of the "mediator" (*nirvāhaka*), for even an action that perishes in a moment can be brought to fruition at a later time through the medium of the unseen potency (*apūrva*).

Since something unprecedented is required in the case of certain deities who are devoid of a body, there is no regard for the grace mentioned in the explanatory passages (arthavāda). Therefore, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that bodiless and insentient deities lack the qualification for the meditations on Brahman.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: In the *Sāmavidhānabrāhmaṇa*, it is heard that "one who employs [the chant] for four years according to this ritual procedure, 'May glory be in me,' attains sovereignty over the three worlds"—thus the station of Indra is declared to be the fruit. Furthermore, elsewhere it is stated that the attainment of the station of deities such as the Maruts is the fruit of the Madhu-vidyā; and since the subjugation of deities is also mentioned in various places as a fruit, and because there must necessarily be an intention regarding the fruit, [it follows that even those meditations situated within the context of worship lead to that result]. Thus, even those situated in the context of meditation [say]: "Those two [Nārada and Sanatkumāra] went to Prajāpati... [and so on].

Through such passages as these, which are supplementary to the injunctions for ritual action (*karmavidhi*), as well as through statements such as "the one with the thunderbolt in hand" (*vajrahasta*), the sentience (*caitanya*) and other attributes of the deities are established. For this very reason, there is necessarily the requirement for the grace (*prasāda*) mentioned in the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). Furthermore, in rites devoid of a deity, the Blessed Lord alone bestows the fruit by means of His own grace.

Furthermore, the authority of both mantras and arthavādas is established on the same grounds as that of injunctions, namely their lack of human authorship and other such qualities. Moreover, remembrance and praise cannot be established if they lack a basis; nor is it possible to generate enthusiasm through the glorification of what does not exist. In the Vedāntas, the fourfold creation beginning with the gods is traditionally taught. Therefore, since the corporeal forms and other attributes of the deities exist, the deities indeed possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman. This very point he states: "By means of more powerful... and so forth.

The term *vigrahādi* (body, etc. is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is more acute (*paṭutara*) than the body and so forth. By the word "etc.," the Veda is included. Its establishment [as being present] occurs either through the understanding that the gods possess Brahminhood and so on—as in the statement "Brahmā is Bṛhaspati"—or through the non-forgetting of the Vedas acquired in other births. Regarding the body's "acute nature," what is intended is its specific state as described in the phrase "one whose son has been born," its fitness for activities such as the *Viṣṇukramaṇa* ritual, and its lack of physical defects such as lameness.

The superior proficiency of the knowledge (*vidyā*) intended here consists in its independence from a teacher and so forth. The term *vigrahādī* ends in the accusative case and is neuter in gender as a general category. *Vahatām* means "bearing" [the burden] by way of being the *Bhārata*. By this, its undeniable nature is suggested. *Bhavatāpavatām* means "those afflicted by the torments of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). The suffix *-matup* is used here in the sense of excellence. The sense is that even for an elephant, there may be a wind-disease corresponding to its own size. By these two [verses], the threefold qualification—being a seeker (*arthin*), being capable (*samartha*), and being learned (*vidvān*)—has been stated.

This indicates that even for such celestial beings—the gods—despite their residence in a realm superior to this one, they may still possess a desire for worship because, in comparison to the eternal glory (*nityavibhūti*), they reside in what is effectively a state of hell. By the term "of the Blessed One" (*bhagavataḥ*), there is intended the source of auspicious qualities that are the opposite of all that is to be abandoned (*heyapratibhaṭa*); by this, specific qualities suitable for being both the means and the goal are meant. "Worship" (*upāsana*) means repeated, revolving contemplation. "Is possible" (*saṃbhavati*) means it is established by authoritative evidence (*prāmāṇika*).

In this context, by the phrase "atropāsanam" (the meditation here), the meaning of the word "tat" (that) in the sūtra "taduparyapi bādarāyaṇaḥ saṃbhavāt" is stated. The word "diviṣadām" (of the inhabitants of heaven) expresses the meaning of the word "upari" (above). By the phrase "manuṣyādhikāratvāt" (because of the qualification of humans), the qualification of humans introduced in the preceding sūtra is connected here as well; this is indicated by the particle "api" (also). And by the phrase "paṭutaretyādi" (more capable, etc.), the meaning of the word "saṃbhavāt" (because of the possibility) is explained.

It has been stated [regarding] the words of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*)—such as "the wielder of the thunderbolt" (*vajrahasta*) and so forth—and also regarding those explanatory passages that serve as supplements to injunctions for ritual acts and meditations (*upāsana*), such as "then both the gods and the asuras... and so forth; and regarding the words of mantras—the portions of mantras intended for the praise of deities and the illumination of what is to be performed. By the word "also" (*api*), the injunctions for rituals that are the means for attaining the state of a deity are included.

The meaning is that the greater strength of a hundred [authorities], even when this is not contradicted by other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), must not be sublated; for the definition of a *pramāṇa* is that which establishes an uncontradicted object. To the question "Of what nature is it?", he says: "faultless" (*apadoṣa*), meaning free from defects (whether of human origin or not); and "according to rule" (*vidhivat*), meaning it is indeed a *pramāṇa* like an injunctive statement (*vidhivākya*). The particle *nanu* is used here as a particle of emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).

Because they share the same quality of being faultless and not of human origin, and because they are free from contradiction by other means of valid cognition (*māna*), the *arthavādas* and so forth possess authority just like the injunctions (*vidhi*). Consequently, since the corporeal form of the deities and the like are established, and since [the qualities] such as desire for knowledge are possible, the gods indeed possess the qualification (*adhikāra*) for the knowledge of Brahman; this is the explicit statement made through the zeal to establish the authority of the mantras and *arthavādas* in the same manner as the injunctions. However, it should be understood that for those [passages] which are supplementary to injunctions, there is an indication by the word "also" (*api*), even though their counterparts (the injunctions) are admitted. || 31 ||

He elaborates on what has already been stated: "In this context, the first [chapter] is primarily for the purpose of generating an inclination toward one's own goal and the task to be accomplished, by drawing from its own qualities of excellence;
otherwise, it would not succeed, just as [it does not] in the case of injunctions for those who know reality."
How can there be praise by mentioning a quality that does not exist? || 32 ||

"Stutiparam" means devoted to the proclamation of qualities. "Here" refers to this collection of *arthavādas* and *mantras* that constitute supplements to injunctions (*vidhi*). "The first," namely that which consists of *arthavādas*, acts as the agent. For the sake of generating "inclination"—that is, for the sake of establishing a specific desire toward the enjoined acts such as sacrifices—it is "like one who has regard" (or possesses intent) toward its own qualities to be expressed, such as being the most efficacious (*kṣepiṣṭhatva*) and so forth; the meaning is that it is directed toward them with purpose.

The phrase "having praise as its primary purpose" is stated with the words "how could it be non-existent," etc., using the very seed of the objection as the seed of the solution. By the prefix *pra-* in the word *prajanaṇa* ("procreation"), the exclusion of those injunctions of meaningless explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) which possess an imagined power of praise is intended. He confirms the stated meaning through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) with the words "that," etc. "That"—namely, the status of having praise as its primary purpose required by the injunction—is the agent. "Otherwise"—without the intentionality toward a quality—it "is not established," meaning it is not possible.

The phrase "as in the case of injunctions" (*vidhiṣviva*) connects with the preceding clause. The sense is that just as an injunction lacks the status of being a eulogy (*stāvaka*) because it lacks an intention directed toward a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), so too an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) lacks the status of being a eulogy because it lacks an intention directed toward a subordinate quality. Alternatively, the meaning is that just as in the case of injunctions, the capacity to impel action (*pravartakatva*) is not established without an intention directed toward its own literal meaning, so too in the case of explanatory passages, the status of being a eulogy is not established without an intention directed toward its own literal meaning. Or else, "as in the case of injunctions" connects with the subsequent clause.

For those who know reality—persons possessing specific insights that consist of valid cognitions regarding objects contrary to the matters they intend to propound—how could there be praise (*nuti*), that is, eulogy (*stuti*) [or inclination (*ruci*) and prior engagement], by means of a quality that is non-existent—that is, whose falsity is certain—even when it is mentioned, even when it is taught through an *arthavāda* (explanatory passage), just as in injunctions such as "Drink the bitter decoction, your crest-lock will grow," where there is a false relationship between the means and the end intended to be propounded? It does not occur; this is the meaning.

(This was stated by the Blessed One: "Delight is not produced by speaking of a quality that does not exist. Praise (*stuti*) is the proclamation of only those qualities that are real, not of those that are unreal, because the term "praise" is used most frequently in reference to such [real] qualities alone; and because it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) to assume that the prohibition "one should not speak untruth" applies to cases other than praise. (Furthermore, by this same logic, it would follow that censure (*nindā*) and defamation (*apavāda*) would also consist of speaking of non-existent faults; thus, the incongruity of passages such as "he defamed Hari with a fault" becomes evident. What [kind of speech] is there regarding a factual matter?

In the *Bhagavad-guṇa-darpaṇa*, it is clearly stated that this word "praise" (*stuti*), following the supplementary portion of the passage at the beginning, signifies that the full extent of the meaning cannot be expressed. For this very reason, even by poets, [the term] "arthavāda" has been indicated as being synonymous with the statement of a non-existent fault—such as "Tell me some fault"—which takes the form of a false accusation.

Otherwise, one might ask: "What real thing is being described? Even if one adopts the view that a hymn (*stotra*) is merely the naming of qualities, there is no contradiction in the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) having their own literal meaning as their purport, for it is accepted that what is non-existent cannot be something that inspires enthusiasm (*prarocaka*). The Vedāntācāryas, however, state in their commentary on the hymns: "I shall praise"—meaning "I shall serve by describing the qualities of the Supreme Reality. Thus says the *Dramiḍabhāṣya*: "Praise is not possible through what is non-existent. And Varadācārya says: "How can there be praise by speaking of a quality that is non-existent? Thus they speak.

This is the intended meaning of this verse for them: here, within the two parts consisting of *arthavāda* and *mantra*, first, that which is of the nature of *arthavāda* is intent upon praise (*stutipara*) in order to generate an inclination toward its own enjoined object to be accomplished; being thus intent on praise for the sake of generating that inclination, it possesses a regard characterized by the intentionality (*tātparya*) regarding the truth of the qualities it propounds. That [regard] is the state of being intent on praise. Otherwise—that is, in the absence of the intentionality regarding the truth of the qualities—it is not established.

The meaning is that since the state of being praise (*stuti*) is pervaded by the description of ultimate qualities, the absence of the pervader entails the absence of the pervaded. "Of those who know reality" means of those who see things as they truly are. "As in injunctions" means as in persuasive statements. How can there be praise through a non-existent quality described? The meaning is: not at all. For praise is indeed the description of ultimate qualities; here, the instrumental case is used with the intention of expressing that qualities are the constituent cause (*ghaṭaka-hetu*) therein. Furthermore, in the commentary, the word *prarocanā* (enticement) in the phrase "enticement does not arise from a non-existent quality described" refers to praise.

In the phrase "the one worthy of praise with meaningful praises" (*stutyaṃ stutibhirarthyābhiḥ*), however, the word "praise" (*stuti*) is used figuratively in the sense of the mere description of qualities. Alternatively, in the term "meaningful" (*arthyābhiḥ*), what is intended is the capacity to bring about the fulfillment of the objects of aspiration; this is according to the maxim that "the meaning follows the word. || 32 ||

[This follows the sequence of injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and mantras. Having established the authority of the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) regarding their own meaning—that is, within their own position—within the sequence of explanatory passages and mantra-utterances, he now establishes that for the mantras mentioned immediately thereafter: "Now, the mantras assist the injunction by way of their function of making known what is to be enjoined; for they are indeed capable of assisting it by generating the cognition of the form of the gods and so forth."
How indeed can a body, so distressed, attain the state of a deity? 33.

Now—[they are] those mentioned immediately [after the injunction]; or rather, when the incentive has been provided by the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), they function at the subsequent time of performance. *Manavaḥ* means mantras. By way of their own function, which consists in illumination—that is, through the act of making known the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*), i.e., that which is to be performed—they assist the injunction; that is, they do something for the injunctive sentence. The particle *hi* indicates the acceptance of the opposing view. *Te* refers to those mantras accepted as being illuminators of the meaning of what is to be performed.

"Producing a cognition"—that is, producing a valid knowledge—regarding "the bodies and so forth" of the "denizens of heaven," that is, the gods; "being [so]," meaning while they are first generating it; "this"—referring to the injunction previously mentioned as being generally assisted by the mantra; "to assist"—meaning to do something for it; "sufficiently"—meaning capable; the sense is that they are those who provide assistance to the injunction by causing the production of a valid cognition concerning the bodies and other attributes of the deities. The suffix *śatṛ* (present participle) is used here in the sense of a cause (*hetau*).

The word "khalu" (indeed) expresses that this [point] is difficult to deny. He states this with the words "how indeed? (*kathamiva*). "Vapurvidhurā" means one who is devoid of a body and so forth. "Devatā" refers to that which is the object of praise in mantras and the intended recipient of sacrifices and other rites. "Dhiyam" means memory. "How does she attain it?"—the sense is that it is difficult for one who is without specific attributes to ascend into memory. For the purpose of establishing that mantras reveal the objects to be performed, it is necessary that they possess authority regarding the form and other qualities of the deity as a preliminary means; otherwise, they would be rendered useless.

Therefore, the intention is that there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). This too was stated by the Blessed One [in the passage]: "For a deity devoid of attributes does not enter the intellect" (*na hi nirviśeṣā devatā dhiyam adhirohati*). In the three verses beginning with "paṭutare," the meter is *natkuṭaka*; for it is said: "The *natkuṭaka* consists of *ya*, *ti*, *ni*, *ta*, *na*, *ja*, *bha*, *ja*, *ja*, and *la*. || 33 ||
He further establishes the eligibility of the deities for the knowledge of Brahman by means of another reason:

"Now, observe that within the scope of the Vedic meters, which enumerate the manifold creation of gods, humans, animals, and stationary beings, the embodied forms of the deities are studied most clearly; and perceive their course in the methods of meditative worship. (34)

The word *atha* introduces another argument. Regarding *chandasām*: this refers to the Vedas. *Antabhāge*: in the final portion; that is to say, in specific Vedāntic passages such as the Chāndogya and Subāla Upaniṣads. *Surāḥ*: gods; *narāḥ*: humans; *tiryañcaḥ*: animals such as deer and so forth; *sthāvarāḥ*: immobile beings such as trees and so forth. Of this entire world—the phenomenal universe (*prapañca*)—which has as its essence (*ātman*) those [beings], there is *prajananam*, meaning creation. Within the *gaṇanāsu*, which are treatises consisting of the mental representation of that [creation].

The "forms" (*vigraha*) of the deities—Agni, Indra, and so forth—are their bodies. This term also implies [their] weapons and other attributes. The plural number in "forms" (*vigrahāḥ*) is used because there are different forms corresponding to the different deities, or else it is intended to show that even a single deity is perceived in various ways in different sacrifices. "More manifest" (*prakaṭatara*) means more clearly evident. By this, the "unprecedented" (*apūrva*) postulated by others is excluded. The sense is: since that [unprecedented force] is merely imagined despite being unmentioned in scripture, how can this [manifest form], which is actually mentioned in scripture, be denied? "Studied" (*adhītāḥ*) means understood. Furthermore:

"In the methods of worship"—that is, in the sections concerning worship. "The course"—the manner of establishing the qualification for the deities. "Consider"—that is, reflect; this is an address directed toward the opponent.

In this context—within [the passage] beginning with "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*sadeva somyedam*)—one should observe such statements as: "The three-eyed Puruṣa, the son of Prajāpati; from his mind the moon was born; from his eye the sun was born; from his downward breath the Niṣādas; from his forehead Rudra, born of anger; having become a god, he created the gods; having become a seer, he created the seers, as well as the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Gandharvas," and so forth. Furthermore, one should observe such passages as "Then, on the next day, both the gods and the Asuras... which belong to the section concerning the meditation on Brahman.
This very point has been stated by the Blessed One: "And the possession of a body, senses, and so forth..."

It is heard in all the Upaniṣads, in the sections concerning creation and in the sections concerning meditative worship (*upāsana*), that [the Supreme] is the source of Brahmā and the others. Here and in what follows, the *mālinī* meter is used; for it is said: "This *mālinī* consists of the syllables *na*, *ma*, *ra*, *na*, *ya*, *ya*, and is praised by the world of serpents. (34)

Stating their authority by way of another method as well, he concludes the section on the deities: "The forms and other attributes of the deities are made most clear through hundreds of Vedic sources, through histories, Dharmaśāstras, and Purāṇas."
Thus it has been said that he is qualified for the worship of Ananta; therefore, this host of gods is capable of seeking that fruit.

By "hundreds of *nigamas*"—meaning the numerous Vedic sentences consisting of *mantras* and *arthavādas* of mixed *brāhmaṇas*; by those whose "sources" (*nidāna*) or roots are such [Vedic texts]; by "histories" (*itihāsa*)—such as the venerable *Rāmāyaṇa* and others which set forth ancient events; by "treatises on Dharma" (*dharmaśāstra*)—specific works of beneficial instruction setting forth the conduct of the virtuous as proclaimed by Manu, Yājñavalkya, Viṣṇu, and others; and by "Purāṇas"—such as the jewel among Purāṇas that set forth the primary creation (*sarga*) and so forth.

Furthermore, "the body of the deity" (*devatāvigraha*) and so forth refers to the bodies of Indra and others who are the intended recipients (*uddeśya*) of the sacrifice. "More clearly" means that it is stated—i.e., recited—by way of the relationship between the door and the one who enters the door (*dvāradvāribhāva*), without depending on the avoidance of a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). The sense is that this is not a conceptual construction based on scriptural implication (*śrutyarthāpatti*). Since there is no contradiction with other means of knowledge (*māna*), the logic of the section on contradiction (*virodhādhikaraṇa*) does not apply here. (In this regard, the *Yajñāgṛhārādhyāya* and other such texts should be consulted.)

Since this is so, therefore—this group of immortals (*amaravarga*), consisting of the host of deities beginning with Brahmā, who possess bodies, sense organs, and so forth as established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); who are seekers of that fruit—that is, seekers of liberation and other results arising from the worship performed in the mind; and who are capable—being capable through the possession of Brahminhood and other such qualities mentioned [in texts] such as "Brahmā is Bṛhaspati," or through the awakening of knowledge acquired in another birth due to their erudition, and because they maintain the sacred fires.

Therefore, because it is heard that sovereignty over Indra and others is the fruit of specific ritual acts (*karma*), and because the mastery over them is also heard in the scriptures; because the Mantras and Arthavādas are authoritative with respect to their own literal meaning; because in the Vedāntas, within the sections on creation as well as the sections on meditation (*upāsana*), the body, senses, and so forth are mentioned; because in the Itihāsas and other texts—which are rooted in the scattered Vedic literature—the corporeal forms of the deities and such are established; and because there is an absence of contradiction by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), [one may conclude] through the logic of the "subsidiary apūrva" (*aṅgāpūrva*) regarding the propitiation of the deities...

The meaning is: because there is no application of the logic of the image and the object of the image (*pratimā-pratimeya-nyāya*) by relying on the grace of the Supreme Self, which stands in the place of the *paramāpūrva* (the transcendental result); and because, in another interpretation, by relying on the fact that the Supreme Self alone—possessing the bodies of the successive Indras and others—is the giver of the fruit through the door of grace, there is an absence of the undesirable consequences of the loss of what was done (*kṛta-hāna*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*). "Of this" refers to this class of immortals. "Eligibility for the meditation on the Infinite"—that is, for the meditation on the Blessed Lord who is devoid of the limitations of space, time, and substance—means the right to perform the practice and the ownership of its fruit.
The word "is" (*asti*) is to be supplied.

By the term *amarapada* (the state of the immortals) and the term *anantapada* (the infinite state), it is indicated that although the immortals (*amaras*) endure for a long time and possess superior sovereignty compared to those such as ourselves, nevertheless—because they lack the experience of the unlimited bliss of Brahman—it is indeed appropriate for them to have a longing for that [bliss] and to practice the means to attain it. Furthermore, by the term *vargapada* (the group), both the deities beginning with the Vasus who desire liberation either through mediation or directly, as well as other deities, are intended. Therefore, it should be understood that the non-mention of those desiring liberation [in the previous categories] is intentional.

"In that very section" means "in that very section [of the *Brahmasūtra*]," specifically in the section concerning the deities (*devatādhikaraṇa*). It refers to the sūtra: "If it be said that [the Veda] is mere word, no, because from this [Brahman] they originate, as is known from perception and inference. This is the remainder [of the context]. For in that [section], in order to avoid [the charge] that words such as "Indra" are devoid of meaning, the fact that they denote *ākṛti* (generic form) was established by refuting the view that they are merely conventional designations for specific individuals.

In this regard, since others admit that *ākṛti* (form) exceeds mere *saṃsthāna* (configuration), and because defects are seen in that [position], and because it is possible for configuration alone to be the cause of the inclusive cognition (*anugatapratīti*) and so forth, it is established that configuration itself is *ākṛti* (in other words, the configuration of the parts is the genus). We indeed perceive a common configuration as a pervasive form; we speak of it, and no other [entity] is seen in the alternative view regarding genera. Just as in the case of many cognitions preceded by "cowness," there is a single commonality.
Even such talk as "birth, birth" occurs in this manner on my path. 36.

The word *tu* has the sense of the particle *eva* (only/just), though its position is displaced. "Understand that configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is the form (*ākṛti*)"—that is, understand that configuration itself is the form. The particle *eva* emphasizes what is well-known. The meaning is: accept the genus (*jāti*) as being nothing other than a specific conjunction of parts, which is admitted by both [parties]. Alternatively, the word *tu* indicates a distinction. What is intended is the distinction between configuration—which is established and observed—and the genus accepted by the opponent.

Even if one admits an entity over and above [the configuration], the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is necessary for the purpose of manifestation, and that [configuration] is indeed perceived; since the configuration is both established and observed, the occurrence of a uniform cognition and so forth is accounted for by that alone, and thus the acceptance of a separate universal (*jāti*) is not appropriate—this is the sense. Here, "form" (*ākṛti*) refers to the general property (*sāmānya*). However, in the expression "universal and form" (*jātyākṛti*), "form" refers to the arrangement of parts (*avayavasaṃsthāna*). Therefore, there is no proving of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). The *Bhāṣya* states: "Configuration is the unique form of an object."

In this context, the word "own" (*sva*) refers to the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*). "Form" (*rūpa*) means an inseparably established qualifier (*apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇa*). The term "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) is used so that the generic property of being a substance (*dravyatva*) or the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) of a jar shall not be [mistakenly considered its form]. Being "under discussion" (*prakṛtatva*) means being present in the intellect by virtue of being the object of specific linguistic usage. Cowness is [the form] relative to a cow; brokenness is [the form] relative to a broken [pot]; but relative to a broken cow, it is cowness as qualified by brokenness that constitutes the configuration.

The meaning is that it is precisely such a configuration (*saṃsthāna*) that sustains the universal (*jāti*); therefore, it is not appropriate to accept a separate category called a "universal" as something manifested by that configuration. Now, one might object: "Since the universal 'cowness' (*gotvajāti*) is manifested by configuration, the configuration itself cannot be the universal. This is not so, because the argument does not withstand analysis. Is this said because [the universal] is perceived as distinct from the configuration, or because it must be postulated? It cannot be the first, because apart from the configuration, no entity is perceived in multiple individuals that could be understood through a single uniform cognition.

For a universal (*sāmānya*) is that which is to be understood through a recurring cognition (*anuvṛttapratyaya*). Since it is precisely the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) that is cognized by such a recurring cognition, the second [alternative] is also not tenable; for the linguistic usage [of "universal"] is established by the configuration alone. Indeed, a conceptualizer is established otherwise [than as a distinct entity]. Therefore, there is no universal as a separate category.

This is what [the author] says with the words "First, we perceive that which is common" (*anugataṃ tāvat*), and so forth. "That" (*tat*) refers to the configuration (*saṃsthāna*). We perceive it as common and we speak of it as such; the word "first" (*tāvat*) indicates a sequence of argumentation. For it is on the grounds of the inexplicability of the cognition of commonality otherwise that a universal (*jāti*) would have to be postulated. However, the meaning is that this [universal] is established otherwise through the commonality of configurations. Furthermore, since the opponent exerts great effort in postulating [a universal] even based on perception, that [perception-based argument] is refuted first.

By the word "hi" (for/indeed), the well-known nature of the conformity to configuration is stated. Now, he refutes [the existence of] "vision" with the words "another," etc. The phrase beginning with "by us" means by us, by you, by me, and by others. "Another" refers to an entity called a universal (*jāti*) that is distinct from configuration.
"Nor was it seen" means it has not been observed, nor has it ever been seen.

The word "tathā" (likewise) serves as an illustration for the exclusion of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). The meaning is: "just as there is no conceptual construction, so too there is no [such] perception. On this point, the venerable Vyāsa favored [the following view]: "This possesses a dewlap and so forth; this also possesses a dewlap and so forth; this has the shape of a broad base and belly; this also has the shape of a broad base and belly. Thus, it is observed that only the dewlap and so forth are the objects of recurring cognition and linguistic usage. Nothing distinct from those [particulars] is seen to be the object of recurring cognition and linguistic usage.

Now, one might ask: "How can a distinct configuration (*saṃsthāna*) be the object of a recurring cognition and linguistic usage? To this he says: "In the alternative view," and so forth. "Just as" (*yadvat*): for example. "In the alternative view" (*pakṣāntare*): in the doctrine that there is a separate universal (*jāti*). "In many" (*bahvīṣu*): in infinite [instances]. "Preceded by cowness, horseness, etc. (*gotvāśvatvapurassarīṣu*): in universals such as cowness, horseness, and so on—namely, in the universals accepted by the opponent. "Common" (*sādhāraṇī*): identical. "The cognition 'universal, universal'" (*jātirjātiriti dhiṣaṇā*): the uniform apprehension in the form "universal, universal."

Such a statement is also as follows: even the uniform linguistic usage "genus, genus" occurs in my own path—that is, in the theory that the universal (*jāti*) consists in configuration (*saṃsthāna*). Thus, the meaning is that the cognition of a universal within universals is based on extreme similarity (*sausādṛśya*). Here, the implied sense is that there is both the recurring cognition "cow, cow" and the recurring word [expressing it]. The point is that, just as the cognition and linguistic usage of "universality" as a qualifier occurs with respect to universals, the cognition and linguistic usage of "cowness" as a qualifier is likewise established with respect to cows and so forth. The mention of "universals" is merely illustrative.

Regarding the phrase "even in the case of individuals and so forth": just as the term 'individual' (vyakti) is applied to many individuals even in the absence of a universal 'individualness' (vyaktitva); or just as the term 'fragment' (khaṇḍa) is applied to [specific cows] such as Khaṇḍā even in the absence of a universal 'fragmentness' (khaṇḍatva); and just as for those who maintain that there are ultimate particulars (viśeṣa) in eternal substances, the term 'particular' is applied to those particulars even in the absence of a universal 'particularness' (viśeṣatva)—in the same way, the application of words such as 'cow' is logically justified.

If it is asked, "What indeed is this *sausādṛśya* (perfect similarity)?"—on this point Vyāsapāda says: "Similarity (*sādṛśya*) is a property of the object that is the unique cause for the conventional usage of 'similar. And this is a category of entity that, like brotherhood, is defined by its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and is distinct in each individual instance. Therefore, there is no difficulty regarding the dilemma of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti-vikalpa*) and so forth. They say that *sausādṛśya* is similarity characterized by the fullness of the aforementioned form. And by the venerable Meghanādāri it was stated: "Now, if it is asked what the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the dewlap and so forth is—we reply that it is simply the similarity of configuration (*saṃsthāna-sādṛśya*). || 36 ||

He states these very prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*) and established conclusions (*siddhānta*) in detail through three verses: "Let it be accepted that there is one genus (*jāti*) which is pervasive across many individuals and complete in each individual; and another, which is without beginning or end, [is] based on configuration (*saṃsthāna*)."

If the recurring cognition and the word "cow, cow" do not exist, how could there be linguistic convention, and how could our words for cows and the like apply to individuals that are innumerable? (37)
That which is followed—meaning persisting—through many individuals; in each individual—

In each and every individual (*vyakti*), it exists as something that is not fully delimited by them. It is "without beginning or end"—where "beginning" (*ādi*) means origination and "end" (*nidhana*) means destruction; it is "devoid" (*nir*) of these two. This compound follows the rule *nirādayaḥ krāntādyarthe*. By this, its eternality is stated, characterized by being a non-counter-positive of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) while simultaneously being a non-counter-positive of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*). It is "one" (*ekā*), meaning undifferentiated across all individuals. That which is of such a nature is the "universal" (*jāti*) distinct from configuration (*saṃsthāna*)—that is, a universal that is distinct from the configuration admitted by both [parties].

Let it be established—let it be asserted; let it be postulated through the otherwise inexplicability (*anyathānupapatti*) of the subsequent cognition and so forth that will be mentioned. For an "assertion" (*pratijñā*) is the communication of a subject (*pakṣa*) qualified by the probandum (*sādhya*). The root *sthā* preceded by the prefix *ā-* functions in the sense of an assertion, as it is stated: "The prefix *ā-* [is used] in the sense of an assertion. By this, the definition of a universal (*sāmānya*) is stated: "It is eternal, one, and inherent in many. By the word "complete" (*pūrṇa*), it is stated that the alternative of its non-existence (*vṛtti-vikalpa*) is contradicted by experience (*pratīti-parāhata*).

By the phrase "others [hold that it arises] from configuration," it is stated that since the existence of permanence and other such qualities in configuration is untenable, the acceptance of a *jāti* (universal) distinct from it is necessary. He then states the reason for this with the words "cow, cow," and so forth: "If not"—that is, if the aforementioned *jāti* is not accepted—how could the recurring cognition "cow, cow" and the recurring verbal expression be possible? How could they be logically established?

The meaning is that since the uniform cognition (*anugata-pratīti*) and linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) cannot be accounted for without a uniform property (*anugata-dharma*), such a property is established by those two. Regarding "of words such as 'cow'": this refers to words like *go* (cow). "In the innumerable"—that is, in infinite—individuals (*vyakti*). "For us"—for us who are not all-seeing. "Cognition" (*vyutpatti*) means the apprehension of the word's expressive power (*śaktigraha*). "How"—meaning, how is it possible? The meaning is that a universal (*jāti*) is necessary for the establishment of the apprehension of the word's power through the inclusion of all instances.

By the word "and" (ca), the apprehension of pervasion, the apprehension of the causal relation, the illusion of silver in mother-of-pearl and the like, and the absence of figurative usage of words such as "cow" with respect to primary and subsequent individuals are all included; for all of these cannot be accounted for by means of a non-uniform configuration. || 37 ||
He elaborates the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with two verses:

"Regarding this, we say: Do we not perceive some other entity, distinct [from the individuals], characterized by the possession of a dewlap and so forth, which is the object of the recurring linguistic usage called 'cowness' (*gotva*)? For such an entity was indeed observed. What was said in the doctrine of universals (*jātivāda*) concerning that other entity which is common to many universals—such as cowness, goat-ness, horse-ness, and so on—and which constitutes the basis for the application of words like 'universal' (*jāti*) and the rest? (38)

To this we reply: regarding this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), we state the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). [The universal] is something other than that which possesses a dewlap and so forth; it is distinct from the configuration (*saṃsthāna*). "Dewlap" (*sāsnā*) refers to the throat-flesh; by "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of horns and other features is intended. By this, the configuration is denoted. "Cowness" (*gotva*) is something else entirely, distinct from the configuration—it is established as the ground for the application of the word "cow" (*go*), and it is the object of inclusive usage (*anuvṛttavyavahṛti*), that is, the domain of recurring linguistic convention. This is a word ending in the accusative case.

The object (*vastu*) is that which is fit for connection with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); this is the action (*karma*). "We perceive" (*pratīmaḥ*)—that is, what do we take as the object of perception? The word "what" (*kiṃ*) here is used in a sense of censure: we do not see it; the meaning is that because it is not observed, there is no additional universal (*jāti*). To the objection that [the universal] must be postulated because otherwise linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) would be inexplicable, he replies with the words beginning "taddhi" and so forth.

Its configuration (*saṃsthāna*); "of such a kind" (*tādṛkṣa*) means that which serves as the cause for the application of linguistic usage and so forth through extreme similarity (*sausādṛśya*). "Was seen" (*aikṣi*) means it was perceived. By this, the impossibility of [the opponent's] conceptual construction is stated. The particle *hi* indicates what is well-known. The sense is that even by the opponent, extreme similarity is put forward for the sake of manifestation (*vyañjakatva*).

The apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth is easily accomplished through a configuration (*saṃsthāna*) qualified by extreme similarity (*sausādṛśya*). Furthermore, the arising of error is easily brought about when there is the perception of a non-contradictory configuration, while its cessation is easily brought about by the perception of a contradictory configuration. A mere trace of similarity brings about figurative usage (*gauṇatā*), whereas extreme similarity brings about primary usage (*mukhyatā*). Therefore, the meaning is that since [the required functions] are accounted for by a configuration qualified by extreme similarity, there is no need to postulate anything further.

On this point, the venerable Vyāsa states: "The etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of a certain word for a specific meaning must be accepted according to observation as the cause for the application of that very same word to a meaning closely resembling it. Rather than postulating an unperceived alternative meaning and attempting to avoid defects such as the dilemma of semantic function (*vṛttivikalpa*) by taking recourse to mere conventional understanding, objections and their resolutions are more appropriately established through the force of perception regarding the actually observed object, in accordance with the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*)."

"In this context, the object perceived is the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) characterized by similarity (*sausādṛśya*); for here, it is possible to include all [individuals] through the configuration as a form unified by similarity," so it is stated in the *Bhāvaprakāśikā*. Also, in the *Mahābhāṣya*, in the *Pratyāhāra-āhnika*: "This is established on account of the commonality of form (*rūpasāmānyāt*); for example: 'We are wearing those very same garments'; 'We are eating those very same rice-grains'; 'That which is in Madhurā and that which is among the Magadhas is the very same *kārṣāpaṇa* coin of yours.'"

It has been stated that when something is perceived in Mathurā and then again in another place, due to the similarity of form (*rūpasāmānya*), the thought arises, "This is that very same thing. Kaiyaṭa also maintains that even when referring to individuals (*vyakti*), there exists a conventional usage of non-difference—just as in common worldly practice—provided there is no consideration of their distinction; thus his desired conclusion is established. Furthermore, he states that whether a universal (*sāmānya*) exists as distinct from the individual or not, in any case, the linguistic usage in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) follows that of the world.

It has been stated that even in the case of the word *kaustubha*, the vowel *u* uttered here brings to mind six highly similar individual instances through the relation known as similarity (*sādṛśya*). Therefore, it is universally accepted that similarity possesses the capacity to subsume other individuals and functions in the same manner as a universal (*sāmānya*). With this in mind, it was said: "For he perceived that which is like that."

Anticipating the objection—“How can a specific configuration (*saṃsthāna*), which is itself excluded [from others], be the determinant for the uniform usage [of a term] and so forth?”—the author states, “In the case of cowness, non-cowness, horseness, and so forth,” with the intention of offering this resolution: just as in the theory of a separate universal (*jāti*), the usage of the term ‘universal’ regarding various universals is explained by means of extreme similarity (*sausādṛśya*) even in the absence of a further universal within those universals; likewise, in the theory of a universal consisting of configuration, it is explained by means of the extreme similarity of configurations. [The phrase] “in the many universals such as cowness” refers to the universals of cowness and the like.

"Anugataṃ" means present. "Ekaṃ sādhāraṇam" means that which constitutes the linguistic usage of words such as "genus" (jāti) and so forth—that is, the cause for the application of terms like "genus. "Aparaṃ vastu" refers to an entity consisting of another genus, or an entity distinct from similarity (sausādṛśya), [which would be required] in the theory of genus—that is, in the position that genus is a separate entity. "Ūce kim? means "What was accepted? The word "kim" here has a dismissive sense; the meaning is: "Certainly nothing was accepted. And thus, the implication is that just as in that case, the derivation of words such as "cow" is also established through similarity alone. || 38 ||

Since the occurrence of linguistic usage cannot be explained otherwise by the non-perception of anything else, and since it is impossible for [the universal] to be postulated [as a distinct entity], the word for "genus" (*jāti*) and so forth is appropriately based on the conventional consensus established by both parties; for here, that [similarity] which is mutually very close is what constitutes the underlying continuous cognition.
It manifests the very form of the doctrines of other systems in such a way that it is indeed worthy of being understood through etymological derivation. || 39 ||

"Of another"—that is, of that which is called "genus" (jāti), distinct from "configuration" (saṃsthāna). By the phrase "due to non-perception," it is stated that there is no perception of it. He rejects the [theoretical] postulation with the words "in practical usage. "Of the formation of practical usage" means of the conformity to worldly transaction. "By being established otherwise" means by being established precisely through the similarity of configuration admitted by both parties. The meaning is: "by that impossibility of being postulated as well. That is to say, because of the absence of perception and because of the impossibility of being inferred.

The term "words such as genus" (*jātyādiśabda*) refers to words such as "cow" (*gavādiśabda*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), words such as "white" (*śuklādi*) are included. For it has been stated that configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is common to both genus and non-genus. The phrase "consistent with the convention of both [parties]" means that it is logical—that is, appropriate—as it provides a unifying factor based on a highly similar configuration accepted by the two positions: the position asserting a genus consisting of configuration and the position asserting a genus distinct from configuration. The compound *jātyādīnāṃ śabdaḥ* is a genitive *tatpuruṣa*; hence, the result is the inclusion of words such as "cow."

"Here," and so forth—here, in the doctrine that [universals] are configurations (*saṃsthāna*). "Mutually" means one another. "Highly similar" means possessing extreme similarity. "Configuration" refers to *saṃsthāna*. "Capable of producing the acquisition of the power for subsequent cognition, linguistic usage, and conceptualization" means precisely fit for generating the grasping of the capacity for inclusive awareness, conventional practice, and the development of linguistic expression. The word "becomes" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The particle "hi" indicates what is well-known. "Of such a kind" refers to the configuration characterized by that extreme similarity; it is the agent. "The form accepted in other systems" refers to the universal (*jāti*) as distinct from the configuration.

"It manifests" (*vyanakti*) means "it makes manifest" (*vyañjayati*). The connection with the preceding clause is that such a configuration is fit for the development of a continuous cognition and verbal expression. The meaning is that, just as in the opponent's view a configuration characterized by extreme similarity serves to manifest a universal (*jāti*), in our own position it is possible for it to be the cause of a recurring cognition and so forth.

For even opponents must admit that the specific configuration (*saṃsthāna*), which consists of a particular conjunction of very similar parts, is the manifester of a genus (*jāti*). As it was stated by the venerable Meghanādāri: "Even on the view that [the genus] is manifested, this same solution applies. When it is asked, 'Why is the cowness (*gotva*) and so forth not manifested in a *gavaya* and the like?', and the answer is given, 'Because of the absence of manifesting parts there'; and when it is further asked, 'How is there an absence of those manifesting parts there?', the only possible answer would be, 'Because of the absence of very similar parts.'"

The experts have stated that "jāti" (universal) is the apprehension of form, meaning it is manifested by a common configuration (*saṃsthāna*). Therefore, the point is that just as a configuration qualified by similarity (*sādṛśya*) manifests a universal, it is also possible for it to account for the occurrence of a recurring cognition (*anugatapratīti*) and so forth. Whether similarity is included within or excluded from the established categories of entities may be debated; however, the essential point is that since the phenomenon can be explained by means of similarity—which is already established—postulating an additional category called "jāti" is refuted by the principle of ontological parsimony (*gaurava*).

In our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*), however, similarity (*sādṛśya*) is not a distinct category. It is a non-substance (*adravya*), for it has been stated that there are exactly ten [qualities], due to the distinctions among the constituents *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, as well as sound, touch, form, taste, smell, conjunction, and power (*śakti*). Meghanādāri Sūri, however, stated that power, number, and similarity are included within the qualities (*guṇa*). Likewise, he stated that power, similarity, dimension (*parimāṇa*), separateness (*pṛthaktva*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), disjunction (*vibhāga*), priority (*paratva*), posteriority (*aparatva*), the relation between substratum and superstratum (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*), and so forth, are qualities common to both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*).

Even in the position that similarity (*sādṛśya*) consists in the possession of many common properties belonging to those two [objects], there is the burden of having to accept a distinct entity called a "universal" (*jāti*), which is something over and above those numerous similar properties and is manifested by them. For us, however, there is parsimony (*lāghava*), because we rely on the establishment of inclusive linguistic usage (*anugatavyavahāra*) through those very properties alone.

In the other view, the resolution of the threefold dilemma regarding the mode of subsistence—namely, that similarity resides in the properties, the manifesting capacity resides in the similar parts, and the universal resides in the individuals—is sought solely by taking recourse to perception (*pratīti*).

In our view, however, there is simplicity (*lāghava*) because the resolution of the dilemma regarding the mode of subsistence (*vṛttivikalpa*) and so forth relies solely on two things: similarity (*sādṛśya*) in the properties residing therein, and the capacity to serve as the basis for the inclusive linguistic usage (*anugatavyavahāra*) with respect to the similar parts. This is true even in the position that similarity is a quality (*guṇa*); for the resolution of that [dilemma] relies, by the force of perception, on only two things: similarity in the parts, and the capacity to serve as the basis for the inclusive cognition with respect to the similar parts. Thus, simplicity indeed exists.

Although similarity is excluded from each individual instance, nevertheless, even though it is thus excluded, its capacity to serve as the cause for a recurring cognition is established by its very nature; just as, according to the opposing view, excluded individuals possess the capacity to manifest an inclusive genus (*jāti*), so it is here. As it has been said: "Because there is no perception of a genus, certain configurations (*saṃsthāna*) themselves have the nature of manifesting 'cowness' and so forth," or rather, that their nature is such.
Thus, in this case as well, the non-perception of cowness and so forth in a *gavaya* and the like due to its configuration is simply due to its own nature. || 39 ||

In the commentary on the first sūtra, two points are stated in the sentence: "Therefore, perception has as its object only that which is qualified by distinctions characterized by the configuration, form, genus, and so forth of things"; namely, that "the genus is the configuration and form of things," and that "the genus itself is the distinction. Therein, the point that the genus is indeed the configuration is established by the commentary beginning with "of that which is distinct from configuration" (*saṃsthānātirekiṇaḥ*). And the point that the genus itself is the distinction is established by the commentary beginning with "because the conventional usage 'it is different' is possible through the very apprehension of the genus" (*jātigrahaṇenaiva bhinna iti vyavahārasaṃbhavāt*).

In this regard, even by the opponent who accepts difference as distinct from "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth, it must be admitted that when there is the absence of an absence, a positive entity (*bhāva*) independent of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) itself possesses the status of an absence dependent upon that counter-correlate; otherwise, there would be an infinite regress and because such an absence is not perceived. Similarly, it has been stated that difference (*bheda*) can likewise consist of a positive entity independent of a counter-correlate, such as "cowness.
