By the same logic, it is intended here that even relative non-existence (*saṃsargābhāva*) is of the nature of a positive entity.
This very point is stated in two verses in connection with the investigation of configuration (*saṃsthāna*) and genus (*jāti*):
Indeed, according to the view of others, the non-existence of a non-entity is itself an entity;
tell me then, is the non-existence of a jar and such things not likewise an entity?
For the destruction of a jar is its state as potsherds, while its prior non-existence is its state as a lump of clay—is any other [non-existence] perceived here at all? (40)

"Of non-existence," and so forth. According to the "opponent's view"—that is, the view of the Naiyāyikas and others—the non-existence of non-existence (the non-existence of the absence of a jar) is indeed accepted as being an existence, namely, having the nature of the jar which is a positive entity (*bhāva*). The implication is that otherwise there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and because it would not be perceived. In this way—just as the non-existence of the non-existence of a jar has the jar as its essence—why would even the non-existence of a jar and the like not be an existence? That is to say, why would it not be an existence characterized by the specific form of the ground, color, and so forth? It certainly is; such is the meaning.

The point is this: the argument that it is logically inconsistent for an absence—which is dependent upon a counter-positive (pratiyogin)—to be of the nature of an existence that is independent of a counter-positive, must be used by him as the reason for postulating an absence distinct [from existence]. However, that argument has already been refuted by him when he asserts that the absence of the absence of a jar is identical with the jar itself. Thus, due to the lack of any such supporting evidence (*kalpaka*), there is no justification for postulating a distinct absence. Regarding the phrase "of the jar," etc.: because of his acceptance of the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), the destruction of a jar consists in its state as potsherds. The other type of absence is the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the jar.

It has the nature of being in a state of massed unity (*piṇḍatva*). The word "for" (*hi*) indicates what is well-known. He [the opponent] accepts that the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of a jar have the nature of the jar at the time when the jar exists. Likewise, he accepts that the prior non-existence of the destruction of a jar has the nature of the jar at the time when the jar exists. Therefore, the point is that it is logically established that even destruction and prior non-existence are positive entities (*bhāvarūpa*). To the objection that they are thus established by the force of perception, he says: "What else is seen here?"

"Here"—that is, in the case of the ground, a potsherd, or a lump of clay—"something else"—an entity consisting of a relational absence (saṃsargābhāva) distinct from the specific features such as the form of the ground—is "seen"? What is meant is: has it been seen? It has not been seen. Thus, the sense is that since neither perception nor non-perception applies, there is no proof for an absence that is a separate entity. || 40 ||

An objection is raised: "If the absence of a jar were identical with the nature of the ground and its color and so forth, then at the time when the jar is present, since there is no destruction or departure of the ground’s color, the cognition of that absence should still occur. Anticipating this, [the author] replies: Even on the theory of an additional (independent) absence (*atiriktābhāvavāda*), since that absence is eternal and inactive, there would likewise be no destruction or departure, and thus the cognition of absence should occur. If you maintain that the non-apprehension [of the absence] at that time is due to the lack of the relation of "qualifier-ness" (*viśeṣaṇatā*) belonging to the absence in respect to the ground as delimited by the time of the jar's existence, then we reply: in that case, since you admit that the color and other qualities of the ground as delimited by that [jar's] time are not of the nature of the absence of the jar, there is no inconsistency. Thus he says:

The wise here understand non-existence as merely the absence of conjunction; however, those who consider existence itself to be non-existence maintain that non-existence is the distinction between the ground and other parts of the earth,
such as the courtyard of a house, which is delimited by specific times.
Others have considered that [the jar] to be the locus for the absence of the jar; but where, in this case, is there the perception of anything additional? || 41 ||

Wise men, regarding non-existence itself as a positive entity, determine that the absence of a jar—consisting precisely of the form of the ground and other factors admitted by both parties—is established by valid means of cognition; these are our own teachers, endowed with correct wisdom dependent upon the grace of the Supreme Person. Here, in response to the objection that if non-existence were of the nature of the ground and its qualities, then the absence of the jar would be perceived even at the time when the jar is present—they accept *saṃsargābhāva* (relational non-existence) as characterized by the manner about to be described.

The word *tu* indicates a disparity consisting of [the former being] established and [the latter being] merely perceived. By the particle *eva*, the "half-old-woman" (*ardhajaratīya*) compromise accepted by the opponent—that among absences some possess the nature of existence while others possess the nature of non-existence—is excluded. To the question "In what manner will this be explained?", he says: "Like a jar, on the ground" (*kumbhavaddhūtale*). [This refers to] the distinction of a particular portion of earth, such as the ground serving as the locus for a jar, which is a specific quality residing in that other [ordinary] ground. The word *tu* has the sense of *eva*. "Absence" means the absence of the jar.

The meaning is that the absence of a jar consists of the nature of the ground and so forth, which is distinct from the ground that serves as the locus for the jar. Here, the author provides an illustration of the opposing view with the words "yaḥ" and so on. "By others"—namely, by those who maintain that absence is a separate entity (*atiriktābhāvavādibhiḥ*). "That which," delimited (*vyatikarita*)—that is, restricted—by the specific time that is not the locus of the jar (*tattatkālabhedena*), namely the particular time when the jar is absent; this refers to a location such as the courtyard of a house, where "courtyard" (*aṅgaṇam*) means a quadrangle.

The locus of the absence of the jar (*kumbhābhāvāśraya*) is accepted as the substratum of the absence of the jar; the sense is that it is the very surface of the ground delimited by a time that is not the locus of the jar which is admitted to be the relation (*saṃsarga*) for the absence of the jar. "That" refers precisely to that place and time, such as the courtyard of a house, delimited by a time that is not the locus of the jar. "For us" (*naḥ*) means in our [view]. "Here" (*iha*) means in the location of the absence; the words "it exists" (*bhavati*) are to be supplied. In the reading *sa hi sa na*, "that indeed" (*sa hi*) refers to the location; "for us" (*naḥ*) means in our opinion.

That—meaning the absence of a jar. The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates firmness [of the position]. The meaning is that for us, the color and other qualities existing in that very place constitute the absence of the jar. Where is there the perception of an "adhika"—that is, an additional or distinct absence? The sense is: nowhere at all. This is because, in the Prābhākara school's view, the locus itself is accepted as the absence; therefore, the cognition of a container-and-contained relationship in the form "there is no jar on the ground" is considered an error.

However, since we admit that the nature of the earth’s surface and so forth consists of color and other qualities even in the absence of a jar, it should be understood that the cognition of those [qualities] possesses validity (*prāmāṇya*). The term "other portion of the earth" refers to that which exists on other parts of the earth; and the word "that" refers to what exists therein—this is understood from the preceding context as referring to the state of being potsherds (*kapālatva*) and the state of being a lump of clay (*piṇḍatva*). In that regard, the intention is that the cognitions "the jar has been destroyed in this potsherd" and "the jar will exist in this lump of clay" possess validity. || 41 ||

It is established in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* that words denoting a genus (*jāti*) or a quality (*guṇa*) denote the individual (*vyakti*) and the substratum of the quality (*guṇin*) as their ultimate referents. However, the view that [words] possess power (*śakti*) directed solely toward the genus and so forth is not rooted in the Sūtras; rather, it was stated by later commentators. In this context, the following Sūtras—*avasthiter iti kāśakṛtsnaḥ*, *aṃśo nānāvyapadeśāt*, *carācaravyapāśrayastu*, and others—are intended to demonstrate that words denoting bodies fall within the scope of the principle established in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*.

In such passages as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) and "All this, indeed, is Brahman" (*sarvaṃ khalvidaṃ brahma*), the state of being qualified by both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*) is understood from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). This follows the logic established in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* (the section on generic form), which is evoked by such texts as "The portion [of the Lord] resides in the moving and the unmoving... because of the various designations" (*aṃśo nānāvyapadeśāt*). In that context, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the identity of the single reality qualified by two states is expressed by the use of the same case-ending (*samānavibhakti*), according to the principle of the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*. Here, in the preceding verses, the meaning of the word "generic form" (*ākṛti*) has been defined.

In this verse, it is stated that the principle of the *ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* applies to words denoting bodies, based on the sūtra beginning with "carācara" (*carācaravyapadeśāt*). In the three subsequent verses, it is stated that according to the logic of the *aruṇādhikaraṇa*, the unity of the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavastvaikya*) is the meaning of grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). (The phrase "based on the sūtras beginning with 'nānā' and 'avasthiteḥ'" is to be supplied to complete the sense.)

Having created [the world] as "Truth" (satya) and "Thatness" (tyat), You enter into both the conscious and the unconscious; therefore You are called the "All" (viśva), because the universe is born from You and dissolves into You, and thus the entirety of it is indeed Your body.
By these various scriptures, which expand the heart's core through the discourse of non-difference, [all distinctions] are cast aside.
O Blessed One, those who postulate a cause [of the world] based on the delusion of difference and non-difference as being non-distinct [from it]. || 42 ||

"O Blessed One"—the Perfectly Awakened One is addressed as the "mine of faultless and auspicious qualities" and the "Supreme Person. Previously, the statement was made by means of a recollection of Brahmā; here, the statement is made by means of an address to the Blessed One. Thus, the purpose of the Smṛti rule—"having looked at their faces, one should look at the sun"—is fulfilled here. By the phrase "by Acyuta-bhānu," his solar nature is expressed, which is manifested here through his being the adversary of the faults denoted by the word "Blessed One."

Here, the meanings of the syllable *bha*—such as being the sustainer (*bhartṛ*) and the creator (*sraṣṭṛ*)—are also intended. "The conscious and the unconscious" refers to sentient beings and the modifications of primordial nature (*prakṛti*). "Having created" means having brought them forth. "You enter" means you penetrate them. The meaning of such scriptural passages as, "Having created that, he entered into it," and "Having entered by means of this living self, let me evolve names and forms," is intended here. "By that" means by entering into the conscious and unconscious entities created by yourself.

"You are the Real and the True, thus you are called the Universe"—by such passages as "It became the Real and the True," "That heat (tejas) reflected, it became those waters," and "From that you are everything," you have been made known as the Universe; the meaning is that you are designated by words denoting the universe because you possess the universe as your body.

It has been stated that the phrase "Truth became That" means that [Brahman] became that which is denoted by those respective words. However, since the manifestation of name and form (*nāmarūpa-vyākaraṇa*) is not possible for one who has not entered [into them], as in the case of a father [entering his son], the manifestation of the body occurs through entry, in order to establish that these two extend as far as oneself. In this context, the extension of name as far as oneself consists in its generating a cognition whose primary qualificand is oneself; whereas that of form...

The meaning established by implication is "the state of being a non-separately existing attribute" (*svāpṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇatvam*). This is also stated explicitly [in scripture]: "Having entered that, He became the existent (*sat*) and the non-existent (*tyat*). This is what was meant by the statement: "And by Him you are called the universe. The word *ca* has the sense of "and"; it is to be construed with the word "His" (*tasya*). In the passage "A part, manifold," the state of sentient and insentient beings being non-separately existing attributes of Brahman—by virtue of being His body—is determined.

In the passage beginning with "resting upon the moving and the unmoving," it was determined that words understood in the world as referring exclusively to sentient and insentient things actually have as their ultimate referent Brahman, which is of that same nature. Therefore, there is neither metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) nor any other distinct power (*śakti*); this has been stated here. The meaning of the Śruti text "All this, indeed... is now expressed by the words beginning with "because it is born from You" (*tvajjatvāt*).

Regarding the passage, "All this is indeed Brahman, from which it is born, into which it dissolves, and in which it breathes; therefore, one should be tranquil," the meaning here is as follows: the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that all this is indeed Brahman, from which it is born (*ja*), into which it dissolves (*la*), and in which it breathes (*an*). The suffix *ḍa* is applied in both cases according to the rule "it is seen [to be applied] after other roots as well. However, in the word *ana*, the suffix *vic* is applied to the root *ana* (meaning "to breathe"). Furthermore, the compound *jalān* is formed like the words *nimna* (low) and *unnata* (high). Since the three case endings are intended to be expressed in accordance with such scriptural passages as "from which these [beings arise]," and since those three cannot coexist in a single word, [the suffixes are applied accordingly].

The compound is formed with the genitive of remainder (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), meaning "of water. "Anana" means living; here, entry into the interior is intended, as it is said, "the Ruler has entered within. Because it is born from that, because it is dissolved into that, and because it breathes through that, all this is indeed Brahman—indeed, Brahman has the entire universe as its body; or rather, the entire universe is indeed the body of Brahman. This very point is expressed here by the address to the Blessed One.

"Because of being born from you" (*tvajjatvāt*) means because of having originated from you (*tvatta utpannatvāt*). In the word *tvad*, the ablative case is either used separately (*vyastā*) or as part of a compound (*samastā*). Regarding "because of being dissolved in you" (*tvallatvāt*): it is called *li* because it dissolves (*līyate*). From the root *lī* with the *kvip* suffix in the sense of an agent, there is a shortening of the vowel according to the rule *hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya*. Thus, *li* ends in a short vowel. The word *ana* means "that which breathes" (*anitīti*); the suffix *ac* is applied because the group beginning with *pacādi* is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*). *Li* and *ana* form a compound like *khañjakubja* (the hunchbacked lame man). The full expression is *tvallyana* (dissolved in you and [yet] breathing), which forms a genitive-possessive compound (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*).

The meaning is: because it possesses the dissolution within you (*tvatsandhilayavattvāt*), and because it does not possess a connection other than yours (*tvatsambandhyananavatvāt*). Here, "connection" refers respectively to being the locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) and being the cause (*hetutva*). Regarding the phrase "as 'you'": "the whole is you" means either that you are the one who has the whole as your body (*nikhilaśarīraka*), or that the whole is your body (*nikhilaṃ tvaccharīram*), or else that everything is your body; the word *ca* (and) here has the sense of *vā* (or). The word *kila* is an explanation of the word *khalu* found in the scripture: "Indeed, the whole is Brahman. (*sarvaṃ brahma khalu*)

In this interpretation, the word "all" (*sarva*) extends up to the embodied beings (*śarīrin*). Here, the referent of the word "That" (*tat*) in the phrase "from which [it] comes, into which it dissolves" (*tajjalān*) is Brahman as qualified by the subtle sentient and insentient principles, being endowed with origination and dissolution. However, the distinction is that when not so endowed, it is Brahman as possessing the attribute of Brahmanhood (*brahmatva*). Indeed, all is Brahman; the entire world is indeed non-different from Brahman (*apṛthaksiddha*). In this interpretation, the word "all" is an abstracting term denoting the world alone, while the word "Brahman" is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) for the body of Brahman.

This entire two-yojana expanse, as well as "you," is indeed said to be your body; thus, the meaning of the two words "iti" (thus) is that they connect non-differently in the heart through the practice of non-difference. Those who expand upon this intent behind the non-dual designations of the individual soul and Brahman, as well as the insentient and Brahman, in the Vedāntas—

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) here is as follows: [these views] have been refuted by those authors of the treatises consisting of the beneficial instruction (*hitānuśāsana*) known as the eternal, faultless, and non-human Vedāntas—namely, by means of those various scriptures in the form of constituent Śruti texts such as "whose body is the Self" and "whose body is the earth," as well as by those such as "having entered that, He became both the existent (*sat*) and the non-existent (*tyat*"), which establish that Brahman is denoted by all words because It is the body of all.

"Difference and non-difference" refers to the difference and non-difference between the world and Brahman. "Non-difference" refers to the non-difference between the world and Brahman, as well as the delusion of manifoldness within Brahman and the superimposition of forms that do not belong to It. "The cause" refers to the reason for the designation of non-difference. By the word "also," those who maintain that there is mere difference between the world and Brahman—apart from the relationship of the mode and the possessor of the mode—and who claim that the scriptural texts on non-difference signify a master-servant relationship (like "the king is the kingdom"), are intended to be refuted. "Refuted" means they have been rejected by the Scripture itself.

Here, by the terms "difference and non-difference" (*bhedābheda*), Bhāskara and Yādava—the proponents of difference and non-difference based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika*) and inherent nature (*svābhāvika*)—are intended. By "non-difference as an error," Śaṅkara is intended. By the word "also" (*api*), the Vaiśeṣikas and others are intended. Regarding the position of difference and non-difference based on limiting adjuncts, it is contradictory for the Lord—who is untouched by afflictions, karma, and so forth—to have identity with those [individual souls] who are subject to them; for since difference exists just as non-difference does, there can be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), as in the case of a "lame" and a "hornless" animal. This is the refutation.

In the doctrine of natural difference-and-non-difference (*svābhāvikabhedābheda*), defects would be as inherent as qualities; for since the three—the object of enjoyment, the enjoyer, and the controller—are all admitted to be parts of Brahman, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the non-sentient and the individual soul, between the non-sentient and the Lord, and between the individual soul and the Lord would be untenable, like the expression "the pot is the bowl. This is the refutation. In Śaṅkara’s position, neither the connection of the self-luminous Brahman with defects nor the delusion rooted therein is possible; furthermore, coreferentiality would be purposeless.

Because the essential nature [of the object] is already understood by a single word; and because it would be contradictory, as that [sentence] is intended to convey the possession of two attributes understood from two words. Furthermore, if its purpose were sublation (*bādha*), there would be the fault that both words would have to employ *lakṣaṇā* (indirect indication)—one for their own essential form and one for the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*). Moreover, since the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "error" (*bhrama*) implies that it is based on the superimposition of a form that does not belong to it, there is the further fault of the sentence becoming invalid (*aprāmāṇya*).

In the systems of the Vaiśeṣikas and others, the non-primary nature of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is evident. A common defect in these four [schools] is their postulation of an intention that contradicts the intended meaning of the coreferentiality found in the revealed scripture (*śruti*). Furthermore, the intention of the scriptural texts regarding non-duality has already been demonstrated. || 42 ||
Now, regarding the incidental section on *aruṇā* (the red cow), wishing to explain that *aruṇādhikaraṇa*, [the author] restates the method of exposition proposed by others:

"In the *aruṇādhikaraṇa*, the Guru has indeed not taught that the connection with redness (*āruṇya*) to the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) is expressed directly by the word; rather, it is established through implication (*ākṣepataḥ*)."

When one says "aruṇayā" (with the red one), the words situated in the sentence—ending in case-terminations denoting grammatical relations and mutually connected—are not merely expressive of a quality, but rather function like the mention of a substance. (43)

"When there is a single purpose, there is a restriction [of the substance] because of the unity of action between the substance and the quality"—this is a sūtra from the Pūrvamīmāṃsā (the "Earlier Section"). The followers of the *Adhvaramīmāṃsā* have provided the following explanation of it: according to the principle of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*, words that denote things qualified by universals (*jāti*), qualities (*guṇa*), and so forth, possess the power to denote those qualifiers, such as the universal; however, in a sentence where a substance has already been introduced, words such as "blue" denote the quality alone. When no substance is mentioned, the substance is understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as in the injunction: "One should sacrifice a white [animal]."

In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is as follows: the word *aruṇayā* ("with the red one") has the power to denote redness (*āruṇya*). Although this redness is capable [of connection], it does not connect with the substance because it is not [conventionally] understood (*avyutpannatvāt*), since factors of action (*kārakas*) connect only with an action. Even if it were understood, it would not connect with the action because, being formless (*amūrta*), it is incapable [of performing an action]. Therefore, being thus isolated, it [connects] through a sentence—constructed by context (*prakaraṇa*) consisting of parts established by direct statement (*śruti*) and inference (*anumita*)—in the form: "One should effect the delimitation of the substance that serves as the means for the transcendental result (*apūrva*) under discussion by means of the red one. Thus, it is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of all substances within the context.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: the cognition of compatibility (*yogyatājñāna*) is not the cause of verbal comprehension; rather, it is merely that the ascertainment of incompatibility (*ayogyatāniścaya*) acts as an obstacle. Therefore, since the absence of such an obstacle exists, the connection of "redness" (*āruṇya*) with the action is logically possible. Subsequently, when one searches for compatibility between those two, the understanding of the connection of redness with the substance [the cow] arises later; thus, there is a restriction regarding its connection with the one-year-old heifer (*ekahāyanī*). He states this very conclusion with the words "unnītam" (it is inferred), meaning "because" (*yat* = *yasmāt*).

Like the indication of a substance (*dravyanirdeśa*), it resides in a sentence—that is, it is situated within a sentence where a single-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) is mentioned as the substance. The word "with the red one" (*aruṇayā*)—that is, the term *aruṇayā*—denotes a mere quality; by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), rather than by denoting a substance, it expresses redness alone through its primary power (*śakti*). However, words ending in case-inflections (*kārakavibhaktyanta*)—that is, words ending in case-suffixes—are not mutually connected; they are incapable of mutual syntactic relation because they lack connection with a verb. This is the ellipsis to be supplied, for there is a rule that case-factors (*kāraka*) must necessarily connect with an action.

Therefore, the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) is [the referent] through denotation—that is, through the word itself. It did not, however, attain connection with *āruṇya* (redness) directly; rather, it attained its subsequent connection with redness through implication (*ākṣepataḥ*). This is because, since that which is formless cannot logically be a means of purchase, or because that which is undifferentiated cannot logically be a means of purchase, it is inferred by means of reasoning (*nyāya*)—namely, the principle that "a quality requires a substance and a substance requires a quality. Thus, since there is a simultaneous connection between the two—*aruṇayā* (by means of the red one) and *ekahāyanyā* (with the one-year-old cow)—there is no application of the "principle of the obstruction of qualities" (*guṇāvarodha-nyāya*); this is what was inferred or envisioned by the Guru in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*. || 43 ||
Refuting this [position], he praises his own intended interpretation which is about to be stated:
"The path of the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa* was correctly established by the venerable sage Rāmānuja."
In an assembly of the learned, what is appropriate becomes clear as well as what is inappropriate. || 44 ||

The path of the Aruṇādhikaraṇa established by the venerable sage Rāmānuja—the method of the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) and the final conclusion (siddhānta) regarding that section—has been considered; this [latter] is appropriate and logical, while the other previously mentioned is inappropriate and illogical. This shall become clear in due course, manifesting as "appropriate" and "inappropriate" in the assembly of the learned—that is, in the gathering of authoritative scholars.

The intention of one who says that this [position] is "inappropriate" (*anucita*) is as follows: For those who maintain that a word denoting a quality within a sentence containing a substance already acquired refers only to the quality, it is contradictory to claim—on the basis of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) involving a split of the sentence—that the word *aruṇā* refers only to redness. Furthermore, if it were to refer only to the quality, there would be the consequence of it being masculine, according to the rule "words for qualities such as white are masculine. Therefore, the prima facie view is untenable. The final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is also untenable.

(Furthermore, because verbal cognition does not arise when one perceives that something is inherently unfit [to be an instrument], moreover, it is impossible to enjoin multiple factors simultaneously by way of restating a purchase already established by the sentence "he buys with ten. Nor should it be argued that this sentence aims at the conjunction of those purchases, for it is more appropriate to regard it as an injunction. Moreover, if redness (*āruṇya*) were also an instrument, there would be a contradiction with the restatement "with ten. If, however, it were intended merely to refer to the substance, it would be inconsistent.)

Precisely because the distinction between purchase [and other acts] lacks scriptural authority, it is also difficult to maintain that redness (aruṇya) is restricted to its connection with the one-year-old cow (ekahāyanī) by virtue of being the means for accomplishing a heterogeneous sequence of actions. Since in cases such as "to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa," even that which ends in a case-ending denoting a kāraka is accepted as connecting with the substance, it is appropriate here as well. || 44 ||

He states his own preferred method: "Even when a substance has been acquired, through the disappearance of a dissimilar case-ending, its distinction indeed transforms according to the nature [of the word], following the principle of *ākṛti* (form)."

The case-ending, being identical for both words, declares the identity of their referents; that threefold ending would likewise indicate the connection with number and the cognition of the kāraka. (45)

The meaning is as follows: in the view of the opponent (*paramata*), regarding such injunctions as "one should sacrifice a white [animal]," it is stated that a word expressing a quality (*guṇa*) extends to include the substance possessing that quality (*guṇin*). In cases such as "the whiteness of the cloth," it is accepted that the word functions as an exception (*apavādaka*) to that rule by virtue of being situated in a sentence containing a substance already mentioned. Furthermore, as an exception even to that, in cases such as "the cloth is white," grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is stated; thus, three distinct grounds for application (*prayojaka*) are postulated. In our own position (*asmatpakṣe*), however, in usages such as "one should sacrifice a white [animal]" or "the cloth is white," the sole ground for a word expressing a quality extending to the substance possessing it is simply the fact that it denotes a property that is non-separately established (*apṛthaksiddha*).

In cases such as "the cloth is white," the use of non-identical case-endings (*asamānavibhakti-nirdeśa*) serves as an exception [to the rule that the qualifier and the qualified must share the same case], and thus there are two motivating factors; this constitutes parsimony (*lāghava*). Consequently, in our view, both in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the word *aruṇā* (red) extends its denotation up to the substance (*dravya*).

Thus, here is the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position: the word *aruṇā* (red) extends only as far as the substance, according to the principle of the section on generic form (*ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*). Even so, the connection of *aruṇayā* (by means of the red one) with *ekahāyanī* (the one-year-old cow) is not possible. For that [connection] must be stated either directly or by way of a connection with the act of purchase (*kraya*). In this regard, there is no direct connection, because it would contradict its status as having a case-ending denoting a factor of action (*kāraka-vibhakti*); for factors of action are invariably connected with an action. Nor is there a connection by way of the act of purchase;

Because there would result a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) if both the substance *aruṇā* (red) and the substance *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow) were enjoined by restating the already-established purchase; and because, due to the absence of a word such as *ca* ("and"), there is no possibility of enjoining them as a collective group—as in the case of "to Agni and to Prajāpati"; furthermore, since no specific substance is perceived in the term *aruṇayā*, the substance *ekahāyanī*, which is presented in its specific form, connects immediately with the purchase, and thus, by the principle of exclusion (*guṇāvarodha-nyāya*), redness cannot connect with the purchase once it has been occupied by the *ekahāyanī*.

Nor is it possible for the meaning of the sentence to be that "one buys with a one-year-old cow, and that [cow] must be red," because this would result in a syntactical split (vākyabheda) by enjoining both the one-year-old cow and the redness in relation to the act of buying. Therefore, since redness connects with all substances within the context, there is no restrictive rule that it must connect only with the one-year-old cow.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: the quality of redness (*āruṇya*) is connected only with the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*). This is because two words with identical case-endings intend the unity of their respective referents. Nor is there a contradiction with the case-ending that expresses a grammatical relation (*kāraka*); for its capacity to convey a *kāraka* related to an action remains intact. Furthermore, there is no rule that connection must be exclusively with an action; otherwise, it would follow that the singularity expressed by the case-ending could not be connected to a *kāraka*. Nor should it be argued that singularity is conveyed by virtue of being a singular number and not by virtue of being a *kāraka*-expressing case-ending.

Even though the identical case-ending conveys identity, there is no contradiction [between the two]. Thus, in this case, the state of being qualified by redness and so forth is to be understood from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). The identity of the substance, which is the substratum of the two properties that serve as the grounds for the application of the two words, is what is expressed by the identical case-ending. However, the relationship between the action and its factors (*kāraka*) is to be understood from the sentence (*vākya*); therefore, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

He states this established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words beginning "even when [the substance] is mentioned" (*upātte’pi*). Regarding the "substance" (*dravye*), it refers to the substance of the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*). "Even when mentioned" (*upātte’pi*) means even when specifically indicated. By the word "even" (*api*), two points are indicated: first, that in the opponent's prior position (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is not even the status of being situated within the sentence as there is in the case of the mention of a substance; and second, that although in his own established conclusion (*siddhānta*) such status exists, nevertheless its function is merely to denote a quality (*guṇa*), because—as in the example "the cloth is white" (*paṭaḥ śuklaḥ*)—it lacks that [function of denoting a substance].

"Due to the absence of dissimilar case-endings"—that is, due to the lack of a designation using non-identical case endings. The meaning is that there is no exception to the general rule (*utsarga*) that [a word] denotes a quality that is inseparably established (*apṛthaksiddha*). "By the primary word" means by the word *aruṇā* (red), which serves as the base for a non-identical case-ending; this is according to the *ākṛti-naya*, that is, the logic of the *ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*. "Qualification" (*vaiśiṣṭya*) means being endowed with a quality. "Indeed, it results" means it becomes the object of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). "Of the two words" refers to the two words *aruṇayā* and *ekahāyanyā*.

"Identical inflection" (*samānā vibhaktiḥ*) means that the two words have a single referent—that is, identity of the qualificanda in the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by the apprehension of their respective word-powers (*śakti*). "It indeed states" (*kathayaty eva*) means "it indeed establishes"; this is made clear by the particle *eva*, which indicates that this alone is the meaning of the section (*adhikaraṇa*). Furthermore, the word *tu* is intended to highlight the difference in purpose from the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*. "Threefold" (*trirūpā*) means endowed with three forms: the state of being a case-inflection (*kāraka-vibhaktitva*), singular number (*ekavacanatva*), and identical inflection (*samāna-vibhaktitva*). "That" (*sā*) refers to the inflection (*vibhakti*).

"Like the connection with number"—that is, like a cognition whose mode (*prakāra*) is oneness and so forth. "Cognition of a case-role" (*kārakadhiyam*) means a cognition whose object is an instrument (*karaṇa*) or other such grammatical roles. "He should impart" (*diśet*) means he should give. This is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); one should also understand that it implies "he should impart the identity of the meanings of the two words," as indicated by the mention of the "three forms" (*trirūpa*). Alternatively, the reading is *saṅkhyānvaya iva diśet*. In this case, *saṅkhyānvaya* is in the locative case. The meaning is that just as there is no inconsistency in the cognition of a case-role when there is the capacity to convey oneness and so forth, there is likewise no inconsistency in the cognition of a case-role when there is the capacity to convey the identity of the word-meanings.

The suffix *liṅ* in *diśet* denotes potentiality (*śaki*). Thus, the sense is that even for a single [word], three potencies are possible due to the difference in the delimiters of its potencies (*śaktatāvacchedaka*).

"This is appropriate" was stated in the preceding verse; its intention is as follows: because the word *aruṇā* denotes that which is qualified by a quality (*guṇaviśiṣṭavācin*), there is no contradiction with the grammatical rule "words such as *śukla* [denoting] a quality [take the masculine gender when denoting a substance]" (*guṇe śuklādayaḥ puṃsi*). For this very reason, the rule "the gender and number of words expressing qualities follow those of their substratum" (*guṇavacanānām āśrayato liṅgavacanāni*) is also naturally consistent. Furthermore, since an incorporeal thing cannot be admitted to enter into a relation of purchase (*kraya*), there is no need to wait for a state where the absence of the certainty of unsuitability (*ayogyatāniścayaviraha*) might arise.

Since the single *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow) itself, indicated by the identity of its case-ending, is enjoined for the purpose of purchase, there is no fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). For this very reason, there is no contradiction with the restatement (*anuvāda*) of ten substances in the phrase "with ten. Furthermore, there is no need for the laborious resort to an implied connection with the *ekahāyanī* as the means for a distinct type of purchase. Moreover, a distinction in the purchase based on the accessory (*guṇa*) lacks scriptural authority. And it is the natural sense of the statement "he purchases with ten" that it functions as an injunction regarding the act of purchase.

The phrase "with ten" (*daśabhiḥ*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the number ten obtained from the respective sentences, intended for the purpose of aggregating the substances used in the purchase (*kraya-dravya*). Since two words with the same case-ending convey the unity of their referents, there is no contradiction with the principle regarding the exclusion of subordinate qualities (*guṇāvarodha-nyāya*). In cases such as "to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa," by this very logic of the *aruṇādhikaraṇa*, there is no syntactic discordance (*vairūpya*), because the two elements ending in case-inflections are mutually connected.

And in the section concerning number and the handful (*saṅkhyāmuṣṭyadhikaraṇa*): when a word denoting a specific number is used in close proximity with a word denoting a specific measure, the non-difference relation of the number denoted by that word occurs only with respect to the measure itself—even if it is a part of the referent of the word—as it relates to the measure, and not to the measured object, due to the peculiarity of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*). Otherwise, in the case of "two *prastha*s of rice," there would be a contradiction because of the greater quantity of the rice. Thus, in the expression "four handfuls" (*caturo muṣṭīn*), even though the measure of the handful is a qualifier of the specific limited substance...

Regarding the number four, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) holds that, in light of the contradiction regarding the qualified object, it is more logical to reject the qualifier—the number four itself. [The reply is: Even when qualified by a number, the word must be construed with a limited substance; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of partial application (*ekadeśānvaya*). Nor is there a contradiction, because the application occurs through the delimitation of being measured by a handful (*muṣṭi*). For rice grains, which are inherently uncountable, can only become countable through limiting conditions such as place and so forth.

Furthermore, since the state of being limited by a fist (*muṣṭiparimitatva*) can function as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), the connection of the number four is logically established precisely through that limitation. Just as in the expression "great hero" (*mahāśūra*), the quality of greatness connects [with the hero] either through the medium of heroism or through the medium of the measure of a fist, so too the connection of the number four with the specific substance to be measured is established. Thus, the status of the number four as a qualifier of the measurable substance is justified.

Therefore, although both the number four and the measure of a handful are qualifiers of the substance (*dravya*), since the number four is heard first, it is the subsequently heard measure of the handful that is sublated without sublating the number four; thus, there is no contradiction even with the *saṅkhyāmuṣṭyadhikaraṇa*. Consequently, it has been stated that this [interpretation] is appropriate, while the other is inappropriate.

Furthermore, for those who assert the combination (*samuccaya*) of the acts of purchase (*kraya*), there would be a contradiction with the twelfth *adhikaraṇa*, which states: "But there should be an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the purchases, because they serve a single purpose. This is because in that [adhikaraṇa], only the combination of substances (*dravya*) is understood. Nor is it appropriate to say that "the purchases" (*krayaṇāni*) are "purchases" (*krayāḥ*); for if that were the case, the formulation would have resulted in "regarding the purchases" (*krayeṣu*). This is because the word *krayaṇa* naturally possesses the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), according to the rule *karaṇādhikaraṇayoś ca*. For this very reason, there is conformity with the wording of the mantra: "This cow is the purchaser of Soma" (*iyaṃ gauḥ somakrayaṇī*).

For this very reason, even in the *Bhāṣya* on that particular section (*adhikaraṇa*), the collection of substances alone is stated as the established conclusion (*adhikaraṇasiddhānta*). Nor should it be argued that—since there is no other sentence enjoining the purchase (*kraya*) devoid of qualities, and since it is necessary for each of those sentences themselves to be the injunction of the purchase—the qualities residing in those respective sentences, being enjoined at the time of origin (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), would preclude the inclusion of other qualities; and thus, because a difference in the purchase would necessarily follow from the difference in qualities, the unity of purpose (*ekārthatva*) would ultimately resolve only within the various purchases themselves. [This is not so.]

For the statement "one indeed purchases it with ten" is logically established as being productive of the act of purchase (*kraya*). Nor is its status as an injunction (*vidhi*) undermined by the particle *vai*, because its injunctive nature is established precisely through the force of its not being otherwise obtained (*arthāprāpti*), according to the principle stated in the section [of the Mīmāṃsā Sūtras] beginning, "But there is an injunction regarding holding, because it is something new. For even in cases such as "one purchases with a cow," since no optative suffix (*liṅ*) or similar marker is heard, the injunctive nature must likewise be asserted on the basis of its not being otherwise obtained. Furthermore, there would be the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*) if the various acts of purchase were distinct. As for the portion "with ten," it is a restatement (*anuvāda*); and it has already been stated that this serves the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

Furthermore, even if the sentences beginning with "aruṇayā" were to enjoin distinct acts of purchase (*kraya*), they would fall under the sixth category [of injunction], which consists in the injunction of a productive operation (*bhāvanā*) where the meaning of the verbal root is the instrument (*karaṇa*) qualified by a quality for the sake of another object. For me, however, it is of the third category, consisting in the injunction of a productive operation where the meaning of the verbal root is the object (*uddeśya*) and something else is the instrument; as in the case of "he purchases with ten [cows] for the sake of another. Thus, it is not the case that...

And it is not to be argued that, because the second type [of injunction] arises from the prescription of a meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) whose instrument is the meaning of the pure element (*śuddhadhātu*), there would follow an undesirable contingency of option (*vikalpa*) between cows and the like—just as with curd and the like—due to the impossibility of the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) expressing independence when the substance is enjoined by the sentence concerning "red" (*aruṇā*) etc. in reference to the purchase already obtained from another sentence. This is because independence remains intact precisely due to the difference in the means (*dvāra*), since the [services] generated by those respective substances (the various prices paid by the sellers) are mutually distinct; thus, no contingency of option arises.

For this very reason, it has been stated that even according to the opponent's view, although the quality of redness (*āruṇya*) and the substance of a one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) are enjoined simultaneously, the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is appropriate in both instances because the substance and the quality are mutually independent, due to the difference in their respective means of operation—namely, the delimitation of the substance and so forth.

Now, it might be argued that by the sentence "one indeed purchases him with ten," a purchase qualified by ten substances is enjoined; since the number lacks grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the action, there is no differentiation of the action by the number. Furthermore, because this is an injunction even regarding the portion "with ten," there is no inconsistency (*vairūpya*). If it is asked, "What are those ten substances? and it is suggested that the specific substances should be enjoined by the sentences concerning the cow and so forth, we say no.

An injunction (*vidhi*) possesses two types of objects of knowledge (*prameya*): making known what was unknown (*ajñātajñāpana*) and impelling one toward what has not yet commenced (*apravṛttapravartana*). However, since [the injunction] here serves merely the purpose of making known what was unknown, it cannot result in producing a specific activity. Even though it might be argued that this is consistent with the principle that "all injunctions regarding substances (*dravyavidhi*) are restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi*)," because the statement regarding the purchase [of Soma] qualified by a substance—such as "he buys [it] for ten" (*daśabhiḥ krīṇāti*)—and the statements regarding cows and so forth (*gavādivākya*), serve to provide what was otherwise only optionally obtained (*pākṣikyāmaprāptau prāpakam*).

Nevertheless, since the restrictive rule (niyama) is established by the prescription of a specific substance alone, there is no need for a prescription regarding the substance in general. Furthermore, when a second type of injunction is possible—namely, the prescription of a productive operation (*bhāvanā*) having as its instrument the meaning of the verbal root in its pure form with reference to another object—it is not logical to resort to the sixth type of injunction, which consists of prescribing a productive operation having as its instrument the meaning of the verbal root qualified by an accessory (*guṇa*) with reference to another object. Therefore, the phrase "with ten" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the collection of substances by way of their number.

And it is logical that the second type [of injunction] consists of an injunction of a productive activity (*bhāvanā*) whose purpose is the pure verbal root-meaning, expressed by the word "buys" (*krīṇāti*) with reference to something else.

However, this must be considered: if one were to rely on the injunction "he buys with ten" as being prescriptive, there would be a contradiction with the established conclusion (siddhānta) of the second section [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*], namely that [the fire-installation] is subsidiary to everything.

For in that case, since the act of establishing the fires (*ādhāna*) is already established by the injunction "He who, knowing thus, establishes the fire" (*ya evaṃ vidvān agnim ādhatte*), which prescribes the establishment with reference to the fire itself, the sentences such as "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the fires in spring" (*vasante brāhmaṇo ’gnīn ādadhīta*) would, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), merely prescribe the times such as spring as being auxiliary to the establishment, contingent upon the Brāhmaṇa being the agent. However, because the sentence "He who, knowing thus" takes the form of a statement of an existing fact (*vartamānopadeśa*) and cannot therefore function as an injunction, it is only the sentences containing direct injunctions regarding spring and so forth that possess injunctive force.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that since the status of being a Brāhmaṇa and so forth lacks the character of being a causal factor (*nimitta*), the injunction regarding the installation of the fires qualified by those attributes is intended for Brāhmaṇas and the other classes. According to the reasoning stated, if there were injunctive force due to the presence of words such as *yat* (the relative pronoun), it would contradict that conclusion.

Furthermore, if this were the case, there would be a contradiction with the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the preceding section, which states: "And [it is] a substance, because of its connection with production. For in that context, following the enumeration "the wooden sword (*sphya*) and the potsherds (*kapāla*)," the statement "these indeed are the ten sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudha*)"—since the word *yajñāyudha* denotes the means of accomplishing a sacrifice—indicates that the *sphya* and other items are means for the sacrifice. Since they cannot serve as such directly [in every instance], the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) holds that, by applying generally to all auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), the *sphya* and others possess the capacity to be the means for all suitable actions, and that statements such as "he digs with the *sphya*" are merely partial restatements (*avayutyānuvāda*).

Because it would result in the meaninglessness of numerous statements such as those concerning *uddhanana* (stirring), because there would be a contradiction with the scriptural hearing of [the word] "always" (*nitya*) due to the absence of constant application, and because of the use of the particle *vai* in the sentence "these" (*etāni*), it has been established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the statement regarding *uddhanana* and so forth is injunctive (*vidhāyaka*), whereas the statement "sacrificial implements" (*yajñāyudhāni*) is merely reiterative (*anuvādaka*). Similarly here, since the statement associated with the word *vai* is injunctive, and because it would otherwise result in the redundancy of the multiple instances of "he buys," the sentence "with ten" (*daśabhiḥ*) is not injunctive.

To this it is replied: the sentence "he buys with ten" (*daśabhiḥ krīṇāti*) is an injunction prescribing the purchase with reference to Soma. However, the phrase "with ten" (*daśabhiḥ*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the ten substances already established by another sentence. Nor is there any contradiction with the two previously mentioned topical discussions (*adhikaraṇa*), because of the greater disparity [in the nature of the cases]. To explain: in the discussion on the Fire-laying (*ādhāna*), the sentence "he who, knowing thus... (*ya evaṃ vidvān*) cannot be an injunction, as it must be a supplement to the injunction regarding the materials (*saṃbhāra*) in the sentence "then they collect the materials" (*atha saṃbhārān saṃharanti*).

The statement "not indeed by ten," etc., is heard as a supplement to another injunction; this is one point of dissimilarity. Furthermore, in the sentence concerning the spring season (*vasantādi-vākya*), there is the hearing of an injunction, whereas in the sentence concerning the cow, etc. (*gavādi-vākya*), there is no such hearing of an injunction. Moreover, in the case of the spring-season sentence, since it prescribes the time of spring as a condition (*nimitta*) for the Brāhmaṇas and others to perform the act—by way of restating the installation of the fires (*ādhāna*) already established by other means of knowledge—there arises the fallacy of a lack of grammatical coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*): because time is not something to be taken up (*anupādeyatva*), even though the ritual action itself is already established, the action would have to be what is taken up while the time is what is enjoined. Thus, in the spring-season sentence, there is the consequence of a mismatch between the locus of the action and the locus of the injunction.

In the case of the sentence regarding the cow and so forth (*gavādi-vākya*), however, there is no lack of co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between the status of being enjoined (*vidheya*) and the status of being something to be adopted (*upādeyatva*), because the cow and so forth are themselves what is to be adopted; thus, there is another point of difference as well. In the sentence regarding spring and so forth (*vasantādi-vākya*), since it is possible for all times to be obtained for the fire-laying (*ādhāna*)—just as all agents are [obtained]—there is no decisive factor (*vinigamanāviraha*) to determine whether the injunction of time applies to the Brāhmaṇa agent or whether the injunction of the agent applies when time is the occasion (*nimitta*). Therefore, an injunction of the fire-laying qualified by both [time and agent] is necessary.

In the case of sentences such as "The cow [is the sacrificial fee]," however, there is no such lack of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanā*), and thus another point of difference also exists. Likewise, the sentence "These indeed are the ten sacrifices and the sacrificial implements" is a supplement to the injunction "They collect the sacrificial implements," and is not itself an injunction; furthermore, there is no finite verb (*ākhyāta*) in this sentence, and the particle *vai* is heard here.

If the sentence concerning the wooden sword (*sphyādi*) were merely a restatement (*anuvādaka*), then many other sentences would be rendered purposeless; furthermore, since there would be no constant application (*nityaprāpti*) of acts such as digging out (*uddhanana*), this would contradict their being heard as constant injunctions. Therefore, sentences concerning digging out and the like possess injunctive force (*vidhāyakatva*). In the present case, however, in the sentence "with ten [cows]," the verbal root *krīṇāti* ("he buys") is heard. If this sentence lacked injunctive force, it would be purposeless. Even if it possesses injunctive force, there is no loss of the injunctive force of the sentences concerning the cow and the other items.

However, it is better to treat the sentence "He buys with ten" (*daśabhiḥ krīṇāti*) as a restatement (*anuvādaka*) of many [sentences] that contain the verb "he buys," because a sentence is more important than a word. For this very reason, one must resort to the sixth type of injunction (*ṣaṣṭha-vidhi-prakāra*) in the sentences concerning spring (*vasanta*) and so forth, due to the lack of any other way; but in the present case, since there is a way out, that [resort] is not appropriate.

In this regard, one should not suspect that the statement "he buys him for ten" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the purchase enjoined by that very sentence, while the substances such as cows enjoined by other sentences are being restated as "for ten" within that same sentence. This is because the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that, by way of a restatement of the Vāyu-sacrifice enjoined by the sentence "One should immolate a white animal for Vāyu," the act of immolation—which is already obtained through the general rule of transfer (*codaka*)—is itself restated within the Vāyu-sentence alone. For this very reason, it was stated by the ritual experts (*tāntrika*) in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the section on the second kind of fire-installation (*dvaitīyīkādhāna*): "The injunction 'He installs the fire upon the ritual materials' is the rule that brings about the installation."

For here, the preparatory materials (*saṃbhāra*) are not enjoined, because they are already established by another means of knowledge; nor is their being the locus [of the fire] enjoined, because that too is already established by the very wording of the mantra, which states "let it be placed upon that. Therefore, this is merely an injunction for the act of laying the fire (*ādhāna*). And thus, since the sentence "he lays the fire upon the materials" is an restatement (*anuvāda*) of the laying of the fire produced by the original injunction, and since the presence of the materials and their being its locus—both of which are already established by the sentence concerning the materials and the wording of the mantra—are accepted as restatements within that very same sentence by the phrase "upon the materials," [the injunction is restricted].

However, there is this distinction: according to the other view (*paramata*), since it is accepted that sentences such as "with a cow" (*gavā*) enjoin distinct purchases qualified by their respective attributes, the words "cow" and so on necessarily involve *matvartha-lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication of the sense of possession). Consequently, the instrumental case-suffix following those words would result in expressing only the instrumentality residing in the purchase. Furthermore, even if *matvartha-lakṣaṇā* were admitted, there would be the laborious effort of explaining how the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākāraka-sambandha*) is not abandoned.

In our own view (*asmanmata*), however, because we accept the injunction of an attribute by way of restating a purchase already established by sentences such as "that [purchase] indeed with ten," neither of these two defects arises.

[The opponent objects: "But surely, if one purchases [the Soma] with a one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*), it must follow that she must be red (*aruṇā*); thus, if one relies on this connection, there arises a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*)—this being the intention of the Siddhāntin. How then can the proponent of the Pūrvapakṣa, having refuted that [position], accept that the quality of redness applies to all substances mentioned in the context? For the syntactical split is equal in both positions. [The Siddhāntin replies: No. For the Siddhāntin, the syntactical split consists of a repetition of injunctions (*vidhyāvṛtti*), namely: first, the injunction of the one-year-old cow in relation to the act of purchase (*kraya*), and second, the injunction of the redness in relation to that same cow. Thus, the two injunctions are distinct.

For me, however, there is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) characterized by the breaking of the sentence; and because of this syntactical split, there is a repetition of the primary injunction (*vidhi*), which constitutes a primary defect—this is the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*). Furthermore, in the expression "with a red, yellow-eyed [cow]," the connection between the quality of redness (*aruṇya*) and the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) is indeed direct (*śrauta*), as they share the same case-ending. However, the connection of the one-year-old cow as a substance with the act of purchase (*kraya*) is to be understood through syntactical context (*vākya*); thus, there is no syntactical split characterized by the repetition of the injunction. This is the actual intention of the proponent of the final conclusion (*siddhāntin*), for it is logical to establish the final conclusion against the prima facie view regarding syntactical split—characterized by the breaking of the sentence—in the manner described above.

[Objection: "But even so, since the instrumental case in *aruṇayā* functions as an adjective-case ending, it would follow that its purpose is merely grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), because non-difference (*abheda*) is a relation (*saṃsarga*). [Response: This is not so, because we accept that a word with a co-occurring case-ending has non-difference as its meaning. Otherwise, there would be the fault of unnecessary complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*) regarding the status of [the cognition of non-difference] as an obstacle to inference. And yet, even so...

It should not be argued that because the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) is already conveyed by the case-ending of the substantive (*viśeṣya*), the case-ending of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) lacks the capacity to convey a *kāraka* (grammatical participant). This is because, according to the maxim "when [two terms] are connected, one of them is redundant," both endings convey the very same single instrumentality. In expressions such as "he brings water with blue [flowers]" (*nīlena jalam āharati*), it is necessary that the case-ending following the word "blue" (*nīla*) conveys instrumentality. And this is likewise the case in "he brings water with a jar" (*ghaṭena jalam āharati*).

The case-ending following words such as *ghaṭa* (pot) is necessarily required [to express the instrumentality]. In expressions such as "he fetches water with a blue pot" (*nīlena ghaṭena jalam āharati*), the single status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is conveyed by both case-endings. This is because there is no evidence that either one of two elements—each of which has been individually determined to possess the capacity [to denote instrumentality]—should fail to convey that instrumentality. Nor should it be argued that, even so, there is some lack of elegance in the case-ending because it does not denote an instrumentality that has not already been expressed by another word.

This is because the natural force of the word rests precisely upon its denoting the performance of an action that requires no other instrument; since that [natural sense] is absent, even in your own view, an unnatural interpretation (asvārasya) is unavoidable. Furthermore, in your view, there is the additional fault of subverting the gender (liṅga), for if the word *aruṇā* were intended merely as a quality (*guṇamātra*), the feminine gender would be untenable. Moreover, since gender takes precedence over case-ending, it is improper to subvert the natural sense of the gender established by the nominative (the first case) merely to conform to a subsequent case-ending.

For this very reason, in the passage "one should not perform the *pravargya* at the first sacrifice," the word *prayoga* (performance) was determined for the term *anantarya-jña* (the subsequent sacrifice), in accordance with the natural sense of the word *prathama* (first) as it is heard in the text.

As for what has been stated by some here—that because gender is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and so forth, it lacks the quality of being perceived first (which is the reason for its predominance), and therefore gender must be understood either through the suffix *ṭāp*—the modification of the case-ending in the word *aruṇayā* which is unique to the feminine—or through the stem itself as a signifier, or as that which illuminates the meaning of the stem and so forth—that is not correct; for in the word *aruṇayā*, there is no modification of the case-ending, since modification applies only to the base (*prakṛti*).

Furthermore, through the study of poetry such as *Rūpamālā* and others during the stage of linguistic training (*vyutpatti*), one acquires proficiency in cases such as *madhurayā madhubodhitamādhvī*, understanding that the word ending in the suffix *-ā* is feminine and in the singular instrumental case; this is because the gender itself is perceived first, and thus the primacy of the case-ending is not established. Moreover, this is confirmed by the fact that such recognition occurs elsewhere as well.

For those who know the grammatical injunctions (*anuśāsana*), however, by the injunction "from a nominal stem ending in *ṅī*, *āp*, or a *prātipadika*," there is a sequence of the denotators corresponding to the sequence of the denoted—namely, self-meaning (*svārtha*), substance (*dravya*), gender (*liṅga*), number (*saṅkhyā*), and case-role (*kāraka*)—either according to the logic of the sequence of secondary suffixes (*śaiṣika-krama-nyāya*) or because gender is understood first; and since this sequence is maintained even elsewhere, the primacy of the case-ending is not established. Furthermore, the cognition of a case-ending as a modification of its own form does not lead to the inference of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*.

However, for those who do not contemplate the grammatical injunctions (*anuśāsana*), that knowledge [of gender]—being dependent on the modification of case-endings—is difficult to attain. But for those who do contemplate it, the priority belongs to the comprehension of gender according to the direction previously stated; thus, there is no obstacle to the application of the "First Sacrifice" maxim (*prathamayajñanyāya*).

Furthermore, if words such as *aruṇā* (red) were to denote substances through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), then the grammatical rule—"the elision of the suffix *matup* is desired after words expressing qualities"—would be rendered purposeless. Moreover, if they were established secondary indications (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇika*), there would be the undesirable consequence that these words could not be used with the intention of expressing only their primary (literal) meaning. Now, one might object: "In a case where a red, yellow-eyed ewe is obtained, as well as a one-year-old cow alone, then according to the opponent's view, since redness (*āruṇya*)—like the substance—is an instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the purchase, the substance must be set aside in accordance with the redness, which is heard first."

In your view, however, since redness (*āruṇya*) is subordinate to the substance, and because when there is a conflict between a substance and a quality, the substance cannot be abandoned, the abandonment must belong to the quality alone in accordance with the substance; thus, a difference in performance (*anuṣṭhāna-bheda*) would result. But that is not tenable—because even when the acceptance of the deity’s corporeal form and so forth is admitted, in the case of an equality between substance and deity, the equality of the substance is the cause for extension (*atideśa*), since the substance is more proximate, and not the equality of the deity, by its very nature.

If it is argued that [the injunctions] are distinct because of their remoteness (*viprakṛṣṭatva*)—that is, because they protect the unity of performance (*anuṣṭhānaikyaparitrāṇa*)—we say no. In the case of the statement "with a red, one-year-old [cow]," both the quality of redness (*aruṇimaguṇa*) and the universal of cow-ness (*gotvajāti*) are subsidiaries (*aṅga*) with respect to the substance used for purchase. Although there is no difference between the two in being subsidiaries of the substance, the universal mentioned subsequently is set aside in favor of redness precisely because of its priority; thus, there is no difference in performance. In this regard, it has been stated that "this [application] is appropriate, while the other is inappropriate."

The phrase "stated by the Guru" is used for the sake of ease in referring back to what was previously mentioned; however, although it should have been stated as "this is appropriate" or "that is inappropriate," the use of the word "another" (*anyā*) is intended to suggest that the other explanation of the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa* offered by others is likewise inappropriate in a different manner.

For instance, some maintain that since it is impossible for an immaterial quality to be connected with the act of purchase, the word *aruṇā* (red) must necessarily refer to a substance through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Thus, they argue that the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*)—qualified both by its reddish-brown eyes (*piṅgākṣī*) and by its redness (*aruṇā*)—is enjoined simultaneously as the means for the purchase; this constitutes their prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). They further state that the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the word refers solely to the quality, just like the position of the opponent.

Since it is appropriate for both the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) and the final conclusion (siddhānta) to proceed precisely by accepting the uniformity of the term *aruṇā*, the word "otherwise" (*anyathā*) has been stated to indicate that [the opponent's position] is also improper. || 45 ||

He states the meaning of the *sūtras* beginning with "There is no inequality or cruelty [on the part of the Lord], because He takes [the individual's] prior actions into account" and "The agent [is the Lord], because the scriptures would otherwise be purposeless," and "But [the Lord acts] in dependence on the effort performed by the individual":
"In the beginning, the person exists, generating within himself various cognitions, volitions, and efforts by means of the power of autonomy granted by the Lord."

In that regard, Hari bestows the fruit of every person's respective actions by first remaining indifferent, then granting permission, and finally performing the corresponding acts of restraint or favor.

This is the refutation of the objections raised by others against the doctrine of Brahman as the cause. Its meaning is as follows: "In the beginning," that is, at the start of creation; "puruṣa" refers to the individual soul (jīva); "jātyekatvam" means the oneness of the genus; [it applies] to every person.

Because it will be stated thus [later]: by that which was given by Īśvara—the Lord who is the sovereign of all and the controller of all—and produced solely through His own compassion. By this, it is indicated that the simultaneity of creation is based on grace (*anugraha*). The meaning already stated is obtained by the word "given" (*dattayā*). Sovereignty (*svātantrya*) is the state of being irresistible when the Will is present; that itself is the power (*śakti*)—the attribute residing in the cause as it is employed for the effect. Although power is not a distinct substance (*adravyaprabheda*);

Nevertheless, "power" (*śakti*) is here figuratively designated as an inseparably established attribute (*apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇa*) that is serviceable for the effect. "Those respective cognitions, desires to act, and efforts" refers to cognitions, desires to act, and efforts directed toward those respective objects. "The desire to act" (*cikīrṣā*) is the wish to do; "the exertion of activity" (*pravṛttyudyoga*) is effort (*prayatna*). "Producing" (*utpādayan*) means generating; [the Lord] exists [thus]. By these two terms, both the initial activity and the subsequent activities are intended.

In that regard—having first acted with indifference, which consists of neither preventing nor producing; then—in subsequent actions from the second onwards; having consented, that is, by assuming the state of being a cooperative cause; [he effects] their restraint and favor—the restraint of the independent person during the initial action.

He performs—that is, he carries out—the resolve to bestow hell and other such states produced by evil deeds, as well as the resolve to bestow heaven and other such states produced by virtuous deeds. He grants—that is, he gives—the fruit of those respective actions, namely the meritorious or non-meritorious results in the form of heaven, hell, and so forth, to every person—in accordance with their resolves, to all men. As to who this is, he says: Hari.
For it is said: "Because he forcibly seizes [the fruits of action] from Brahmā, Śitikaṇṭha (Śiva), Yama, and Varuṇa himself, he is therefore called Hari."
The meaning is that the Blessed One is the ruler of all as thus described; by means of the power of autonomy granted by the Lord,
there shall be no futility in injunctions and prohibitions.
The limitation [of the Lord's sovereignty] is only as much as is required by the scriptural texts concerning His being the controller; it does not extend beyond that.

Through the pervasion of the external and internal organs, and through the bestowing and sustaining of their powers, the Supreme Lord acts as the cause of will and the other [faculties] by means of these common auxiliary functions.

Since the mind arises from desire and so forth— which are accompanied by latent impressions (vāsanā) and consist of objects brought about by past experience or inherent nature— the Lord’s state of neutrality is logical.
When an object intended for one purpose is employed for another by someone else,
the person who procured it is indeed excluded from that [result].
Because it cannot be prevented when [the body] has capacity, the individual soul (jīva) is said to be independent;
for by the knowledge of poison even in cooked rice, it restrains its own will.
Even when there is an absence of a prompter regarding a particular matter, the Lord, awakening the intellect of the virtuous,
becomes at each such occasion both the instigator and the consenter.
Furthermore, as a result of prior engagement, there would be consent and so forth;
and for virtues such as compassion, another object [of action] is easily found.
When a minister possesses independence, it does not detract from the sovereignty of the king; likewise, it does not detract from the sovereignty of another who grants independence to a living being.
Freedom does not fall away from that whose very nature is dependent on another,
because the person who bestows freedom does not prevent its operation.

Thus, the summarized meaning declared by the venerable Vyāsa has been indicated. Consequently, the independence of individual souls (*jīvas*), the efficacy of the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions, the status of the Supreme Self as the cause of all, and its possession of unrestrained sovereignty—all of this is logically established. || 46 ||

To the objection that there would then be the fault of [the Lord] not turning back [the soul] from evil deeds and so forth, he says: "When a person consents to the non-cessation of evil deeds, Acyuta acts by means of his own untrammeled sovereignty; that is a merit for him, not a fault of Hari, according to the Śruti."

Furthermore, the subduing of enemies is observed in the world as a virtue, not as a fault; thus, there would be no lack of establishment of the locus [of the argument], provided that the Vedic word is accepted as a valid means of knowledge. (47)

The Blessed Lord possesses greatness such as being the cause of non-dislodgement and the controller [of all], despite those with external and wicked views who rely upon fallacious means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and fallacious reasoning (*tarka*). By His absolute sovereignty—meaning by the cause that is unrestrained, unimpeded, and not co-located with dependence—and by His autonomy—which consists in being irresistible when His will is present—He acts toward the person: that is, toward the individual who, having been assisted by common benefits such as the provision of instruments and bodies in the manner previously described, proceeds toward sinful acts under the influence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

In "duṣkarmasu" (in evil deeds), that is, in sins; the locative case is used because there is an intention to express the locus (adhikaraṇa) as the point of departure (apādāna). In "anivartanānumanane" (the non-prevention and the approval)—

[The Lord] does not prevent the initial commencement [of an action], nor does He give His consent for subsequent occurrences. Here, the locative case (*saptamī*)—in the word *duṣkarmasu* ("in evil deeds")—is used because the substratum (*āśraya*) of the action is intended to be expressed as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). "He performs" means that He becomes the possessor of that [action]. "He" refers to independence (*svātantrya*). "By revelation" (*śrutyā*) means by the eternal, faultless, and non-human-authored Veda. "Of Hari" means of the Blessed Lord, the controller of all, who is the adversary of everything to be abandoned (*heya*). "Quality" (*guṇa*) means an attribute that brings about excellence; it is masculine (*puṃstva*) in relation to "quality. "He" refers to independence.

"It is not a defect"—that is, it is not a property that brings about diminution. The word "by scripture" (*śrutyā*) is to be supplied [from the previous context]. The meaning is that by the very scripture which apprehends the subject (*dharmin*), its independence, its status as a quality, and its absence of defectiveness are established. He states the support of reasoning for this scripture: "And it is observed," etc. The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "moreover.
