In the world, regarding enemies—that is, those who transgress one's own commands—there is "restraint," which consists in being the cause of inflicting suffering proportionate to their offense; this is observed to be a "quality" (on the part of kings). The phrase "of kings" is to be supplied [as the subject].

"By way of defect"—that is, its nature as a defect has not been observed. For even among kings, it is observed that toward those who are disliked, the granting of successive permissions for offenses is itself a form of punishment. Likewise, the acquiescence to sins is also a form of punishment resulting from past demerit (*durita*). Thus, the sense is that the independence (*svātantrya*) consisting in the bestowing of the fruits of actions is indeed a merit (*guṇa*), and not a defect. In this way, both scripture and supporting reasoning have been stated regarding the merit of independence.

Here, this alternative is intended: is it said that independence is a fault because of the non-acceptance of God, or because of the acceptance of Him? Regarding these, he refutes the first [alternative] with the words, "there would be no establishment of the locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*). The meaning is that if it is said that independence is a fault due to the non-acceptance of God, then the alternative of non-acceptance is untenable because of the absence of a locus (*āśrayabhāvāt*). He rejects the second [alternative] with the word, "the Upaniṣadic" (*aupaniṣadam*). "Upaniṣadic" means originating from the Upaniṣads; "speech" (*vacaḥ*) means a statement (*vākya*).

If it were not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—that is, if its validity were not accepted by you—then there would be the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), for the locus of the property consisting of independence would not be established. The *Upaniṣad* is that specific portion of the Veda which teaches Brahman without mediation. It is called *upaniṣad* because "it sits near" (*upa-ni-ṣīdati*). It is said that "this [knowledge] is seated in the deep" (*gahane hy eṣopaniṣannā*); the explanation of this is that it is "seated in the profound Brahman. The suffix *-aṇ* is applied to the word *upaniṣad* according to the rule governing the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava-adhikāra*). And the state of being "belonging to" (*bhavatva*) here consists in being a constituent part (*ghaṭakatva*).

In this regard, the intention of one who says, "That quality [of independence] would not be established through scripture because it is unrestrictedly independent," and "If the Upaniṣadic word is not our means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)," is as follows: By you, who assert that independence is a defect in the case of inference, is scripture accepted as a means of valid cognition, or not?

In the first case, since the quality of the Lord’s independence is established by the very scripture that constitutes the means of valid cognition apprehending the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇa*), the inference that this independence is a defect would be *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (vitiated by the lapse of time). In the second case, since the Lord—who is cognizable solely through scripture—is unestablished, it must be stated whose independence is the defect; thus, there would be the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). This has been explained in detail by Vyāsapāda.

And thus, because it is prompted by the independence inherent in the quality established by the very means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇa*), and because it consists in the bestowing of the fruits of the misdeeds committed in other lives, the Lord’s non-prevention of the soul’s evil actions and His acquiescence therein are a quality, not a defect; such is the meaning (and so forth). || 47 ||
He states the scope of virtues such as compassion:
"For that man who has desisted from the pursuit of evil deeds, [compassion] disregards the countless sins previously accumulated over many births."
And for the sake of attaining infinite bliss for him, Lakṣmī herself exerts effort;
preceded by His compassion, this multitude of His qualities unfolds. (48)

The person who has desisted from the undertaking of evil deeds—that is, who has turned away from the determination to perform the three kinds of transgressions—is described by the word "tu" (but) and the singular number as being rare and preeminent. He is "accompanied by Lakṣmī" (*lakṣmīsahāya*), meaning he is protected by the Goddess in the form of compassion; according to the stated method, he is endowed with Lakṣmī, who manifests qualities such as compassion. It is said by the Tantrikas that the wife possesses both the status of the one who accepts (*aṅgīkartṛtva*) and the one who consents (*anumantṛtva*). This is also stated in the *Lakṣmītantra*: "I alone am his supreme Śakti, the Goddess [who is] seated upon him."
She performs every duty, following after all states of being.

Thus, compliance with the Lord in all activities has been stated by [the Lord] himself. Furthermore, it has been stated in various places that she (Prakṛti) receives designations such as "cause" because she is presided over by the Lord’s primordial nature, His intelligence, His power, and His ego. Such is the Lord; for Him—who has completely ceased from any resolve of hostility—these [deeds] were performed in former times, through many previous births, in greater numbers. They were accumulated through the three modes of speech and so forth, gathered intentionally like wealth, and were beyond counting even for the Omniscient One.

Even by the Blessed One, these offenses—transgressions—are difficult to discern due to their magnitude. Having disregarded them—that is, having resolved not to apply punishment—he [the Lord] exerts himself personally to bring about the attainment of that person’s infinite happiness; that is, for the sake of attaining unsurpassed bliss born from the experience of the unlimited Brahman and its subsequent service. He exerts himself personally; the word "personally" (svayam) excludes Lakṣmī and merit (sukṛta).
By this, the scope of his role as the instigator is shown.

Therefore, from this [verse]: "Of the Lord of Lakṣmī, [the qualities] beginning with compassion, preceded by compassion..."—by this, it is stated that among the qualities that render Him worthy of being sought as a refuge, compassion is preeminent. For here, compassion is defined as the inability to endure the suffering of others, regardless of one's own interest. And in this context, the [suffering] of others is understood [to be real]; since that [suffering] is experienced precisely as something disagreeable, it is thereby stated that compassion consists in being pained by the suffering of others.

And this is indicated here by the employment of the word "compassion" (*kāruṇya*). For it has been said: "Compassion arose in that holy-souled sage; grief attained the state of a verse. This [compassion] is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); or rather, the author intends its establishment through his own experience as its object. "The multitude of qualities" (*guṇagaṇa*) refers to the collection of qualities such as affection (*vātsalya*) and others conducive to the granting of liberation. "It unfolds" (*ujjṛmbhate*) means it shines forth through the attainment of an unrestricted range of objects. By this, the object of compassion and the other qualities is stated.

This which has been spoken by the Blessed One is as follows: by the mere resolve to transcend his own teaching and by accepting infinite, unbearable offenses accumulated over beginningless and endless eons, he himself strives for the sake of increasing unsurpassed bliss. || 48 ||
Now begins the section on the refutation of the proponents of illusion (*māyāvāda*).

Thus, the objections raised by others against the doctrine that Brahman is the cause have been refuted. Now, he proceeds to refute the opposing view—beginning with the fact that, at the outset, the scriptural texts concerning difference have as their object the unreal, and those expressing unity possess an indirect meaning (*lakṣaṇā*).
The abandonment of that [doctrine] is far indeed from those words intent on the synthesis of both;

furthermore, there is a subversion of the natural course of means of valid cognition such as perception, as well as extensive refutation by reasoning (tarka) in the Māyāvāda. All of this, however, is otherwise in the position of Lakṣmaṇācārya.

By the refutation of this single doctrine of illusion (*māyāvāda*), the positions of the Buddhists, the Sāṅkhyas, and those of Yādava and Bhāskara are also rejected; thus, it is that very [doctrine] which is refuted here. Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣika has already been dismissed in the context of defining configuration (*saṃsthāna*) and genus (*jāti*). As for the Śaiva position, it will be refuted in detail starting with the passage, "Who are you? I am a knower of reality," and so forth. Therefore, the entire purpose of this discourse on the refutation of opposing views has been stated.

For it has been stated that "there is secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) for words denoting identity. In that regard, according to Śaṅkara’s position, there is no secondary signification, because he accepts that [the sentence] has as its purport the identity of the substantive (viśeṣya). However, there is merely the capacity of a word—whose natural inclination is to denote the qualified entity (viśiṣṭābhidhāna)—to produce a cognition that does not have the qualifiers (viśeṣaṇa) as its object. Thus, in this context, it must be said that the word *lakṣaṇā* refers to something other than its primary sense. Since even the primary meaning of the word *lakṣaṇā* is possible here, that too should indeed be accepted; therefore, the statement "and there is secondary signification for words denoting identity" is intended to include the views of Yādava and Bhāskara.

In that regard, according to the Yādava school, since the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two terms denoting the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*)—which are both transformations of Brahman as pure Being (*sanmātra-brahman*)—is untenable (just as it is between the words "pot" and "bowl"), one must resort to the view that one of the two terms functions as a *lakṣaka* (indicative) of Brahman as the pure Being which is their material cause (*upādāna*). Likewise, even in the Bhāskara position, because he accepts both difference and non-difference conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-bhedābheda*), the coreferentiality of the two terms denoting the individual soul and the Lord is untenable (just as it is between the words "space in a pot" and "space in a cloth"); therefore, it is necessary that one of the two terms functions as a *lakṣaka* of the [Brahman] unconditioned by adjuncts (*anupahita*).

(And on Śaṅkara’s view, there is an inherent lack of naturalness due to the abandonment of the qualifying portion. Therefore, the summary of Yādava and Bhāskara regarding the statement "and because of the identity expressed by the words" is as follows: [lakṣaṇā caikyavācām].

The refutation of the Buddhists by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and other proofs is clear, because they deny the existence and origination of objects, both of which are established by the direct perception of all people. Furthermore, their acceptance of error even while asserting that defects (*doṣa*) and so forth are unreal is contrary to direct perception. The view that pure consciousness alone is real while everything else is unreal is common to both Śaṅkara and the Yogācāras. Moreover, the view that the changeless, self-luminous, and uniform pure consciousness is the witness distinct from itself is common to both Sāṅkhya and Śaṅkara.

For this very reason, in the sūtra "And because of contradiction, it is inconsistent," the author of the Bhāṣya, the venerable Śaṅkara, extended the refutation of the Sāṅkhya position to the Śaṅkara position as well. Since, according to the reasoning already stated, the witnessing of ignorance, superimposition, and so forth are impossible for them as well, there is indeed inconsistency; therefore, by the refutation of the Śaṅkara position, everything becomes refuted, and thus that alone is explicitly refuted here. As it has been said: "The emergence of the Śaṅkara [view] arises from a mixture of Sāṅkhya, Saugata, and Cārvāka;
the refutations [of that] are the same as those [already given], and even more extensive."

"At the beginning" (ādau) means: in the position that accepts *avidyā*—which is indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), logically untenable (*anupapanna*), and has the singular form of being the cause of the delusion regarding Brahman—in the doctrine of Śaṅkara, namely the theory of Illusionism (*māyāvāda*). "At the beginning" (*ādau*) means first. Its primacy is indicated in relation to the faults that will be stated later. The analysis of the compound is "the scriptures of difference" (*bhedasya śrutayaḥ*). The meaning of the genitive case is both the state of being expressive of that [difference] and the state of being expressive of its pervaders, such as duality. Of those [scriptures], "having falsehood as their object" (*anṛtaviṣayatā*) means having a false referent (*mithyābhidheyakatā*).

The masculine form [of *śaradaḥ*] is applied according to the rule of *puṃvadbhāva*, as in the expression *śaradaḥ kṛtārthatā*. The intention is that, like a sentence such as "this is silver" (*idaṃ rajatam*), having an unreal object constitutes a primary defect; the underlying point is that its validity, characterized by the revelation of reality (*tattvāvedakatva*), would be lost.

Here, by the term "scriptural mention of difference" (bhedaśruti), there is intended the entire first part [of the Veda], which consists of injunctions for rituals—comprising sacrifices, gifts, oblations, and so forth, whether high or low—and which are embellished by various substances, deities, places, times, procedures, fruits, qualified agents, and expiations; and also that portion of the second part [of the Veda] which concerns the conscious and unconscious, their creation and so forth, their fruits of pleasure and pain, their causes such as sound and touch, and the controller of both.

The intended compositions are those that set forth the thousandfold distinctions of the Lord’s qualities, His divine form, the specific knowledge that is the means to attain Him, the specific states of liberation that are its fruit, the experience of the perfect Brahman preceded by that [knowledge], the service to Him preceded by that [experience], and the celestial queens, retinue, and other such attendants that facilitate that service. These are the works of those who speak of oneness.

In sentences such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), which are endowed with grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) that establishes non-difference, there is *lakṣaṇā* (indication), consisting in the abandonment of the qualifying portions (*viśeṣaṇāṃśatyāga*). The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to include the avoidance of the redundancy of other words. Following the apprehension of the primary power (*śakti*), the first to arise is the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) characterized by the property that serves as the ground for the application of the term (*pravṛttinimitta*).

Immediately thereafter, due to the agitation caused by fallacious arguments—such as the mutual identity between the genus, qualities, and so forth mentioned therein—the term "indication" (*lakṣaṇā*) is employed because it produces a cognition whose object is the qualified entity alone, excluding the qualifying attributes; this is on account of its similarity to "delayedness" (*vilambitatva*). As for the purpose, it has already been stated.

Regarding the passage beginning with "tadubhaya" and so forth: in establishing the authority of those two types of scriptural statements—namely, the statements concerning difference and the statements concerning non-difference—by first pacifying their contradiction through demonstrating a distinction in their respective objects; [this refers to] the words of those [scriptures] intent on reasoning, such as "He whose self is the body" and so forth. The form "tadubhaya" is a masculine compound according to the rule *sarvanāmno vṛttimātre* (Pāṇini 1.2.72). This was stated with reference to the actual entity (*vastu*).

Because the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is understood through scriptural texts concerning difference, while their non-difference is understood through scriptural texts concerning non-difference; and because, since difference and non-difference are contradictory, it is impossible for both to be true without the sublation of one of them; and because, through such passages as "He whose self is the body," the fact that both the conscious and the unconscious are the body of Brahman is understood; and because a body, like a genus or a quality, has the nature of being inseparably established (*apṛthaksiddha*) as a mode (*prakāra*) with respect to the substance—as in the case of a substance with respect to its genus or qualities—and because words denoting a mode have their power extending to the possessor of that mode (*prakārin*), [this applies] in such passages as "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*).

The identity between Śvetaketu’s body and that which is qualified by omniscience and other attributes is understood through the use of a common case-ending, just as in the expression "the blue lotus," where there is identity between that which is qualified by blueness and that which is qualified by lotus-ness. Furthermore, the scriptural texts concerning difference demonstrate the mutual distinction between the modes (prakāra) and the possessor of the modes (prakārī). Therefore, the fact that there is no contradiction between the scriptural texts on difference and non-difference is understood through the "reconciling" (ghaṭaka) texts; thus, it was said [in the commentary] that these texts are intent upon the reconciliation of both, in accordance with the actual state of things.
However, one should not think that this status of being a reconciler (ghaṭakatva) is accepted by the opponent.

"Abandonment from afar" means absolute renunciation. First, there is invalidity resulting from those [scriptural passages] such as "whose self is the body," because they are indeed texts teaching difference (*bheda-śruti*). Second, there is invalidity regarding that same portion [of the text], because—unlike the acceptance of a conventional relationship of cause and effect between the world and Brahman—the acceptance of a relationship of body and embodied being (*śarīra-śarīribhāva*) of that kind is absent; for while the texts teaching difference have unreal objects, the texts teaching non-difference, according to the aforementioned reasoning, merely present the essential nature (*svarūpa-mātra*), and thus both difference and non-difference are non-existent.

Since contradiction does not even arise [in this case], there is no need for a reconciling factor (*ghaṭaka*) to pacify it; thus, the third type of invalidity, which consists in being such a reconciling factor, is also excluded. This is what is intended by the phrase "by its very removal from afar" (*dūreṇaiva prahāṇam*), because when there is removal from afar, both the act of removing and the abandonment [of the third type] are established as a matter of course. Furthermore, by the phrase "that both," there is a general reference to all statements of identity, after which the determination of the specific [meaning] is established through logical fitness (*yogyatā*). In that regard, the scriptural testimony of identity (*aikya-śruti*) is of various kinds. Some conveys non-difference through the employment of identical case-endings (*samāna-vibhakti-nirdeśa*), such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) or "The Brahmas are the Dāśas" (*brahma dāśāḥ*), and so forth. And some...

One type of statement expressing oneness consists in the cognition of a unity characterized by the absence of a second of the same class, such as "the Teacher is one, without a second," and so forth. Another type, however, negates difference, such as "but where everything is this Self, how can there be duality here? or "here there is no diversity," and so forth. The purport of all three kinds of statements regarding unity is made known by the *ghaṭaka-śruti* (the unifying scriptural passage). Among these, the meaning of the non-difference scripture (*abheda-śruti*) is the non-distinction between the two entities that serve as the substrata for the two qualifiers.

The meaning of the scriptural texts concerning oneness (*ekatva*)—which consist in being devoid of a second of the same class—is that there exists no other entity of the same genus because [the Lord] is qualified by the sentient and the non-sentient as His body. The meaning of the scriptural texts negating difference is that there exists nothing whatsoever established independently of the Lord, since He is the mode (*prakāra*) of all things. This threefold purport of the scriptures on oneness is made known by such scriptural passages as "He whose self is the body" (*yasyātmā śarīram*).

Since even the scriptural teaching of absolute unity, when in conflict with the teaching of difference, cannot establish its own validity without a reconciling scripture that does not subvert one by the other, [the following must be understood]: therein, the meaning of the first and second teachings of difference is the mutual distinction between the qualifier and the qualified, and among the qualifiers themselves. In the third, however, although the non-Brahman nature [of the world] is negated, because its essential nature is not negated, the meaning of the teaching of difference is precisely that distinction [between Brahman and the world].

Therefore, by means of those constituent Śrutis that establish the relationship of qualifier and qualified through the body-and-body-possessor relation between the world and Brahman, the authority of both the Śrutis concerning difference and the Śrutis concerning non-difference is justified through the resolution of their apparent contradiction; thus it was said, "the conjunction of both," and so forth.

"Direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*) means that which is produced by the sense organs; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), inference (*anumāna*) is included. For such a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), "natural operation" (*svarasagati*) refers to its inherent capacity to bring about the cognition of an object possessing specific qualities (*saviśeṣa*). The "contradiction" (*hati*) of this—meaning its abandonment—is the point.

The meaning is that there is a loss of the inherent consistency of the means of valid cognition, such as perception, because perception is admitted to have "pure being" (*sanmātra*) as its object; because inference establishes properties such as eternality by taking a featureless entity as its subject (*pakṣa*); and because the inference establishing the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva*) is admitted to sublate the perception that apprehends the subject (*dharmin*). Regarding the phrase "tarka," etc.: *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) is the attribution of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) based on the attribution of the pervaded (*vyāpya*).

It is a specific type of knowledge, witnessed by such experiences as "I infer" or "I postulate," which assists the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and other means. Since this too has a qualified entity as its object, the disregard for it by those who maintain that the reality is devoid of qualifications (*nirviśeṣa*) is evident. For if perception were to grasp only pure existence (*sanmātra*), there would be the undesirable consequence of all cognitions being indistinguishable from one another, leading to the collapse of the distinction between purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*) and desistance (*nivṛtti*).

If one attempts to prove the oneness and other attributes of a featureless reality (*nirviśeṣavastu*) through inference, it follows as a consequence that it would possess specific qualities (*saviśeṣatva*) by virtue of the properties of the probandum and the probans. If Brahman were self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśatva*), it would follow that its concealment (*tirodhāna*) cannot be established; even if concealment were admitted, it would follow that it could never cease; and if there were concealment of that whose very nature is light, it would follow that its essential nature would be destroyed. Furthermore, if Brahman were an object of knowledge, it would follow that liberation could not be achieved through the knowledge of it.

If the production of the indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) is admitted, there follows the undesirable consequence that it would be perceived by those standing nearby. Furthermore, there is the consequence of the absence of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*) and so forth; and if a word were to produce immediate perception (*aparokṣa*), there would be the consequence of a confusion between the definitions of perception and other means of knowledge. If one accepts the reasoning called "the application of the definition of the apprehensible" (*grāhyalakṣaṇayoga*), which states that the relation between the seer and the seen is untenable, there follows the consequence that the empirical usage of consciousness (*caitanya*) could not be established.

And because they disregard reasonings such as the collapse of the category of difference (*bheda*) leading to the identity of Brahman and the insentient (*jaḍa*), it has been stated that there is a great deal of subversion by reasoning (*tarkabādha*). This is indicated by the word "and" (*ca*).

The overturning of the established order regarding the relative strength and weakness of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when they do not correspond to reality is here subsumed; likewise, the sublation of the principles (*nyāya*) set forth in the Sūtras is quite evident, and that too is included by the word "and" (*ca*).

He states that all of this does not exist within his own school with the words "tadetad" (this very thing). This refers to everything previously mentioned: the scripture on difference, the scripture on non-difference, the scripture on reconciliation, the means of valid cognition such as perception, and reasoning—[all of which are absent] in the system of Lakṣmaṇācārya, namely, in the established doctrine of Bhagavadrāmānuja.

The meaning is as follows: otherwise, [the text] would possess a mode of operation distinct from the modes mentioned in the alternative views; specifically, it would possess a correct mode characterized by being sequentially endowed with: (1) having truth as its object, (2) being expressive [of that truth], (3) removing contradictions, (4) having a qualified object, and (5) the absence of sublation by counter-arguments (*pratitarka*). However, the demonstration of this is not written here for fear of making the book too voluminous. In this context, the phrase "all this otherwise" refers first to the fact that the Śrutis concerning difference have truth as their object and are primary, while those concerning oneness are only indirectly compliant; and furthermore, it refers to those statements whose purpose is the reconciliation of both of these.

It is indicated that the study [of this work] should consist of a vast understanding of logic (*tarka*) and the comprehension of the natural course of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). By the phrases "in the Māyāvāda" and "in the view of Lakṣmaṇācārya," the analogy of Lakṣmaṇa and Meghanāda is suggested between one's own position and the opposing position. [End of verse 49].
*gaḍḍhandya ghddhaḍḍhadhtdṛdvadma* [Corrupt scribal notation].

He now states at length, through many verses in sequence, the very refutations of the opponent's views mentioned in the preceding verse: "The words of the Upaniṣads do not propound duality, for that is well-known; rather, let non-duality be accepted as that which is to be known, since it is beyond the scope of other means of cognition. Indeed, scripture is purposeful only regarding what has not been previously established; therefore, [your] effort is in vain."
But the distinction between that which is well-known and its opposite, which is the subject matter of the scriptures, is like your own non-duality.

"Upaniṣad-vācaḥ" means the Vedānta statements. "Dvaitam" means duality or difference. "Na pratipādayanti" means they do not teach or make known. "Dvitā" is the state of being two; "dvaitam" is simply that state of being two. The suffix *aṇ* is applied in its own sense (svārthe) because it belongs to the class beginning with *prajñā*. Furthermore, by the word "dvaita," which denotes duality, its pervader—namely, difference—is indicated, according to the statement: "Because it is based on distinctness, there would be a difference in ritual action due to the number. Thus, the meaning is that the Vedānta statements do not establish difference.

To the question "Why?", he says: "For it is well-known. That is, duality. "For it is well-known" means it is indeed apprehended through perception and other means of knowledge. Therefore, the meaning is that difference is not something to be established by the scripture (*śāstra*). The intended sūtra here is: "But the scripture [is authoritative] regarding an object not in contact [with the senses], because of the cognition arising from the word."
And by the term "not proximate" (asannikṛṣṭa), two things are here intended to be excluded:
either its determination through that very form, or its determination through the opposite of that.

The sense is this: according to the method stated above, since the fact of not being known by other means of knowledge (*māna*)—in the form of being the subject matter of the scripture—is required for something to be the subject matter of the scripture, this [difference] cannot be the subject matter of the scripture due to the absence of that [requirement]. Here, what is intended is that the difference between a jar and a cloth is established by perception, as well as the perception of the difference from the Lord in the form "I am not the Lord. To the question "In that case, what is it that is taught by the scripture?", he says: "But rather... That is to say: but rather, in the absence of difference being the subject matter of the scripture.

Non-duality (*advaita*) means non-distinction (*abheda*). By the reason of being "not within the scope of anything else"—that is, by virtue of not being the object of any means of valid cognition other than scripture—that which is to be known is what is propounded by the *Upaniṣads*. "Let it be accepted" means "let it be affirmed by you"; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "Because [it concerns] what has not been attained," and so forth. Scripture—consisting of the Veda—is instruction for one's welfare, whose sole inclination is to make known what was previously unknown. "In regard to what has not been attained" means in regard to an object that is not the province of any proving or subverting means of valid cognition. Indeed, it is "purposeful"—that is, it certainly possesses the purpose consisting in making known what was previously unknown.

Therefore, the meaning is that because it is not apprehended by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), non-difference alone is what is to be understood from the scripture. Thus, "effort" refers to an exertion involving hardship directed toward establishing the aforementioned point. That effort is "vain," meaning purposeless. To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "Because..."—that is, because [non-difference] is distinct from well-known differences such as those between jars and cloths, which are the objects of other means of valid cognition.

The other type of difference—namely, the difference consisting of the relations of cause and effect, part and whole, controller and controlled, object of meditation and meditator, and goal and means—is, like your non-dualism, a subject matter of scripture, being equal to the identity between the individual soul and the Lord as accepted by you.

The meaning is that [the Self] possesses a connection with the scripture (*śāstra*) in the form of being the subject matter (*pratipādya*) of that scripture. It is called "object" (*viṣaya*) because it binds (*visinoti*); from the root *ṣiñ* in the sense of "binding," the suffix *vatip* is justified by the rule "if the action is similar to that. Alternatively, its justification may be through the supplied verb "to be" (*bhavati*). Just as in the perceptual cognition of identity such as "This is that Devadatta," you yourself accept that the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*para*), though not the object of that perception, is nevertheless established by the scripture.

Similarly, although the distinction between jars, cloths, and so forth is established by perception and other means of knowledge, we maintain that the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para)—consisting of the relationship between the controller and the controlled—is not an object of such [empirical] cognition, and therefore it is to be understood through the scriptures. Consequently, this effort of yours, expressed in the statement "they do not teach duality" and so on, is fruitless because it is useless for defeating an opponent; this is the response of the proponent (siddhāntin) directed at the proponent of falsehood.

Regarding this, the venerable Bhaṭṭa Sudarśana says: "If it is argued that because mere difference is established by worldly experience, non-difference alone is what is to be known through scripture—on the basis of the maxim that 'scripture is purposeful only with regard to what is not already established'—then that is incorrect. For in such cases as 'this is that Devadatta,' since mere non-difference is established by worldly experience, and since scripture is purposeful only regarding what is not already established, the teaching of non-difference by means of scripture would be improper. Indeed, the identity of Devadatta and others is established by the world, but [the identity] of the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para) is not."

If it is argued that, therefore, the non-difference between those two is what is to be known from the scripture (*śāstra*), then [we reply]: in that case, while the difference between a jar and a cloth is indeed established by common worldly experience (*lokasiddha*), the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*)—characterized by the states of being the controlled and the controller, the supported and the supporter, the subordinate and the principal, and the pervaded and the pervader—is not established by worldly experience; thus, that difference is indeed to be established solely by the scripture. || 50 ||
He states that the mutual difference between individual souls is established by the Śruti:
when the Śvetāśvatara Śruti declares, "One among many," the injunction therein refers to a qualified subject, just as in the case of the eight-pot-sherd (aṣṭākapāla) sacrifice and others.

How could one know from any source other than the Veda that the Self is eternal and manifold? Furthermore, how could there be a clear distinction between self and other, and between the internal and external states, in the state of liberation? (51)

The Śvetāśvatara Śruti: "The eternal among the eternals, the conscious among the conscious, the one who bestows desires upon the many"—this is a mantra from the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad. By the phrase "the one among the many," [it] speaks of—that is, makes known—the plurality of selves (ātman). "Therein" means: in the doctrine that the aforementioned Śruti makes known the plurality of selves. "Like the eight-potherd [cake]" refers to the passage: "That which belongs to Agni is the eight-potherd [cake]."

"According to such rules" means according to the rule for enjoining the *āgneya* sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) as qualified by its being prepared on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*). Here too, the justification for the suffix *-vat* should be understood as before. "An injunction concerning a qualified object" refers to an injunction in the form of making known what was previously unknown, concerning the *pradhāna* (the primary matter) as qualified by eternal, multiple conscious beings. "Is accepted" (*āsthīyate*) means it is asserted (*pratijñāyate*). The connection with the recurring term "let it be accepted" (*āsthīyatām*) is made by changing the case-ending. The word "but" (*tu*) serves to dispel doubt. "Eternal among the eternal... (*nityo nityānām*)... [text fragment].

There are two doubts: first, that because the verse "The one conscious being among the conscious, who ordains the desires of many" is intent upon the ordaining of desires, it has no purport regarding [the Lord's] eternality or plurality; for if that were the case, there would be the consequence of a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*); and second, that this demonstration of the Lord's consciousness, eternality, and plurality is unnecessary.

The use of the word "tu" (but) is intended to indicate that [the objection] has been refuted by demonstrating the necessity of [accepting] the dependence [of the texts on the plurality of selves], based on the desire to understand the excellence of the granting of desires; for when it is stated that even though many eternal [desires] are granted, the granting of many eternal desires constitutes an excellence over the granting of a few non-eternal desires by resorting to a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), then the excellence of the granting of desires is established. Now, an objection might be raised: "Since the plurality of selves is already established in the world, the scripture has no purport regarding that; for scripture is meaningful only with respect to what is not already known. To this doubt, he says: "Because of its eternality," and so forth.

“Nityatvātmānaḥ” means selves accompanied by eternality. The compound is formed either with the word “sup” (as a case-ending) or by splitting the rule (*yogavibhāga*) as “tṛtīyā. “Nityatvātmabahutvam” refers to the plurality of selves characterized by eternality. Here—meaning in the world—and “elsewhere than the Veda” (*nigamād anyatra*) means other than the scripture shown above, namely from perception and so forth. “How do we know? means “we do not know. The locative case in “anyatra” is used because the cause is intended to be expressed as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

The meaning is as follows: the perception of a plurality of selves conjoined with non-conscious matter (acit) is established by worldly experience. However, since a plurality of the nature of the pure self is not established by worldly experience, it is indeed possible for the scripture to have its purport there. For in the Śruti, through the connection "of many eternal conscious beings," and according to the principle that "the qualified [is understood] by means of the qualification," a plurality qualified by eternality is obtained; thus, the status of being the delimiting factor (avacchedakatā) for plurality is obtained within eternality.

Since the conditioned form is impermanent and the extracted essential nature alone is eternal, when the multiplicity of selves is understood through that [essential nature] as its delimitation, the multiplicity of the pure self-nature is established; thus, it is indeed possible for the purport of the scripture to lie therein. Nor should it be argued that in the Śruti, the connection "the eternal among the eternals, the conscious among the conscious" is due to mere proximity.

Since grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible, it is inappropriate to assume a lack of coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*); furthermore, in the case of "one [rite] for many," a discrepancy in form would result, which is untenable. As for proximity (*sānnidhya*), its function is exhausted by merely indicating that the prescription of optional rites is appropriate for a permanent rite (*nitya*); thus, it does not contradict coreferentiality. Moreover, because proximity is a weaker means of proof, it is not capable of subverting coreferentiality in the form of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).

In the Śruti passage "of many eternal [souls]," the author has adopted the phrasing "eternal-ness-and-the-multiplicity-of-selves" (*nityatvātmabahutvam*) as a compound containing a third-case tatpuruṣa (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*), specifically to indicate that the understanding occurs according to the principle of "the qualification of the qualified" (*viśiṣṭasya vaiśiṣṭyam*). It is not, however, a compound containing a karmadhāraya such as "eternal-self-multiplicity" (*nityātmabahutvam*). Alternatively, it may be a collective dvandva (*samāhāra-dvandva*) meaning "eternal-ness and self-multiplicity" (*nityatvaṃ cātmabahutvaṃ ca*).

Since that [term "eternal"] signifies a collection (*samūha*), and since a collection consists of multiple entities existing in one place at one time, it is established that eternity and plurality reside in the self (*ātman*) at one and the same time; thus, the plurality of the pure nature of the self is attained. Furthermore, this is because the scripture (*śruti*) accepts the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "of many eternal ones.

And since the Tantrikas maintain that even identity of time (*kālaikya*) is manifested therein, the fact that eternity and plurality reside in the selves at one and the same time is secured by the scripture—

The grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) [of the term "souls"] in the verse is explained by employing a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). This has been stated by the venerable Sudarśana Bhaṭṭapāda: "When plurality is expressed as being coreferential with eternity, it is indeed the plurality of the nature of the pure selves that is stated. Therefore, the essential point is that the multiplicity of selves, established through the principle of distinctness (*pṛthaktva*), is the means for establishing the difference between selves.

He states that even in the state of liberation there is mutual difference among liberated selves whose natures have been extracted from adjuncts, by means of the passage beginning with "by way of interiority" (*pratyaktvena*). "By way of interiority" means by being cognizable through the notion of "I" (*ahaṃ-buddhi*); "by way of exteriority" means by being cognizable through the notion of "this" (*idaṃ-buddhi*). The meaning is that the mutual difference between oneself and others—that is, between liberated beings and another liberated being—is clearly evident in the scriptures. The point is that because of the superimposition of contradictory attributes in the form of interiority and exteriority, the difference between selves is established by scripture even in the state of liberation.

In the Śrutis, the conventional usage of "I" and "this" among liberated beings is to be observed here and there. (Alternatively, the portion ending with "of oneself and others" refers to the establishment of difference during the state of transmigratory existence; "in liberation," however, refers to the establishment of that [non-difference] in the state of mokṣa. Furthermore, this refutation of the claim that the Śrutis concerning difference have as their object what is unreal (anṛta)—namely, the position that scriptural mentions of difference are merely restatements (anuvāda) for the purpose of negating difference—is also an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) of the rejection of other such positions. || 51 ||

First, the opponent’s position—that the scriptures concerning difference have falsehood as their object—was refuted in detail. Now, he refutes in detail the position stated [by the opponent] that there is metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for words denoting oneness:
"In all collections of words that share grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the non-dualist must state what distinct entity is conveyed by each individual word."

Alternatively, if [the word] "not" (na) were not recited because it would be meaningless, then the term "non-one" (nekātirikta) would not be recited; however, for the opponent, otherwise, this logical consequence (yukti) would apply to himself. || 52 ||

Vyā—For others have asserted that a sentence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) has an indivisible meaning (*akhaṇḍārtha*). To explain: since it is established by linguistic convention that coreferentiality refers to a single referent, and since it is not established that the words [in such a sentence] refer either merely to qualifiers or to qualified entities, it follows that words in grammatical coreferentiality with "Being" (*satya*), etc., refer solely to the identity of their essential natures (*svarūpa-mātra-ekya*). He refutes this with the passage beginning "sāmānādhikaraṇya... and so on. [The word] "in all" refers to those [sentences] that are not in grammatical coreferentiality (*vyadhikaraṇa*).

And "in the case of coreferential [words]. Among the clusters of words—that is, among sentences—[it occurs] in those that possess coreferentiality: in words that are coreferential (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Those whose expressed object (*vācya*) is a single common substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) are thus called coreferential; the state of being so is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and "possessing that" means having a connection to it. The locative case is used here because one intends to express the instrument (*karaṇa*) itself as the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*). "To be conveyed" means to be understood. "In each word" means in those respective individual words.

"Is it distinct? means "is it different. Alternatively—"or else"—"no" (*na*) refers to the question "it is not distinct. "By the Advaitin" means by one who accepts a reality devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣa-vastu*), that is, by a proponent of falsehood (*mṛṣāvādin*). "What is to be said?"—the word "what" (*kiṃ*) here has the sense of negation or censure; the meaning is that not even one of the two aforementioned alternatives can be stated. This refers to the question: in the case of words in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa-pada*), does there exist a distinction between what is conveyed by one word and what is conveyed by the other, or not?

The meaning is that a liar is able to offer any answer whatsoever. To the question "Why?", he says: "If not," and so forth. Because it resides in the intellect, the second head is refuted first. "If not what is to be made known" means "if it is not distinct. "Exceeding the one" means exceeding each respective single word intended [by the speaker]. The word is "meaningless" by reason of the absence of a purpose consisting in the communication of a meaning not already communicated by other words.

"It would not be recited"—the meaning is "it would not be studied," based on the maxim that words whose meaning has already been expressed are not employed; such is the intended sense. And thus, the underlying point is that there would be the consequence of the recitation being rendered purposeless.

This is an illustration: [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the words are synonyms; because of the absence of a difference in the grounds for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*), there would be the undesirable consequence of losing the defining characteristic of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); if the unity conveyed by coreferentiality were distinct from the essential nature (*svarūpa*) [of the referent], there would be the undesirable consequence of its being determinate (*sakhaṇḍatva*); and if it were not distinct, since it would not contradict the essential nature already understood through the nominal stems, there could be no abandonment of the qualifiers—this too should be understood.

By the phrase "in all collections of words," it is indicated that in all sentences whatsoever, what is to be conveyed is merely a specific relation between the meanings established by the etymological derivation of the words. Therefore, in the case of coreferential (samānādhikaraṇa) terms, it is not appropriate to abandon the primary denotative causes (pravṛttinimitta) established by their respective derivations. Rather, the meaning suggested is this: the identity understood from the common case-ending is, without contradicting the connection with the qualifiers understood from the nominal stems, primarily the identity of the qualified entities themselves.

First, he refutes the initial position with the words "Otherwise," and so forth. "Otherwise" means: if the object to be conveyed (*pratyāyya*) were distinct in each word, such that the words "Satya" and the others were intended merely to exclude what is contrary to their respective referents (*tattatpadārthavirodhivyāvṛttimātraparatve*), or if they were intended to denote the essential nature (*svarūpa*) as delimited by the exclusion of the contrary (*virodhivyāvṛttyavacchinnasvarūpaparatve*). In this case, the opponent's argument—the reason consisting in the non-establishment of unity as understood through the identical case-endings (*samānavibhaktyavagataikyāsiddhi*), which is accepted by our opponent as proving the indivisible sentence-meaning (*akhaṇḍavākyārtha*)—would undermine his own position. "His own" refers to the position belonging to the opponent.

"Āsīdati" means that it "attains" by way of the absence of contradiction. The opponent's objection—that if the words "satya" (truth) and so forth refer merely to the exclusion of their opposites, then oneness is not established because the exclusions differ according to the difference in their counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*); and if they refer to the essential nature as delimited by those exclusions, then if the exclusions are mere secondary indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*), other words become redundant, whereas if they are primary qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), oneness of meaning is not established—this same defect applies to the proponent’s own position as well. This is the intended sense.

That the unity of meaning is established in the primary sense of the substantive (viśeṣya), even though there is a difference in the meanings of the qualifying attributes (viśeṣaṇa), is common to both positions. However, the meaning of the word "but" (tu) is that the distinction lies in this: in the final doctrine (siddhānta), words possess their primary (mukhya) denotative power, whereas in the alternative position, they function as indicators (lakṣaka) by excluding their respective opposites. || 52 ||

Thus, with these three verses, the two positions previously accepted by the opponent—that first, the scriptural texts concerning difference have falsehood as their object, and second, the texts expressing unity possess figurative meaning (*lakṣaṇā*)—have been refuted in detail. As for the statement that "the texts intent on effecting the union of those two [truths] are set aside from afar," this has already been refuted by the refutation of the falsehood of the scriptural texts concerning difference, since even the "uniting" texts are themselves texts concerning difference; therefore, they were not refuted separately.
This was indicated by the separate mention in the phrase "set aside from afar," regarding words such as "body" (*śarīra*) in passages like "He whose self is the body."

Since the opponent accepts that [the word "world"] indicates dependence on that [Brahman], even the charge of metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) would follow in that respect; however, such an additional refutation is far from necessary, as it has already been stated in this very context, so there is no need for further elaboration there. Therefore, he now clarifies how the order of presentation here results in a loss of the natural consistency of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), such as perception:
"Regarding those who have declared that 'what is censured is unreal because it is perceptible,' citing the silver superimposed on mother-of-pearl as an example, we say this in response."

Furthermore, this "conditionality" (sopādhikatva), established by a means of knowledge that apprehends the subject itself, is clearly of the same nature [as the probandum], unbroken, and a deviating mark; it shall lead to your own destruction. // 53 //

Others have stated as follows: the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is established by the inference: "The disputed phenomenal world is false because it is perceptible, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. Here, the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*) is falsity, defined either as being perceived in the locus of its own absence, or as being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence that resides in the same locus as itself, or as being removable by knowledge. The reason (*hetu*) is perceptibility, which consists in being an object of knowledge.

Since the relation of inherence-in-the-conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*) is necessary for the perception of a substance as inherent [in another], and since that relation is absent here, an "otherwise-appearance" (*anyathākhyāti*) of silverhood is impossible; therefore, an unprecedented silver, which is indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) and manifested by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣibhāsya*), arises within the mother-of-pearl. And because that substance is sublated by knowledge (*dṛṅnivartya*), it alone serves as the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) on the basis of being the locus for determining the pervasion (*vyāpti*). He restates this very point with the words beginning "because of perceptibility" (*dṛśyatvāt*). Here, the meaning is "certain proponents of falsity" (*mṛṣāvādinaḥ*).

Silver superimposed upon mother-of-pearl—meaning silver that constitutes the objective qualifier (*prakāra*) of an error having mother-of-pearl as its substantive object (*viśeṣya*); or else, because of the absence of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) established for the production of silver.

And because it is not perceived when standing beside [the mother-of-pearl], that silver—whose production there is simply impossible—is merely said to have been produced in the mother-of-pearl through one's own mental fabrication (*kusṛṣṭi*). Being "those who cite an example" (*dṛṣṭāntayantaḥ*) means those who state an example that serves as the ground for the ascertainment of pervasion (*vyāpti*). It is stated that the silver is "superimposed on the mother-of-pearl" in order to reveal the opponent's intended refutation, namely the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the example. The word *utpanna* is derived from the root *ud-bhū*, meaning "to arise," with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) applied and the past passive participle suffix (*kta*) added in the sense of the object (*karman*).

And here, regarding the phrase "citing an illustration" (*dṛṣṭāntayanta*), the causative suffix *ṇic* has the sense of narration, according to the rule *tat karoti tad ācaṣṭe*. The underlying intention is that there is no requirement for the production of silver there [in the shell], because either (1) the theory of misapprehension as something else (*anyathākhyāti*) is accepted on the grounds of the proximity of cognition and the established existence of the silver perceived in the bangle, or (2) the theory of apprehension of the object as it is (*yathārthakhyāti*) is accepted, whereby the apprehension of silver is logically accounted for. The term "disputed" (*vigītam*) means "subjected to controversy"; the word "world" (*jagat*) is to be supplied as the remainder, since the word "of the world" (*jagataḥ*) is used in the following verse.

This is the statement of the subject (*pakṣanirdeśa*). "Unreal" (*anṛtam*)—meaning possessing falsity in the form of being sublatable by knowledge (*jñānanivartyatva*). This is the presentation of the probandum (*sādhyasamarpakam*). "Because of being visible" (*dṛśyatvāt*), that is, because of being an object of knowledge (*jñānaviṣayatvāt*). This is the statement of the reason (*hetūkti*). Thus, the inference of the form: "The world under dispute is unreal because it is visible, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell"—this is what they "sang" (*jaguḥ*), meaning they said. The term "singing" (*gāna*) is used because it is intended to delight people who are like children or cattle.

"In the presence of that crest-jewel of the Vedic assembly, what possibility is there for an opponent?"—thus they spoke according to the manner previously described; the use of the third person ("they spoke") is an indirect reference. To this, we reply: in that inference, there are these three refutations, namely: the designation of a lapse of time (*kālatyayāpadeśa*), the presence of a limiting condition (*sopādhikatva*), and contradiction (*vyāghāta*).

The meaning is that by the latter half of the preceding verse, we—who follow the heart of the author of the Sūtras—state [our position]. Therein, with the second half of this verse, beginning with the words "dharmigrāhaka... (by the grasper of the locus), he first states the "indication of the lapse of time" (*kālātyayāpadeśa*) and the "presence of a limiting condition" (*sopādhikatva*). "This" refers to the inference of falsity (*mithyātva*) which has the world as its subject (*pakṣa*) and perceptibility (*dṛśyatva*) as its reason (*hetu*).

By means of the perception that apprehends the subject (*dharmin*)—which apprehends the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) as its subject while grasping its truthfulness—this inference is sublated (*bādhita*) because it apprehends the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), which has been set aside by the very cognition that apprehends the subject as having the nature of falsity. Therefore, the meaning is that this inference is defective. As the venerable Bhaṭṭa Sudarśana said: "In that case, is the substratum (*āśraya*) cognized or not? If it is not, there is the fallacy of the unestablished substratum (*āśrayāsiddhi*)."

[The objection that] "the proof of its falsity by means of perception and other valid cognitions [is contradicted] by the very cognition that apprehends the subject" is refuted. Thus it is also stated in the *Caṇḍamāruta*: "Cognition regarding the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is self-luminous and intrinsically valid."

Therefore, since the perception that apprehends the objectivity and the truth-status (*pramātva*) of objects such as a jar has already grasped the fact that the jar is an object of valid cognition, the inference of falsity (*mithyātva*) is sublated—just as the inference of non-heat is sublated by the perception of heat—and thus [the reason] is "vitiated by a limiting condition" (*sopādhika*), and so forth. (The word *punaḥ* here signifies "again," and the particle *ca* serves to aggregate the three qualifiers. This is stated in the Sūtra: "And because of dissimilarity, it is not like dreams and the like. (*Vaidharmyācca na svapnādivat*).

*Abhaṅguram* means "unbroken," that is, not refuted because it possesses both subsistence in the locus of the probandum (*pakṣadharmatva*) and co-extensive pervasion with the probandum (*sādhyasamavyāpti*), and thus cannot be dismissed as a pseudo-reason (*upādhi*). *Vyabhicarat* means "erring," i.e., existing in that which lacks the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavadvṛtti*). That by which the reason—namely, "because of visibility" (*dṛśyatvāt*)—is so characterized is described as such. The state of being made known (*jñāpyatva*) is the meaning of the third case (*tṛtīyārtha*) in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*). The sense is: "that which makes known the errancy of the reason. It is stated thus because the pseudo-reason (*upādhi*) is precisely what brings about the cognition of errancy. *Sopādhikatvam* (the state of having a pseudo-reason) consists in possessing a pseudo-reason in the form of being sublated (*bādhitatva*) when a [specific] pseudo-reason is apprehended.

The word *punaḥ* is a rhetorical ornament (*vākyālaṅkāra*). The word *ca* (and) is a conjunctive particle (*samuccāyaka*) that collects the previously mentioned defects. *Vaḥ* means "of you," the disputants (*vādin*). *Bhaṅgāya* means "for the sake of defeat" (*parājayahetu*). The sense is that the "indication of the lapse of time" (*kālātyayāpadeśa*) and its being "actually characterized by a limiting condition" (*sopādhikatva*) bring about the defeat of the disputant, either directly or through the medium of the "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) fallacy. Alternatively, *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* refers to "visibility" (*dṛśyatva*), and *abhaṅgura* refers to the "limiting condition" (*sopādhikatva*) found in the Sūtra; in this case, the word *punaḥ* has the meaning of the word *ca* (and).

The logical mark (*liṅga*) "because it is seen" (*dṛśyatvāt*), which you employ [to prove that Brahman is not the cause], is non-conclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to Brahman; this is the construction of the argument. It has been stated thus because the quality of being "seen" exists in Brahman according to the natural force (*svārasya*) of the Śruti and Smṛti. Regarding this, they say: "And the quality of being seen is fallacious (*vyabhicārin*) with respect to Brahman. By the general term "logical mark," the refutation of other reasons such as "being excluded from the world" (*vyāvartamānatva*) is also established. This very point regarding the presence of a limiting condition (*sopādhikatva*) has been explained at length by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Sudarśana; that should be investigated in his own work.
By this statement, "It is evident," the proponent reveals his extreme lack of skill in formulation, [thinking] that even for children this qualified nature (sopādhikatva) is clear. || 53 ||
Now he states the contradiction:

"If the falsity of the world, established through delusion, is indeed sublated, then the reason [of yours] proves what is already proven; or if the manifold world (prapañca) is real, then there is the loss of non-duality."
If the object to be established (*sādhya*) is the very nature of Brahman, then it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatva*);
and thus, the path of refuting the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is discarded by you from afar.

In this context, the two words *yat* and *tat* must be supplied. Thus, the construction is: "If that falsity which is being established for the world is established by error. "Established by error" means existing as a mode of error; that is to say, it is false. The meaning is: "if there were falsity in the falsity of the world which one intends to prove. The reason (*hetu*) consists of such factors as "being an object of perception" (*dṛśyatva*). "Siddhasādhya" is a compound analyzed as: "that whose probandum (*sādhya*) is already established (*siddha*)—i.e., already known through another means of valid cognition (*māna*)."

In this context, there is an elision of the word *syāt* (might be). Here, it would appear that, according to the literal reading, the reason (*hetu*) suffers from the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*). However, that is not the case. As stated in the *Caṇḍamāruta*: "Even if falsity (*mithyātva*) is in fact false, since falsity in that [specific] form is not the intended probandum (*asādhya*), the fallacy of proving the already established is impossible; therefore, it is merely a different matter (*arthāntara*). Furthermore, if falsity were false, there would be no contradiction with ultimate reality, just as there is no contradiction between the superimposed yellowness of a conch shell and its actual whiteness; thus, it is a different matter."

Therefore, the meaning is that here the reason would be one whose probandum is already established (*siddhasādhya*), which would result in a shift of the subject matter (*arthāntara*). He states the consequence of this: "the world-phenomenon (*prapañca*) becomes real. The meaning is that there is no loss of the reality of the world-phenomenon, because there is no contradiction between that which has superimposed falsity and ultimate reality (*pāramārthikasatyatva*). If...

“*Vetyādi* (‘or... etc.’): the meaning is ‘if that falsity were real (*satya*)’. Regarding the phrase ‘there would be the loss of non-duality (*advaitahāni*)’, the sense is that in that case, it [falsity] would be distinct from the nature of Brahman, and so forth. The meaning is that if the falsity intended to be proven were real, and if it were distinct from the nature of Brahman, it would follow that Brahman possesses a second entity (*sadvitīyatva*) by virtue of that real thing. Anticipating the objection that it might not be distinct from the nature of Brahman precisely because it is real, he refutes it with: ‘If the probandum [falsity] were the very nature of Brahman...’”

The intention of the doubt is this: "If [the world] is not distinct from the nature of Brahman, then there is no loss of non-duality (advaita), nor is there the reality of the world; thus, it would merely be a case of proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatva), or rather, it would be a different point altogether (arthāntara), since we ourselves accept the nature of Brahman. By the use of the word "eva" (only/merely), it is indicated that the previously mentioned fault indeed follows. He states the resulting conclusion: "And so" (evañca). "In this way"—that is, by the aforementioned method—your path for the elimination of the phenomenal world (prapañcavyudasana), namely your procedure of inferring the falsity of the world as stated by you, is refuted from afar.

The meaning is that [the argument] is refuted because it leads to a logical contradiction (*vyāghāta*) through the alternative options regarding whether the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*) or not ultimately real. Furthermore, the use of the word "and" (*ca*) is intended to indicate that this is not a "perpetual fault" (*nityasama*) consisting of a refutation by establishing a succession of non-authoritative properties, since you yourself admit the sublation (*bādhyatva*) of the very sublation of knowledge asserted by the Mādhyamika. Regarding this, the venerable Bhaṭṭa Sudarśana said: "When the alternative between the ultimate reality or non-reality of the property to be proven is raised, if it is ultimately real, there is a loss of non-duality (*advaitahāni*)."

Furthermore, the reason "being perceptible" is inconclusive (anaikāntya), because it applies even to the ultimate reality (paramārtha). If [perceptibility] were not ultimate, it would follow that the phenomenal world (prapañca) is real, according to the logical principle that "when the sublater is sublated, the nature of the sublated is not sublated," and so forth. || 54 ||

If it is objected: "But since the sūtra *vaidharmyācca na svapnādivat* is intended to demonstrate that the Yogācāra inference—'The cognition of the waking state is without an external object (*nirālambana*), because it is a cognition, like a dream-cognition'—is fallacious due to the presence of a limiting condition (*sopādhikatva*), how can it be said that this sūtra demonstrates the presence of a limiting condition in the inference of falsity (*mithyātva*) put forward by the proponents of falsity (*mṛṣāvādins*)? To this they reply: There is no fault, because there is no difference between the proponents of falsity and the Yogācāras regarding their acceptance of the falsity of objects.
This has been stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Sudarśana: "Because the fact of being sublated while yet being perceived is accepted by both parties."

Thus, since the status of being a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is equally established even in the view that [the world] is indescribable (*anirvacanīya*), with respect to both the defect in the cause and the subverting cognition (*bādhapratyaya*), so too has it been stated in the *Caṇḍamāruta*: "The Buddhist inference—that waking cognition is without a real object (*nirālambana*) because it is a cognition, like a dream cognition—was refuted by the Blessed One in the *Sūtra-bhāṣya* on the grounds of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). [The Māyāvādin] has stated: 'The world is false because it is an object of perception, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, dream objects, and the like.'"

And thus, since there is no distinction between proving that [the world] has a false object by means of its being a cognition and proving its falsity by means of its being an object of a cognition, the very refutations of the reason "being a cognition" apply equally to the reason "being an object thereof. Therefore, in order to demonstrate that the [reason] stated in the Sūtra is *sopādhika* (vitiated by a limiting condition), he states the lack of distinction between the Yogācāras and the proponents of falsity (*mṛṣāvādins*) regarding their acceptance of the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*): "In the view of the Yogācāras, when it is proclaimed that 'everything other than pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) is false,' that which is to be made into an Upaniṣadic truth is thereby drawn forth [into the fold]."

For the proponents of Māyāvāda, following a system based on scriptures not recognized by others and devoid of other means of valid cognition, cast aside those very means of valid cognition along with their underlying logical principles. || 55 ||

According to the Yogācāra school—among the four disciples of the Buddha, namely the Vaibhāṣika, Sautrāntika, Yogācāra, and Mādhyamika, this refers to the view of the third, known as the Yogācāra: consciousness alone (*cideva cinmātram*). The compound is formed with the word *mātra* according to the rule for the *mayūravyaṃsaka* class of compounds. The lexicon states: "The word *mātra* [is used] in the sense of 'only' (*kārtsnya*) or 'restriction' (*avadhāraṇa*). "Distinct from that" (*tadvyatireki*) means devoid of all particularities designated as internal differences distinct from its own nature (*svarūpa*). "Apart from consciousness" (*saṃvidvyatiriktam*). "Everything" (*sakalam*) refers to the forms of the knower, the known, and so forth.

*Vastu* means the collection of objects. The statement of "being a real entity" (*vastutva*) refers either to its status as an established conclusion (*siddhānta*) or to its being regarded as real according to the opponent's own accepted conventional truth. *Mithyā* refers to that which is proclaimed repeatedly—that is, the inference of falsity (*mithyātvānumāna*) stated over and over again. This is derived from the root *ghuṣ* with the suffix *yaṅ* (indicating repetition) and the suffix *yat* in the sense of the object (*karman*). The inference of the world's falsity, such as "the cognition of the waking state [is false]," etc., has been stated many times by the Yogācāras. *Tat* (that) refers to the inference of falsity; it is the object (*karman*).

And this [word "to"] connects with the phrase "to do this. "Unperceived" means not cognized. "Of the Vedas" refers to the *nigamas*—the scriptures—which are intent upon the truth of the manifest world, intent upon the negation of things established in themselves, and intent upon the negation of qualities to be abandoned in Brahman. "Of the principles of reasoning" refers to the principles of general rule and exception (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*), general injunction and specific prohibition (*utsarga-apavāda*), initial statement and contradiction (*upakrama-virodha*), the principle of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and the principle of all Vedic branches being consistent (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya*).

And [this applies] to the principles of *apaccheda*, *jaratila*, and so forth; as well as to the two other means of valid cognition, namely perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). By those who have set forth their systems—that is, by those who have established the sequence for making known the objects of knowledge—by the proponents of Māyā, the followers of Śaṅkara who maintain that ignorance (*ajñāna*) is an indefinable positive entity (*anirvacanīyabhāvarūpa*); [they act] in order to "Upaniṣad-ize" it—to make it the subject matter propounded by the Upaniṣads. By the use of the suffix *cvipratyaya*, it is indicated that the Upaniṣads do not have that as their primary purport; the ellipsis is "the Upaniṣads are drawn away" from that meaning.

The meaning is this: having drawn away even the poor Upaniṣads—which, being inclined toward the reality of phenomenal diversity (*prapañca*), do not desire [the world's falsity] for that very reason—one intends to cast them into the great well consisting of the world’s falsity. Although the denial of the world is common to both, the core point is that the Māyāvādins commit a greater betrayal of the Śruti than the Yogācārins. Thus, the intention is that the "conditioned nature" (*sopādhikatva*) mentioned in the Sūtra applies equally to the position of the Māyāvādins as well.

Regarding this, he concludes the refutation of the inference for the falsity [of the world] stated in the passage beginning with "tatredamācakṣmahe" by means of the verse beginning with "apahastayanti. "Pramāṇas" refers to those consisting of perception, inference, and scripture. "Together with the nyāyas" means together with the favorable logical arguments (anukūlatarka) that constitute its own retinue, as well as the nyāyas such as "introduction" (upakrama) and so forth, which are woven into the Mīmāṃsā treatises. "That" refers to the action of the inference for the falsity of the phenomenal world (prapañca). "They cast aside" (apahastayanti) means they drive it out from the assembly of authoritative evidence by seizing it by the hand—that is, they refute it.

Alternatively, *yadvā tad* is in the nominative case. *Tat* refers to that inference of falsity (*mithyātvānumāna*), which is being "drawn"—that is, brought by force even against its will—to be made "Upaniṣadic," meaning to be rendered in the form of reasoning that supports the Upaniṣads. *Tat*—the inference of falsity being drawn—is the object. The meaning is that they "dismiss" the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇas*) along with their logical arguments (*nyāyas*) by seizing them with the hand and turning them back. And here, there is no need to supply the word *upaniṣad*. For in the previous construction:

The attainment of a superior state by that which is inferior cannot be "drawing" (ākarṣaṇa); for since the inferior, desiring the superior state, proceeds spontaneously of its own accord, it has no need for being drawn. Therefore, it is appropriate that the Upaniṣad itself—which does not even wish to contemplate an inferior state with its mind—be what draws [the soul] there. Since the question "In what sense do we cause it to fall? is well-known, the word "falling" (pātana) is supplied by ellipsis.

In this analogy, however, just as certain individuals of the Caṇḍāla caste—though restrained by their own lack of qualification and held back by others who speak with the authority of Brahmins—are nevertheless dragged toward being admitted into the Brāhmaṇa fold despite their own unwillingness due to an awareness of their unfitness, and are then cast away from afar by the best of Brāhmaṇas along with their followers, the Kṣatriyas and others; so too is the inference of falsity (mithyātva) stated by the Yogācāras, though it is inherently weak due to the very nature of the object, dragged toward being made Upaniṣadic by those who propound falsehoods.

And since they cast aside the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) along with the logical arguments (*nyāya*), the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) is justified by the force of the context; for the word *hi* functions in the sense of "and" (*ca*). In the previous construction, however, the word *hi* signifies "well-known" (*prasiddhi*). [This is according to the rule: "The meaning of the verbal root [is expressed] from the agent and the instrument. || 55 ||

[Objection: But surely, since the Yogācāras accept multiplicity and momentariness regarding the aspect of consciousness (*cidaṃśa*), whereas the proponents of falsity (*mṛṣāvādins*) accept permanence and unity therein, how can it be said that "every entity distinct from pure consciousness is false," and so forth? Anticipating this objection, [the author] replies that because there is no difference in their being distinct from consciousness, the falsity of multiplicity and other such attributes belonging to consciousness is likewise identical in both systems; therefore, it is entirely appropriate to state that "every entity distinct from pure consciousness is false," and so on. Thus he refutes [the objection]: *avaṃ—nanu cidaṃśe yogācārairnānātvakṣaṇikatvayorupagamānmṛṣāvādibhiśca tatra nityatvaikatvayorupagamāt kathaṃ cinmātravyatireki vastu sakalaṃ mithyā ityādikamuktaṃ ityāśaṅkya ciddhyatiriktatvāviśeṣācciddharmabhūtanānātvāderapi mithyātvaṃ matadvaye’pyaviśiṣṭamiti cinmātravyatireki vastu sakalaṃ mithyā ityādikaṃ vaktuṃ yuktameveti pariharati—*

If it is argued that there is a disparity between the cognitions regarding multiplicity and momentariness on the one hand, and unity and permanence on the other—both within one's own system and in the other's—we reply: this is not so for the Māyāvādin’s position compared to the Buddhist position; for in neither of these two systems is there any real property other than the nature of the cognition itself. (56)

Because of the consequence that even for the conscious aspect (*cidaṃśa*), the proponents of falsity (*mṛṣāvādinaḥ*) do not admit any attributes distinct from its own nature, they are entirely identical to the Yogācāras; thus, the author states their exclusion from the Vedic fold with the words beginning "nānātva" (diversity), etc. In one view—that of the Yogācāra position—there is the acceptance of diversity and momentariness in consciousness (*dhiyaḥ*, i.e., *saṃvid*), meaning the admission of plurality and being the counter-positive of a destruction occurring in a second moment. In the other view—that of the proponents of falsity—[the same applies].

Because of the acceptance of oneness and eternity of the intellect (*dhi*), and because of the admission of its being devoid of a second of its own kind and its being delimited by all time—for these reasons—there is a difference, that is, a distinction, from the Buddhist position, namely the Yogācāra school which follows devotion to the Sugata. If it is argued that there is such a difference, this is not so; the meaning is that the aforementioned difference is not supported by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*). Why? To this he says: "Since," and so forth. "Since" (*yat*) means "because."

In that regard, "in both systems" means in both the previously mentioned Yogācāra position and the Māyāvāda position. "Distinct from its own nature" means other than the essential nature (*dharmisvarūpa*) of the subject. "Any property whatsoever"—whether it be multiplicity and so forth, or unity and so forth—"does not exist as real" means it is not true. This is because properties are non-different from cognition, and because cognition itself is devoid of internal differentiation; such is the meaning.
