Therefore, the statement that [the self] is distinct from pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) and so forth is not untenable.

The meaning is that because the same logic applies even to the aspect of consciousness (*cidaṃśa*), the Yogācāras and the Māyāvādins are completely outside the fold of true Vedism. Furthermore, it is indicated here that for both the Yogācāras and the proponents of falsity (*mṛṣāvādins*), there is a lack of natural fitness for inference; for when they debate with one another regarding the plurality or unity of the probandum (*sādhya*)—such as whether it is distinct from or non-distinct from the nature of the subject (*dharmin*)—the first alternative leads to the consequence of the existence of external objects and their possessing specific qualities, while the latter leads to the consequence of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*). || 56 ||

By the statement "established by a means of knowledge that apprehends the substratum," the natural consistency of the means of perception (*pratyakṣa*) is undermined; and by the statement "distinct from pure consciousness" and so forth, the natural consistency of inference (*anumāna*) is said to be undermined. Here, the undermining of the natural consistency of perception is stated by another approach: it is observed that only two real defects in the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) serve as the cause of error. Therefore, the production of error even when the defect itself is false contradicts perception.

Likewise, even if the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) were unreal, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the arising of error, which would lead to the victory of the Mādhyamika position. Furthermore, because one would require a further defect to account for the initial defect, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

If you argue that this infinite regress is avoided by asserting that the locus is beginningless by its very nature (*svarūpa-anāditva*), then that same solution applies equally to the doctrine that the locus is ultimately unreal; thus, along with the loss of the natural consistency of perception, the proponent of falsity reaches the extreme of being excluded from the Vedic fold. [The *Mūla* states: "In the case of the combination of self and other, the impossibility of beginninglessness is difficult to establish."
Furthermore, regarding the beginninglessness of the stream: for there are four modes of existence (gatis).
If ignorance were non-existent, these [four] would clearly be considered equal in the path that lacks a real substratum, in order to avoid the fault of infinite regress. (57)

In this context, the phrase "of those who speak falsely" (*mṛṣāvādinām*) is to be supplied. Regarding "unreal ignorance" (*asatyāvidyā*): that which is both unreal and ignorance is "unreal ignorance"; [the genitive] refers to that. For, since it has been accepted as unreal—lest the non-duality (*advaita*) be lost in the ultimate sense—it is the ignorance denoted by the term "positive nescience" (*bhāvarūpājñāna*), which has its locus in the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman. [The phrase "of that ignorance having the soul and Brahman as its locus" (*jīvabrahmāśrayāyāḥ sā avidyāyāḥ*) is to be understood. In order to avoid the infinite regress (*anavasthā*) that was raised—since, for the sake of avoiding that very regress, [this ignorance] would itself require a root defect because it is itself imagined—[the author speaks of the falsity of that regress]. To resolve that [regress], [he says the following].

The connection is as follows: "It is considered that there are four possible ways (gatis) to describe those who speak falsely. Regarding the compound *svarūpānāditva-svaparaghaṭane*: it is a copulative compound (*itaretarayoga-dvandva*) consisting of "intrinsic beginninglessness" (*svarūpānāditva*) and "the conjunction with itself and others" (*svaparaghaṭanā*). "Intrinsic beginninglessness" (*svarūpānāditva*) means the state of not being the counter-positive of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva-pratiyogitva*); the meaning is that it has no beginning in its own nature. For if something were produced, it would depend upon a producer; however, for that which is unproduced, there is no dependence on a root cause—this is one way. And this is stated by the proponent of Brahman-ignorance (*brahmājñāna-vādin*).

This has been stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Sudarśana: "The objection raised by the proponent of Brahman’s ignorance—that it would lead to an infinite regress—is avoided by [the Advaitin] on the grounds that its nature is beginningless. The term *svaparaghaṭanā* (the coordination of self and other) means that in the conceptualization of itself and in the conceptualization of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), the very same principle serves as the solution to the defect; thus, it possesses the quality of being self-sufficient (*svaparanirvāhakatva*) in terms of resolving defects. For if something were not self-sufficient and were merely sufficient for others, there would be a requirement for another resolver with respect to itself. However, when it is both self-sufficient and sufficient for others, no such requirement exists; this is another way of explaining the matter.

As it has been said: "Because a defect establishes itself and others, and because it is independent of any further defect, there is no infinite regress. "Inexplicability" (*durghaṭanatā*) means the state of being difficult to establish (*durghaṭatva*). It is the independence from logical justification (*upapatti*). For if it were dependent on justification, there would be a requirement for a further establishing factor; however, if it is independent of that, there is no requirement for an establishing factor—this is another way of putting it. As it has been stated: "For the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) depends upon justification."

In cases such as the swallowing of palaces and the like, the reasoning that "the swallowing of a palace and so forth by a small mouth is impossible" does not apply. Therefore, independence from logical justification (*upapatti*) is the proof of its non-ultimate reality (*apāramārthya*). "Beginninglessness in terms of a stream" (*pravāhato'nāditvam*) means a succession of individual instances of the same kind that are subject to origination and destruction. And this [beginninglessness] consists in possessing a property whose delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) is not the counter-correlate of an absence that pervades the time prior to its own substratum. Thus says the author of the *Tātparyadīpikā*.

"There is no infinite regress because of the logic of the seed and the sprout; this is the other way. This [latter] view was stated by the proponents of the ignorance of the individual soul (*jīvājñānavādin*). As it was said by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Sudarśana: "By the proponents of the ignorance of the individual soul, [the objection of infinite regress] is avoided through the beginninglessness of the stream (*pravāhānāditva*), according to the logic of the seed and the sprout. Here, the first [view] was stated by the proponents of the ignorance of Brahman (*brahmājñānavādin*), while the last was stated by the proponents of the ignorance of the individual soul. The distinction is that the middle one was stated by both.

Thus, there are four alternatives (*gati*): these are the logical options intended and desired by those who propound falsehoods to be stated—that is, asserted—in order to establish the avoidance of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) regarding ignorance (*avidyā*). The suffix *tumun* is used here in the sense of desire (*icchārtha*). These four alternatives—consisting of [ignorance's] having an intrinsic nature, being beginningless, being self-sustaining, being independent of the proof [of its existence], and being a beginningless stream—are the means for avoiding infinite regress regarding ignorance.

"Even in the Mādhyamika position, which maintains that the ultimate reality is pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*) serving as the locus for the delusion of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), [the faults] are equal—that is, the same. 'Clearly' means even for children, it is evident."

This has been stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭasudarśana: "If [the substrate] were not ultimately real, then even its beginninglessness would not avoid the fault of infinite regress. For if that were the case, it would follow that the Madhyamaka position is victorious. In that case, since the substrate is established through illusion, that illusion would require another substrate; and since that too would be established through illusion, the same would apply—thus, by means of this infinite regress, the ultimate reality of the substrate is established."

If the Mādhyamika accepts that the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is beginningless in its own nature while being non-ultimate (*aparamārtha*), then the charge of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) is avoided; thus, it would follow that the substrate itself is merely non-ultimate. Furthermore, if a defect can account for itself and others (*sva-paranirvāhaka*), then the substrate could likewise do so—thus rendering the infinite regress untenable. Moreover, if the avoidance of infinite regress is achieved even when the substrate is non-ultimate, then infinite regress would be easily avoided even in the absence of an ultimate substrate. Even in the view that the stream is beginningless, if the substrate is non-ultimate, the infinite regress is easily resolved.

And because, like the succession of fathers and so forth, one accepts the beginninglessness of the succession of substrata (*adhiṣṭhāna*). The word "but" (*tu*), however, serves to dispel the suspicion of a discrepancy regarding defects in the substratum, such as its inability to account for itself or its difficulty in being self-sustaining.

Regarding this, the venerable Bhaṭṭa Sudarśana says: "If it is argued that once its status as a substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) with respect to another is established, it follows that it is self-sustaining (*svanirvāhaka*), [we reply: it is self-sustaining only if it is a defect with respect to another; but that very status does not exist. Thus, since the arguments based on its being non-ultimate (*aparamārtha*) are unavoidable, there must indeed be a dependence upon a substrate, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthiti*). This is what must be stated.

And since this fault applies equally [to the opponent's position as well], the Blessed One, intending all of this, has declared: "As long as there is no acceptance of ultimate defects distinct from Brahma, to that extent error cannot be established. || 57 ||

Just as the reason that establishes universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyatva*) results in the "unestablished nature of the reason" (*svarūpāsiddhi*) because it destroys its own very form, so too the reason that establishes the ultimate unreality of everything apart from pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) likewise destroys its own form; thus, once again, the lack of logical consistency in inference is asserted. In that regard, it was previously stated that the arguments establishing the position of the Proponent of Falsity (*mṛṣāvādin*) serve to establish the position of the Mādhyamika. Here, however, it is stated that the arguments refuting the Mādhyamika position serve to refute the position of the Proponent of Falsity—and so forth, the author of the *Khaṇḍana* refutes [the opponent], and your position is rejected.
If it is asked, "What follows from those arguments stated by you?", [we reply: our position remains;

for just as your own position persists despite being closely associated with the refutation of consciousness as taught by the Mādhyamikas, so too in the world, when a subverting factor is destroyed, one's own essential nature remains established.

*Re* is a contemptuous address. The repetition (*dvirukti*) expresses an excess of disdain. [It refers to] the author of the work titled *Khaṇḍana*. "Shatter" (*khaṇḍaya*): this is the imperative (*loṭ*) used in the sense of granting permission; the meaning is, "Nothing of ours is cut away. To the question "Why?", he says: "By your arguments," and so forth. By the arguments stated by you—on the occasion of refuting the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so on—when addressed to the Mādhyamika; "your position" (*bhavatpakṣaḥ*), i.e., your accepted view that everything other than consciousness (*cit*) is false; "is rejected" (*pratikṣipyate*), i.e., is cast aside.

The meaning is that your stated inference and other arguments are refuted by means of such conceptual distinctions as whether the properties of the means of proof (*sādhana-dharma*) are ultimate (*pāramārthya*) or non-ultimate (*apāramārthya*). If one asks, "What follows from this?"—the meaning is: by permitting the demolition of your own position while failing to establish your own thesis, you fall into the state of a mere caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*); thus, your purpose is not accomplished. He offers a rebuttal with the words beginning "Our view" (*asmanmatam*), etc. "Our view" refers to the reality of the world (*jagat-satyatva*) which we maintain.

"It remains" means it becomes stable. The intention is that since both the refutation of the opponent's position (*parapakṣadūṣaṇa*) and the establishment of one's own position (*svapakṣasthāpanā*) are accomplished simultaneously (*tantreṇa*), there is no consequence of being a mere caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*). Regarding this point, they cite his very position as an illustration with the words "just as," and so forth. (Just as) because of the immediate rejection of the negation of consciousness (*cidvyudāsana*)—that is, the falsity of the substratum—as stated by the Mādhyamika, i.e., the proponent of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*).

By means of the alternatives concerning the existence of valid knowledge, its objects, and the instruments for attaining them—as formulated by you—your own position, namely the reality of consciousness as the underlying substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), remains intact; such is the meaning. He provides another illustration with the words "And just as... In the world, in places such as a room, when there is a sublation—that is, when a statement that makes known the absence of a jar is countered by another statement that produces the valid cognition of the jar's presence right there—the nature of the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), such as the jar, [remains].

The meaning is that stability (*sthiti*) is the state of being stable (*styatva*), just as [the destruction of the cause is the state of being destroyed]. There is no contradiction with the maxim: "When the killer of Devadatta is slain, Devadatta does not rise again," because there is a difference between a causal agent (*kāraka*) and a cognizer (*jñāpaka*). This very point was stated in detail by the venerable Bhaṭṭasudarśana in the passage beginning, "This was said for the purpose of illustrating the refutation of the fallacious arguments (kutarka) advanced by the author of this critique (*Khaṇḍana*) and others"; it should be investigated in that very place. || 58 ||

Furthermore, he states the lack of cogency in inference: "If it is argued that 'because it is cognition, its own establishment follows like a jar'—that is, because it possesses the nature of cognition—it would follow that it is an object of knowledge; if anyone here says this, it is incorrect."
For one's own cognition is indeed independent with respect to its own substratum; yet, when directed toward another person, it becomes an object of knowledge for that other.
Even so, this does not undermine its status as a cognition. || 59 ||
"Ko'pi" means someone unworthy of having their name mentioned; that is to say, a certain liar. "Iha" means in this [work], which abounds in authoritative sources.

In the world, regarding consciousness (*dhiyaḥ*)—that is, experience (*anubhūteḥ*)—if it were an object of knowledge (*vedyatve*), meaning if it were the object of another experience (*anubhavāntaraviṣayatve sati*), then non-experience (*adhītvaṃ*), that is, the state of not being an experience (*ananubhūtitvam*), would follow; it would entail (*prasajati*), i.e., it would result. "Like a jar" (*kumbhavat*): this suffix *vati* is used after a word ending in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyantāt*). This favorable argument (*anukūlatarka*)—"If experience were to be experienced, then it would be a non-experience, like a jar"—is stated as a constituent part of the inference to be presented hereafter; therefore, [it is said] "for this reason," i.e., for the reason of the aforementioned argument. Now he states the inference itself with the words beginning "its own establishment" (*svasiddhi*).

That—[referring to] experience (*anubhūti*). This is the statement of the subject (*pakṣanirdeśa*). "Established by itself" (*svasiddhi*) means that its establishment and its conformity with worldly usage (*vyavahārānuguṇya*) are by itself alone; thus it is so described. Given its self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*), [the meaning is: "it becomes an object of another cognition" (this is the sense). Because the term contains an emphasis (*avadhāraṇagarbhatva*), the stated meaning is established; and that [emphasis], namely "if it were cognizable, it would be knowable by another," is adopted in accordance with what precedes and follows. And this is the statement of the probandum (*sādhyānirdeśa*). "Because of being a cognition" (*dhītvāt*), i.e., because of being experience (*anubhūtitvāt*). This is the statement of the reason (*hetunirdeśa*).

The phrase "like a jar" (*kumbhavat*) is supplied from the preceding context. This is a negative instance (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*). For in the case of jars and the like, the absence of self-luminosity and the absence of not being an object of another cognition are observed along with the state of not being an experience (*ananubhūtitva*); thus, this is a negative inference (*vyatireki-anumāna*). Regarding what was said—that he stated, or states, an inference of the aforementioned form—that is incorrect. That [inference] is "incorrect" (*asat*), meaning it is defective, being beset by faults such as proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), the lapse of the time for the argument (*kālātyayāpadeśa*), and the presence of a limiting condition (*sopādhikatva*).

And here, regarding the probandum of self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*), does it mean with respect to its own locus or with respect to another? In the first case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*); in the second, there is sublation (*bādha*). This is because the cognition of another person does not manifest for that other person without [that person’s] own cognition. Furthermore, the claim that experience is not an object of another cognition is sublated; for the cognitions of one person are objects of the inferential cognitions and so forth of another person. Otherwise, there would result a contradiction with all worldly and Vedic transactions.

Furthermore, the fact that a jar or similar object is not an experience (*ananubhūtitva*) is due to its being non-opposed to ignorance (*ajñāna*), and not due to its being an object of experience (*anubhāvyatva*); thus, this [argument] is fallacious because it is subject to a limiting condition (*sopādhika*). This very point is stated by the words beginning with "svasiddhi" (its own establishment). "In relation to its own substratum" means in relation to the referent of the "I" (*ahamartha*), which is perceived as the locus of knowledge in the cognition "I know. "Its own establishment" (*svasiddhi*) means that, in the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) where it is itself the agent, having the "I"-referent as its substrate and itself as its object, it is itself the cause of its own manifestation. It is self-luminous.

By the word *prati*, which denotes "remainder" (*śeṣin*), the status of being the locus and the agent is obtained. Its denotation of "remainder" (*śeṣatva*) is established by the rule: "The words *prati*, *pari*, and *anu* [are used] in the senses of indication (*lakṣaṇa*), description of a state (*itthaṃbhūtākhyāna*), and distributive repetition (*bhāga-vīpsā*). For this very reason, the accusative case is used in the expression *svādhāram*. By the word *hi*, which indicates that the [property] is already established through another means of knowledge in the form of the delimitor of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka-prakāra*), the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*) is signaled. This is expressed by the phrase "not merely," and so forth.

The meaning is that even with respect to another person—that is, even with respect to a person other than its own substratum (or even with respect to a different person)—its own establishment does not occur. The word *hi* (for/indeed) connects both to the preceding and the following according to the "middle gem" (*madhyamaṇi*) maxim. Therefore, the meaning is that this [reason] is "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), as stated in the passage beginning with "to be known by others" and so forth; for this very cognition—which, with respect to its own substratum, consists in its own establishment, yet with respect to another person is not of such a nature.

"Knowable by another" (*parajñeyā*) means [knowable] by another experience—that is, by a different cognition. "Knowable" (*jñeyā*) means that which is to be made an object; that is, possessing the status of being an object for another cognition. Regarding the compound *parajñeyā*, there is the substitution of the masculine form (*puvadbhāva*) when it occurs as a simple derivative. Furthermore, the two types of "other" experience (*anubhūti*)—the coordinate (*samānādhikaraṇā*) and the non-coordinate (*vyadhikaraṇā*)—are both applicable. Thus, experience (*anubhūti*) is knowable by both these two kinds. In this regard:

Because the past and future experience belonging to a particular person is an object of the present experience belonging to that same person, it is experienced by the former [experience]; and because the cognitions of one person are seen to be inferable by another person, they are experienced by the latter [experience]. Thus, in order to include both the co-referential and non-co-referential experiences, it is explained that [the experience] is "to be known by the other. Therefore, the claim that experience is not an object of another cognition is refuted—this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "that too" (*tadapi*) and so forth: here, the word *dhiyaḥ* (of the cognition) is to be supplied.

Even so—that is to say, even if it were known by another, or in other words, even while being the object of another cognition—the nature of consciousness (*dhiyaḥ*) as experience (*anubhūti*) does not fail; it is not contradicted. The meaning is that the property of being experience is not the counter-positive of an absence residing in an experience that possesses the property of being cognizable. The absence of the property of being experience in things such as a jar is not caused by their being cognizable; rather, it is caused by their not being opposed to ignorance (*ajñāna*). Since experience, however, is indeed opposed to ignorance, the [proposed] probans is shown to be fallacious due to a limiting condition (*sopādhikatva*). This is the sense.

The nature of being an experience (*anubhūtitva*) is the unique, defining characteristic (*asādhāraṇadharma*) of experience. This "nature of being an experience" consists in its manifesting to its own substrate by its very existence during its present state. On the other hand, "being an object of experience" (*anubhāvyatva*) is common to jars and the like; for a unique form does not cease to be established by the means of knowledge that apprehends the subject simply because a common form is present. If it were so, it would follow that jars and the like would possess "jar-ness" and so forth merely by virtue of being objects of experience. Thus, he refutes the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between "being an object of experience" and "not being an experience," as demonstrated by the group of cognitions beginning with perception: For indeed, [it is] manifested by the entire range of cognitions such as perception and the rest...

If it is argued that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of entities departs [from them] because they are objects of cognition, what [of it]? If there is a connection with intrinsic nature by virtue of being an object of cognition, then it follows that a cloth, insofar as it is an object of knowledge, would lack the nature of a cloth, just like a jar. (60)

To explain: the meaning is that what was stated previously—that even this does not undermine the nature of cognition—is indeed so. Why is this? To this he says: "perceptual," and so forth. "Those" refers to entities or objects. "Vedyāḥ" means objects of knowledge, i.e., objects of cognition. The word "iti" has the sense of a reason; the meaning is "because of their being objects of knowledge. "Of entities" means of objects. "By the groups of cognitions beginning with perception" means by the collection of valid cognitions consisting of direct intuition, inference, and verbal testimony.

"Manifested" (*prakaṭita*) means that which was already existent has been made manifest; by this, its status as something produced by scientific intervention is excluded. By the word "class" (*varga*), it is understood that it is improper to alter many things. "Intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to a unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*). "Does it depart? means "does it not cease?"—the meaning is that the common properties of objects, such as being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*), are not established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because they are contradictory to those respective unique properties. If that were the case... [tathātve]... at such a state.

He states the consequence (*prasaṅga*) with the words beginning "svabhāva" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of the cognition" (*dhiyaḥ*): "on account of being cognizable" (*vedyatvaśataḥ*) means because of its connection with the state of being experienced, that is, because of its connection with the common property consisting in being an object of knowledge (*jñeya*). "Of its own nature" (*svabhāvasya*) refers to its own unique property, which is the state of being consciousness (*anubhūtitva*). "Exclusion" (*pratyāsaḥ*) means rejection (*pratikṣepaḥ*).

The root *asu* is listed in the sense of "throwing" (*kṣepaṇe*); from the prefix *prati-* combined with this root, the suffix *ghañ* is applied to denote the abstract state (*bhāve*). "If it happens" (*bhavati yadi*) means "if it should be the case. The meaning is: if the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) consisting in being knowable (*jñeyatva*) were pervaded by the absence of the unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) consisting in being an experience (*anubhūtitva*). "Of the cloth" (*paṭasya*) refers to that which possesses the unique property of cloth-ness (*paṭatva*) established through perception. "While being knowable" (*jñeyatve sati*) means [the reason] "because of being an object of knowledge" (*prameyatvāt*), which is a common property. "Like a jar" (*ghaṭavat*) means like a jar which is endowed with the property of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*). "Non-cloth-ness" (*apaṭatva*) is the absence of cloth-ness (*paṭatvābhāva*).

When there is no [separate] object, it forms an *avyayībhāva* compound. "Entails" (*prasajati*) means "occurs. The meaning is that the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of knowability with the absence of cloth-ness in a jar would, by mere virtue of that co-occurrence, entail its co-occurrence with cloth-ness as well, which contradicts perception. This is an illustration: it would follow that fire on a mountain, which is inferred from smoke, lacks the nature of being "fire-on-a-mountain" because it is knowable; or, in the theory of the postulated *apūrva*, it would follow that the *apūrva* lacks its status as *apūrva* (the unprecedented) because it is knowable.

It should also be understood that since heaven (*svarga*), which is knowable solely through verbal testimony (*śabda*), is an object of cognition (*prameya*), it would follow that it lacks the nature of being heaven (*svargatva*). This is because [heaven] has been stated to belong to the class of cognitions such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth. Thus, the point is that while in the case of a jar or the like, the absence of the nature of being a cognition (*anubhūtitva*) coexists merely with the state of being an object of experience (*anubhāvyatva*), in the case of self-luminous cognition (*anubhūti*), the absence of the nature of being a cognition due to its being an object of experience is contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣabādhita*).

In the case of a jar and the like, however, it is precisely the state of being non-opposed to ignorance (*ajñāna*) that is the cause for the absence of the nature of experience (*anubhūtitva*), not the state of being an object of experience (*anubhāvyatva*). This very point was stated by the Blessed One himself: "In that case, let it be accepted that it is precisely the state of being non-opposed to ignorance that is the basis for the lack of the nature of experience, and not the state of being an object of experience. Therefore, the essential point is that there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the state of being an object of experience and the lack of the nature of experience. || 60 ||

In the phrase "the natural flow of perception and other means of valid cognition is obstructed," the lack of intrinsic validity (*asvārasya*) regarding inference—which was intended by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*)—was stated by the passage beginning with "because it is visible, it is unreal. Here, he explains what was said regarding the "abundant sublation" (*bādha*) of that [inference] in the passage beginning with "illumination" (*prakāśa*). Illumination (*prakāśa*) exists in jars and the like, which possess insentience (*jāḍima*), as well as in the cognitions directed toward them; and its concealment (*tirodhi*) is the non-cessation of this [insentience]. However, in the case of Brahman, who is non-insentient, its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*); its manifestation (*sphuraṇa*) is itself its own cessation (*nidhana*). Its concealment is merely the absence of that manifestation. Thus, since the nature of the object is established through perception and other means of valid cognition, inference is sublated by them. Furthermore, the sublation of that [inference] is manifold. This is because the nature of the object is determined by perception and the rest, while the nature of the subject is determined by inference. Since the subject is subordinate to the object, the sublation of the subject by the object is more powerful. Moreover, the sublation of the subject by the object is direct (*sākṣāt*), whereas the sublation of the object by the subject is indirect (*pāramparya*). Therefore, the sublation of the object by the subject is not possible. Consequently, the inference is sublated by perception and the other means of valid cognition. Thus, the view that "the world is unreal because it is visible" is refuted. Furthermore, the statement "the world is unreal because it is subject to contradiction" is also refuted. For instance, the Vedas are not subject to contradiction, as they are the source of all knowledge. Nor is the world subject to contradiction, for it is established by perception and other means of valid cognition. Therefore, the view that "the world is unreal because it is subject to contradiction" is refuted. Furthermore, the statement "the world is unreal because it lacks a cause" is also refuted. For the world has a cause, namely Brahman, who is the creator of all. Therefore, the view that "the world is unreal because it lacks a cause" is refuted. Furthermore, the statement "the world is unreal because it is momentary" is also refuted. For the world is not momentary, as it is perceived to persist over time. Therefore, the view that "the world is unreal because it is momentary" is refuted. Furthermore, the statement "the world is unreal because it is devoid of essence" is also refuted. For the world possesses an essence, namely Brahman, who is the substratum of all. Therefore, the view that "the world is unreal because it is devoid of essence" is refuted. Thus, the view that "the world is unreal" is refuted by perception and other means of valid cognition. Therefore, the world is real. Q.E.D.
Brahman would either be insentient, or else it would be devoid of concealment; otherwise, it could not be so.

The proponents of illusoriness (*mṛṣāvādins*) accept that the nature of Brahman is eternal, devoid of distinctions, and self-luminous; that it is concealed by positive ignorance (*bhāvarūpājñāna*); and that this concealment is removed by knowledge. Regarding these points, a mutual contradiction among the attributes is stated:

"Manifestation in the jar and so forth" refers to the following: "in that which possesses dullness"—that is, in that which possesses insentience (*jaḍatva*) and is necessarily manifested by another; "in the jar and so forth"—that is, in the pot and the like. "Manifestation" is the property that is the object of the linguistic usage "it shines" or "it is manifest. "Cognition having that as its object" means there arises a cognition whose content is that [manifestation]. Furthermore, "concealment in the jar and so forth" refers to the state of being concealed residing in the pot and the like—that is, the state of being concealed which is the object of the linguistic usage "it does not shine. "Of this" refers to the cognition whose object is the jar and so forth.

“Cessation” (viratiḥ) means that there is non-existence. Thus, the authoritative nature of the manifestation and concealment of jars and other objects has been shown. Furthermore, since this concealment consists in the absence of the jar and so forth—and is distinct from the essential nature of the jar itself—it does not consist in the destruction of that essential nature; thus, the distinction from the point to be explained later is stated. [The opponent asks: “Let it be so; what follows from that? To this, he says: “In the non-inert,” and so forth. “In the non-inert” means in that which is not self-luminous. “But in Brahman”—that is, regarding the object that is Brahman—however...

"Consciousness alone" (*cideva*) means pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), which is devoid of attributes such as illumination that are distinct from its own nature. "Its own nature" (*svarūpa*) refers to the essential nature of the subject (*dharmin*). "Manifestation" (*sphuraṇa*) means illumination; the word "becomes" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "Concealment" (*apidhi*) and "covering" (*apidhāna*) mean obscuration (*tirodhāna*); this is derived from the root *dhā* preceded by the prefix *api*, with the suffix *kip* applied according to the rule for verbal roots ending in *ghu* after a prefix. "Self-destruction" (*svanidhana*) means the very destruction of its own nature; here too, the word "would be" (*syāt*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

The sense is that since light is of the nature of its own essence (*svarūpa*), its concealment would necessarily be its destruction; thus, there is a mutual contradiction regarding [Brahman's] eternality and other attributes. Furthermore, the Lord has stated that for that whose sole nature is light, the concealment of light is indeed the destruction of light. "Or else," and so forth: otherwise—that is, if one were to admit that Brahman is the object of a cognition distinct from its own nature.

Furthermore, if one accepts that there is an eternal manifestation (*sphuraṇa*) of light distinct from its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), then Brahman would either be sequential, inert (*jaḍa*), or devoid of concealment (*apidhividhura*). The implication is that Brahman would face the undesirable consequence of being inert like a jar or the like, or else the consequence of an absence of concealment. By the word "also" (*api*), the impossibility of a remover for concealment and the impossibility of its removal are indicated. In this context, one should reflect upon such passages as "the supreme Brahman is of the nature of knowledge."

It should be resolved that either the suffix *ki* is applied to the root *tiras* even though it is not a prefix due to its inclusion in the category of "various" (*bāhulaka*), or that the suffix *in*—as prescribed by the rule *sarvadhātubhya in*—is treated as having the *kit* designation by way of *bāhulaka*, or that the suffix *ik* is used here to indicate the verbal root itself; or alternatively, that the term *dadhāti* functions to indicate the meaning [of the root]. Thus they explain the grammatical correctness of the word *tirodhi*. Furthermore, this has been employed by the venerable Yāmunamuni: "The concealment of His true nature by primordial matter (*prakṛti*) is the taking of refuge. (61)

The proponents of falsehood have stated that ignorance has two functions regarding Brahman: concealment (*ācchādana*) and projection (*vikṣepa*). Among these, the aspect of concealment was refuted previously; here, the aspect of projection is refuted. Projection is superimposition (*adhyāsa*), which is the attribution of the nature of one thing to another. Here, it is argued that neither its essential nature nor its cessation is established: even the manifestation of the substance present before one is capable of sustaining the error of silver, whereas the manifestation of the "this-ness" (*śuktitva*) alone is what is capable of subverting the error.

If Brahman were not as it was before, the cessation of the superimposition upon the world could certainly not be established; for if there were superimposition, it would be like [the perception of] silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.

"Purovartin" means that which exists in front (*puro vartate*). The suffix *ṇini* is applied according to the rule *supyajātau*. "Of the object existing in front"—that is, of an object such as mother-of-pearl—its "manifestation" (*sphuraṇam*) is its apprehension through its "this-ness," its being mother-of-pearl, and so forth. "Compatible with the error of silver" means it is not opposed to the error of silver; rather, the meaning is that it is actually conducive to it. The word "api" (even/also) indicates the contradiction inherent in the manifestation and the error having the same objective substrate (*viśeṣya*). That contradiction is resolved by the fact that the manifestation does not have the unique, specific property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) as its object.

"Not by the manifestation of 'shell-ness'," and so forth. "The manifestation of shell-ness" means the flashing forth of the specific quality of shell-ness that is unique to the shell. "Not capable of sustaining the error of silver" means it is opposed to the delusion of silver. To the question "Why?", he says: "By the error," etc. "That"—namely, the manifestation of shell-ness—"is capable of preventing the error of silver"—that is, it has the power to bring about its cessation and non-arising.

And thus, the apprehension of a common form (*sādhāraṇākāra*) produces error, whereas the apprehension of a unique form (*asādhāraṇākāra*) is its opposite; this is the meaning of what is established for all. He states the undesirable consequence if both of these were to have Brahman as their object, beginning with "If" (*yadi*). "Brahman" refers to Brahman, which is self-luminous and of a single essence. "If, as before"—meaning, if it were like the manifestation of the substance present in front mentioned first in the first half [of the verse], and if it were of the nature of the apprehension of the substratum (*dharmin*) which is the cause of error.

In that case, there would indeed be no cessation of the superimposition upon the world; that is to say, the delusion of phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*) would not cease, because the knowledge [of Brahman] would not be the remover of the cause of delusion. The implication is that this leads to the undesirable consequence of the impossibility of liberation (*anirmokṣa*). If Brahman were like the "mother-of-pearl-ness" (*śuktitva*)—that is, if it were equivalent to the apprehension of the unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) of mother-of-pearl, and if it were of the nature of an apprehension that contradicts delusion—then where could the superimposition—the delusion of the phenomenal world—be established? The meaning is that it would not arise due to the presence of its inhibitor.

And thus, the meaning is that there is a contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*). It is not the case that the nature of Brahman (*brahmasvarūpa*) is inherently opposed to superimposition (*adhyāsa*), but rather that it becomes so only when delimited by an immediate mental modification (*aparokṣavṛtti*); however, this is impossible because there is no difference in the object. Is there some aspect (*ākāra*) of Brahman that is not made the object of the nature of Brahman yet is made the object of the immediate modification, or is there none? In the first case, Brahman would possess attributes (*saviśeṣatva*); in the latter case, the nature itself would be the sublater [of ignorance]. These and other points should be examined in works such as the *Vedāntavijaya*.

In that system, two types of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) are accepted regarding Brahman: the superimposition of the non-conscious (*acetana-adhyāsa*) and the superimposition of the conscious (*cetana-adhyāsa*). Among these, the superimposition of jars, cloths, and the like is the superimposition of the non-conscious; whereas the superimposition of a person endowed with agency, enjoyership, and so forth, is the superimposition of the conscious. Therein, the superimposition of the non-conscious was already refuted previously on the grounds that it does not entail the cessation of the superimposition of the world. Here, however, the untenability of the superimposition of the individual soul (*jīva*)—which is characterized by agency, enjoyership, and so forth—and the consequent untenability of its cessation are stated. These various objections raised against the doctrine of Māyā are presented here.

If Brahman is self-luminous and devoid of all distinctions, how can it be so? For only when that [Brahman] is perceived as the Self by one who sees [it], can such things as the superimposition of what is not its nature—such as the notion that "the person possesses distinctions"—and the cessation thereof be logically established. || 63 ||

Vyā—In this view, namely the position of Māyāvāda, if Brahman is self-luminous and devoid of distinctions—that is, if it is of the nature of a non-distinct self-luminosity—then, in our perspective, within that Brahman which is the object of the "I-notion" (*asmat-pratyaya*) and whose essential nature is non-distinct self-luminosity; for that [Māyāvādin] says that [Brahman] is the subject (*viṣayin*) within the range of the "I-notion. The word *tu* (but) indicates its being devoid of those attributes necessary for being an underlying substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*). It is "with distinctions" (*saviśeṣa*), meaning it is endowed with attributes such as agency and enjoyership by virtue of being an object (*viṣayatayā*).

The superimposition of "man" (*puruṣa*)—that is, the attribution of that which is not its true nature—is as follows: "man" refers to that which is not his true nature, namely the property consisting in the non-manifestation of the essential nature of Brahman, which serves as the substratum; the superimposition of that [property] is *adhyāsa*. Its cessation is its removal. "And so forth" (*ityādi*) means all that was previously stated starting from that point. How is this consistent? How is it logically established?

Because Brahman is devoid of distinctions, it lacks both common and uncommon attributes; and because its nature is solely self-luminous, there is an absence of both manifestation and non-manifestation of those attributes. Therefore, the possibility of error does not exist. Even if such a possibility were granted, there could be no cessation of that error, since that which is not opposed to it cannot be its remover. Furthermore, it is not logical that clarity (*vaiśadya*) should be the remover of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), for being insentient (*jaḍa*), it lacks the power to remove anything; you yourselves have admitted that only knowledge (*jñāna*) is the remover of ignorance (*ajñāna*).

Furthermore, if knowledge whose object is merely that [superimposed thing] were the sublater [of error], then because such knowledge is beginningless, it would follow that there is a sublation of what is beginningless. If the witness-consciousness (sākṣijñāna) of the self alone were the sublater, it would follow that it is something produced. If the state of being the witness of the self alone were produced, it would follow that it itself is the sublater. Moreover, it is untenable for the state of being the witness of the self alone to be the delimiting condition (avacchedaka) for the status of being a sublater;

for it is observed that the cognition of nacre and the like, even when its object exceeds the underlying substrate (adhiṣṭhāna), acts as a sublater. These points should be investigated in works such as the *Caṇḍamāruta*.

In this context, the meaning of the phrase "but in our view" (*tasminnasmaddṛśi tu*) is as follows: the word *tu* (but) has the sense of *ca* (and). "In that" refers to Brahman, which is devoid of distinctions and self-luminous; "and in our view" refers to the substance called the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), which is the object of our cognition. "Qualified" means having agency and so forth as its content. The superimposition of the nature of "person" (*puruṣa*) upon that [ego]—that is, the superimposition of the individual soul (*jīva*) and so on—is the intended sense. To begin with, the existence of a soul endowed with agency and other attributes is not established through the reflection of consciousness (*cit*) in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

Because consciousness (*cit*) is devoid of distinctions, agency and so forth do not exist therein; furthermore, because it is formless (*nīrūpa*), a reflection cannot occur within it. Nor is the establishment of the individual soul (*jīva*) as qualified by agency and so forth possible through the reflection of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in the nature of consciousness, since the internal organ—being insentient—is itself devoid of agency and the like. Furthermore, the establishment of the soul cannot result from the reflection in the internal organ of cognition (*jñāna*) which is itself devoid of the status of knower or agent.

"Because cognition is not visual, a reflection is impossible; therefore, such things as 'the superimposition of what is not that nature' and 'the cessation thereof' are untenable. This is the manifold refutation of the Māyāvāda that has been stated; thus, the detailed exposition introduced with the words "in the Māyāvāda" is concluded. || 63 ||

Objection: "But surely, in your view, there is a constant manifestation of the knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*); and since the delusion of identifying the body with the self cannot occur without the concealment of their true nature, the logical inconsistency is equal [in both systems]. To this, he says: "While the substrate, the Person (*puruṣa*), shines forth by itself as 'I', the superimposition of the mode [of the body] occurs in the form of 'I am an animal,' 'I am a human,' and so forth."
When minuteness and other qualities are established as being far removed from the body, there is indeed concealment—that is, contraction—of the cognition directed toward them. || 64 ||

"In the male"—that is, in the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field), the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), which is the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the locus of error. "It flashes forth as 'I'"—the meaning is that while it is manifesting itself as "I" spontaneously. The form *sphurjati* is derived from the root *ṭuosphūrjā*, listed as "the thundering of a vajra," where the present tense suffix (*laṭ*) has been replaced by the suffix *śatṛ*. The designation "thundering of a vajra" is used to highlight the extreme firmness of the self's manifestation, which is occasioned by its self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*).

By this, the insentience (*jaḍatva*) of the Self is refuted; and herein, the manifestation of the substratum required for error is stated. He describes the non-manifestation of qualities contrary to error with the words beginning "atomicity" (*aṇutva*), etc. "Confusion of the body" (*dehavyatikara*) refers to the error of mutual identity between the body and the Self; it is described as that which has its removal (*nirvartya*) far off.

Because the word *vyatikara* denotes mutual intermingling, it follows by implication that its purpose here is to indicate an error regarding that [intermingling]. Since qualities such as atomicity (*aṇutva*) do not reside in the body, the knowledge of them is opposed to the error of identifying the body with the Self; thus the phrase "the intermingling of the body" (*dehavyatikara*) and so forth is stated. Regarding "atomicity and so forth" (*aṇutvādau*), the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes eternality (*nityatva*) and partlessness (*niravayavatva*). The phrase "when [the substrate] is manifested or concealed" means when it is manifesting; the particle *ca* (and) conjoins this with the previously mentioned manifestation of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

The statement regarding the non-manifestation [of qualities] such as atomicity is because they are to be known through scripture (*āgama*); for those [qualities] are not within the range of the "I-notion" (*ahaṃ-pratyaya*). Thus, the manifestation of the substratum required for error and the non-manifestation of the contradictory quality have been stated. Now, he describes the arising of the error with the words beginning with "as a beast" (*paśu*): "I am a beast," "I am a human"—this is the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of the mode of the body.

The delusion has the body as its qualifier (*prakāra*) through identity (*tādātmya*). The word "occurs" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied here. The sense is that a delusion is logically established in which the self is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and the bodies of animals, humans, and so forth are the qualifiers, by means of the relation of non-difference (*abhedasaṃsarga*). Here, being a qualifier means appearing as subordinate while its internal difference [from the qualificand] is not apprehended; this is because properties distinct from the essential nature (*svarūpa*) are admitted. Even if those [properties] do not manifest, there is no consequence of the destruction of the self's essential nature; thus, the delusion of the body as the self is established.

The meaning is that in the alternative view, since no attribute distinct from the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is admitted there, its impossibility—due to the consequence of the destruction of the essential nature and so forth—is unavoidable. "Of the cognition directed toward that" refers to the contraction of the attribute-bearing knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*), which is capable of extending by way of being the object of the soul's qualities of atomicity, eternity, and partlessness, [but] through the influence of karma and the non-occurrence of auxiliary factors such as scriptural injunctions, there is simply an absence of extension toward those qualities. The word *nanu* is used here for emphasis. "Concealment" (*tirodhi*) means non-manifestation; the words "it occurs here" are to be supplied. This is because the non-manifestation of atomicity and the other qualities is logically consistent, given that the substrate...

The core point is that the delusion of identifying the self with the body is possible because of the manifestation [of the self]. Thus, the venerable Bhaṭṭasudarśana said: "It is true that the manifestation of the essential nature (svarūpa) indeed exists; its concealment is not admitted. Furthermore, the manifestation of the essential nature is not opposed to delusion; rather, it is eternality, atomicity, and partlessness themselves that oppose delusion. These are known through scripture. Their concealment consists in the absence of the expansion of knowledge regarding them, which is a state of contraction."
Therefore, because one accepts a mode distinct from the essential nature [of the self], there is no consequence of the self's destruction. || 64 ||

[Objection: But surely, since the "I-ness" (ahaṃtva) and the knowerhood (jñātṛtva), which are the unique forms of the Self, manifest [to consciousness], error is untenable. To this, he says: Verse 65: Surely "I-ness" and "knowerhood" are attributes of the Person (puruṣa), not qualities of the body; yet in reality, that is not so. Indeed, because of beginningless superimposition (adhyāsa), those two are understood [as belonging to the body]; however, now, through the method of scripture and one's own yoga, it is realized that the Person is other than the body and so forth.

Regarding "I-ness" (*ahaṃtva*) and "knowership" (*ajñātṛtva*): by their actual state of being, they consist respectively in being cognizable by the notion of "I" as the inner self (*pratyaktvena*), and in being the substratum of attribute-become-knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*). The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used here in the sense of a characteristic (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*), or alternatively, it follows from the category of "starting with *prakṛti*" (*prakṛtyādi*). Furthermore, due to the inherent nature of word-derivation (*vyutpatti*), even though these are attributes of the Person (*puruṣa*), the meaning of the third case is construed with a part of the referent (*padārthaikadeśe*)—namely, the two attributes of the Person. Indeed, these two attributes of the Self are precisely those characterized by their actual existence (*vastusadbhāva-viśiṣṭa*).

The *Abhidhānakośa* states: "Puruṣa, ātman, and mānava [are synonyms]. (In reality, by the phrase "the two qualities of the person" (*puruṣadharmau*), the possibility that they might be qualities of the self (*ātmavṛttitva*)—which was previously suspected—is excluded. However, they are not qualities of the body (*na tu vapurguṇau*), meaning they are not qualities of the physical frame (*na tu dehadharmau*). The designation "quality" (*guṇatva*) is used because they are eternally dependent upon that [person]. Here too, the phrase "in reality" (*vastusthityā*) is connected [to the preceding]. The meaning is: they lack the status of being bodily qualities as established by actual existence. Furthermore, the status of being a bodily quality—which was here suspected due to their non-perception in the interval—is also excluded.

By these two statements, it is stated that "I-ness" (*ahantva*) and "knowership" (*jñātṛtva*) possess the unique characteristic of the Self (*ātmasādhāraṇākāratva*), which consists in residing in the Self while not residing in the body. The word "even though" (*yadyapi*) should be supplied at the beginning [of the following sentence]. The construction is: "Even though 'I-ness' and 'knowership' are indeed attributes of the Person (*puruṣadharma*) and do not belong to the qualities of the body. This statement is intended to raise an objection: that because the unique characteristic manifests, error (*bhrama*) is untenable. He refutes this with the words beginning "even then" (*tadāpi*).

Nevertheless, the "suchness" (*tathātva*) of those two—agency and knowership—consists in their residing in the Self while not residing in the body; that is to say, they are unique to the Self. This is due to *adhyāsa*—that is, the cause which is the delusion of identifying the body with the Self—a process that is beginningless in its stream, according to the analogy of the seed and the sprout. It has not been "cognized"—that is, it has not been grasped [as distinct]. Therefore, the delusion is possible; this is the sense of the remaining portion of the sentence.

In reality, although those two possess unique (asādhāraṇa) forms, there is no contradiction with the occurrence of error because their suchness is not apprehended. The point is that the apprehension of the uniqueness of "conch-whiteness" (*śuktitva*) and so forth alone is what sublates the error of silver and the like. Because the error of identifying the body as the self arises from the non-apprehension of the uniqueness of "I-ness" (*ahaṃtva*) and so forth to the Self, and the non-apprehension of that [uniqueness] arises from the error of identifying the body as the self, there would be a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*); therefore, the term "beginningless" (*anādi*) was stated to avoid this. As the venerable Bhaṭṭasudarśana said: "If it is argued that error is impossible because the unique form of the Self is manifest to cognition, we say no."

This is because that [consciousness] does not manifest as something unique (asādhāraṇa). For it is observed that a property which manifests as unique possesses the capacity to contradict error, as in the case of "shell-ness" (*śuktitva*) and so forth. Shell-ness, having been previously known as the unique property of a shell, subsequently dispels the error. However, consciousness has never been observed anywhere as a unique property of a self distinct from the body; therefore, error occurs. Furthermore, superimposition (*adhyāsa*) arises because the property of being common to the self is not perceived.

"The non-apprehension of specific properties [of the object] arises from superimposition; thus, the mutual dependence [between these two] is resolved by their beginninglessness. If that is so, then [the objection remains] regarding the non-apprehension of specificness and so forth.

In the passage beginning with "gaḍḍhandya... and ending with "...ghaṭate," the intended meaning is as follows: that which is not in contradiction with an error cannot be its remover; furthermore, verbal immediate cognition (*śābdāparokṣa*) does not possess the power to remove such error, because if it did, there would be a confusion between the definitions of the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) of verbal testimony and direct perception, resulting in the impossibility of the former itself. Precisely because verbal immediate cognition does not remove error, it is said that even liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) is not possible.

As stated by the Blessed One: "Since ignorance does not cease through the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence—because direct, immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) cannot arise from a sentence—liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) is likewise cast far away. The two verses beginning with "In the substrate, the person" (*adhiṣṭhāne puṃsi*) and "In the state of 'I'-ness and knower-ship" (*ahaṃtvajñātṛtve*) are incidental, as they are intended to establish the delusion of the body being the self within his own [the opponent's] position. Furthermore, the conclusion "This is the doctrine of Māyā" (*idaṃ māyāvādaḥ*) was made to highlight that liberation while living is independent and distinct; for the view of liberation while living does not survive when struck by the weapon of the scripture (*śāstra*).
Since this [system] is cut down and established in opposition to the world,
the Sage named Dvaipāyana— the Teacher who likewise rejected the Upaniṣadic path that was discarded by Āpastamba— has indeed refuted it even at the very outset.

"Jīvat" means one who possesses a body; "muktiḥ" means liberation (mokṣaḥ); "tasya matam" refers to the acceptance of his doctrine as authoritative. "Na jīvati" means he does not sustain life—that is, he does not maintain the vital breath (*prāṇa*). This is because a multitude of powerful proofs has demonstrated its lack of authority; the meaning is that it is devoid of the sustenance of the vital breath, which is characterized by the truthfulness of its own subject matter. To the question "Why?", he says: "yataḥ" and so forth. Because it has been "lūnam"—cut down—by the weapon of scripture, namely the Śāstra consisting of such scriptural passages as "For him, there is delay only so long... (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.14.2).

The sense is that it is indeed difficult for one who is severed to maintain his life-force. Since the word *uttara* (the latter) does not depend on the word *tat* (that), it follows from the scripture itself that because he has been severed by the weapon in the form of the teaching (*śāstra*), he does not live. This is because [this case] is a "success contrary to worldly experience" (*lokaviruddhasiddhi*), just like obtaining a self that contradicts direct perception; for liberation from bondage is not seen to occur merely through the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence. The particle *ca* (and) joins this with the prohibition found in the scripture.

By that—by virtue of its nature being contradicted by scripture and perception. "At first"—previously. "This"—the doctrine of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). It is also rejected by Āpastamba; the meaning is that it is forbidden by Āpastamba. And thus says the venerable Āpastamba: "Having abandoned the Vedas, this world, and the next, one should seek the Self. That attainment of security through the intellect is contradicted by the scriptures."

By stating, "If [liberation] were attained through the Buddha, one would not experience suffering even here and now," he refuted the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). He [refers to] the Vedas as the means for accomplishing the three aims of life (*trivarga*), and this world and the next as their fruit—namely, sovereignty pertaining to this life and the life hereafter—within the knowledge of the meaning of the Buddha's words.

Liberation (*mok�ṣa*) is the attainment of security. And what is that? It is the practice of action prohibited by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, according to the doctrine of liberation-in-life (*jīvanmukti*). "Aupaniṣada" means belonging to the *Upaniṣads*; the suffix *-aṇ* is applied here according to the rule "tasyedam. It refers either to the portion of the four Vedāntas skilled in propounding the Brahman that is difficult to grasp, or to the path (*panthānam*) which begins the journey to the further shore of the ascertainment of reality. "Of those who have stood upon it" (*ātasthuṣām*) means of those who have taken their stand—such as Bodhāyana, Ṭaṅka, Dramiḍa, Bhāruci, Guhadeva, and others.

The Teacher (Ācārya) is one who performs the instruction of the meaning of the scriptures, their implementation, and so forth. He is named Dvaipāyana—one whose name is Dvaipāyana according to the direction [of the etymology] "on the island of Badarikāmiśra," and so on; he is a sage (muni), meaning one whose nature is reflection (mananaśīla), which is to say, Vyāsa. He indeed refuted (nirācakāra)—that is, he has indeed rejected it. For in the second section (pāda) of the fourth chapter (lakṣaṇa) of the Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā, the venerable Vyāsa formulated the aphorism: "Therefore, there is no sublation" (nopamardena ataḥ). And that aphorism was explained by the venerable [Śaṅkara] as being intent upon the refutation of liberation while living (jīvanmukti).
"Therefore: 'When all desires that dwell within his heart are released, then the mortal becomes immortal; he attains Brahman even here.'"

"This statement does not declare immortality through the crushing of bondage. Regarding this, the venerable Bhaṭṭasudarśanapāda commented: "This sūtra was stated with the intent of refuting *jīvanmukti* (liberation while living). Since there is the injunction for meditation (*upāsana*), the scriptural teaching that it persists until death, the scriptural teaching on departure (*utkrānti*), and the scriptural teaching that all bonds are released upon reaching a specific location—due to the consequence of contradicting these and other such numerous scriptures, as well as the contradiction with direct perception, the sense is that *jīvanmukti* is untenable.
The form *ātasthuṣām* is derived from the root *sthā* preceded by the prefix *ā*, using the *liṭ* (perfect) tense suffix *kvasu*. 66.

By these two statements—“the scriptural texts concerning difference have falsehood as their object” and “there is figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in those words denoting oneness”—it is impossible for the proponents of falsity (*mṛṣāvādins*) to maintain the authority of the Veda; for the quality of revealing reality (*tattvāvedakatva*), which consists in having an uncontradicted meaning, is difficult to find in the earlier portion [of the Veda], and because that [quality]—defined as the capacity to convey a thing in its own form—is absent from the non-dualistic (*advaita*) passages, since they accept that those passages produce only a cognition devoid of any specific mode (*niṣprakāraka-jñāna*).

It has been indicated that since "the state of not having a qualifier residing in a different locus" (vyadhikaraṇāprakārakatva), when combined with "being other than an illusory object," results in the same conclusion as "having an uncontradicted object," the aforementioned defect remains. Furthermore, those [opponents]—like actors assuming the role of non-Vedic persons, entering while appearing to assert the authority of the Vedas, and stating that the Vedas possess an authority which is in fact nothing but a lack of authority because their objects are merely empirical—fearing exclusion by the Vaidikas if they were to speak thus in their entirety, have ascended into the midst of the Vaidika assembly as if asserting that [the Vedas] reveal reality, yet even of that...

By stripping away the capacity of statements such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*)—which are considered to reveal reality—to convey a relation between words, and by asserting that the meaning of a sentence consists solely in the word-meanings themselves, they even discard that [position] on the grounds of the resulting redundancy, thereby suggesting that there is no cognitive power at all; how then can there be validity? This approach, which is favored by the venerable Mahācārya, is also intended by those two [authors]. However, here their inability to maintain the authority of the Veda through another route is stated:
"Where is the Vedānta, and where are these people whose minds are fixed on the system of Śaṅkara? (and so forth).
Proclaiming that the authority of the Vedic words is but a manifestation of delusion—
just as they do for the compositions woven by Buddha— they were nonetheless counted among the Vedāntins by those seized by the crocodiles of the Kali age. (67)

Where are the Vedāntas—in what manner do the Upaniṣads exist, being devoid of any possibility of being rooted in error, negligence, a desire to deceive, or incapacity of the senses? (The word "here" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. This means they are free even from the slightest scent of invalidity. According to the view of Śaṅkara—those whose minds are fixed upon the doctrine of Māyā accepted by Śaṅkara—having restrained the natural flow of their intellects, they have applied their minds with extreme difficulty.

By this, it is revealed that even for those who possess faith, their doctrine is subject to repeated ascents and descents due to internal contradictions between earlier and later statements. [This applies to] the words of the Veda—that is, the faultless, non-human (apauruṣeya) Vedic utterances—as if they were the compositions of Buddha, like the words bound together by the deceitful Buddha. "The play of delusion" means being the object of delusion, being false because it is rooted in defects. Those who assert its validity [must admit that] the authority of the Buddhist scriptures is false because it is rooted in the defects of Buddha.

Thus, those wicked disputants who assert that the authority of the Veda is likewise false because it is rooted in the defects of Brahmā—where and in what manner do they stand? The meaning is: they are not far removed from the direction shown by the venerable Upadēśaka Ācārya, being devoid even of the scent of accepting Vedic authority. Śaṅkara, however, is not like them.

And here, because it is rooted in defects, the falsity of the Veda’s authority is stated; thus, it is shown that the acceptance of the Veda’s authority is untenable by way of another argument. Having thus established the absolute impossibility of the relationship characterized as the status of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the knower (*pramātṛ*) between the Vedāntas and the followers of Śaṅkara, the author addresses their continued usage of the term "Vedāntin" with the words beginning "atha ca": "And yet," even though there is a connection with the Vedāntas through the aforementioned relationship and despite the existence of that [connection], those [followers] are the Śāṅkaras.

"Seized by the crocodile of the Kali age"—meaning those gripped by the obsession induced by the defects of the Kali age, or the dull-witted who are overwhelmed by the crocodiles characterized as the faults of the Kali age. "They were counted among the Vedāntins"—meaning they were accepted as possessing a relationship defined by the Vedāntic categories of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the knower (*pramātṛ*). "Oh!"—expressing astonishment. The meaning is that the use of that word (*Vedāntin*) for those who are devoid of even a trace of the grounds for its application is truly astonishing. By the phrase "seized by the crocodile of the Kali age," it is shown that this is not the fault of those engaged in worldly discourse.

Rather, it is implied that [the error] belongs to those who engage in worldly discourse (*vyavahartṛ*) and to the ignorance (*kala*) which is its root. This very point was stated by the Blessed One: "If you say that this [error] is rooted in delusion, then you yourself have stated that this [statement] is also rooted in delusion. The form *agaṇiṣata* is the aorist (*luṅ*) of the root *gaṇ* (to count) in the passive voice.

Even if the Vedas lack authority according to their own school's position, nevertheless, he refutes the application of Mīmāṃsā logic—which they have employed for the purpose of deceiving authoritative people as a means to determine the meaning of the Vedas—starting with the words "That which... and so forth:

"That which [is the rule] regarding the relative strength and weakness among all the Upaniṣads devoted to Janārdana, which possess both general and specific qualities and consist of the proximity of attributes and injunctions."

A few have reached the stage of *prastāva* under the pretext of the rules for interruptions (*apaccheda-nyāya*); however, the discourse on the laborious path of *mīmāṃsā* remains far off—this indeed is its beauty.

Some disputants whose minds are fixed on the system of Śaṅkara maintain that "sāmānyaviśeṣa" refers to the method of the sixth and final section [of the *Brahma-sūtras*], where both the universal (*sāmānya*)—defined as a positive entity delimited by a pervading property (*vyāpakadharma*)—and the particular (*viśeṣa*)—defined as a positive entity delimited by a property pervaded by that [pervader] (*tadvyāpyadharma*)—are present as objects to be determined; the suffix *-ac* is applied here according to the rule for words beginning with *arśas*. [The compound thus means] "in the paths," that is, in those subjects which are the scope of that method. Alternatively, it means "in those [arguments] concerning universals and those concerning particulars."

However, the word "guṇa" in the phrase *guṇapratyāsa* is used for the sake of obtaining the general qualities (*guṇasāmānya*) and the specific qualities (*guṇaviśeṣa*) through injunctions and prohibitions. [It refers to] those consisting of the injunctions regarding the proximity of qualities (*guṇapratyāsa*), and those consisting of the prohibitions regarding qualities; [those] devoted to Janārdana—that is, those Upaniṣadic portions which, even without the effort of commentators, are dedicated to the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa; [those] at the end of the three Vedas (*trayyanta*)—the Upaniṣadic sections whose sequence of sentences, words, and phonemes is unerring.

In this context, the statement "the negation of qualities in general results in the negation of specific qualities" is expressed by the words "sāmānya... and so forth, in order to indicate that the sentence negating specific qualities and the sentence stating the absence of qualities (nirguṇa) fall under the scope of the principle of the general and the particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣanyāya*). Furthermore, by the mention of "general and particular," and by the contradiction indicated between the injunction and the prohibition, it is suggested that the negation of qualities in general and the injunction regarding specific qualities fall under the scope of the principle of the general rule and its exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*).

By the phrase "in the case of qualities, proximity, and injunctions" (*guṇapratyāsavidhyātmasu*), it is indicated that the status of being a prohibition for an injunction of qualities is not tenable; for if that which is enjoined by itself were prohibited by itself, the scripture would result in the absurdity of the ravings of a madman, and it would also contradict the maxim of "cleansing away [the stain]" (*prakṣālanāddhi*). Furthermore, by the same phrase "qualities, proximity, and injunctions," it is indicated that it is also not logical for the sentence concerning qualities to serve as the provider of the object to be prohibited, since the words "quality" (*guṇa*) and so forth found within sentences such as "devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇam*) themselves provide that object.

For this very reason, it is also indicated that there is no contradiction between the injunctions and prohibitions regarding qualities, form, and so forth, because they have distinct objects; for since the injunction and prohibition concern the general and the particular, the prohibition does not prevail [over the injunction] as in the case of the sentences concerning the taking or not taking of the *ṣoḍaśī* cup.

It is also indicated that [these two] follow a prescribed method (*vidhinayanam*). By the phrase "in the case of those [two]," it is understood that they consist of a performance characterized by a fixed sequence; thus, it is indicated that these two do not fall under the scope of the *apaccheda-nyāya* (the logic of the "severance"), which concerns specific instances of performance where the sequence is not fixed. By the phrase "devoted to Janārdana," it is shown that the distinction of subject matter—namely, that sentences describing qualities (*saguṇa-vākya*) have the lower Brahman as their object, while the meaning of sentences describing the qualityless (*nirguṇa*) has the higher Brahman as its object—is not tenable.

This is indicated by the natural consistency of the statement beginning with “this is the Self” (*eṣa ātmā*), which conveys that both [the Upanishadic texts and the Smṛtis] have a single subject matter. By the term “Janārdana,” the ultimate reality of the Deity—established through the maxim of the general and the particular—is also incidentally indicated. Furthermore, by the term “Janārdana,” it is indicated that because the Vedāntas have the Blessed Lord as their purport, they likewise have a qualified entity as their purport. Why, then, is it not reasonable for the injunction of attributes to be for the purpose of meditation? For if that were the case, it would follow that even those statements whose purport is the essential nature [of the Self] would likewise be for the sake of meditation.

Therefore, it is indicated by the phrase "among those devoted to Janārdana" that the qualities are indeed established by the scriptural statements concerning the qualities [of the Lord] precisely through the nature of the Blessed One's own essence. Furthermore, it should be understood that qualifiers such as "possessing both the general and the particular" have been employed to indicate the entire aforementioned meaning.

"By means of the pretext of the rule of subsequent annulment (*apacchedanyāya*)," that is, by invoking the logic stated in the section concerning subsequent annulment (*apacchedādhikaraṇa*). By the word "pretext" (*chala*), the dissimilarity between the sentences regarding the qualities (*saguṇa*) and the sentence devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) and the sentence on subsequent annulment is indicated. [This refers to] the introduction—that is, the consideration—of the strength and weakness respectively: namely, the strength of the sentences negating qualities which serves as the cause for subverting the sentences regarding qualities, and the weakness of the sentences regarding qualities which serves as the cause for being subverted by the sentences devoid of qualities.

They attained—that is, they resorted to—the realization that the discernment of the strength and weakness of investigators arises within the injunctions and prohibitions concerning qualities; or rather, they understood this. That which is the *Mīmāṃsā*—consisting of twelve chapters (*dvādaśalakṣaṇī*), composed of a collection of sūtras that set forth the principles useful for determining ritual action (*karmanirṇaya*)—is itself the path, the means for determining the meaning of the Veda:
"When Dharma is being cognized by the Veda acting as the instrument (*karaṇa*), Mīmāṃsā shall fulfill the path of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)."

[The text] is devoid of such [qualities]; therein, "exertion" (*pariśrama*) refers to the constant hardship of studying and teaching; "discourse" (*kathā*) means talk. It is fitting—that is, it becomes beautiful—only for those who are distant from it, namely, those who are dull-witted. The meaning is that only those ignorant of Mīmāṃsā are fit to speak or hear this. There is also a reading *paribhramakathā*; the meaning is the continuous coming and going on the path of Mīmāṃsā, and so forth.

On this point, the venerable Sudarśana Bhaṭṭapāda states: "The principle of simultaneous disqualification (*apacchedanyāya*) indeed concerns cases where the contradiction and the sequence [of events] are not fixed. There is no fixed rule that both the *udgātṛ* and the *pratihartṛ* must be disqualified simultaneously; even there, the sequence of their disqualification is not fixed. For if such a rule were established, there would necessarily be a contradiction between the requirement of giving away one's entire property as a sacrificial fee (*sarvasvadakṣiṇā*) and the requirement of not giving any fee (*adakṣiṇā*). In the case of the simultaneous disqualification of both..."

They say: "Even if there is a sequence of occurrence, there is no fixed rule that the interruption (*apaccheda*) of the *udgātṛ* must occur first and the other later, or vice versa. Therefore, the scope of the *apaccheda*-rule concerns a contradiction occurring within the limits of a single ritual performance (*prayoga*). However, the contradiction between the passages concerning the qualified (*saguṇa*) and the unqualified (*nirguṇa*) [Brahman] is based on their essential nature (*svarūpa*), and possesses a fixed priority and posteriority in the form of injunction and prohibition (*vidhi-niṣedha*).
