Consequently, even if a contradiction is admitted, the *apaccheda*-rule—which deals with a non-fixed priority and posteriority of contradiction—does not apply here."

And this principle has been transcended by the venerable feet of the Great Teacher: "In the case of a sequential disjunction, why does the principle of the opening statement (*upakrama-nyāya*) not apply? If superiority results in greater strength, how can the principle of the opening statement be set aside?"

Therefore, when there is a mutual conflict between these two principles (*nyāya*), the determination here should be made as follows: since the earlier meaning is understood due to its lack of contradiction with what follows, and because the subsequent portion is seized by doubt at the very moment of its arising, the determination of the later meaning must follow the earlier determination; this is the principle of the opening statement (*upakrama-nyāya*). However, in the case of understanding the meanings of two occasional injunctions (*naimittika-śāstra*), the principle of the opening statement does not apply, because there is no priority or posteriority (*paurvāparya*) between those two texts.

Consequently, when there is a doubt as to which of two contradictory contingent rites (*naimittika*) should be performed after considering the specific details of their application, one must perform that which is caused by the second contingency, because of its proximity to the time of the performance of the contingent rite. Therefore, the meaning of the expiatory scripture (*prāyaścitta-śāstra*) is held to be: "If there is no subsequent interruption of the *pratihartṛ* following an interruption of the *udgātṛ*, this is to be done; if there is no subsequent interruption of the *udgātṛ* following an interruption of the *pratihartṛ*, this is to be done. This is the principle of interruption (*apaccheda-nyāya*), and regarding the phrase "by not subverting the prior," the subversion (*bādha*) is as follows:

The sense is this: because there is no interruption of the cognition of the duty regarding the first occasional rite by the arising of the cognition of the duty regarding the second occasional rite during the interval between the two, and because no sublation other than this can be established—and because the *upakrama-nyāya* (the principle of the beginning) cannot be invoked—it is only those ignorant of Mīmāṃsā who find it "delightful" to claim that the two sets of passages concerning the Saguna and Nirguna Brahman fall under the scope of the *apaccheda-nyāya* (the principle of the later annulling the earlier).

By the two qualifiers "in those whose nature consists of the proximity of qualities" (*guṇapratyāsattidharmasv*) and "in those whose characteristics are general and particular" (*sāmānyaviśeṣadharmasv*), the author expresses both the injunction regarding specific qualities and the injunction regarding general qualities; thereby, the refutation of the denial of intrinsic qualities in Brahman is indicated. Since knowledge is never observed to be the locus of [another] knowledge, the demonstration that Brahman is pure consciousness results in its being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*); this is what constitutes the denial of intrinsic qualities.

The refutation of that [objection] is as follows: Is the absence of knowledge being the substratum of knowledge stated on the basis of logical pervasion (*vyāpti*), or due to the superior authority of Śruti and Smṛti? If it is by way of pervasion, then since knowledge—which illuminates its object—is observed to be the attribute (*dharma*) of something that is not itself a substratum of knowledge, let it be accepted as an attribute. If, however, it is accepted as independent on the strength of Śruti, then by the very force of that same Śruti, let its status as the substratum of knowledge also be admitted; thus, this denial of the quality of the Self is refuted by the acceptance of the scriptural injunctions prescribing those qualities. (68)

Thus, because it has been stated that [the case of Brahman] does not fall under the principle of "exclusion" (*apaccheda-nyāya*), and because it will be explained that it does fall under the principles of "general and particular" (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-nyāya*) and "exception and general rule" (*utsarga-apavāda-nyāya*), he states that the injunctions and prohibitions regarding qualities and so forth have distinct objects:

"Those words which enjoin or prohibit qualities, transformations, bodies, distinctions, actions, and so forth regarding Brahman, have mutually distinct objects; they do not deserve even a scent of contradiction. Therefore, the injunctions are not sublated by the prohibitions. (69)

Alternatively, it is said that a prohibition does not sublate an injunction because, if that which is enjoined by scripture itself were prohibited by scripture itself, it would follow that the scripture is the prattle of a madman; therefore, since the injunctions regarding qualities and the like and their prohibitions must necessarily have different objects, the prohibition cannot override the injunction. "Yat" means "because. "Brahmaṇaḥ" means "of the Supreme Self (Paramātman)."

Those things beginning with quality (*guṇa*), modification (*vikāra*), body (*śarīra*), distinction (*bheda*), and action (*karman*)—those which are thus described—are the "objects" (*gocara*) or domains of the two [types of] injunctions and prohibitions, or of the two states; the "words" are the expressive sentences. Being "possessed of mutually distinct objects" means that they have mutually different things to be enjoined and prohibited. Such [words], due to the absence of a single common object, do not "admit" contradiction—that is, they do not become capable of the aforementioned contradiction, which consists in the lack of a single object and which instigates the relationship of sublated and sublator through the mere scent of opposition.

Therefore, injunctions—words that make known the existence of qualities and so forth—are not sublated by prohibitions; they are not sublated by sentences that make known the non-existence of qualities and so forth. For this reason as well, the principle of the "successive annulment" (apaccheda-nyāya) does not apply; such is the meaning.

Injunctions regarding qualities include such passages as "His qualities [are not exhausted] even in ten thousand years" and "He consists of all auspicious qualities. Prohibitions regarding qualities include such passages as "devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) and devoid of action (niṣkriya). Injunctions regarding modification include such passages as "He made Himself by Himself," "As a spider emits and withdraws [its thread]," "When he beholds that which is cherished," and "Through the grace of the Creator, [he perceives] His majesty."

Negations of modification: "to the changeless," "truth-knowledge," "the truth of truth," and so forth. Descriptions of a body: "having the color of the sun," and so forth. Negations of a body: "bodiless," "partless," and so forth, as well as "of him [there is no...]"

There are also such [scriptural passages] as "the instrument exists in the effect. The injunctions regarding difference include such [passages] as "He makes himself separate. The prohibitions regarding difference include such [passages] as "There is no diversity here. The injunctions regarding action include such [passages] as "The one teacher" and "The deeds of Viṣṇu. The prohibitions regarding action include such [passages] as "actionless"; by the word "etcetera," the inclusion of colors such as dark-blue is intended. The injunction regarding that [color] is such as "situated in the midst of a dark-blue cloud," and so forth.

The negations of these are expressed by such terms as "without lineage" (*agotra*) and so forth. Here, the word *guṇa* signifies the qualities of *sattva* and the rest; the word *vikāra* signifies the state of being subject to change, referring to the body which is prone to disintegration. The word *nānā* in the phrase "neither here nor manifold" (*neha nānā*) signifies "without" (*vinā*). Alternatively, the word *kriyā* signifies motion, or the words beginning with *guṇa* may refer to universals (*sāmānya*). In the first case, because they refer to different objects, the principle of general rule and exception (*utsargāpavāda*) does not apply. In the second case, however, that principle does apply.

Therefore, by the operation of the principles of general rule and exception (*utsarga-apavāda*) and of generality and particularity (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*) among these [texts], the prohibitions regarding qualities and so forth have as their object those qualities and forms that are to be rejected, being distinct from the qualities and forms that are ordained. By the operation [of these principles], the prohibitions regarding qualities and so forth have as their object qualities and forms that are to be rejected, being distinct from the qualities and forms that are ordained: "Where the material qualities such as *sattva* and the rest do not exist," and "No longer existing in a collective configuration..."

Alternatively, it is appropriate that [the scripture] culminates in the negation of specific attributes as stated in passages such as "The body of this Supreme Self," and so forth. Furthermore, since the distinction between the qualifier (*prakāra*) and the qualified (*prakārī*), as well as the mutual distinction among qualifiers, is established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*), it is logical that the negation of difference—which is intended to negate a difference that contradicts the unity enjoined—refers to a difference consisting of a separate, independent entity whose nature is not Brahman.

It should be understood that even when referring to transformation (*vikāra*), the scope is restricted to those transformations that are to be rejected—distinct from the transformation consisting of the world-form assumed as a manifestation of supreme sovereignty—and that it refers to objects distinct from the transformations consisting of joy produced by sacrifices, meditations, and so forth, as established by injunctions such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) and "one should worship" (*upāsīta*). || 69 ||

Regarding the phrase "in the paths of general and particular [rules]," he explicitly states that the scope of the principles of *utsarga* (general rule) and *apavāda* (exception), as well as the principles of the general and the particular, applies to the injunctions and prohibitions concerning qualities and so forth—beginning with the words "Agnīṣomīya," etc.

The killing of the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma is enjoined by its own specific injunction; is it not prohibited by the statement "one should not harm living beings"? Through these two principles, it is determined that the word "animal" (*paśu*) refers specifically to the goat. Furthermore, based on the principle that "the goat [is meant] because of the wording of the mantra," the mention of the absence of qualities (*nirguṇa*) is intended to exclude undesirable attributes according to both those principles; thus, the Brahman heard in scripture to possess auspicious qualities would be "stainless" (*nirmala*). // 70 //

Alternatively, as for what others have stated—that there is "possessing qualities" (*saguṇatva*) in the form of being a cause and "being devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇatva*) in its essential nature (*svarūpa*), and that since the objects of the injunctions and prohibitions regarding qualities are distinct, the principle of the general rule and the exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*) does not apply—furthermore, since even the prohibition "not gross" (*asthūlam*) and so forth pertains to specific particulars, the principle of the "burnt foot" and the "Agnihotra fire" (*padāhavanīyanyāya*) does not operate here. For this very reason, it is also not the case that it falls under the principle of the general and the particular (*sāmānyaviśeṇanyāya*). This [objection] is incorrect; for if the meditation on qualities were non-real knowledge, it would follow that liberation could not be established. If that were so, it would contradict such passages as "He manifests in his own true form" (*svena rūpeṇābhiniṣpadyate*).

Furthermore, since the possession of qualities (*saguṇatva*) is the object of meditation that serves as the means to liberation, its reality is necessarily required; thus, it is unavoidable that the injunctions and prohibitions regarding qualities share a single object. Consequently, because a difference in objects is impossible, the application of the principle of general rule and exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*) proceeds without obstruction. Moreover, arguments such as "what more [could there be]" (*kiṃ ca*) are also untenable, for that principle is applicable in relation to statements such as "devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇa*).

This is what he states with the words beginning "agnīṣomīya" and so forth. By the statement "na hiṃsyādbhūtāni" (one should not harm living beings)—that is, by the sentence "na hiṃsyāt sarvā bhūtāni" (one should not harm any living beings)—the killing of the animal prescribed by one's own injunction, namely the injunction "agnīṣomīyaṃ paśumālabheta" (one should sacrifice the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma), is [raised]. Is it prohibited? The word "kim" is used for the purpose of censure; thus the meaning is that it is indeed prohibited. The point is that the sentence "na hiṃsyāt" and so forth has the function of prohibiting all acts of violence other than the killing of the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma.

This has been stated in the tenth [book]: "When there is a general scriptural injunction, because an option is improper, that which is specifically enjoined from afar should set aside the doubtful one. Here, regarding the general injunction "one offers in the Āhavanīya fire," although it is like a specific injunction such as "one offers on the footprint" in terms of being established and being directly heard in scripture, it cannot be sublated due to the disparity with the extension by indicative mark (*liṅga-atideśa*). Consequently, because they possess equal force, there is an option.

As stated in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "Since the general rule is also obtained, just like the specific one through direct perception, there is no sublation by means of indicative marks and the like, nor is there sublation as in the case of extension (*atideśa*)."

"Attainment [of a general rule] occurs through the function of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding a particular, whereas that of a specific rule occurs through direct statement (*śruti*); therefore, there is a difference in strength. According to this principle, because the presentation of an object under a specific property occurs more rapidly than its presentation under a general property, the status of being the place for the *pad* and other offerings—which is immediately obtained in the case of the *patnīsaṃyāja* and other oblations—sets aside the *āhavanīya* fire, which is obtained more slowly in the case of oblation in general; thus it was established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). By that same logic, it applies even to the case of ritual injury (*hiṃsā*).

Because there is a contradiction between incitement (*pravartanā*) and prohibition (*nivartanā*), specifically, since incitement is connected with the Agniṣomīya sacrifice which is explicitly heard in scripture, prohibition is connected with violence other than that; thus, the meaning is that the Agniṣomīya sacrifice is indeed not prohibited. This is precisely the principle of the general rule and its exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*).

He states the *sāmānya-viśeṣa-nyāya* (the principle of the general and the particular) with the words "paśupadena" (*by the word 'animal'*). According to the sixth book of the *Mīmāṃsā-sūtra*, in the section concerning the sacrificial animal, it is established that "it is the goat because of the wording of the mantra. Thus, the object of the word *paśu*—that which is denoted by the term 'animal'—is specifically the goat; no other form has been determined. [The word] *nirūpitaḥ* is derived from the root *rūp* preceded by the prefix *ni*, meaning "to investigate," in the sense of the object (*karman*), in the *luṅ* tense, with the elision of the suffix *ta*. "It is the goat... [and so forth].

Regarding the statement "from the wording of the mantra," [the *Tantravārttika*] says: "The injunction, having first settled upon the general [animal], due to the resulting split in the sentence, may—without contradicting that—incline toward the specific goat, either as a contingent option or through its etymological sense. In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is argued that the injunction "One should sacrifice the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma" settles upon the general category of animal; therefore, even though it is dependent on that generality, it is justified—either by its etymological function (*yogavṛtti*) or by referring to a performance involving the substance of a goat—as applicable to the goat.
[The reply is: "The injunction would make known the general animal as a subsidiary;
however, that [subsidiarity] is deficient even in the case of the goat, because [the generic property] is fully realized in each individual instance."

Because it is recited within the specific context [of the sacrifice], the *mantra* is understood to be a permanent auxiliary (*nityam aṅgam*). Furthermore, by virtue of its established conventional power (*rūḍhi-śakti*), it denotes specifically a goat.
"Therefore, the ritual procedure, by accepting such [an animal] that is contrary to its own requirements, prescribes the goat itself as the limb; hence, there is the inclusion of the goat."

The meaning is that, because this has been established as the final conclusion (*siddhāntita*), it has been determined that the word *paśu*, although denoting a general class, ultimately refers specifically to the goat. The particle *ca* serves to aggregate what was stated previously. To the question, "Granted there are these two principles (*nyāya*); what follows from that?", he says: "By those two," and so forth. This means "by both of those principles. In the compound, the suffix *vṛtti* [is applied] to the word *ubhaya* as a pleonastic (*svārthika*) element. Precisely because of its connection with the word *ubhaya*, the suffix *tasi* is employed even after the word *nyāya*, which ends in the dual number.

Regarding *śrutaśubhaguṇake*: it means that whose auspicious qualities are made known by scripture (*śruti*). The suffix *kvip* is applied here according to the rule *śeṣādvibhāṣā*. Regarding *nirmale*: "impurity" (*mala*) is a property that brings about the degradation of its own substratum; [the term refers to Brahman] because it is devoid of such [impurity]. Regarding the statement "devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇa*) in relation to Brahman: the expression "devoid of qualities" should be understood as intended for the exclusion of rejectable attributes (*heyadharma*), meaning it is appropriate for it to either indicate the absence of rejectable attributes other than those auspicious qualities known from scripture, or to have the purpose of making known the absence of rejectable attributes.

If *kṣepa* (rejection) is non-existence, then it is the *artha* (meaning), that is, the expressed object (*abhidheya*). If, however, *kṣepa* is the cognition of non-existence, then it is the *prayojana* (purpose). This is the distinction.

In this context, [the phrase] "one whose virtuous qualities have been heard in due order" expresses a meaning established by the principle of general rule and exception (*utsarga-apavāda*), for the purpose of setting aside inferior qualities (*heyadharma*); [the phrase] "in the stainless one" expresses a meaning established by the principle of the general and the particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*), for the purpose of setting aside inferior qualities; and [the term] "devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇam*).

This is because it is appropriate that the cognition of the absence of the commonality of qualities (guṇasāmānya) should ultimately conclude even in the absence of those properties—such as the qualities of *sattva* and so forth—which bring about proximity (*nikarṣa*) with their own substrates. Furthermore, it should be understood here that the refutation of the previously mentioned objection raised by others is established both by the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of "possessing heard auspicious qualities" and "purity," and by the statement [of the author] that the expression "devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇa*) is used in the singular. The statement regarding the *hiṃsā* injunction being subject to the principle of general rule and exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*), however, was made in accordance with the method accepted by Bhaṭṭa.

But it was not done so according to our own position, because of the established doctrine that the immolation of sacrificial animals (*paśusaṃjñapana*) does not constitute violence (*hiṃsā*). As it was stated [in response to the objection] "that [immolation] is impure": in the commentary on the sūtra "Because of the word" (*śabdāt*), the venerable Bhaṭṭasudarśana said: "This alone is the correct and unassailable resolution. Therefore, this is precisely what constitutes the difference between the *śyena* sacrifice and the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice. An activity that, even if it causes slight pain, accomplishes an extraordinary degree of prosperity (*abhyudaya*), is 'protection' (*rakṣaṇa*); whereas an activity whose ultimate result is misfortune (*anartha*) is 'violence' (*hiṃsā*)."

And it has been stated by the teacher Campakeśa in the *Vedāntakaṇṭakoddhāra*: "In reality, since the established conclusion is that the immolation of sacrificial animals (*paśusaṃjñapana*) is not indeed violence (*hiṃsā*), the Nyāya perspective is merely presented here in accordance with the conventional usage of the Mīmāṃsakas; therefore, there is no insistence on that [view]. And: "Because there is no evidence that an action intended for the purpose of death constitutes violence; for only an action that results in an undesirable fruit and does not produce a powerful desired [fruit] is considered violence."

It should be understood that the application of the principles regarding contradiction (*virodha*), commencement (*upakrama*), and the governing rule (*adhikaraṇa*) concerning passages on the qualified (*saguṇa*) and unqualified (*nirguṇa*) [Brahman] must be stated as a further elaboration (*abhyuccaya*), depending upon the restriction of priority and sequence (*paurvāparya-niyama*) regarding the contradictions asserted by others; therefore, that [restriction] is not explicitly mentioned here. || 70 ||

Beginning with the words "In the beginning, regarding the scriptural texts on difference" and continuing up to this point, the author of the Sūtras has, with the intention of showing that the proponent of falsehood (the Mṛṣāvādin) faces the same defects as those raised against the positions of the Sāṅkhya, Yoga, and other schools, has explained at length the refutation of the doctrine of falsehood. Now, in order to state—following the direction determined by the Sūtra "On account of the lack of consistency in [the doctrine of] a Lord"—that the supremacy of another deity is untenable because it contradicts the Vedānta, since the Vedānta texts are intent upon the supremacy of the Blessed Lord, he declares their purport (*tatparatva*):

"Who are you? "I am indeed the Knower of Reality. "What then is that supreme reality? "It is Viṣṇu. "How is that reality known? "From the observation of the three Vedas, specifically from the *Taittirīyaka*, which is the final portion [of the Vedas]. "If that is so, how then are other words [applied to him]? "Due to his qualities (*guṇa*). "In this regard, how is it that Rudra speaks here?"
According to that view, how could anything else arise, how could it descend, or how could it be led away? (71)

Regarding the statement "those who are devoted to Janārdana," the fact that the Upaniṣads have the Blessed Lord as their ultimate purport was mentioned there in brief; here it is stated somewhat more elaborately: "The one Blessed Lord Janārdana alone assumes the designations of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, which bring about creation, maintenance, and dissolution."

This is for the sake of identification—that the Blessed Lord alone, possessing the body of Rudra, is the object of worship in the two forms of meditation taught in the *Atharvaśiras* and the *Śikhā*. However, the word "Janārdana" is employed in the phrase "janārdanapraṇayiṣu" for the sake of facilitating the comprehension of the meaning that is about to be stated: "clearly [the Lord] who has the body of the enemy of the cities (Śiva), for the sake of non-return."

Since it has been stated, "Where can there be the emergence of an opponent before [me]?", this series of verses in the form of questions and answers was spoken by Varadaguru to a certain seeker—there being no possibility of a question from one desiring victory—and it serves as a summary of the detailed exposition that is about to be presented.

"Who are you?"—this is the question of one desiring to know. The answer to that is, "I am a knower of reality (*tattvavit*). One who knows *tattva*—the ultimate reality of the Supreme Deity—is a knower of reality. By the statement "knower of reality," there is an exclusion of the claim that one is a proponent of the supremacy of a deity imagined according to one's own personal preference. If that is so, regarding the state of being a knower of reality...

"What is the supreme reality?"—the meaning is: what is that which is superior to everything, devoid of any other entity in relation to itself, and endowed with unconditioned existence? "What is the deity?"—this is the sense of the question regarding the supreme deity. The neuter gender of the word "what" (*kim*) follows the gender of the word "reality" (*vastu*). This question arises because of the diversity of scriptural statements. The answer to it is: "Viṣṇu. The phrase "supreme reality" is supplied from the context. Viṣṇu alone is superior to everything and is devoid of anything else in relation to himself.

And here, the word "Viṣṇu" is employed to clarify a specific statement regarding the Void (śūnya), even with the suspicion that the phrase "Viṣṇu was then Hari alone, partless" might be a mere restatement (anuvāda). How so? Here, the term "Viṣṇu" is understood as "the supreme reality. The meaning of the question is: "Since various scriptural texts are observed, how can Viṣṇu’s supremacy be determined? The answer to this is: "tattvedaṃparā" (those [texts] intent on the truth of that [reality]).

The meaning of the reply is as follows: "That which has this as its supreme object" means that whose ultimate aim is this; regarding the reality (*tattva*)—the ultimate truth concerning the Deity—"this as its supreme reality" refers to such [texts]. Of those Vedānta texts beginning with the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka* from the *Taittirīyaka*, as well as the *Puruṣasūkta*, *Subālopaniṣad*, *Āruṇeyopaniṣad*, *Mahopaniṣad*, and others, through their "manifestation"—that is, through the correct perception characterized by being established as authoritative by virtue of possessing the sixfold marks of interpretive intent (*ṣaḍvidhatātparyaliṅga*)—there is the determination of Viṣṇu’s supremacy.
This is the sense of the reply.

By the phrase "tattvedampare" (intended for the knowledge of reality), there is an exclusion of those statements whose primary purpose is other than the injunctions for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*). The sense is that passages such as "Śambhu is to be meditated upon in the midst of space" are intended for the injunction of meditation on the sky (*dyu-pāsanā-vidhi*) and do not aim at determining the specific nature of the object of meditation (*upāsya-viśeṣa-nirṇaya*); whereas the *Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka*, however, is solely intent upon that [determination]. As stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Sudarśana: "The sentence 'He offers with the *juhū* ladle' has as its sole purport merely the fact that the *juhū* is the instrument for the oblation (*homa-sādhanatva-mātra*)."

There is no intention [in these texts] to determine a specific substance; for the sentence "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa-wood" does not have as its primary purpose the determination of a specific substance, even though the sentence "One offers with the *juhū*" is consistent with that [meaning]. Likewise, because sentences such as "Śambhu is to be meditated upon in the midst of space" are intended as injunctions for meditation (*upāsana*), they do not have the purpose of determining a specific object of meditation.

However, since the Nārāyaṇānuvāka does not have as its primary purpose the injunction for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*), it has as its sole purpose the determination of the specific object of meditation (*upāsya-viśeṣa-nirṇaya*). Therefore, one must admit that sentences such as "Śambhu in the midst of the ether" have meanings that are consistent with that [determination].

He asks with the words beginning “anyā” (others): “If that is so—if the Blessed One alone is the Supreme—then how are other statements such as ‘Neither being nor non-being, Śiva alone exists,’ or ‘Śambhu is to be meditated upon in the midst of space,’ and so forth, to be reconciled? This is the meaning of the question; the underlying sense is that it would result in the abandonment of the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of words such as “Śiva. The answer to this is: “By virtue of qualities” (*guṇavaśāt*). The word “are reconciled” (*saṃgacchante*) is to be supplied here.

The sense is that the application of words such as "Śiva" to the Blessed Lord is dependent upon qualities such as auspiciousness (*maṅgalatva*), because there exists the mark of the subversion of conventional usage (*rūḍhibhaṅga*) in the form of unsuitability for other meanings, and because [qualities like] being auspicious or being a bringer of happiness are common to other objects; thus, this is intended to exclude the suspected defect of [the word] being a cause [of those qualities]. He asks [this objection] with the words "Here he says," and so forth.

Regarding Rudra, in this context of transcendence (*paratva*), how does he say: "There is nothing whatsoever other than me," and so forth? The meaning is: how does he utter such a statement that brings about the cognition of supremacy (*pāramya*) as residing in itself and not residing in anything else? The answer to that is: "By his own observation" (*taddṛṣṭyā*).

The meaning is as follows: because it has been stated, "He entered from within to within," Rudra—thinking that, like Prahrāda, Vāmadeva, and others, the Supreme Self (Paramātman) residing within his own body would be the specific object of the cognition generated by the word "I" used by himself, and thus the aforementioned supremacy would reside in that very [Self]—said, "There is no other whatsoever," and so forth. The indeclinable *āha* means "he said"; it is either an indeclinable with this sense, or it is a present-tense (*laṭ*) form of the verb meaning "to speak. He asks: "How does he arise? Here, the word "Viṣṇu" is to be supplied.

The meaning of the question is: "How does Viṣṇu arise? How can the birth of the Blessed One, as stated in the passage 'Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—they all are brought forth,' be consistent with the supreme nature of the Blessed One? The answer to this is: "He descends"; the word "Viṣṇu" continues [from the previous context]. According to the Śruti text, "Being unborn, he is born in many ways," the birth of the Blessed One is not rooted in karma, but rather consists of incarnations by his own will. This is the meaning.

Since the introductory passage to "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra" is understood to be intent on prescribing the object of meditation by asking "Who is to be meditated upon?", the state of being an effect (kāryatva) is restated. And this is a restatement (anuvāda).

It would be according to the requirements of the means of attainment (*prāpaka*). In this passage, regarding the *Uttaranārāyaṇa* which concerns the Lord of Lakṣmī, the birth of the Blessed One in the form of an incarnation is heard; thus, there is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the incarnations of the Blessed One. The sense is that because there is no scriptural mention of incarnations for Brahmā and Śiva, their birth is restated as being equal to that of Indra, Varuṇa, and others. He asks: "How is it otherwise? [The answer is: passages such as "That which is higher than the high" (*tato yaduttarataram*) and "That which is within it" (*tasmin yadantaḥ*) constitute the etymological derivations (*nirvacana*) of the names of Rudra and the others.

The meaning of the question is: how can such things as the prescription for the substance of ashes be justified? The answer to that is: "Let it be led [to this context]. The meaning is that it is appropriate to lead [these matters] here because: (1) the word "thence" (*tataḥ*) does not denote a limit but functions as a reason; (2) the phrase "that which is within it" refers to the eightfold qualities mentioned in the passage "and these true desires"; (3) the etymological explanation of the names Rudra and others pertains to the *praṇava* (the syllable Om), which is a constituent part of the subsequent knowledge (*vidyā*); and (4) the prescription for the ashes is an auxiliary to the worship of the Lord whose body is Paśupati. || 71 ||

He elaborates upon the meaning already stated by means of twenty-four verses: "That Supreme Person whose boundless majesty was described in the *Yājñikī Upaniṣad* is described in the *Puruṣasūkta* as the cause."
Furthermore, in the Saubālika Upaniṣad, the great Upaniṣadic path is likewise; understand that it is the same for the Kaṭhavallī and the others as well. || 72 ||

In the *Yājñikī Upaniṣad*—that is, in the *Taittirīyaka*—the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) of boundless majesty is mentioned. That Supreme Person is spoken of as the cause in the *Puruṣasūkta*. This is determined by such passages as: "The lightning within the ocean, from the Puruṣa... ("*yam antassamudre vidyutaḥ puruṣāt adhi*"); "Lakṣmī and Hri are Your two wives" (*"hrīśca te lakṣmīśca patnyau"*); "Salutations to You, the Universal Form" (*"viśvarūpāya te namaḥ"*); "He who is beyond is Maheśvara" (*"yaḥ paraḥ sa maheśvaraḥ"*); and "We know the Puruṣa of a thousand eyes" (*"puruṣasya vidmaḥ sahasrākṣasya"*), as well as by the passage beginning with "A thousand heads" (*"sahasraśīrṣam"*). Thus, it is established that the *Taittirīyaka* has the Blessed Lord as its subject.

Because lying upon the ocean, having the color of lightning, and being the Lord of Lakṣmī are characteristics of the Blessed One; because the word *viśvarūpa* is understood through its conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) for the Blessed One according to Halāyudha’s lexicon—"Viṣvaksena, Viśvarūpa, Murāri, Śauri, Śārṅgin, Padmanābha, Mukunda"; and because, having referred to the Blessed One by means of the letter *a*, which is well-known as denoting the Blessed One in such statements as "The letter *a* denotes Viṣṇu," His supreme sovereignty is enjoined [in the passage] beginning with "We know the Person."

Because the attainment of the Blessed One is mentioned, and because meditation on Rudra is prescribed as a means to that end—given the statements, "We meditate upon Mahādeva" and "One should seek knowledge from Śaṅkara"—the *Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka* of the Taittirīyas is established as being devoted to the Blessed One. Just as the sentence, "Whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa* wood," has the purpose of specifying a particular material for the sacrificial implement prescribed by the rule, "He offers with the *juhū*," so too this *anuvāka* has the purpose of determining the specific object to be meditated upon in each respective *vidyā*. Thus, its devotion to the Blessed One is proven.

Regarding the term *paramapuruṣa* (the Supreme Person): this is a statement of the meaning established by such scriptural passages as, "There is nothing whatsoever higher than Him. Regarding the phrase *nissīmamahima* (of boundless majesty): this is a statement of the meaning established by such passages as, "He is the Great Lord (*maheśvara*). Furthermore, the fact that the word *puruṣa* is unique to the Blessed Lord is established through Śruti, Smṛti, lexicons, and reasoning. As for the statement, "Rudra is indeed the Puruṣa," that refers to the Blessed Lord Puruṣa having Rudra as His body.
[As it is said: "In the midst [of the ocean], there is a most terrible division situated in the waters of the great ocean..."

"Having meditated at the time of dusk, one shall attain union with Śiva. This [view] also is not to be accepted because it is *tāmasa* (of the nature of darkness). For when that which is well-known in the *Śruti* is possible, that alone is to be accepted. Furthermore, its being so [i.e., referring to Śiva] is not established, as it is merely supplementary to the meditation [on the Supreme]. Therefore, on account of attributes such as "lying upon the ocean," the *Taittirīyaka* passage refers to the Blessed Lord. Likewise, the *Puruṣasūkta* also refers to the Blessed Lord, due to the recognition of the meaning of the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka*.
[As it is said: "By means of *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, designation (*samākhyāna*), application (*viniyoga*), and corroboration (*upabṛṃhaṇa*)."

"In this manner, according to the statement, 'The wise know that this Puruṣasūkta has the Blessed Lord as its ultimate referent,' it is established through the Śrutis and other authorities that the Puruṣasūkta is devoted to the Blessed Lord. A detailed exposition may be sought in the works of the ancient teachers, such as the Vedāntavijaya. Furthermore, the Blessed Lord's status as the cause is stated therein by passages such as, 'From Him Virāj was born. This very point is expressed here: 'He is declared in the Puruṣasūkta as the Supreme Person (Paramapuruṣa) by virtue of being the Cause.'"

In the *Saubāliky-upaniṣad*—that is, the *Subāla-upaniṣad*—it is understood that the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) is stated to be the cause. The word "again" (*punaḥ*) refers to the occurrence of the act of stating what is taught in the *Subāla-upaniṣad*, in relation to the act of stating what is taught in the *Puruṣasūkta*. The meaning is that the *Subāla-upaniṣad* also has the Blessed Lord as its sole subject, because of its association with such terms as "the thousand-headed Person" (*sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ*). And the course of the *Mahopaniṣad* is likewise; that is, the manner in which the *Mahopaniṣad* establishes the reality [of Brahman] relies, in the manner described, upon the supremacy of the Blessed Lord. "Eko ha vai... [and so forth].

The meaning is that by the use of the term *Nārāyaṇa*—which is not shared by any other—and by the specific injunction [of him as the cause], the text declares that the Blessed Lord alone is the cause. Similarly, the *Kaṭhavallī* and other such texts are also devoted to the Blessed Lord; this is the meaning. In the *Kaṭhavallī*, beginning with "That goal which all the Vedas proclaim," and concluding with "He reaches the end of the path—that supreme abode of Viṣṇu"—it is stated that the *Kaṭhavallī* is also devoted to the Blessed Lord.

By the word "etcetera," the Maitrāyaṇīya and other scriptural texts are intended. Thus, in the passage, "The desirable splendor of Savitṛ—firm, immovable, immortal, named Viṣṇu, the support of all, the abode"—the fact that the reality taught in the Vedāntas, characterized by firmness, immovability, and so forth, is named Viṣṇu is enjoined; therefore, the Maitrāyaṇīya scripture has the Blessed Lord as its subject.

"The *Nārāyaṇopaniṣad*, beginning with 'Now, indeed, the Person Nārāyaṇa desired: "May I create offspring"'; the *Mahānārāyaṇopaniṣad*, beginning with 'Now, indeed, the Person Nārāyaṇa desired: "May I create offspring"' and 'Then he created the waters'; and the *Paiṅgirahasya*, beginning with 'There was only Nārāyaṇa alone; neither Brahmā nor Śaṅkara existed'—these and others are included by the word "etcetera. (Consider)—consider, that is, know, that the *Taittirīyaka-puruṣasūkta*, the *Subālopaniṣad*, the *Kaṭhavallī*, and so forth, are devoted to the Lord as the cause. Who are you?"

This is an injunction intended to demonstrate the credibility of the speaker’s own statement to one who has asked and desires to know; it is like the case of the sentence "See, the deer runs," where the meaning of the entire sentence functions as the object of the verb.
Now, as to the question "What is the course of the Mahopaniṣad?", he says:
Nārāyaṇa has proclaimed himself as the sole cause of the universe through the resonant declaration of the Mahopaniṣad, which begins with the words "Eko ha vai... and is full of intentional meaning.
He who, manifesting at the appointed time, brings about the destruction of the entire world—beginning with Brahmā, Īśa, the heavens, the earth, the waters, Svāhā, Īśa, Soma, and the Sun.

Nārāyaṇa: The Blessed One, whose name is unique and not shared by others, is one whose etymological derivation is beyond the reach of mere conjecture—contrary to the etymologies found in the *Manusmṛti* and the *Nirukta*, such as "the waters are called *nārāḥ*" and so forth. [He is described] with intent—that is, with a specific underlying purpose—by the opening passage beginning with "Eko ha vā," namely, "Eko ha vai nārāyaṇa āsīt" (In the beginning, indeed, Nārāyaṇa alone existed), and by the proclamation of the *Mahopaniṣad*—that is, by the clearly recited and unrefutable sentence of the *Mahopaniṣad* whose meaning is manifest.

As the single cause of the world—meaning as that cause which, by virtue of being the sole cause, is one, being without a second of its own kind due to its identity as the non-different efficient and material cause—he addressed him; he was addressed.

In the Sadvijñāna [Saddhida], the status of *sat* as the cause is established by the statement: "In the beginning, my dear, this was indeed *sat* alone. That very same *sat* is further specified as being *brahman* by the statement: "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman alone. Here, the phrase "this was alone in the beginning" is a restatement (*anuvāda*), while "Brahman" is the injunction (*vidhi*). Similarly, in the passage: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone," that very same entity is specified as being the *ātman*. Here too, "the Self" is the injunction, while "this" and so forth are the restatement.

Likewise, in this *Mahopaniṣad*, [the Lord] is specified as Nārāyaṇa in the passage, "In the beginning, indeed, there was only one Nārāyaṇa. Here too, "Nārāyaṇa" is the injunction (*vidhi*), while "one," and so forth, is the restatement (*anuvāda*). And here, by the principle of the convergence of all recensions (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-nyāya*) and the principle of the general and the particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-nyāya*), since all statements regarding the cause culminate in the Blessed Lord alone, the meaning is that the Blessed Lord alone is the cause; this is understood from the *Mahopaniṣad* and other such texts.

Terms such as *Hiraṇyagarbha* and others have meanings that are not uniquely appropriate, just like the terms *ākāśa*, *prāṇa*, and so on. Furthermore, terms such as *Śiva* are common to many referents due to their usage in various senses; thus, like terms such as *sat* (Being), they are incapable of bringing a specific [referent] to mind. Therefore, it is the term *Nārāyaṇa* alone that possesses a single, uniquely appropriate meaning;
the intention of the Śruti in designating him alone is expressed by the word "sākūtam" (with a hidden purpose).

Furthermore, in the passage "He who is Para is Maheśvara," the Lord is first referred to as "He who is Para" in accordance with the well-known fact that He is denoted by the syllable *a*. Then, when there is a desire to express the conventional meaning (*rūḍhy-artha*) of the word "Maheśvara," identity cannot be predicated between two things whose difference is already established. Moreover, there is no purpose in specifically enjoining here that [the Lord] has Rudra as His body. Furthermore, since the word "Maheśvara" is seen to be used extensively elsewhere in its etymological sense (*yogārtha*), it is used here specifically in reference to the Lord.

Furthermore, it is logical that the term *maheśvara* (the Great Lord) is prescribed here to denote one possessing the great quality of unsurpassed sovereignty, as this is seen to be the predominant usage. In this context, however, because the universal denoted by words such as *sat* (Being) requires a specific individual for its final determination (*paryavasāna*), and because the word *nārāyaṇa* is not observed to be used anywhere except in its conventional sense (*rūḍhi*), and because the Blessed One alone—being the body of all—is declared in the *Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa* and other texts to be the inner controller, it is impossible for anyone else to be the intended referent even through a secondary or non-literal application (*aparyavasāna-vṛtti*). Thus: "One..."

In the passage "Verily, Nārāyaṇa alone existed," by the word "Nārāyaṇa," it is Nārāyaṇa himself—who is capable of being the supreme cause—who is enjoined as being identical with the reality denoted by words such as "Being" (sat). Therefore:

The intention expressed here by the word *sākūtam* (with significance) is that, because the state of being the cause (*kāraṇatva*) is pervaded by the state of being Nārāyaṇa (*nārāyaṇatvavyāpyatvāt*), the possibility of causality does not exist for anyone other than Nārāyaṇa. Alternatively, the word *sākūtam* expresses the intention that this [statement] is properly understood as an injunction (*vidhi*) precisely because its meaning would otherwise not be established, and thus it does not become a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) simply on account of the words "not indeed" (*na ha vai*). Furthermore, since the disclosure of this very intention is carried out by the following verse, there is no tautology.

Even though the status of being Nārāyaṇa was predicated of the causal entity, because they are cognized by the same consciousness, it was stated that Nārāyaṇa, as the sole cause of the world, abandoned [the body] once the causality of Nārāyaṇa was established.

(And here, because the word *yat* in the subsequent clause is independent of the word *tat*, there is no need for the ellipsis of *tat*. "When" (*yaḥ*) means at the time of dissolution, at the time of the commencement of the cosmic withdrawal. "Manifests" (*samunmīlati*) means when [the Lord] possesses the excellence characterized by the union with His own volition, being present at that moment. However, in the doctrine of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) as the cause, the state of dissolution is fixed [by necessity]; such is the sense of the prefix *sam-*.

Brahmā is the four-faced one; Īśa is Rudra; dyau is the sky; Vasundharā is the earth; uḍūni are the stars; salilam is the waters; Svāhā is the beloved of Agni, and her lord is Fire; Soma is the Moon; Aṃśumān is the Sun. [The compound] is analyzed as: "that which has [the aforementioned] as its beginning" (pūrvādi), and that which is "entire" (aśeṣa), and that which is the "world" (jagat)—thus, in this *karmadhāraya* construction, it takes the second case ending. He causes the world to rest, meaning he causes it to dissolve. Nārāyaṇa has declared himself to be the cause; the meaning is that he alone is the agent of the dissolution of the world. Regarding this, the latter half [of the verse] states: "Neither Brahmā nor Īśāna..."

This passage is intended to explain the meaning of statements found in the Mahopaniṣad, such as, "Neither heaven and earth, nor the stars, nor the waters [are able to destroy it]. Therefore, since it is understood that the four-faced Brahmā, Īśāna (Śiva), and others are subject to destruction and so forth, it is impossible for them to be the cause of the universe. Consequently, the sense is that words such as *Hiraṇyagarbha* must ultimately terminate in the very same entity denoted by the word *Nārāyaṇa*, either through secondary application (*yoga*) or through a figurative extension (*aparyavasāna-vṛtti*). || 73 ||

He reveals the underlying intention: because [the world] has not yet been established, there would be no restatement of the cause of the universe in the Great Upaniṣad, according to the principle of passages such as "Eko ha vai" and "Upari hi devebhyaḥ."

For, by the natural force of the statement, the Lord’s status as the cause and the status of others as the effects were considered non-contradictory; yet, there remains nothing further to be enjoined here.

Because the cause of the world has not been previously established—since the fact that the causal entity denoted by terms such as "Being" (sat) is Nārāyaṇa is not understood from other passages—in the *Mahopaniṣad*, the portion beginning with "Eko ha vā" refers to the passage: "Eko ha vai nārāyaṇa āsīt."

According to the principle beginning with "For above the gods," as determined by the two sūtras—"But [these] are injunctions because they convey something not previously known" (*vacanāni tv apūrvatvāt*) and "The injunction, however, applies to the holding, because it conveys something not previously known" (*vidhis tu dhāraṇe ’pūrvatvāt*)—even when there is a connection with words such as *yat* (the relative pronoun) or *hi* (the particle indicating a reason), which suggest the status of a restatement (*anuvāda*), the sentence is indeed an injunction and not a restatement, because its meaning is not apprehended through any other means of knowledge (*māna*). However, in cases where the meaning is already apprehended through another means of knowledge, [the status of the words employed...]

[The opponent argues: "The investigation of the *gati* [the destination] is for the purpose of indicating that [the statement] is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what has been established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)," according to the maxim [that a statement is not an injunction if it merely repeats what is already known]. [The response is: It would not be a restatement—meaning it is unfit to be a restatement. Now, one might object: "Non-establishment indeed consists in being beyond the scope of other means of valid cognition, whether supportive or subversive. In this case, even if there is no supportive means of cognition (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*), an injunction cannot stand because of the existence of a subversive means of cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*); for the text 'neither being nor non-being, Śiva alone' exists as a destroyer of its status as an injunction. To this, he says: "By the sentence," and so forth.

"Non-contradictory" means not sublated by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Regarding the Lord Nārāyaṇa, His status as the cause is established by the natural sense of the scriptural statement; for, according to the principle that "scripture is purposeful where [the matter] has not been previously established," the character of being an injunction (*vidhi*) is inherently established, and thus it is indeed determined to be enjoined. Likewise, regarding others such as Brahmā and Īśāna, their status as effects is also determined from the natural sense of the statement. Therefore, the meaning is that because it is not sublated by other means of valid cognition, it possesses the character of an injunction.

The point is that because the word *śiva* is common [to many], it does not destroy its status as an injunction (*vidhi*), just like words such as *sat* (Being) and so forth. Thus, the established meaning has been stated; even though the particle *ha vai* destroys its status as an injunction, here [it is said]: "Indeed, one alone was Nārāyaṇa..."

However, in the sentence "He existed," there is nothing at all to be enjoined; rather, it is appropriate that this [sentence] functions as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of a meaning already established by another explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) within its own context, namely, "At that time Viṣṇu alone existed, the partless Hari. It does not, however, mean that it is a restatement of a meaning expressed in a sentence containing common terms such as "Śiva" and the like, which have distinct and incompatible referents. This is the sense.

Here, by the word "param" (supreme), it is indicated that while the sentences concerning the *āgneya* sacrifice and others function as injunctions (*vidhi*) because their meaning is not otherwise established, the sentence "In the beginning, indeed, Nārāyaṇa alone existed" is appropriately an explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*); thus, its difference from the sentences concerning the *āgneya* sacrifice is pointed out. This very point is supported in the *Tātparyadīpikā* on the *Vedārthasaṃgraha*.

The venerable Bhaṭṭasudarśana states: "Indeed, in the passage 'Nanveko ha vai nārāyaṇa āsīt' (Now, indeed, Nārāyaṇa alone was), because of the hearing of the word 'ha vai', which indicates the nature of a restatement (anuvāda), this sentence—like the sentence 'Sarvāṇi ha vā imāni bhūtānyākāśādeva samutpadyante' (All these beings, indeed, arise from Ākāśa alone)—is dependent on another sentence, as it is primarily a restatement."

In this regard, it is argued that by the statement, "The particle *eva* and its occurrence therein constitute the characteristic of a predicate," the very soul (*jīva*) mentioned in the sentence, "He is neither being nor non-being, but Śiva alone," which contains the particle *eva* indicating an injunction, is merely being restated (*anūdita*). To this, it is replied: according to the maxim, "A scripture is purposeful only with respect to what has not [otherwise] been established," the particle *hi* does not subvert the injunctive force that is inherently present.

In the case of the statement, "The cake on eight potsherds is for Agni," although there is the presence of the word *yat*, which indicates a restatement according to the rule that "the connection with *yat*, being first mentioned, and so forth, is the characteristic of the subject (*uddeśya*"), its status as an injunction (*vidhi*) is established by the sūtra, "But [these] statements are injunctions because they convey what is not already known" (*vacanāni tvapūrvatvāt*). Similarly, in the case of "For he holds it above for the gods," although the word *hi* is present, its status as an injunction is established by the sūtra, "But it is an injunction regarding holding, because it conveys what is not already known" (*vidhistu dhāraṇe’pūrvatvāt*).

Therefore, the word *havai* does not inherently subvert the status of an injunction; rather, it indicates the scope of a word that has been employed after the injunctive status has been subverted by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). In the passage concerning the cause of space (*ākāśa*), however, because the injunctive status is subverted by factors such as logical incompatibility (*ayogyatva*), the word *havai* serves to indicate its character as a restatement (*anuvāda*). In this case, however, since the matter is not established by another means of knowledge and there is no factor to subvert the injunctive status, the word *havai* does not inherently subvert an already established injunctive status.

If it is argued that by the phrase "Śiva alone," the status of [the passage] as an injunction (*vidhi*) is destroyed, we say no. This is because in such expressions as "May your paths be auspicious" (*śivāste santu panthānaḥ*), "May the action be auspicious" (*śivaṃ karmāstu*), and "Auspicious for the auspicious, inauspicious for the inauspicious" (*śivaḥ śivānāmaśivaḥ śivānām*), we observe that the word "Śiva" has other meanings; thus, the word "Śiva" is common to many things (*sādhāraṇa*). Even though it is common, if it were to subvert the status of an injunction—as in the case of words like "Being alone" (*sad eva*)—then the sentence "Śiva alone" would become a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). Furthermore, let it be a restatement; [that does not invalidate its authority].

Nevertheless, because one hears statements of identical meaning such as "At that time Viṣṇu was indeed Hari, partless," it is merely a restatement of that [fact]; thus, it is not a restatement of a statement intended to convey a contradictory meaning.

Alternatively, even if one were to disregard the Lord’s causality and the others’ effect-status based on the literal sense of the sentences, that too—the Lord’s causality and the others’ effect-status—is not contradictory.

The meaning is that it is worthy of being enjoined because it does not contradict other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). It is not only on account of its intrinsic consistency and lack of contradiction that it is worthy of being enjoined; rather, since there is no other thing to be enjoined here, he states that the Lord’s status as the cause alone is what must be enjoined: "There is nothing else whatsoever to be enjoined here."

The sense is that since the status of being an injunction (*vidhitva*) is intrinsic, since [the cause] is already established, since the word *ha vai* does not negate the status of being an injunction, since the Lord’s causality is not known through any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and since the fact that the four-faced Brahmā and others are effects is not contradicted by other means of knowledge—and likewise the Lord’s causality is not contradicted by other means of knowledge—furthermore, because there is no other thing to be enjoined in this sentence, the Lord’s causality is indeed what is to be enjoined. The underlying intention is that other passages which appear to concern the injunctions for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*) should be interpreted in accordance with this [text]. || 74 ||

Granted that the Blessed One is the cause; yet, within that very Lord Nārāyaṇa—who is designated by the word "ether" (ākāśa) and is well-known as the cause—there exists a certain specific principle (tattva-viśeṣa) mentioned in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad as the object of meditation for those seeking liberation.

Now, regarding the passage: "Now, that which is within this city of Brahman, the small lotus-palace, within that is the small ether; what is within that is to be sought, that indeed is what one should desire to understand"—because it is heard that this ether possesses the quality of being the bearer (*nirvoḍhṛ*) of name and form, and because in the *Puruṣasūkta* the Puruṣa is seen to be the agent of name and form, it might be thought that something other than the Puruṣa (who is a synonym for ether) is to be sought and meditated upon. To refute this doctrine of a [Brahman] transcending space (*vyomātīta-vāda*), [the author states]:
"Whatever [is created] from the Supreme Person, who is the maker of names and forms, [that belongs to] the one named 'ether'..."
That Supreme Being, who is to be worshipped in the lotus of the heart and whose glory was sung at the summit of the Vedas by the chanters of the Sāmaveda,

is described there through questions and answers as possessing eight qualities— beginning with the destruction of sin and ending with the power of true resolve— which are distinct from His own nature and which the learned proclaim as ever-arising attributes of His.

The phrase "in the *Śrutiśiras*" refers to the *Chāndogya* Upaniṣad among the Sāma-veda chanters; the word "param" (supreme) is used to indicate the opponent's misconception that even the *Taittirīya* and other texts rely solely on the *Chāndogya* as their source for asserting that the Supreme is beyond the ether (*vyomātīta*). Alternatively, the term "param" may be construed with a shifted word order as "paramapuruṣataḥ param" (higher than the Supreme Person). [The text continues: "of the one named Ākāśa"—meaning from the one designated by the name Ākāśa—referring to the "creator of names and forms" (*saṃjñāmūrtikartṛ*).

Therefore, that which is other than the Supreme Person—the Supreme Person spoken of in the Puruṣasūkta as the agent of name and form, which are heard in scripture to have Ākāśa as their agent—is not [the creator].

Something—one [entity]—which is to be worshipped in the heart-lotus (*hṛtpadma*), the lotus of the heart, has been proclaimed as that which is enjoined to be sought after. The form *upāsyaṃ* is derived from the root *gā* (to proclaim) in the passive voice (*karmaṇi*) with the suffix *luṅ* and the *ciṇ* augment. The word *syāt* is used to demonstrate that, in accordance with the suffix *tavya* in the scriptural passage "That is to be sought after" (*tadanveṣṭavyam*), it is appropriate to supply an auxiliary verb in the optative (*liṅ*) mood. Thus, in the passage beginning with "Now, as for this," the subject (*dharmī*) of the matter suspected by others has been indicated along with the grounds for their doubt. Now, regarding that subject...

It is not possible that the specific qualities (tattvaviśeṣa) are stated by another [source]; rather, the collection of qualities is what is expressed by the phrase "that which is within it. He states this with the words beginning with "tatra," etc. In the expression "tadguṇān," there are two words: *tat* and *guṇān*. Otherwise, there would be the fault of redundancy with the word *tadīyān*. Furthermore, since the preceding word *yat* requires a correlative *tat*, there would be the necessity of supplying an unstated *tat*. Moreover, *tat* ends in the accusative case. That which was sung (*agāyi*) is the object (*karman*).

"They proclaim the qualities" means they speak of them as being qualities; this refers to the authors of the Śruti, the Sūtras, and the Vākyas, as well as our own teachers who follow them, and so forth. In that regard—specifically in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad—by means of a question containing an objection, namely, "What is found there?", and the answer, "As vast as this space (ākāśa)... [it is established].

By such [passages] as these, which contain the refutation of that [objection], and by the subsequent [text], [the qualities] beginning with the destruction of evil—namely, being free from sin and so forth—and ending with having true resolve (*satyasaṃkalpatā*), are [meant]. These remaining [qualities] are those taught in such passages as: "He is free from sin, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger, free from thirst, his desires are true, his resolves are true"; "and these true desires"; and "in him all desires are contained. They are *tadīyān*: belonging to the Supreme Person who is the inner space (*daharākāśa*).

The term *anidamudayinaḥ* means those that do not arise at this time—that is, those which are not subject to manifestation (*āvirbhāva*) at this moment; they are eternally manifest. The meaning is that they proclaim the eight qualities (referring to the multitude of qualities of the Supreme Person, who is the substrate [dharmin] designated as "that which is within it" in the context of the small ether). Therefore, the intended sense is that there is no possibility of a particular ontological principle being the object of meditation.

The Great Teachers have provided an explanation of the question and its answer in that context: "If they should say: 'In this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-palace; within it is a small ether (ākāśa). What is there that ought to be sought, or that ought to be understood? This is a question containing a challenge (*codyagarbha*). Otherwise, the restatement beginning with "that which is this" (*yadidam*) would be purposeless. Therefore, the intention of the question is: "Because of its subtlety, what could possibly exist within the small ether?"

This being the case, why has the form of a question regarding the subject (dharmin) implied by the word *svam* been revived? Furthermore, the resolution of the objection was stated on the grounds that the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished [in the statement]: "As great as this space is, so great is this space within the heart. By the expression "so great," a doubt regarding limitation [of the self] arises.

By stating that he is the support of all through the passage beginning with "In him both heaven and earth," the intended meaning of the preceding sentence—that [Brahman] is not limited—is made manifest. Thus, when the objection has been refuted, the answer to the question "In whom are desires contained? has been stated. Immediately thereafter, having described the desires with the passage beginning "The Self, free from evil," the text says, "Now, those who depart here having discovered the Self and these true desires"; by the word "true" (*satya*), heaven, earth, and so forth are excluded.

The extraction of the meaning of "freedom from sin" (*apahatapāpmatva*) has been elucidated by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Sudarśana as follows: "There is a certain specific nature of the Lord which consists in His being an adversary to the power of actions—whether they be those that produce results or even those performed for His own sport—to generate their fruits within the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*). This is precisely the meaning of the term 'freedom from sin' (*apahatapāpman*) when it refers to the perfectly pure Self; however, in that case, [the quality] is not subject to concealment. Upon the removal of obstacles, it becomes manifest. The distinction is this: while [in the soul] it is not subject to concealment by the Lord and is eternally manifest."

This has been refined by the venerable Vīrarāghava in his commentary on the *Advaitavidyāvijaya*: "The state of being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*) is the absence of evil whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a relation of objective content that is not restricted to a different locus [from the self]. Its manifestation and concealment consist respectively in its co-occurrence with and non-co-occurrence with the counter-correlate [evil]. Alternatively, freedom from evil is a quality that serves as the cause for the non-arising of evil at a time when the causes of evil are present."

Its manifestation consists in the possession of the property that delimits its causal agency (*prayojakatāvacchedakadharma*). For the cause of the aforementioned non-production is the nature of the Self (*ātmatva*) as qualified by the absence of being the object of the Lord’s volition for bondage at a time delimited by the period preceding the separation from the final body. Otherwise, the non-clinging of karma in the state of liberation would be untenable. Nor can this be established through knowledge (*vidyā*), because knowledge serves merely to prevent the clinging of accidental sins (*prāmādikāgha*), and because it would apply equally to the eternal Lord (*nityeśvara*).

Furthermore, because non-origination is predicated of that which is insentient, there is no redundancy in the qualifier. And "the state of having true volition" (satya-saṃkalpatva) consists in being the substratum for a substance capable of transformation that does not depend on any other effort for the production of its own object. That substance is indeed the knowledge of volition itself, and its manifestation is its distinction by such a particular state. Thus [it is said].

By the phrase "not arising from this," there is the exclusion of qualities such as being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatā*) and so forth, which were stated in the subsequent speech of Prajāpati regarding the individual soul (*jīva*). These [qualities] have been concealed within the heart. Furthermore, the mention of "eight" is for the purpose of illustration, referring to the multitude of attributes such as being the creator and sustainer of heaven, earth, and so forth.

This has been stated by Bhaṭṭa Sudarśanapāda in the *Vedārthasaṅgraha-tātparyadīpikā*: "The meaning is that the collection of qualities such as being the creator and sustainer of heaven, earth, and so forth, as well as the collection of qualities such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and the like, are intended [to be attributed to Him]. Thus the scripture (*śruti*) has been cited. The aphorism (*sūtra*) is: "Desire and the rest [belong] elsewhere, because of the abode and so forth. (Brahma-sūtra 3.3.39).

And the author of the *Vākya* says that there is a designation of desires in the phrase, "that which is within it. The venerable authors of the *Bhāṣya* explain: "The meaning is that 'desires' (kāmāḥ) are those qualities such as freedom from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth, because they are desired. Therefore, the meaning is that the Śruti, the author of the Sūtras, the author of the *Vākya*, and the venerable authors of the *Bhāṣya* all maintain that what is situated within [the city of Brahman] according to the phrase "that which is within it" is not a separate reality (*tattvāntara*), but rather the quality of the Supreme Person.

The position that the phrase "that which is within it" (tasmin yad antaḥ) refers merely to the small ether (daharākāśa) was previously refuted by the argument beginning with "the fourfold lack of natural fitness" (asvārasyacatuṣṭaya). Here, however, there is no tautology, because what is being rejected is the specific nature of the reality residing within the small ether. The form *udgṛṇanti* is derived from the root *gra*, listed in the *kryādi* class, in the third person plural with the *śnā* affix. || 75 ||

He refutes the claim that the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad has as its purport a reality superior [to Brahman]: having introduced the Primordial Person as the cause of immortality, and having set aside other paths, it proclaims the supremacy of the Goddess who is the Mistress of All for the sake of attaining Him.
Therefore, that which is superior to what has been stated therein— that which bestows liberation—
is the conclusion declared in the Śvetāśvatara Āgama, which contains the statement of the reason for what was previously proclaimed.
In this regard, the following passage from the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad is relevant to the subject at hand: "I know this great Puruṣa,
resplendent like the sun, beyond darkness."
Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death;
there is no other path for this journey.
Than whom there is nothing else higher;
than whom there is none smaller and none greater.
Like a tree, he stands alone, motionless in heaven; by him, this entire world is pervaded as the Puruṣa.
That which is higher than that is formless and free from suffering.
Those who know this become immortal.
But others enter only into suffering.
He whose face, heads, and necks are everywhere, who dwells in the secret cave of the heart of all beings—
"That Blessed One is all-pervading; therefore, Śiva is omnipresent.
He is the Great Lord, the Supreme Puruṣa, the impeller of this [universe] consisting of sattva. Thus [it is said].

In this context, regarding the statement "there is nothing whatsoever beyond or superior to Him," the negation of anything superior to the Puruṣa refers to objects other than the "Supreme" (para) which is about to be described. However, in the phrase "that which is higher than that," the meaning is that there is a reality consisting of Śiva which is higher—that is, more supreme—than the Puruṣa previously introduced. Therefore, the position of the opponent is that Śiva is all-pervading because He is about to be described [as such].

In the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), however, because of the scriptural declarations that [the Lord] is the Great Person (*mahāpuruṣa*), has a complexion like the sun, and is beyond darkness, it is stated in the passage beginning with "I know Him" (*vedāham*) that the Blessed One is the means to liberation, while anything else is not so. To substantiate this, the passage beginning with "Than whom there is nothing higher" (*yasmāt param*) declares that the Supreme Person is devoid of any equal or superior. The meaning is: than whom there is nothing else higher; in no way whatsoever does anything distinct from the Person possess superiority. Than whom there is none smaller and none greater.

Thus, the meaning is that there is no one superior to or more sovereign than the Puruṣa. Therefore, regarding the passage beginning with "that which is higher than that" (*yad uttarataram*): since the principle of Puruṣa alone is the highest (*uttarataram*), for that reason—whatever is higher than that is formless (*arūpam*) and free from affliction (*anāmayam*), being opposed to the body produced by karma and the suffering caused thereby; those who know this become liberated, whereas others—those devoid of this knowledge—attain only suffering. This is the meaning.

By this [verse], that which was asserted at the outset—that the knowledge of the Person (*puruṣavidyā*) is the cause of immortality while anything other than it is not the means—is concluded along with its supporting reason. Since a proposition requires a reason, it is appropriate that the word "from that" (*tataḥ*) has the sense of a reason. Furthermore, it is logical that the word *tat* refers back to and functions as the reason for what is indicated by the instrumental case-ending in the word "by the Person" (*puruṣeṇa*), which lacks any formal primacy in the verbal expression.

And thus, since the natural sense of the phrase "from that" (tataḥ) is to denote a cause rather than a limit, and since no entity superior to the Person is prescribed in this sentence, this sentence cannot serve to restrict the negation of what is superior as stated in the passage, "Than whom there is none higher, nor any other."
This is what he says with the words "having introduced," and so forth; [it refers to] the Primordial Person (Ādipuruṣa) who is the cause, as stated in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad.

Having introduced the Blessed One as the cause of immortality (*amṛta*) and established him at the outset as the means to liberation, [the author] sets aside—i.e., rejects—any other path, i.e., any other means, to that immortality. This refers even to a single part of the subject, just as in the expression: "These ten are the royal elephants; these very ones are his horses. To establish this—that is, to demonstrate that [the Blessed One alone] is the means while others are not—the sense is that if another alternative were to exist, then even that [other] might become a means.

"Niṣpratibhaṭām" means without rival; that is to say, uncontracted and not merely occasional. "Sārveśvarīm" refers to the state of being the Lord of All (*sarveśvaratva*). The feminine suffix *ḍīṣ* is applied because the suffix *ṣyañ* added to *sarveśvara* is marked with the letter *ṣ*. "Udghuṣya" means having clearly established. If only "sārveśvarīm" had been stated, there might arise the notion that this is merely the common case; therefore, "niṣpratibhaṭām" is said. By this, the meaning obtained from the words *kiṃcit* and *kaścit* found in the Śruti is restated. Here, in the first half-verse, the meaning of [the passage] beginning with "I know this... is restated by the first quarter-verse.

The meaning of the passage beginning with "than which there is nothing higher" (*yasmāt paraṃ nāparam*) is stated by the second quarter [of the verse]. In that regard—the reference to the *Śvetāśvatara*—the statement "that which is higher than the highest" (*tato yaduttaratam*), the statement "which bestows liberation, which grants release" (*muktidāyi mokṣapradam*), and the statement "those who know this become immortal" (*ya etadviduramṛtāste bhavanti*) all have this same meaning. Furthermore, the word "this one" (*ayam*), though singular, by its inherent power (*sāmarthyāt*) refers both to the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and to the objective reality (*artha*).

Then, that which takes the form of the statement "that which is higher than this" is the *ukti* (statement). It is called *nigamana* (conclusion) because it conforms to the gender of the predicate (*vidheya*). Regarding "of what was stated at the beginning": it refers to the meaning stated in the introduction—that the Lord is the means (*upāya*) and everything else is not the means. The conclusion consists of a summary accompanied by the statement of the reason; it is the final recapitulation together with the explanation of the grounds for the Lord’s unique status as the means to liberation. This [status] is defined by the Lord’s uncommonness as the means to liberation.

The meaning is that this summary of the Lord’s being the means and others not being the means is presented following the statement of that causal nature which consists in being a communicator, culminating in the unsurpassed and supreme excellence belonging to the Blessed One. Therefore, the intention is that there is no room here for the doctrine of a superior entity [other than the Lord]. This very point has been aphorized as: "And likewise because of the negation of another."
"He whose face, head, and neck are everywhere; who dwells in the secret cave of all beings;
who is all-pervading—that Blessed Lord is therefore Śiva, present everywhere.
This explains that the word "Śiva" occurring in this passage refers to the Blessed Lord (Bhagavat)—(beginning with the words "yad," etc.).

Since the arrival of the White Horse (Śvetāśvatara) [Upaniṣad] indicates another clear application regarding the Blessed One— who is certainly the abode of Śiva, the bestower of liberation as previously described,
all-pervading, and possessing faces, heads, and necks on every side— he alone is the Lord.
This Great One is the instigator of the sentient being; thus, the Puruṣa is once again made manifest. || 77 ||

The *Śvetāśvatara-āgama*—specifically the passage beginning with "He who is all-pervading" (*śvetāśvatarastha-sarvānana*) and so forth—is the agent that employs the term "Śiva" found in the phrase "therefore Śiva is all-pervading. Because of the necessary connection between the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative *tat*, the word *tat* is to be supplied [as the correlative]. That [term] refers to the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa. Another clear usage is the phrase "the eternal Śiva" (*śāśvataṃ śivam*), which is employed without doubt. The expression "another usage" (*prayogāntaram*) is a compound formed according to the *mayūravyaṃsaka*-type group.

The analysis of the compound is *bahuvrīhi*: "that whose interval between [the word] *śiva* and [the word] *pada* is clear. The sense is that since the fact that the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka* has the Blessed Lord as its subject matter is established by many authorities, it is "clear" (*spaṣṭam*) that the word *śiva* occurring therein refers to the Blessed Lord. Such a word *śiva* is the object (*karman*). The *Śvetāśvatara-āgama* is the agent (*kartṛ*). Regarding the analysis "that which is both commenced (*prakrānta*) and bestows liberation (*muktiprada*)," the compound is formed like *nimnonnata* ("low and high") and so forth; it refers to that which bestows liberation, being introduced by the passage beginning with "I know this one" (*vedāhametam*).

"Having pervaded all-pervading [reality], Nārāyaṇa remains"—thus, by virtue of being the nature of the Blessed One, he is established as "all-pervading" because he possesses that all-pervasiveness taught in the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka*. Furthermore, he is described in the present passage as "having faces, heads, and necks on all sides," because he possesses the quality of having faces, heads, and necks everywhere, as stated in the *Puruṣasūkta*.
