It is precisely in that Blessed One that [the word "Śiva"] is pointed out; the meaning is that this word "Śiva" refers exclusively to the Blessed One by means of the aforementioned indicators of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
The word "dhruvam" (certainly) denotes certainty. That Blessed One, the Great Lord, is indeed the Puruṣa who sets this *sattva* into motion;

thus, by the subsequent statement, He is again made manifest and further established. For there, because of the hearing of the word "Puruṣa" and because of the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of the Blessed One consisting in being the impeller of *sattva*, His reference to the Blessed One is clear; therefore, the intended meaning is that the word "Śiva" occurring here also refers to the Blessed One.

Indeed, according to the Maitrāyaṇīya Śruti, "That which is his *sattvika* portion is this Viṣṇu who is the *brahmacārī*," it is understood that the quality of promoting *sattva* is a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of the Blessed Lord (*bhagavat*). Furthermore, it is understood from such statements as "the word *bhagavān* is [used] for the Blessed Lord alone" that [this term] is unique to the Blessed Lord. Therefore, the intention is that the word *śiva*, due to its preceding and succeeding context, refers to the Blessed Lord. Since he is the Blessed Lord, the meaning is that *Śiva* is auspicious (*maṅgala*), even though he is all-pervading;
otherwise, there would be the fault of tautology between the two words *sarvavyāpin* and *sarvagata*.

The word *Śiva* refers to the Blessed Lord (*bhagavat*) because its conventional meaning—as in words such as "space" (*ākāśa*)—is inappropriate [in this context]. Regarding this, the venerable Bhaṭṭa Sudarśana has said: "The possession of all faces, heads, and necks serves as a reminder of the meaning of the *Puruṣasūkta*," and so forth. Furthermore, the Blessed One (the Commentator) has explained this in detail in the *Vedārthasaṅgraha*: "That the Puruṣa alone is denoted by the word *Śiva* through his connection with the qualities of *śabda* and *dhī* is already known from such passages as 'the eternal Śiva'."

Immediately thereafter, [the text] states that the Puruṣa alone is the one denoted by the word Śiva. Regarding the verse, "The Puruṣa is indeed the Great Lord, the impeller of this Sattva," the *Tattvārthadīpikā* explains that the word Śiva is expressed and recognized here by means of the term "this" (*eṣa*). Furthermore, in the verse, "He whose faces, heads, and necks are everywhere... [it is stated].

Because [the attributes] such as "having faces on all sides" would contradict the fact that all [beings] have their faces on the front of the Lord's face, the term *sarvatomukhaśirogrīvaḥ* ("having faces, heads, and necks on all sides") is stated with the intention that this is a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* (a possessive compound with non-co-referential members), where "faces," "heads," and "necks" are understood to exist everywhere. Furthermore, with the intention that this designation by the word *śiva* refers specifically to the Blessed One (*bhagavat*) who has been described as "all-pervading," it is said that he "designates him"—that is, he designates the one already designated by the word *bhagavat*. || 77 ||
When there was neither darkness nor light, neither night nor day, neither being nor non-being—Śiva alone existed.
That is the Imperishable, that is the most excellent splendor of Savitṛ; from it the ancient wisdom issued forth.

Thus, he establishes that the word *Śiva* occurring in the subsequent passage refers to the Blessed Lord: "(Yadityādi)"— that the term *Śiva* which the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad employs when *Hara* is foremost, and which pertains to the Supreme Cause of the universe, is indeed appropriately applied to Him alone.

Those who seek that [liberation] and are well-versed in the Upaniṣads call this cause by such names as Sādhāraṇya, Vidura, Viṣṇu, Bhagavat, Nārāyaṇa, and so forth, according to their respective portions.

The Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad employs the term "Śiva" in reference to that state of Śiva which it declares further on: "Neither being nor non-being, Śiva alone. It designates this state of Śiva later in the passage: "The eternal, auspicious [state]... and so forth, where it is applied to the Blessed Lord who is the destroyer of all—namely, the Supreme Cause of the universe, the subject concerning the cause of the world. That is the term "Śiva."

The word "agre" (in the beginning) is also connected here. "Agre" means at the time prior to creation. As stated in the passage, "In the beginning, that One breathed, windless, by its own inherent power" (*svadhayā*), He exists by His own power of sustenance, remaining unabsorbed like Brahmā, Īśāna, and others. It is in Him alone—in the Blessed Lord designated by the word "Hari"—that this occurs.

It is appropriate [to use the term *yukta*] because it is fit for the application (*yoga*) in the sense of a relationship consisting of being an enlightener; or, when the world is described as void in passages such as "darkness" (*tamaḥ*), it is fit for application in that very context to manifest its auspicious nature, or to exclude the defects suspected in its being a cause—the meaning is that it is fit for application in that very context.

Because this word "Śiva" refers to the Cause—since it is established in the *Mahopaniṣad* and other texts that the Blessed Lord alone is the Cause; because the word "Śiva" is seen used elsewhere for the Blessed Lord; because the well-known Śiva (the deity) is heard to be subject to destruction while the Blessed Lord is not; and because the manifestation of auspiciousness and so forth is necessary here even without the conventional application to another deity.

The sense is that because of the great frequency with which the word *śiva* is employed, this word *śiva* refers to the Blessed Lord (*bhagavat*). Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that, in order to favor both meanings of the word *śiva*, this term *śiva* refers specifically to Rudra? To this, he says: "Because of its commonality," and so forth. For (*hi*), the Upaniṣadic portions—specific sections found in the *Mahopaniṣad* and other Upaniṣads—being desirous of that [word], and seeking that common term *śiva* in order to exclude any suspected defects regarding [Rudra’s] causality, or else to demonstrate auspiciousness even in the state of universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyatva*).

By means of names such as Viṣṇu, Bhagavat, Nārāyaṇa, and so forth—found in scriptural passages such as "At that time there was Viṣṇu, the all-pervading Lord; indeed, there was only one Nārāyaṇa"—which are remote from common usage, which are established through yogic derivation, and which lack application to any other individual, [the scriptures] declare this very Lord whom I have previously cited in the first half [of the verse] as the subject of the word *Śiva* in the Śruti to be the Cause—they establish Him as the cause of the universe. (The term "and so forth" includes names such as Puruṣa. They declare this very Lord, who is the object of the word *Śiva* occurring in the Śruti and whom I have taken up in the first half, to be the Cause—they designate Him as the cause of the world.

Therefore, the meaning is that it is logical for that state of Śiva to exist in that very place; however, there is no possibility for the names of Nārāyaṇa and others to apply elsewhere, according to the scriptural statement: "Viṣṇu alone is proclaimed as the destination for all other names."

By the passage beginning with "This word 'Bhagavān'... and so forth, it is understood that the names Viṣṇu and others are common [to other deities] and thus remote [from the primary subject]. In this context, if two types of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) were to support the word *Śiva*, there would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the word *Nārāyaṇa*. However, if one abandons the specific conventional usage of the word *Śiva* and accepts only its general conventional usage, then there would be no figurative indication anywhere; therefore, the specific conventional usage should not be favored. Moreover, according to the principle of the "external ghee" (*bahirājyanaya*), the word *Śiva* does not possess a specific conventional usage.

Nor should it be argued that, this being the case, there would likewise be no specific conventional usage (*viśeṣarūḍhi*) for the word *puruṣa*; for we accept a specific conventional usage for the word *puruṣa* on the strength of the evidence establishing it as His name. Precisely because it would entail the fault of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the word *nārāyaṇa*, the failure to admit two modes of operation (*vṛtti*) even for Vedic words such as *īśa* and others is refuted. Furthermore, it is well known that if one were to accept a derivative etymological application (*yoga*) of the word *nārāyaṇa* to anyone other than the Blessed Lord, the nasalization of the *ṇa* sound (*ṇatva*) would be impossible.

The sense is that if one were to justify [the form] by some particular derivation—such as through the rule *aṇ-kyaṅ-luṭ-sukṛteṣu* and so forth—it would mean abandoning the well-established usage found in the *Manusmṛti* and other texts. Furthermore, the refutation of the justification for the suffix *ṇatva* as conceived by the moderns (navya) in another manner should be sought in our own work, *Ṇatvatattvaprapañca*.

The meaning of this statement has been elucidated by the Great Teachers (*mahācāryas*): when "darkness merges into the darkness beyond the divine," that darkness is in an undivided state, and there is neither day nor night; rather, it is the Blessed Lord alone, devoid of all effects. At that time, by the term "the Imperishable" (*akṣara*), the absence of modification in the essential nature of the Blessed Lord is enjoined. Furthermore, the designation of the Blessed Lord here by the word "Śiva" is intended to manifest His auspicious nature even amidst universal voidness. Alternatively, let the word "Śiva" itself be the enjoining term.

Furthermore, by the word "Śiva," there may indeed be an injunction [of the Lord] as the cause, in accordance with the injunction of Nārāyaṇa as the cause. Nor should a contrary view be suspected; for words such as "Śiva" are designations of the Blessed Lord, they possess a conventional meaning that submerges other specific etymologies and shares commonality [with other names], and they are seen to be used for the Blessed Lord in actual usage. || 78 ||
He explains what was stated in the two verses beginning with "yacchvetāśvatare" (that which [is taught] in the Śvetāśvatara): "(yadagre...
etc.)"—that supreme Brahman, the cause of the universe, the auspicious state revealed by the Śruti, who is awake at the beginning, is that Blessed Lord at the end of the Āgama of the Śvetāśvataras.
Since the word "Śiva" employed in that Yajurvedic mantra is not uncommon to others, it was not reckoned as being exclusive to the name of Nārāyaṇa.

In the *Śvetāśvatara-nigama*, that is, the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*: at the beginning, the term "Śiva" is heard; therefore, in the subsequent sections, He is designated by the word "Śiva" in the passages, "Therefore, Śiva is omnipresent; Śiva alone is absolute," and "That Supreme Brahman which is awake. That which is the cause of the world—that is, the causal ground of the universe—is recognized from the two opening statements: "What is the cause? Brahman," and "This indeed is the supreme Brahman. He is that Brahman who is designated by the word "Śiva" in the *Śvetāśvatara*.

"The Blessed One is all-pervading; that Blessed One is the Puruṣa"—thus one should contemplate. They call Him the "Foremost Puruṣa. Because He is designated by such terms as "Puruṣa" and "Bhagavat" in the beginning, middle, and conclusion [of the text], He is indeed Nārāyaṇa. The use of the masculine gender in "sa" (He) is due to His being the primary subject of the injunction. To the question "Why?", he says: "Because," and so forth. "Yat" means because; in the *Yajus*, in the *Śrutiśiras* (the Taittirīyaka), the word "Śiva" refers to that Blessed One.

The meaning is that because [the Lord] is described as "eternal, auspicious, and infallible," the Blessed One alone is the one denoted by the word *Śiva* occurring in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*. Now, to the doubt—"How can the *Taittirīyaka* have the Blessed One as its ultimate referent?"—he replies with the words beginning "atatsādhāraṇyam" (its non-commonality with others), stating that even setting aside the indicative marks such as "lying upon the ocean" and "being the husband of Lakṣmī," the direct scriptural mention of the word *Nārāyaṇa* itself is sufficient to establish that the *Taittirīyaka* has the Blessed One as its ultimate referent. "Of the word *Nārāyaṇa*" means of the term *nārāyaṇa*.

"Atatsādhāraṇyam" means not being common to those other than the Blessed One—that is, among [the deities] such as Brahmā and Rudra; it refers to the state of being a general term (*sāmānyaśabdatva*) consisting in having the property of residing [in many], while residing specifically in the Blessed One. "Na samagaṇi" means it was not understood. Here, the phrase "by means of Śruti, Smṛti, and Vyākaraṇa," and so forth, is implied.

Because of its identity in meaning with the *Mahopaniṣad* and other texts, and because of the frequent repetition of the word "Nārāyaṇa," the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad] refers to the Blessed Lord. Therefore, the one denoted by the word "Śiva" occurring therein is indeed the Blessed Lord; and since it is identical in meaning to that, the one denoted by the words found in the *Śvetāśvatara* Upaniṣad is also He alone—this is the sense. This very point was stated by the venerable Mahācārya: "This is the etymological derivation of the word 'Nārāyaṇa' as referring to the Cause, based on the context. And yet, you maintain that this very word 'Nārāyaṇa,' which has the Cause as its scope, refers to Rudra. Therefore, it functions there through that same [etymological] application."

The impossibility [of his being the creator] is unavoidable. Nor is it reasonable to suspect that the etymological derivation of that term refers to the Four-faced One (Brahmā), because it is impossible for one who was born immediately after the production of the cosmic egg to be the cause of the principles (tattvas) such as Mahat and the rest. Furthermore, the explanation of the words of Manu should be consulted in the *Vedāntavijaya*. || 79 ||

Having thus introduced [the topic] with the four verses beginning with "ityam," the fact that the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* has the Blessed Lord as its ultimate subject was established. Now, with the eleven verses beginning with "yaddevairanuyuktaḥ," he establishes that the *Atharvaśiras* has the Blessed Lord as its ultimate subject: "Since Rudra, when questioned by the gods, having opened himself up, proclaimed in the head of the *Atharvaśiras* a great answer concerning the office of the Supreme Lord... (beginning with *yaddevair...*) [Root Text:
*yaddevairanuyukta uttaramuśan rudro vivṛtyātmani vyājahre mahatīmadhīśvaradhurāmātharvaṇe mūrdhani |*
He manifested as the inner self, the Lord, the Infinite; he hissed and entered from within into the very core, according to the method studied, like Vāmadeva and others.

From this point onward, the following passage from the *Atharvaśiras* is employed, consisting of six verses: "The gods indeed went to the heavenly world. Those gods asked Rudra: 'Who are you? He replied: 'I alone existed in the beginning, I exist now, and I shall exist in the future. There is nothing whatsoever other than me. He entered into the interior of the interior; he entered into the interior of the quarters."

Thus, by means of such attributes as "I am eternal," "I am impermanent," "I am Brahman," "I am the one facing east," "I am the one facing west," "I am the one facing south," "I am the one facing north," "I am below and above," "I am the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions," "I am male," "I am female," "I am the three-eyed [Śiva]," "I am Sāvitrī," "I am Gāyatrī," "I am Triṣṭubh, Jagatī, and Anuṣṭubh," and so forth, I satisfy [all beings] with my own splendor—thus ends [the passage].

This is the meaning: Having gone to the heavenly world, the gods saw Rudra wearing the garb of an ascetic and established in *yoga*. Although they recognized him as Rudra upon seeing his appearance as a sage, yet—either because they were unable to determine his true nature or out of a desire to know whether he was independent or dependent—they asked, "Who are you? He replied; that is, Rudra gave the answer to the question of the gods. The intent of the question was: "Are you merely a deity like ourselves, or are you the Supreme Cause?"

He said, and so forth: "I alone existed"—that is, I was in the state of the causal condition characterized by unity, which is the opposite of the multiplicity consisting of names and forms existing at the time of creation. "I existed first," and I exist now, and I shall exist; I am the Self of all things existing in the three periods of time. There is nothing else whatsoever distinct from me—there is no one other than me. Here, the word "I" (*asmad*) used by Rudra refers to the Blessed Lord who dwells within Rudra as his inner controller (*antaryāmī*); therefore, it is that [Lord] residing within him whom Rudra has designated through such attributes as being the cause.

The word *iti* has three meanings: the sense of cause (*hetu*), the sense of manner (*prakāra*), and the sense of completion (*samāpti*). Among these, when it signifies cause, there are two ways of construing the sentence. When it signifies completion or manner, there is only one construction for each. The first construction is as follows: "There was no other whatsoever distinct from me; because of the absence of anything other than myself, I alone existed at the beginning. This is the single construction [in the case of the sense of completion].

In this context, that Supreme Self, who exists as consciousness and consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), entered from within the one consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*) and from within the one consisting of mind (*manomaya*) into the individual self (*jīva*) consisting of cognition (*vijñānamaya*). It also entered "from within the quarters" (*diśaścāntaram*); that is, it entered the individual self which is internal to the insentient external world characterized by the quarters. The statement "it entered from within the quarters" is intended as an illustration for its own entry into the Supreme Self; such is the meaning of the passage beginning with "from within the internal."

When it is stated that because nothing exists apart from me, I alone possess the nature of being the cause and the state of being the self of all—"The Person alone is all this"—it is indeed the Person who possesses universal selfhood (*sārvātmya*). In response to the inquiry as to how this is so, the passage beginning with "He entered into that which is within the sun" is intended to clarify the logic of Prahlāda. Alternatively, the meaning is that because the Supreme Self entered the individual soul (*jīvātman*) as its inner controller (*antaryāmin*), as expressed in "He entered into that which is within the interior," there is nothing other than the Supreme Self whose body is I.

"It is because of the all-pervasiveness of the Infinite that I myself am established as That," thus it was said by Prahlāda. In this way, two ways of construing the word *ittham* (thus) as having the sense of a reason (*hetu*) have been shown. When it is stated, "There is nothing whatsoever other than Me," one might ask: what kind of designation of universal selfhood (*sārvātmya*) is this? In response to this expectation, he says: *iti*. This means "in this manner"; that is to say, in the manner about to be described.

Regarding the question "Who is he who is about to be described?", [the author] says: "He is within the sun," and so forth; the meaning is that his universal selfhood (sārvātmya) is due to his being the body of all things. Thus, it has been shown that the word *ittham* signifies "in this manner. Alternatively, let this word *iti* signify "conclusion. After the passage beginning with "So am I," the phrase "He said" (*so’bravīt*) will be supplied as an ellipsis.

"He said, 'There is no other whatsoever distinct from me'"—this [statement] is not out of order. "He entered within," and so forth: that Rudra entered into the Supreme Self, which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), which is more internal than that which consists of mind (*manomaya*) and more internal than that which consists of knowledge (*vijñānamaya*); he entered it by means of his intellect. Therefore, the meaning is that Rudra taught, like Vāmādeva, Prahlāda, and others, "I alone possess the nature of being the All-Self" and so on. In these three interpretations, the word *iti* remains in its own original position.

Regarding the interpretation that "he entered from within to within" means "there is no other whatsoever distinct from me," the distinction [from the previous view] is that there is movement from his place. Furthermore, according to the interpretation stated as having the sense of completion (*samāpti*), one must supply the words "he said" (*so’bravīt*) later on. However, in the alternative view where the particle *iti* is applied to mark the conclusion of the entire speech of Rudra, there is no such ellipsis; rather, there is only the movement from his place, as expressed by the verb itself, "he entered."

Referring to the Supreme Self as "He," Rudra proclaims his universal identity—that he, the Supreme Self, and I are both eternal and non-eternal—through the passage beginning with "I am He" (*so'ham*); this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

However, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), they excise the phrase "He entered into that which is more internal than the internal" and insert it after the completion of the entire speech of Rudra, asserting that its meaning is: "The god Rudra, abandoning his visible gross form, entered into his subtle form. But that is not a correct interpretation.

Because it is inappropriate to assume the extraction and insertion [of words], and because it would be improper to subvert the recognition of the term *antarādantara* as meaning "from within" (the womb), as well as the recognition of the well-known entry described in the manifestation of name and form (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*) expressed by the word "entered" (*prāviśat*), [the author] will explain that the word *atra* here has the sense of "because" and so forth in the five subsequent verses; meanwhile, he states the meaning of the sequence of Vedic sentences consisting of questions and answers with the words beginning "yad daivaiḥ" (that which by the gods).

In the *Atharvaṇa-mūrdhan*—that is, in the *Atharvaśiras*. Rudra, being questioned by the gods—"Who are you?"—asked out of a desire to know his independence (*svātantrya*), [spoke] with longing; "longing" here means desire. [He assumed] the great office of supreme lordship—the burden of being the sovereign Lord. [The form *adhīśvaradhurām* is derived] from the word *dhur* ending in *ā*, according to the rule "ṛkpūrabdhūḥ," etc. Having unfolded it—having explained it at length with "I am He" (*so’ham*) and so forth—he [placed it] within himself—within his own self.

He spoke—by means of the textual passage beginning with "I alone existed in the beginning" and ending with "by my own splendor"—that which was said constitutes the *karman* (the object). He is Rudra. According to the rule established by the study of the Veda—"He entered from within, even deeper within"—this refers to the manner described in the Śruti: "He entered from within, even deeper within," which consists of an entry characterized by the Supreme Self as the agent and the individual self (*jīvātman*) as the object, and an entry characterized by the immersion of the intellect where one's own self is the agent and the Supreme Self is the object; in that manner [he entered].

Being one for whom the abundance (*bhūmā*) of the Lord as the inner self has become manifest—namely, that which is both the inner self (*antarātmā*) and the Blessed One (*bhagavān*), the Lord who is well-known in the Vedas as the inner self through such passages as "This Blessed One is the inner self of all beings and is all-pervading"—his "abundance" (*bhūmā*) means his manifoldness, his state of being the self of all; thus, he is one whose abundance as the Lord and the inner self is manifest by his own word, shining forth in the intellects of the gods and in his own intellect, like Vāmadeva and others—the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) including Prahlāda.

The construction is: *aphaṇat* means "he spoke. This statement in the *Atharvaśiras*, namely Rudra’s words beginning with "I alone existed first," is his speech; or rather, like the speech of Vāmadeva, Prahlāda, and others beginning with "I became Manu," it is rooted in the recognition of his own identity as the Blessed One (*bhagavadātmakatva*) due to the Blessed One's entry everywhere as the Self (*ātmatayā*). Thus, it has the Blessed One’s universal selfhood (*sarvātmya*) as its ultimate purport.

The meaning is not that this refers exclusively to Rudra’s being the self of all and so forth; rather, the statement "He entered from the innermost to the innermost" is an indication of the meaning of the scripture, not a literal citation of the scripture itself, and thus there is no inconsistency regarding the word "innermost. || 80 ||

Regarding the phrase "nānyaḥ kaścinmatto vyatiriktaḥ," [the author] will explain in two verses that the word *iti* functions as a reason (*hetu*) and that the passage "so’ntarādantaraṃ prāviśat" connects with its own proper place immediately following it; meanwhile, he refutes the notion that *iti* signifies completion (*samāpti*), which would contradict its function as a reason. (The verse begins: "nānya... etc.
Following the forceful statement "There is nothing other than Me," the word *na* does not signify the conclusion of that statement, because—as before—the forceful statement continues thereafter.
Thus, by means of such formulations as "I am eternal" or "I am non-eternal," [and so forth]. || 81 ||

In the *Atharvaṇa*, the term "in the head" (*mūrdhani*) is understood. In the *Atharvaśiras*, as before, it refers to what precedes the word "as before," namely the speech of Rudra beginning with "I alone existed in the beginning. It follows from the word "afterwards," meaning according to the manner [of the text] beginning with "That I am eternal, yet not eternal," and so forth. This is because of the continuity—meaning the non-interruption—of the utterances of the fierce Rudra.

Regarding the phrase "nānyaḥ kaścicanmatta ityugravākyādūrdhvamiti": the word *iti* heard in the expression "there is no one other than me" indicates the conclusion—that is, the completion—of Rudra’s speech. [The opponent claims: "It does not state [the conclusion]," meaning it does not express it. Even though the lexicon (*kośa*) teaches that the word *iti* has the sense of conclusion in the rule "the word *iti* [is used] for cause, context, manner, and so forth, as well as for conclusion," its sense of conclusion is set aside here; furthermore, because it would entail the necessity of supplying an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) later on, this word *iti* does not have the sense of conclusion.

The meaning is that, because the phrase *so’bravīt* requires an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) later on, it is more logical for the word *asya* here to signify merely the movement from its place [rather than referring to the entire preceding context]. As it was stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭasudarśana: "Even though the word *iti* has 'conclusion' as its only meaning and no other, nevertheless, according to the maxim 'it is better to postulate a property (*dharma*) than to postulate a substratum (*dharmin*)', it is logical to assume the connection of the employed word *iti* with the conclusion of Rudra’s speech, rather than the ellipsis of another unmentioned word."

Having thus refuted the sense of completion (*samāpti*), he states that [the passage] has the sense of a reason (*hetu*) and its connection immediately following "He entered from within to what was more internal" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1), beginning with "So 'taḥ" and so forth.
He says: "So 'taḥ" expresses the reason; the word "no" indicates the manner; the reason stated by Prahlāda is the entry into the interior.
The speech of Prahlāda, beginning with "Because Ananta is omnipresent," is clearly stated in the Purāṇa known as the Vaiṣṇava. (82)

Therefore, because it is untenable for [the particle *iti*] to signify completion (*samāpti*), the word *iti* mentioned previously is used here; it expresses a reason (*hetu*) and does not express a manner (*prakāra*). The ellipsis is "lest there be a split in the sentence" (*vākyabheda*). The syntactical connection is: "He entered from the interior into the interior," and so on, up to "none other than this. The meaning is that because the Blessed One has entered into all living beings as their very Self, the Supreme Self alone—having Me as His body—is the one who possesses the nature of being the Self of all, and there is nothing distinct from Him.

Regarding the statement that the entry of the Supreme Self (paramātman) as the self within all living beings is mentioned elsewhere as the reason for designating that Supreme Self—who is one's own embodied self—with the word "we" (asmat), he says: "As stated by Prahlāda. "Internal entry" means the Lord's entry into all living beings as their inner self. "The reason stated by Prahlāda" means that this very designation of the Supreme Self—who is one's own embodied self—by the word "we" was also stated by Prahlāda as the underlying reason. To the question, "What is that statement of Prahlāda?", he says: "As stated by Prahlāda."

The statement by Prahlāda in the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*—namely, "Because the Infinite One is omnipresent, He alone exists as I," and so forth—is clear and explicit. Therefore, just as in that case, it is appropriate here as well to interpret the phrase as stating a reason (*hetu*). Consequently, even though there is a shift in location, it is logical that the word functions to express a reason; its meaning is not to signify the conclusion of a methodological section, which would necessitate a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) and the supplying of ellipses (*adhyāhāra*). This is the intended sense. While one might have expected the expression "in the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*," the designation "*named Viṣṇava*" is used to emphasize:
"Among the Vedas, the *Puruṣa-sūkta*; among the Dharmaśāstras, the [Code of] Manu... and so on.

This is for the purpose of indicating its superior status compared to all other Purāṇas, by means of the recollection of the scriptural statement: "In the Bhārata, the Bhagavadgītā is the supreme Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa. || 82 ||
Regarding the fact that [the word] has the sense of a reason (*hetu*), he states the position of internal connection (*svasthānānvaya*) [beginning with]: "Or else" (*atha vā*), and so forth.
By the words "or else," it is understood that the reason stated here is the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), and not anything else.
For one who has stated the logical connection as "I am alone," the position of the mode (prakāra) is easy to comprehend. || 83 ||
Alternatively, [the word *iti*] [is used] in the sense of: "He entered from within to what is more internal," or "There is nothing else whatsoever distinct from me."

Regarding the absence of logical concomitance (*anvaya*) due to movement from one's place: here, by the word *iti*, meaning "by that which remains in its own place," there is the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) understood as "none other," that is, "nothing whatsoever distinct from Me. This signifies the non-existence of any entity established independently, apart from the Supreme Self whose body is Rudra, as conveyed by the statement. Regarding the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) expressed as "I alone," which is taught by such passages as "I alone existed first," this refers to the presence of universal selfhood and so forth within the Supreme Self whose body is Rudra. The reason was stated—that is, it was made known as the logical ground—for [the existence of] another entity established independently. If there were such an entity...

The meaning is that the Lord’s universal selfhood (*sārvātmya*) is not unestablished; rather, the absence of any other entity residing independently [of Him] is stated by the word *iti* in the Śruti as the reason for His universal selfhood. Regarding the previous interpretation, although there is a displacement of the word *iti*, it possesses natural elegance (*svārasya*) because it makes known the cause of entry well-established in another Śruti. In this [present] interpretation, however, even in the absence of that [displacement], there is natural elegance because the word connects precisely where it stands. This is the distinction.

He states that the word *iti* can also have the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*), saying: "The position of 'manner' is easy to understand. This is because if the word *iti* were taken in the sense of "cause" (*hetu*), it would result in [the faults of] displacement from its proper place (*sthānacalana*) and being a mere supplement to what precedes (*pūrvaśeṣatva*). Since it is said, "In this world, the learned desire both brevity and expansion," there is no fault even in the division of the sentence when it contains both summary and detail; thus, the meaning is that the position of "manner" is indeed appropriate. || 83 ||

Since the word *iti* has the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*) and constitutes an independent sentence, he states that the sentence "He is within the inner [space]" (*so’ntarādantaram*) is its explanation (beginning with "of Rudra"): "The utterance of Rudra is 'He is within the inner';
therefore, He is someone other than that, the Inner Self of that."
And it is said "of others" because he is included by the expression "the one within"; thus, that Viṣṇu is also well-known [as such] through his fierce (raudrī) nature. || 84 ||
From this word "iti," which functions as a particle indicating a specific manner and constitutes an independent sentence, [the following] is subsequent.

The statement "He is within the sun" belongs to Rudra, not to the deity [of the Upanishad]; however, if the word *iti* is taken to mean "conclusion," then it will be stated that "He is within the sun" and so forth constitutes a Vedic sentence (*vedavākya*), while this [statement] belongs to Rudra. It should be understood that the mention of Rudra’s authorship at the conclusion of the demonstration that the word *iti* signifies "reason" or "manner"—rather than "conclusion"—is intended to clarify that this status is indistinguishable in both cases. He states the meaning with the words beginning "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). By "Rudra's" (*raudryā*), he means by that which resides in the Śruti and has Rudra as its speaker.

By the statement "He entered from within," according to the passage "He entered from the innermost interior," there is none other than him—none other than Rudra. Of that Rudra and of the other individual souls (jīvātman), there is an Inner Self (antarātmā) who, because he cannot be designated by any specific individual form, is referred to as "some unknown one" (ko'pi). This is what is being stated; this is what is being established. By the phrase "from the innermost interior," the meaning is that an Inner Self distinct from Rudra—one common to both Rudra and the other individual souls—is being established.

Even when the teaching is given merely as being the inner self (*antarātman*), it is established that the Blessed One alone is the subject to be taught here; for the status of being the inner self is well-known to belong to Him alone. Thus he says: "He too is Viṣṇu, as is well known. "He" refers to the inner self. Viṣṇu is well known [as such] from passages such as: "The inner controller of beings," "This is the inner self of all beings," and "Thou art my inner self and mine."

He is well-known as Viṣṇu. By the word "also" (api), the glorification of the Lord as the inner self of all is included, as found even in the *Atharvaśiras* Upaniṣad: "He who is Rudra is indeed the Blessed One, and he who is Brahmā," and so forth, through the designation of the term "Blessed One" (bhagavat). The inclusion of the word "Viṣṇu" is for the purpose of recalling the scriptural passage, "To Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa," for that [passage] is also well known as referring to Viṣṇu. Indeed, its meaning is "he who has entered, i.e., pervaded, the *śipis*, which are the animals, by way of being their inner controller."

Alternatively, in the phrase "the method of categories (*prakārapakṣa*) is easy to comprehend," the word *iti* is intended by the term "easy" (*sukara*) to signify inclusion, while "So [He who is] within the Sun" (*so’ntarāditya*) and so forth signify elaboration. However, in this verse, because the word *iti* has the sense of indicating a reason (*hetu*) and a mode (*prakāra*), the passage beginning with "So [He who is] within the Sun" is indeed the statement of Rudra; thus, he states its meaning with the words "of Rudra" and so on. Therefore—because the word *iti* has the sense of indicating a reason and a mode—the rest is as before.

In stating alternative interpretations of the word "iti," the refutation of other interpretations is intended to reveal the specific natural aptness and relative equivalence among those interpretations; thus, there is no fault. || 84 ||

He states the position that the word *iti* serves to mark the conclusion of Rudra’s speech (*itītyādi*): "Whether this expression 'iti' denotes the completion of the words of Hara, or whether it [denotes] the end of that [inner Āditya], let it be so; even if it were Rudra’s own utterance, there would be no contradiction whatsoever in this view."
Rudra, having entered Hari—who is his own self—with a pure intellect, desiring to act as if he were another man under his own control, is thus manifested by the voice of the Veda. (85)

The word *vā* is for the purpose of indicating an alternative position (*pakṣaparivṛtti*). The word *iti* [in the phrase] *ityuktiḥ* means that the statement "There is no one else whatsoever distinct from me"—this is the word *iti*. *Haragiraḥ* refers to the speech of Rudra, such as the words beginning with "I alone existed in the beginning. *Samāptim* means the conclusion or end. *Vadatu* means let him speak or let him make known; this is the *loṭ* (imperative) mood used in the sense of permission (*atisarga*). *Atisargaḥ* means permission.

The permission for acting at will (*kāmacārānujñā*). Because of the word "thus" (*iti*) having the sense of completion, let there be no [claim] that "He who is within the sun" is a statement of Rudra; that is, the passage beginning with "He who is within the sun" should not be considered a statement of Rudra. Let it also be the case that this is not a statement of Rudra, and rather let it be a statement of the Śruti—this is the intended meaning. This being so—that is, even while the word "thus" has the sense of completion and the passage "He who is within the sun" is indeed a statement of the Śruti.

There is not even the slightest disintegration—meaning there is no contradiction even in a single part—of our desired position, which conforms to the natural force (*svārasya*) of the Śruti, Smṛti, Sūtra, and Vṛtti, and consists of this very meaning: "Rudra is not what is propounded by the *Atharvaśiras* as the inner self of all; rather, it is the Blessed Lord alone, who is his inner controller (*antaryāmī*), that is propounded therein as the inner self of all."

In this context, if the word *ati* signifies completion (*samāpti*), then in the passage beginning with "He entered within the sun" (*so’ntarāditye*), it is Rudra alone who is referred to by the pronoun *tat*;

consequently, it would be he alone whose status as the inner ruler (*antar-yāmitva*) is being stated—this is one objection. On the other hand, if the word *antara* refers to the Lord (*bhagavat*), then because of the lack of syntactic connection with the phrase "he entered" (*prāviśat*), the word *antara* cannot refer to the Lord—this is another objection. Neither of these two objections applies. Even if, in the sentence "He entered within the inner [of the inner]" (*so’ntarādantaraṃ prāviśat*), the pronoun *tat* were to refer to Rudra, it would not be possible to assert through this that he possesses the nature of being the Self within all.

Because the multitude of scriptural authorities beginning with "This is the inner Self of all beings" establishes that being the inner Self of all is a characteristic mark (liṅga) of the Blessed Lord; and because, through the recognition of the *Ānandavallī*, the phrase "from within, even more within" refers specifically to the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) as "from within, even more within"; therefore, regarding Him [it is said]: "That which is here in the person and that which is yonder in the sun."

Thus, because he is understood to reside within the solar orb, and because it is heard in scripture that the one residing within the solar orb is the lotus-eyed Lord, it is the Blessed One himself who is spoken of as "the innermost of the inner. Furthermore, through specific statements such as "Viṣṇu is the Self of the Blessed One" and "Thou art my inner Self," it is understood that the Blessed One is the inner controller (antaryāmin) even of Rudra.

Therefore, since the root *praviśati* (to enter) signifies perfect comprehension, the meaning of the passage "He entered from the innermost to the innermost" is that Rudra has perfectly understood the Blessed Lord who dwells within the individual soul (*jīva-antaryāmin*); thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. This very point is stated in the words beginning with "Rudra," etc.

Furthermore, a wise man desiring to bring another person under his own control—just as Rudra [controls] another man—enters Lord Hari, who is the self of himself and the self of all other selves, by means of a stainless intellect, that is, through perfect knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). This is expressed by the Vedic word: "He entered within, from the interior to the interior. The meaning is that this very point is stated by the scriptural passage: "He entered within, from the interior to the interior."

From the statement "another man," it is understood that the wise one is a man. And in this regard: "Whatever the disposition of each person may be, by means of that very disposition, the wise one, having entered into that person, should quickly bring them under his own control."

This is the intended meaning of Cāṇakya’s statement. For the phrase "having entered that man by means of this or that" means having known him through being endowed with those respective dispositions (*bhāva*). Thus, just as in that statement there is a person who is a learned scholar (*medhāvin*) acting as the agent, whose action is an entry consisting of the penetration of the intellect (*buddhi*) of another person as its object; similarly, in the Vedic sentence as well, the result obtained is that Rudra is the agent of an entry consisting of the penetration of the intellect of the Blessed Lord—who is the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all living beings other than himself.

It has been stated that the root *praviśati* (to enter) signifies the act of mental penetration (*buddhyavagāhana*). In the case of the mental penetration performed by Rudra as the agent in the context at hand, there is an intended similarity with the penetration performed by the intelligent man (*medhāvin*) mentioned in Cāṇakya’s statement—a similarity consisting in the fact that both are expressed by the verb *praviśati*. Furthermore, since the determination of the specific relationship between word and meaning in the Veda depends upon worldly convention, the statement of Cāṇakya is cited as an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). And in this instance, the very fact that *praviśati* means mental penetration is what is relied upon for the illustration. Therefore, [there is a similarity] of the intelligent man who serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).

The statement “like Medhāvī” is inappropriate because [the comparison] lacks worldly established usage (*lokasiddhatva*). There is no room for the doubt that, as in the case of “Yajñadatta goes like Devadatta,” only a similarity of meaning (*arthasādṛśya*) would be obtained here as well. Furthermore, the citation of Cāṇakya’s words is for the sake of illustration. It should also be noted that even when entering our own system of thought, the term *anupraviśati* is seen to mean “entering into practice” as well as “penetrating with the intellect. As stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Sudarśana: “That the word *anupraveśa* has the sense of ‘perfectly understanding’ is established by common worldly usage. And likewise is the usage of Cāṇakya: [followed by the verse].
"For whatever the disposition of any person may be, by entering into that very [disposition] through that same [means], the wise man should quickly bring that person under his own control.

This means that Rudra has, through his intellect, contemplated the Supreme Self—who is his own inner controller as well as the inner controller of all things—as having that [Rudra] as His body. Furthermore, the fact that the Blessed Lord alone is the inner self of all is well-known from other Vedic texts; and with the intention of stating here as well that "He who is Rudra is indeed the Blessed Lord," the term "Hari" was used.

In passages such as, "This is the inner self (antarātman) of all beings, free from evil, the self of Being, the inner controller, the immortal," although the Blessed One is the inner self, it is taught that He is not touched by the defects residing therein; for after stating, "the inner self of all beings, the self of Being," it is further stated, "free from evil, immortal. To indicate this, it is said here that Hari is one's own self (svātmātmabhūta). This is because of the etymological derivation of the word *hari*: "He is called *hari* by the wise precisely because of His taking away (*haraṇa*) of sins."

If it is argued that the word *nanu*—when used in conjunction with a verbal root having the sense of "speaking"—is always observed to refer to the very form or meaning of the sentence with which it is co-occurrent, and thus its function as indicating completion (*samāpti*) is not logical; and furthermore, if the word *iti* were to signify completion, it would be proper for it to be mentioned before the word denoting that which completes what is expressed by itself (as in "ity upaniṣat"), then they reply: although there is such a sequence—first the mention of the sentence to be understood, then the word *iti*, and then the mention of the verbal root having the sense of speaking—in cases possessing this order...
"O slender-limbed one, abandon your silence; behold me prostrate at your feet;
indeed, never before has your anger been such as this.
Thus spoke the lord.

In such cases, the word ending in *iti* has the property of intending a cognition that is identical in form to the cognition produced by the sentence with which it is co-uttered; furthermore, that cognition appears as a qualifier in the act of "speaking" (ukti)—denoted by the verb meaning "speaking" that follows the word *iti*—through the relation of being its generator;
and the verb meaning "speaking" following the word *iti* possesses the capacity to convey a sentence whose word-order is identical to that of the sentence with which the word *iti* is co-uttered.

Although this [usage] is established by conventional derivation (*vyutpatti*), nevertheless, because such a sequence is absent here—as in the case of "Look, the deer runs," where the sentence-meaning consisting of the deer's running is understood as the object (*karman*) of the verbal action of speaking expressed by "He said"—it is appropriate that the word *iti* has the sense of completion (*samāpti*). Furthermore, the placement of the word *iti*, which signifies completion, after a word denoting that which is completed by its own expressed meaning is observed in practices such as the recitation of syllables (*akṣarapāṭha*).

Therefore, it is appropriate that [the word *saḥ*] has the sense of completion (*samāpti*). This being the case, in the phrase *so’ntarād*, the word *saḥ* has the same referent as the word *saḥ* in the phrase *so’bravīt* (or *saḥ... ityena*), which shares the same case-ending as its stem. Thus, in accordance with the natural consistency of the opening statement, there is no fault in supplying the ellipsis *so’bravīt* in the subsequent sentence beginning with *so’haṃ nityo’nityaḥ*. Furthermore, since the sentence beginning with *so’ham* serves as an elaboration of the sentence beginning with *ahamekaḥ*, it does not require another verb; thus, its having the sense of completion is indeed logical. || 85 ||

Thus, it has been established that the statements of Rudra found in the first section of the *Atharvaśiras* have as their ultimate referent the Lord who dwells within Rudra as its inner controller (*antaryāmī*). Now, the statements in the second section consisting of the deities’ hymns of praise are established as having as their referent the Supreme Self whose body is Rudra: "Having heard those words of Rudra, the immortals, emboldened to offer a hymn to His majesty, even attempted to seize the universal sovereignty [residing] in the head of the *Atharvan*."

For these Rudras, who are here clearly manifest as the causes of the Antaryāmin-samādhi, are joined with that [state] and follow after it; they possess the speech of the gods and have their minds fixed solely upon Him. 86.

In this regard, the collection of sentences found in the second section begins as follows: "He who is Rudra is the Blessed One; and he who is Brahmā—to him indeed, salutation after salutation! He who is Rudra is the Blessed One; and he who is Maheśvara—to him indeed, salutation after salutation! and so forth, up to: "He who is Rudra is the Blessed One; and that which is Satya—to him indeed, salutation after salutation!"

Thus ends [the section]. And here—the meaning is as follows: he who is Rudra is indeed the Blessed Lord (Bhagavān), and he who is Brahmā is also indeed the Blessed Lord; therefore, "salutation to the Blessed Lord who consists of both," and so forth. Furthermore, that which is called Viṣṇu is stated to be worthy of salutation by virtue of being distinguished as an incarnation. Since the qualification "Rudra" is employed in every successive turn of the verse, the meditation here enjoined is upon the immanent ruler of Rudra (rudrāntaryāmin) as the universal self (sārvātmya).

On this point, the venerable feet of the Great Teacher [state]: "If the word 'Bhagavat' were also intended to refer to Rudra, one would have to say, 'Salutation to him who is Rudra and to him who is the other'; therefore, the use of the word 'tasmai' (to him) would be entirely incoherent. If one accepts the meaning 'he who was Rudra became Brahmā,' then the second occurrence of the word 'yaḥ' (who) becomes inconsistent. If one accepts the meaning 'he who was Rudra and he who was Brahmā,' then a separate substratum (*dharmy-antara*) would be obtained by the natural force of the text. In either case, the word 'saḥ' (he) in the phrase 'sa bhagavān' (that Blessed One) would lose its capacity to function as a natural correlative reference back to the word 'yaḥ'."
The meaning is: "He who is indeed Rudra is the Blessed One; salutation to him," and likewise, "He who is indeed Brahmā is the Blessed One; salutation to him. The word *brahman* extends up to Rudra.

Even if this is accepted, the same fault remains; however, the repetition of "to him, obeisance" (*tasmai namaḥ*) is additional. Furthermore, since Brahmā is also the Blessed Lord (*bhagavān*), the repetition of the word "Blessed Lord" (*bhagavat*) is not a fault, as it is illuminated by the particle *ca* (and). Thus, having stated the identity of both through the two sentences "He who... and "And he who...", the third sentence, "To him, obeisance," performs an act of salutation precisely to such a Blessed Lord.

Furthermore, if it is argued that "whatever is Rudra is the Blessed One (Bhagavān)," and thus the word *bhagavat* must be accepted as having only its etymological meaning (*yaugikatva*), we say no; for it is improper to abandon the natural conventional sense (*rūḍhi*) without a subverting reason (*bādhaka*). Moreover, if it were stated that "whoever is Rudra possesses qualities such as omniscience, and whoever is Brahmā also possesses qualities such as omniscience," then since this would apply elsewhere as well, the meaning would become inappropriate (*ayogyārthatā*). There would also be a contradiction with the hymns of praise to Rudra. Therefore, they concluded: "It is more reasonable that [the term] refers to the Blessed One (Viṣṇu) by way of its conventional sense (*rūḍhi*). Thus they supported their position.

This is what he says with the words beginning "having heard," and so forth. In the *Atharvamūrdhan*, that is, in the *Atharvaśiras* [Upaniṣad], the immortals—the gods—having heard the words of Rudra, namely the speech of Rudra beginning with "I am one," and being endowed with effort—that is, being diligent—in order to compose a collection of words for the sake of praising the majesty of that reality (the object expressed by Rudra's words), which is the excellence resulting from its universal selfhood and other attributes.

By means of the repeated designation of the word "Rudra" in every verse, they [the gods] recognized that his sovereignty extends toward all, including the four-faced Brahmā and others—that he is the Lord over them all—exclaiming, "He is indeed Rudra."

The construction is as follows: "Because they spoke by having gone into Rudra, those dwellers of heaven were endowed with that same intention. For (hi) because, here in the first section of the *Atharvaśiras*, the utterances of Rudra—which are the causes for the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) upon the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin)—are manifest; such words of Rudra as "I alone existed first," and so forth, become the cause for the gods' meditation on the Lord who is their own Inner Controller, through their own hearing.

And because they are the causes for the meditation on the Lord who dwells within Rudra, they are *vyaktāḥ*, meaning clear or manifest. Therefore (*tat*): those utterances of the gods (*diviṣadvācaḥ*) spoken subsequently to that [statement]—the divine declarations beginning with "Vai rudraḥ" and so forth—which reiterate Nārāyaṇa’s status as the inner controller of all, which constitutes the meaning of Rudra’s speech; being "joined with a single intent toward Him" (*tadekāśayā yuktāḥ*) means that their primary (*eka*) and principal (*mukhya*) intention (*āśaya*) or purport (*tātparya*) is directed toward that inner controller. Thus they are so described; the meaning is that they are appropriate (*ucitāḥ*). [The form *yuktāḥ* is derived from the root *yuj* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract state, with the substitution of *ku* for *j*.]

Because a word ending in a verbal suffix conveys the action in the form of "sādhyatva" (the state of being something to be accomplished), which consists in possessing a property that precludes the arising of an expectation for another action; and because, in the case of *vyājahnire*, the gender and number inherent in the action of speaking (*vyāharaṇa*) are not manifested, the relative pronoun *yat* used as its qualifier is indicated by its natural neuter gender and singular number.

However, regarding that very action, its state as an accomplished entity (siddhabhāva) is based on suffixes such as *ghañ*; for, according to the stated principle, it is presented by a verbal root ending in *ghañ* in an accomplished state capable of manifesting gender and number, [in accordance with the rule]: "An action expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix appears like a substance (*dravyavat*)."

Since it is necessary to employ case endings that convey gender, number, and so forth—just as one does for a substance—the masculine gender of the word *vāk* is appropriate because of the rule "words ending in *ghañ* are masculine," and its plural form is justified due to the multiplicity of sentences. Therefore, it should be understood that the word *tat* (that), which serves as its qualifier, is also indicated with masculine gender and the plural number, just like the word *pad*. Furthermore, the word *api* (also) conjoins the fact that the statements of Rudra have as their ultimate referent the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) within them.

The word *tu* (but) indicates the resolution to the following doubt: since the word *rudra* is repeated at every turn, does this not imply that the passage is devoted solely to Rudra? It indicates that there is no loss of the sense of the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*), because the repetition is intended for the purpose of meditating on the Lord whose body is Rudra. Here, the meaning of the two sentences at the end of the first section—namely, "Having heard the words of Rudra, [they said] 'Praise his greatness,' etc. and "Those gods praised Rudra"—is stated.

"They did not see Rudra" means they did not see him as characterized by his prior independence. "They praise Rudra" means they praise the Blessed One who has Rudra as His body (*rudra-śarīraka*). By the phrase "the causes for the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) upon the Inner Ruler," the meaning of the final sentence in that context—"those gods meditate upon Rudra"—is restated. "They meditate upon Rudra" means they meditate upon Rudra as being identical with the Blessed Lord, according to the instruction.

The meaning is that they meditate. This has been stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭasudarśana: "The second section, because it is intent upon praise through the restatement of Rudra’s words, concerns the Inner Controller (antaryāmin)"; and [he further states]: "The sense is that it is intent upon praise by way of restating Nārāyaṇa’s status as the Inner Controller of all, which is the subject matter of Rudra’s speech. The *Tadbhāvaprakāśikā* says: "For the sake of praising His greatness. The dative case is used according to the rule beginning with *kriyārtha-* (Pāṇini 2.3.14). || 86 ||

Thus, it has been established that the first and second sections of the *Atharvaśiras* have the Blessed Lord as their subject matter. As for the third section, since it sets forth the majesty of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), it is already effectively established as having the Blessed Lord as its subject by the very same reasoning used to establish the subject-matter of the second section. Now, [the author] refutes the view that the fourth section has Rudra as its subject—a view which might otherwise be suspected due to the hearing of specific names such as "Rudra" and "Īśāna"—which would act as an obstacle to establishing its subject-matter as the Blessed Lord. (The passage beginning with) "Oṃkāra...
[states]: "Surely the other names taught as preceded by the syllable *oṃ* do not have Rudra as their primary referent."
However, those [passages] in the *Atharvaśiras* are not capable of establishing the well-known status of Rudra as the Lord (*īśitṛtva*). || 87 ||
In this regard, the textual sequence of the third section is as follows:
"All deities reside in the heart; the vital breaths (prāṇas) are established in the heart.
You are eternally in the heart; he who is beyond the three measures (mātrās) is indeed that."
"To its north [is the head]; the south is the feet. That which is to the north is the syllable *oṃ*, that is the *praṇava*. That which is the *praṇava* is all-pervading;

that which is all-pervading is infinite; that which is infinite is the *tāra*; that which is the *tāra* is subtle; that which is subtle is white; that which is white is the lightning-like; that which is the lightning-like is the Supreme Brahman. He is the one Rudra; he is Īśāna; he is the Blessed One; he is the Lord; he is Mahādeva. Here, the names of the syllable *oṃ*—which was introduced in the preceding section as a synonym for the Supreme Self and serves as a constituent part of the present meditation—are specified.

Regarding this, the venerable Bhaṭṭasudarśana says: "The names of the syllable *oṃ*, which denotes that [Brahman], are given in the fourth [chapter]," as stated in the passage beginning with "preceded by the syllable *oṃ*," etc., in the *Atharvaśiras*, that is, the *Atharvaśira-upaniṣad*.

The word "in the fourth section" (*turīyakhaṇḍe*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. "Preceded by Rudra" refers to the specific names such as Rudra, Īśāna, Īśvara, and Mahādeva. The term "other" (*antara*) is used with the intention that these names are distinct from each preceding name already specified, according to the passage: "He who is Rudra is indeed the Blessed One. The word "other" is explained here as signifying a particular distinction, just as in expressions such as "another deity" (*anyadevatāntara*) or "another form" (*anyākārāntara*). These [names] are presented as being preceded by the syllable *Oṃ*.

Now, [the opponent may object]: "The meaning is that those names—Rudra and so forth—which were indeed prescribed as his designations by referring to him with the pronoun 'he' (saḥ) in the passage, 'He who is beyond the three measures,' using the syllable *oṃ* as a designation for the Supreme Self; these names, being thus spoken of as the designations of *oṃ*, are not capable of, nor are they fit to, establish or state the lordship and supremacy of Rudra, who is well-known from the Śrutis and other sources as being created and so forth. The word 'but' (*tu*) serves to set aside the aforementioned doubt.

The meaning is that because they are understood through their designation as *oṃ*, these [mantras] do not refer to the well-known Rudra. However, the term "well-known" (*prasiddhe*) is used to indicate that it is appropriate for them to refer to the Lord who dwells within Rudra (*rudrāntaryāmī*).

As stated by the venerable Mahācārya: "The words 'Īśāna' and so forth, by denoting their etymological meanings through such passages as 'He who [rules] all,' being expressive of the Lord, cause one to understand the Praṇava, which is His designator. (87)

He states that the fifth section has the Blessed Lord as its subject matter (beginning with "samākhyā"): "The designations— namely Rudra and the others— which are explained at every step concerning the previously introduced Praṇava, indeed belong to the head of Mahādeva."
This very manifestation of the power of the Tāra (Om) is revealed at the head of the Atharvaṇa Śruti; Oṃkāra is the preparatory support for the higher knowledge that follows.

"In the head of the Atharvaṇa Śruti" means in the *Atharvaśiras*, specifically in the fifth section (*khaṇḍa*), as is understood from the context. "Concerning the Praṇava under discussion" means those [mantras] which, in the fourth section, reveal the Praṇava as denoting the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). The suffix *-ini* is applied here according to the rule for *karmadhāraya* compounds, based on the indicative mark [of the text]. "Beginning with Rudra" means starting with the word *rudra*; "ending with Mahādeva" means ending with the word *mahādeva*. These are the designations—the names—occurring at every step, that is, at every word.

That which has been "etymologically explained" means it has been commented upon by demonstrating the meaning of each individual word-derivation (*yogārtha*). That [explanation] constitutes the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the designations "Rudra" and so forth. This [derivation] reveals—that is, makes known—the "vibhava," or the excellence, of the *tāra*, the *praṇava*. By the word "also" (*api*), it is indicated that even the etymological derivation of those names, such as "Rudra," does not establish that [the *praṇava*] has Rudra as its ultimate referent.

The meaning is that the mention of the Praṇava—which denotes the Supreme Self—as being associated with the words Rudra, Īśāna, and so forth, which signify the meanings residing within that Supreme Self, is for the purpose of making known the excellence of the Praṇava. (Now, one might ask: "What is the use of making known the excellence of the Praṇava, since it is not enjoined as a subordinate element? To this he says: (To the objection that "praising the Praṇava when it is not being employed is improper," he says: "Oṃkāraḥ" and so forth. *Oṃkāra* means the Praṇava.

The "higher knowledge" (*uparitanī vidyā*) is the knowledge consisting of the worship of the Lord whose body is Rudra, which will be enjoined in the sixth section with the words, "This is to be worshipped. Its *parikara* means its auxiliary or limb (*aṅga*). *Syāt* means "it may be" or "it would be."

By the word "subsequent," it is indicated that the *praṇava* is understood to be an ancillary (*aṅga*) to the specific knowledge (*vidyā*) consisting of the meditation on the Lord whose body is Rudra—by virtue of the means of application called "position" (*sthāna*), which is defined as proximity in the form of sequential recitation; thus, it is shown that it is logical for the etymological definition of the names "Rudra" and so forth to serve the purpose of praising that [knowledge]. Furthermore, by the word "syāt" (it may be), which denotes worthiness (*arhatva*), there is expressed the "indicative mark" (*liṅga*) characterized by the objective capacity (*vastu-sāmarthya*) of that which expresses [the name], namely its fitness for the accomplishment of that meditation.

Therefore, since it is established by both indicative marks (liṅga) and position (sthāna) that the Praṇava is an adjunct to the knowledge under discussion, the etymological explanation (nirvacana) is for the purpose of praising it; thus, the sense is that there is no room here for the interpretation that Rudra is the subject.

Now, although etymologies have been provided for the names of Oṃkāra, Praṇava, Sarvavyāpin, Ananta, Tāra, Sūkṣma, Śukla, Vaidyuta, and Parabrahma—beginning with the statement, "Why is it called Oṃkāra? Because as soon as it is uttered, it causes the entire body to rise upward; therefore it is called Oṃkāra"—nevertheless, because the etymologies of Rudra and others serve as the basis for the prima facie arguments (pūrvapakṣa), the phrase "Rudra and the others [are] from the head of Mahādeva" was stated in order to indicate the necessity of establishing their consistency within the final conclusion (siddhānta).
For this very reason, it is also indicated that the etymological explanations of names such as "Oṃ" serve as illustrative examples. || 88 ||
He explains the sixth section as prescribing the worship of the Lord, whose body is Rudra together with the limbs and the *praṇava*: "(The path, etc.
The path to the cessation of bondage is here in this *Atharva-śiras* declared to be the worship of Paśupati;
by that statement, Hari shines forth as its essence, and thus He is to be worshipped here.
Just as in the Madhu-vidyā and other meditations, the state of being the creator and the created of other celestial bodies is scripturally established,
so too here [in the case of the ash], that which is heard equally in scripture is merely a subordinate element of the meditation under discussion.
In the *Atharvamūrdhan* and the *Atharvaśiras*, having established the worship of Paśupati, one attains oneness with Rudra.

In accordance with passages such as "Rudra, the eternal, the ancient," it consists of the worship of the perfected Rudra (*siddharudra*). It is the path to the pacification of bondage, meaning the means for the cessation of bondage as stated in the phrase "for the sake of liberation from the bonds. Here, in the sixth section situated within the intellect, it is enjoined by the statement, "This very thing should be worshipped. Now, the particle *nu* is used for emphasis. There is also the reading *nirvihā*; *vihā* means a destroyer, so *nirvihā* means one who is free from that, i.e., unimpeded (*niṣpratyūha*). This is the meaning therein.

"May you accomplish the path to the cessation of bondage through the worship of Paśupati"—this is also the reading "may you accomplish. And "accomplish" (*nirvaha*) is an instruction directed toward the disciple regarding the manifestation (*saṃsthāna*) [of the deity], like a form (*ākṛti*). The meaning is that although the worship of Rudra is already prescribed here, nevertheless—this is the ellipsis—the Lord Hari, whose essence is that [Rudra], shines forth as the one to be worshipped; such is the syntactical connection. Here, in this worship of Rudra mentioned in the *Atharvaśiras*, the Lord Hari, being the inner controller (*antaryāmī*) of Rudra, is the one to be worshipped, that is to say, the object of worship.

By that statement from the beginning of the first section, namely the statement "He [is] within the innermost," the statement "Rudra is indeed the Blessed One," and the statement similar to the one regarding the waters, "This is indeed the God," He shines forth—that is, He is manifested. The meaning is that it has been understood from the preceding statements that the Blessed One alone, as the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin), is the object of the worship of Rudra. This is also an elliptical indication for the subsequent passage: "The Lord, the Person, the God, the Praised One, by whom this fivefold [world] [is pervaded]."

For here, the word *śāsana* (teaching/authority), being intended in its etymological sense of "presiding over," serves as an epithet of the Person (*puruṣa*); furthermore, it should be understood that the word *puruṣa* is unique to the Blessed One. And in this context, the first sentence of the sixth section is: "This is the conduct of Rudra. [The mantra] with the *praṇava* in the heart...

The meaning [of the verse] is that the contemplation (*anusandhāna*) of the Lord, characterized by His being the Self of all (*sārvātmya*), was performed by Rudra. And thus, according to the principle of the Madhu-vidyā, it is possible for Rudra to be the agent in the worship of the Lord who has him as His own body; this is stated in the passage beginning with "Just as" (*yadvat*). The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Just as in the Madhu-vidyā and other [vidyās], [the worshipper] having the body of another god—just like one having the body of another god—here, Hari, whose self is that [body], is to be worshipped. By the phrase "Madhu, Āditya, etc.," the Prāṇa-vidyā is included.

In the Madhu-vidyā, the Prāṇa-vidyā, and others enjoined by such passages as "This sun, indeed, is the honey of the gods" and "Worship me," [the meaning is as follows]: just as in other Vedic texts there are deities like the Vasus, Ādityas, and Indra who possess bodies distinct from Rudra—the subject of the present vidyā—just as the Vasus and others [worship the Self], so too in this vidyā, it is the Supreme Self alone, having Rudra as its body, that is to be worshipped by Rudra. [Objection: But surely, on the strength of scriptural texts concerning causality and so forth, He (Rudra) must be worshipped here as independent.

If it is argued that [Brahman] is not to be worshipped as a mode (*prakāra*) of the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*), then for Indra and the others as well—given that their causality and so forth are understood from such passages as "Indra, by means of his *māyās*, moves in many forms," "Worship me," and "They have perceived Indra in the highest heaven"—there would likewise be the status of being an independent object of worship. If it is objected that they do not possess the status of being independently worshipped because they are understood to be effects (*kārya*), then the same applies here: since this [Brahman] too is understood to be an effect, it does not possess the status of being independently worshipped. He states this with the words beginning "the relation of creator and created," etc.; "śrautaḥ" means declared in the Śruti.

The state of being the creator and the created, as well as causality and effectuality—the word "etcetera" (ādi) including such qualities as being subject to dissolution—is the same here; that is to say, it is identical even in the case of Rudra. Furthermore, the word "but" (tu) [indicates this].

Because the birth of the Blessed One is heard of as an incarnation (*avatāra*), this [term] indicates partiality. Here, by the word *panthā* (path), the statement "this path is extended" is indicated. Regarding the sentence "this is the *pāśupata* vow," the term *paśupata* is intended to mean "connected with Paśupati" because it is a limb of the meditation on the Supreme Self in the form of Paśupati; thus, it is called "the worship of Paśupati. By the intent of the sentence "Therefore, salutations again and again to the Withdrawer, the Great Devourer," he is called *hari*.

The phrase "just as in the Madhu-vidyā and others" was stated to indicate that this vidyā is also included by the term "Madhu-vidyā and others. Thus, the portion concerning the injunction for the primary rite (*aṅgin*) has been explained. He now explains the injunction for the subsidiary rites (*aṅga*) with the words beginning "It is heard," etc. Here, what is heard is the ash-observance (*bhasita-vrata*): "This is Pāśupata"; "Fire is ash, wind is ash, water is ash; indeed, all this is ash"; and "the mind, these [senses], and the eyes."

"Having taken ashes with [the mantra] 'ashes, fire,' and so forth, one should rub them and touch the limbs; therefore, this is the Pāśupata vow for the sake of liberation from bonds"—thus is the taking of ashes heard in the *Atharvaśiras*. This constitutes a subsidiary (*śeṣa*) to the meditation under discussion, being a limb of the primary knowledge (*prakṛta-vidyā*) consisting of the worship of the Supreme Self whose body is Rudra. The word "subsidiary" (*śeṣa*) is neuter even though it ends in the suffix *ghañ*, like the word "connection" (*saṃbandha*), because the relationship continues.
Furthermore, in the phrase "to the meditation under discussion" (*prastutopāsti*), the word "under discussion" (*prastuta*) indicates the means of application known as context (*prakaraṇa*).

Context (*prakaraṇa*) is defined as the requirement for a proximate, fruitful element whose status as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) is not otherwise understood, specifically in terms of its being a constituent part of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Since the meditation on the Lord whose body is Rudra is proximate, and since it possesses a fruit—namely, "He attains ultimate peace"—and because the taking up of ashes is not the subject of the triad of means such as direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), yet is of the nature of an action, there exists a requirement for it as a constituent part of the procedure. Thus, the meaning is that the taking up of ashes is a subsidiary of the meditation on the Supreme Self whose body is Rudra, by virtue of context.

Regarding the phrase "heard here [is] spoken," the term *pāśupata* does not denote that which is taught in the *Pāśupata-tantra*, because that would entail the fault of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Nor is it denoted by the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), for that would entail the application of the suffix *cha* according to the rule "vṛddhāccha" (Pāṇini 4.2.114), and it would also result in the unnecessary complexity of postulating two separate secondary derivatives. Therefore, the venerable Sudarśana Bhaṭṭapāda maintains that *pāśupata* refers to that which is connected to Paśupati as an ancillary (*aṅga*) to the worship of the Supreme Self in the form of Paśupati.

The Great Teacher [Sadyojyotiḥ] maintains that this is the *Pāśupata* system because it begins with the phrase "this is the conduct of Rudra" (*tadetadrudracaritam*), indicating that it was practiced by Paśupati. In both interpretations, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule "tasyedam" (Pāṇini 4.3.120). Furthermore, the specific meaning is understood from the context; or rather, the specific meaning is understood because pronouns such as *tyad* and others generate a cognition characterized by their respective specific forms. Nor should it be suspected that this suffix *aṇ* has the sense of "deity" according to the rule "sāsya devatā" (Pāṇini 4.2.24).

Since the nature of a deity (*devatātva*)—consisting of being the intended object of an oblation being offered, and being the object of praise through a mantra—is defined by its status as a counter-correlative residing in the oblation and the mantra, and since the specific ritual act consisting of the non-grasping of ashes lacks such a relationship with a deity, the suffix *kāṇ* (in the word *pāśupata*) cannot signify a deity. Furthermore, the phrase "for the sake of liberation from bonds" (*pāśavimokṣāya*), which describes the fruit of the primary rite (*aṅgin*), is mentioned merely for the purpose of praising the subsidiary rite (*aṅga*). Thus, because it lacks the character of being an auxiliary to the vows prescribed in the *Pāśupata-tantra*, Rudra is not to be worshipped independently within this present knowledge (*vidyā*).

This very vow is expounded in the Kālāgnirudra Upaniṣad. Therefore, the Great Teachers maintain that this [Upaniṣad] also has the Lord as its ultimate purport, because it is devoted to the injunctions regarding the ancillaries of the worship of the Lord. Consequently, it does not have Rudra as its ultimate purport. || 89 ||
Now, regarding the taking of ashes:
"Having drunk liquor, having approached the wife of one's guru, having committed theft, and having even committed the murder of a Brahmin— "
"Covered in ashes, lying on a bed of ashes, meditating upon Rudra, one is liberated from all sins"—

since this passage in the *Śātātapa-smṛti* records that [this practice] is the cause for the destruction of all sins, and since the destruction of sin is required by all knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), one must conclude— by means of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting in the force of the matter characterized by such requirement— that it serves the purpose of all knowledge of Brahman, thereby setting aside the context (*prakaraṇa*).

For this very reason, although the Dahara-vidyā is the subject under discussion in the passage, "This very [Self] by the study of the Vedas... (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.10), sacrificial rites and other such actions are common to all meditations. This is because the door consisting of the destruction of sin produced by karma—which is established by the scriptural statement, "By dharma he drives away evil"—is required by every meditation.

Likewise, in the scriptural passage beginning with "Therefore, one who knows thus is calm, self-controlled," even though the word "one who knows thus" (*evaṃvit*) refers specifically to the knowledge under discussion, one might suspect that because mental one-pointedness—which is to be accomplished through calmness and self-control—is required for all forms of knowledge, this [meditation] must be common to all vidyās.
