Anticipating this objection, [the author] states: "If things mentioned in a specific context were common to all merely by virtue of being required, then the *sannipatyopakāraka* (directly contributing) auxiliaries such as the sprinkling and threshing of rice-grains, which are mentioned in the context of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, would also apply to the *Varma-vājapeya*..."

There would be the undesirable consequence that even the auxiliary rites such as the *prayājas*—which produce the assistance required by the sacrifice as understood from explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as "this is performed for the sake of the sacrifice"—would be common to all sacrifices simply by virtue of their being taught [in a general context]. However, in cases such as "by sacrifice, by charity," although their commonality to all forms of knowledge (*vidyā*) is established by the force of other scriptural texts which teach their commonality to all knowledge—such as "When the impurity has been cooked away by actions, then knowledge arises"—there is no evidence for such a status elsewhere. This applies to the case of tranquility (*śama*) and so forth as well.

Since the meditation on Brahman (*brahmopāsana*) is to be accomplished solely through mental one-pointedness (*cittaikāgrya*), which in turn is achieved by tranquility (*śama*) and other such means, tranquility and the rest are common to all forms of knowledge (*vidyā*). However, as there is no authoritative evidence that the destruction of sins required for the knowledge of Brahman is achievable solely through the smearing with ashes (*bhasmoddhūlana*), the latter cannot be considered an ancillary (*aṅga*) to all meditations on Brahman. With this resolution in mind, he says:
"Having introduced [the topic] of the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*) in the form of Rudra... and so forth.
The Atharvaśiras-vidyā is declared to be an ancillary (aṅga) of this [Upaniṣad],
whereas there is no application of ashes elsewhere, just as there is no application of the cup of surā liquor mentioned in the context of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice.

In the *Atharvaśiras*, the remainder being that it is in the sixth section (*khaṇḍa*). Of the one whose body is Rudra—that is, of the Lord Puruṣottama—[it teaches] the *vidyā*, which is the mode of worship (*upāsanā*). Having praised [it] and enjoined it by means of the preceding statement, "This very thing is to be worshipped," [the text] declares: "Agni," and so forth; and it is prescribed by such passages as, "Having taken the ashes and rubbed them, one should touch the limbs. Thus, the ash (*bhasman*) becomes an ancillary (*aṅga*) to this—the aforementioned *vidyā* whose nature is the worship of the Supreme Self whose body is Rudra. This refers to what was stated in the context of the Sautrāmaṇi—that is, in the context of the specific sacrifice named Sautrāmaṇi.

Regarding the "prescribed" [act], such as the taking of wine (surāgraha), or as in the case of the taking of wine: in other instances, there is no application elsewhere of that which belongs to its own context; there is no possibility of ashes becoming a subordinate element (aṅga); the meaning is that there is no possibility of those things grasped within their respective contexts becoming subordinate elements elsewhere. By the word "ca" (and), the *prayāja* offerings and others grasped within the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) are included as corroborative examples.

Here, by the phrase "of Puruṣottama, whose form is Rudra," the meaning of these two statements—"that Lord, the Person, the adorable God"—and "having meditated upon Him with the intellect and established Him in Rudra"—is recalled. || 90 ||

Thus, by means of these eleven verses, it has been established that the *Atharvaśiras* has the Blessed Lord as its ultimate subject. Now, the fact that the *Atharvaśikhā* has the Blessed Lord as its ultimate subject is being established. In this regard, the intended meaning of the word "but" (*tu*) in the statement, "The relationship between the creator and the created, etc., is equally scriptural here as well," is explained as the Blessed Lord’s birth being an incarnation: "In the *Atharvaṇī Śikhā*, the birth of the Blessed Lord—which occurs in that [Upaniṣad] whose sole purpose is to establish Him as the single object of meditation for the cause [of the universe]—is for the benefit of the world; this is an incarnation by His own will."

Since the teaching of Viṣṇu’s causality is clearly seen through his statements whose sole intent is to establish that causality, even the word *śambhu*— which is commonly used for Śiva— is applied to him because he is the generator of the gods.

In the *Atharvaśikhā*, Paippalāda, Aṅgiras, and Sanatkumāra said to Atharvan: "O Blessed One, what is employed at the beginning? What is meditation (*dhyāna*)? What is that which is to be meditated upon? Who is the meditator (*dhyātṛ*)? And what is the object of meditation (*dhyeya*)? Thus it is heard. Here, the first question concerns meditation alone;

The second is the question concerning the deity who possesses the conceit of being the meditator in the second *dhyāna*; the third is the question concerning the deity who possesses the conceit of being the one who meditates; and the fourth is the question concerning the object of meditation with its specific qualifications. Among these, the answer to the first question is: "The syllable 'Om'—this imperishable which is employed at the beginning—is the meditation that is to be meditated upon. The answer to the second is: "Having established all the organs in the mind, the meditation is Viṣṇu."

The answer to the third question is: having established the meditator together with the organs in the mind, [one should know] that Rudra is the fourth. The answer to the fourth question is: Īśāna is to be meditated upon; all this is Brahman, for Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, and all the senses along with the elements are produced from Him. He is not a cause, but the meditator, the sustainer, and the cause of causes. Endowed with all sovereignty, the Lord of All, Śambhu is to be meditated upon in the midst of space.

On this point, the Great Teachers [state]: "He states the answer to the fourth question: 'Īśāna is to be meditated upon. Because it corresponds to the form of the question, 'And who is to be meditated upon?', this alone is the answer to the fourth question, just like the answers to the preceding questions; it is not, however, 'one should meditate on Īśāna,' because that would differ from the form of the question and differ from the form of the previous answers. The masculine designation 'Īśāna' is employed here. Since no specific object to be ruled over is mentioned, the meaning is that the reality which is the Lord of all is to be meditated upon."

In order to state the preeminence of the object of worship among the principal deities, he declares the preeminence of Brahmā and the others: “All this is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra. This grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—between everything established by valid means of knowledge and Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—is based on the relationship between that which is to be manifested and its manifestor, just as in the expression “the king is the kingdom. There is another sentence: “They are all brought forth. This being the case, the use of the word *tat* (that) achieves its purpose.

In order to manifest the preeminence of the Blessed One (*bhagavat*), and because his lack of birth among these will be stated in the subsequent sentence, the word "all" (*sarve*) was used so that there might be no suspicion that anyone other than him [the Blessed One] could be born among them; for only when this is the case is the purpose of this [statement] achieved. Nor is the purpose of the phrase "all those" (*te sarve*) fulfilled merely by referring to the two previously mentioned groups as "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra."

It should not be argued that because of the absence of the word *ca* (and), there must be an expectation for a collective reference (*samudāyaparāmarśa*) such as "all those [beings]"; for otherwise, the grammatical fault of *napuṃsakaśeṣa* (the remainder being neuter) would result. Furthermore, from its association with the senses (*indriya*) and so forth, it is understood by the natural sense of the passage that the "progeny" (*prasūti*) of Brahmā and others is dependent on another. The text denies the progeny of the Blessed One: "He is not the cause of causes; He is the meditator, the creator. Among the three types of causes, the modification (*vipariṇāma*) and the ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) are to be supplied as follows: "He is not produced as a cause among the causes, nor as a meditator, nor as a creator."

The consequence regarding transformation is the same even for the opposing side. It is understood that the term "Dhātṛ" (the Ordainer) refers to one who is established as the meditator in the causal state, as in the passage: "The Blessed One Nārāyaṇa himself desired," and "He meditated upon another desire with his mind. Furthermore, the word "Dhātṛ" is well-known in its application to the Blessed One in the verse "Smaller than the small," which is corroborated by the commentaries of Śaṅkha and Likhita; and in the *Sahasranāmastotra*, it says: "The Ordainer, without beginning or end."

Let it be simply the genitive of remainder (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), with "the cause" (*kāraṇam*) as the understood object; the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) is obtained through the context. Alternatively, let there be no obtainment of selection through the context. Let the manifestation (*saṃprasūti*) of Viṣṇu himself be what is propounded. And that manifestation is established by such passages as: "Though being unborn, he is born in many ways; the wise know his source," and "That birth is not produced by karma," and "His birth is by his own will alone. Thus, it is dependent on himself, and not dependent on karma like Brahmā, Rudra, and others.

Alternatively, no modification need be made here, nor should the well-known meaning of the word *dhātṛ* be abandoned. The meaning is that the four-faced one (*caturmukha*) is the meditator (*dhyātā*), and Rudra is the meditator; [Vishnu] is the cause of the causes. The sense is that Vishnu alone is the cause. Since it was previously stated that "Rudra is the meditator," Rudra, as the deity who sustains (*dhātṛ*), is designated as the meditator. Or rather, no origination of anything at all is being propounded here. The form *saṃprasūyante* is derived from the root *ṣūñ* in the sense of "impelling" (*preraṇe*), used in the passive voice (*karmaṇi lakāre*).

However, [the root] *ṣañ* in the sense of “birth” (*prāṇiprasave*) or *ṣūñ* in the sense of “delivery of the fetus of living beings” (*prāṇigarbhavimocane*) cannot be accepted here, because they relate specifically to living beings (*prāṇin*), and thus would be incompatible with the connection to the phrase “all the senses together with the elements” (*sarvāṇi cendriyāṇi saha bhūtair*). Furthermore, this would necessitate the forced insertion (*adhyāhāra*) of the word “are born” (*jāyante*). Moreover, since the preceding sentence states that “the Lord (*īśāna*) is to be meditated upon,” and since this serves as a direct justification for the Lord’s sovereignty over all—which was established without restriction—the verbal root must be understood here in its sense of impelling (*preraṇā*).

The meaning of the passage beginning with "the creator is not impelled by anyone" is that the meditator (*dhyātā*) is the supreme cause, yet he himself is not impelled by any other. In the phrase "And who is to be meditated upon? (*kaśca dhyeyaḥ*), because the qualification of the object of meditation is also intended to be expressed, [the text] prescribes the heart as the locus for that which is to be meditated upon: "But the Cause is to be meditated upon—Śambhu, endowed with all sovereignty, the Lord of all, in the midst of space. In the compound *sarvaiśvaryasaṃpannaḥ*, it is a *karmadhāraya* meaning "that which is both everything and sovereignty" (*sarvaṃ ca tad aiśvaryaṃ ca*).

However, the suffix *ṣyañ* is not applied here from the compound *sarveśvara* (master of all) because that would entail the initial *vṛddhi* strengthening [of the first vowel]. What is intended to be expressed is one who is the Lord (*īśvara*) or Sovereign (*īśāna*) in every respect. And there is indeed a distinction of modes in the act of ruling: namely, ruling by entering within like a king, and ruling by remaining outside, which concerns such matters as sustaining and setting in motion, whether through a medium or without a medium. This sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) of every mode—not limited to a few objects—is what is expressed by the term *sarveśvara*.

Thus, because of the delusion that the two terms *sarvaiśvaryasaṃpanna* ("endowed with all sovereignty") and *sarveśvara* ("Lord of all") have the same meaning, the attempt by some to avoid redundancy by resorting to *lakṣaṇā* (indication) for the word *sarveśvara*—taking it to refer to what is denoted by that [other] term—is refuted. The actual state of things has been stated; even if that were so, there is no fault in our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), because the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of the word *sarveśvara* for another deity is not established. Let this very figurative interpretation (*kalpanā*) apply instead to the Blessed Goddesses.

And here, the separate mention of the word "senses" (*indriya*) in the phrase "all the senses" (*sarvāṇīndriyāṇi*) is intended to establish the meaning of the term *hṛṣīkeśa*—which consists in the impelling of the senses—as a mark (*liṅga*) of Nārāyaṇahood. Alternatively, it serves as the answer to the fourth question, "But the Cause is to be meditated upon. By way of introduction, the sense is that in order to demonstrate that, [the text says] "the Lord of lords is to be meditated upon"; thus, since only the Sovereign of all possesses the power to bestow liberation, it is logical that He alone is the object of worship. In the phrase "But the Cause is to be meditated upon," the word "Cause" (*kāraṇa*)...

It is either the supreme cause of all causes or the supreme cause of the three forms (trimūrti). That the Blessed One alone is the cause of the three forms is well-established, because in the *Subālopaniṣad*, in the sections explaining the maintenance of effects, the maintenance within the three forms is heard; and because in the *Paingi-rahasya* it is heard: "Yama, Varuṇa, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra. Therefore, in this *Subālopaniṣad*:

By restating the well-known causality, it is enjoined that the Blessed Lord alone is to be meditated upon. Furthermore, the word *Śambhu* is well-established in lexicons and other works as a name for the Blessed Lord. Since the *Subālopaniṣad*, the *Tāpanīya Upaniṣad*, and others—through passages such as "Śambhu [is] among the Creator, Hari, and Īśa"—reveal His universal lordship, the word *Śambhu* used in grammatical apposition with Him refers exclusively to the Blessed Lord. If it is argued that the natural meaning [of *Śambhu*] applies only to Rudra—that is true.

However, that [creation] is included within the Trimūrti itself, and its inclusion therein is untenable because of the scriptural hearing of [the soul's] being an object of creation and its state of having an unremoved nature (anapahatapāpmatva). Furthermore, its inclusion is not accepted by others. Therefore, its inclusion is logical only for the Blessed Lord. Although there is scriptural hearing of Viṣṇu’s creation, they have explained that he is not dependent on another, because his status as an incarnation is understood from the passage: "Being unborn, he is born in many ways; the wise know his source."

This is stated by the passage beginning with "In the Atharvaṇīya," and so forth. The meaning is: regarding that which is the singular object of meditation for the Cause—[the text refers to] that [Upaniṣad] which is intent upon this [Cause], and which, while restating the causality well-known from the *Puruṣasūkta* and other sources, is devoted to the injunction that He is to be meditated upon. Furthermore, the word "single" (*eka*) is intended to indicate the preeminence of the focus on His being the sole object of meditation.

Regarding this, the venerable Bhaṭṭasudarśana says: "Since this section begins with 'And who is to be meditated upon? and concludes with 'But the Cause is to be meditated upon,' it is understood that its purpose is to enjoin meditation; therefore, this statement is intended to enjoin the Lord—already established in the Puruṣasūkta and other texts—as the object of meditation. This refers to the *Atharvaśikhā*, which is a part of the *Atharvaṇī Śikhā*.

The meaning is this: that birth of the Blessed One—which was without a womb (*agaṇi*), a mine of faultless and auspicious qualities, and which is the birth of Nārāyaṇa as taught [in scripture]; by the statement, "All these—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—are born from Him," it is indicated that even the Blessed One has an origin. This very [birth] is expressed as: "Though unborn, He is born in many ways."

"The wise know its source"—referring to that from which the sun shines, kindled with splendor; "the father becomes possessed of a son through the son, in womb after womb"—such is the manifestation [of the Lord] which is well-known from these and other scriptural passages that establish His nature. This manifestation is restated here for the purpose of making Him easily accessible to the practitioner, as He has descended in a form similar to other created beings, even though this text is primarily devoted to the injunction for meditation. "For the benefit of the worlds" means for the sake of assisting the worlds.

Thus, the term "descent by will" (*icchāvatāra*) refers to the Lord’s manifestation caused by His own will, which has as its purpose the benefit of the world in the form of protecting the virtuous and so forth. By the word "will," it is stated that this manifestation is not rooted in karma, as is the case with the birth of ordinary living beings (*jīva*). The expression "descent by will" is used with reference to such scriptural passages as, "I manifest myself through my own *māyā*" and "and my birth is solely by my own will."

The designation "this is that" (so'yam) follows the gender of the predicate. The purpose of this restatement of the Lord’s birth is to serve as an injunction for meditation; the sense is that it restates the incarnations already established by preceding passages such as "He who is not born" (ajāyamānaḥ), in order to make [the Lord] easily accessible. This is because, in one [place], by means of eloquent utterances—namely, the Upaniṣads such as the Puruṣasūkta, the Subāla-upaniṣad, and the Paiṅgirahasya—which are intent upon [this truth] and possess its underlying purport.

The teaching on Viṣṇu’s causality—the prescription of the Blessed One’s status as the cause—is clear and manifest. [The root] *vana-ṣaṇ* means "to desire" (*saṃbhakti*). Here, *saṃbhakti* signifies "prayer" (*prārthana*). By this, the intended purport (*tātparya*) is expressed.

Regarding that Blessed Lord Śambhu, who is declared by the Śruti to be the cause [of the universe], the word *śambhu* is also used in its observed (dṛṣṭa) application through its etymological (yoga) meaning—derived from the sense of producing happiness (*śam*) by the process of "He brings about (*bhāvayati*) happiness (*śam*)"—as seen in corroborative texts such as, "Listen to my words, O Śambhu, the grandfather of the Grandfather," and in Vedic passages such as, "The all-seeing one, the source of happiness for the universe."

Therefore, having referred to the Blessed One by such terms as "Kāraṇa-Śambhu," the meaning is that in this [passage] which is devoted to His being the object of meditation, the mention of the Blessed One's birth is a restatement of His birth in the form of an incarnation.

This has been stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Sudarśana: "The syntactical function [of the sentence] is not 'Śambhu is the cause,' but rather 'the Cause is Śambhu, who is to be meditated upon. Otherwise, the subsequent question 'And who is to be meditated upon? would be inappropriate. Even though the word 'Śambhu' is not common [to other deities], it is logical that it refers to the Supreme Self (paramātman), just as in the case of the words 'ether' (ākāśa) or 'vital breath' (prāṇa). Nor is this word uncommon, because it is recited in the list of names [in the Purāṇas]: 'Śambhu, Svayambhū, Druhiṇa,' and so forth."

In the section concerning the technical term *kṣiprasūlibādva*, it is stated that there is an "addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) from *mitadru* and others. Thus, the grammarians have derived the word *śambhu* by means of the suffix *ḍhuk* [with the addition of *u*], as follows: "He who flows measuredly is *mitadru*; *śatadru* and *śambhu*—here the root *bhū* contains an implied causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*). Furthermore, this word *śambhu* is based on a connection with a quality (*guṇayoga*), just like the word *śiva*.

And thus it is employed: "O lotus-eyed one, Śambhu, the Self-born, shall become the crest-jewel upon the moon for which fortunate man’s breast will he [touch] with his fingernail? Furthermore, its usage alongside the term *bhagavatī* (the Blessed Lady) has been demonstrated by the Abhidhānakośa lexicon. Since its reference to the Blessed Lord (*bhagavat*) is also possible through the function of inexhaustible implication (*aparyavasāna-vṛtti*), this *Atharvaśikhā* is indeed devoted solely to the Blessed Lord. || 91 ||

Regarding the position that the *Atharvaśikhā* is devoted to the Lord through its inexhaustible application to Śambhu alone, [the author] states that even in the *Atharvaśikhā*, just as in the *Arthaśiras*, the meditation on the Supreme Self whose body is Rudra is indeed enjoined. He says:
"The two meditations taught in the *Atharvaśiras* and the *Śikhā* for the sake of non-return [to saṃsāra] clearly concern the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva) who has assumed a body."

[This is] for the lotus-eyed one, and for the wise man who dwells within the center of the heart, which is the abode of the sun, as ordained by the Veda—the supreme scripture concerning the reality of causes—here and there [in various places]. 92.

In the *Atharvaśiras* and the *Atharvaśikhā*: in the *Atharvaśiras* and the *Atharvaśikhā*, [the teaching] is "spoken for the sake of non-rebirth"—that is, spoken for the sake of liberation (*mokṣa*), meaning it is prescribed. "The two modes of worship": the two modes of worship stated as "this is to be worshipped" and "Śambhu is to be meditated upon in the midst of space. [This refers to] that which is prescribed by certain Śrutis concerning the causal principle (*kāraṇatattva*).

In various places—in certain instances within the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka*, the *Mahopaniṣad*, the *Subālopaniṣad*, and so forth—by means of scriptural passages that declare the true nature of the Cause, which are intent upon the reality of the Cause and are entirely free from even a trace of being subordinate to injunctions for meditation or other purposes, such as "He is Brahmā, He is Śiva, He is Indra," [the Lord] is taught as the one who possesses those respective bodies and is the object of worship in those respective meditations (*vidyās*).

Of the wise one who dwells in the center of the cavity of the heart—that is, situated within the hollow of the devotee’s heart; for the lexicon states: "randhra, śvabhra, vapā, and suṣi [mean] cavity. The suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *juṣ* (meaning "to delight in" or "to serve"). Of him whose body is that of the Enemy of the Cities—namely, Rudra; the suffix *ini* is used here after the *karmadhāraya* compound *rudra-śarīrin* because there is an intention to express excellence relative to humans and others. The prohibition "not after a *karmadhāraya*" does not apply here.

Grammarians have stated that the prohibition applies only to the *matvarthīya* suffix—which expresses a mere relationship and is synonymous with a *bahuvrīhi* compound—and not to those [suffixes] employed to convey specific meanings such as praise. Thus, "of the lotus-eyed one" (*kamaladṛśaḥ puṇḍarīkākṣasya*) clearly refers to the Blessed One whose body is Rudra; this is evident.

And here, because it is enjoined that the Cause alone is to be meditated upon; because the Blessed One alone is known from other Vedic texts to be the Cause; because the well-known Rudra is heard in scripture to be subject to birth and so forth; because the scriptural accounts of his incarnations are not intended to establish his identity [with the Supreme]; because the Blessed One is established as the object of worship for all branches of knowledge by the *Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka* which has no other purpose; and because there is a recognition—through the passage beginning "The heart is like the interior of a lotus bud"—that he who is to be meditated upon in the middle of the space within the eye is the same one whose worship is prescribed in the center of the heart.

The meaning is that, because of the realization of identity between the one who is within the person and the one who is within the solar orb—as expressed in passages such as "He who is here in the person and he who is yonder in the sun are one"—and because of the scriptural declaration of His having lotus-eyes (*puṇḍarīkākṣatva*), it is clearly understood that the Blessed Lord alone is the object of worship here, by virtue of having Rudra as His body.

In this context, the mention of the *Atharvaśiras* is for the sake of illustration; for it has been established that the meditation taught therein has as its object the Lord who dwells within Rudra. Furthermore, this is intended to clarify that although Rudra alone is the meditator—as expressed in the words "Rudra is to be meditated upon"—it is not contradictory for the Supreme Self, whose body he is, to be the object of meditation according to the principle of the Madhu-vidyā.

And here, although the object of knowledge is indeed the Supreme Self whose body is Rudra, the statement that there are two meditations is made with the intention that there is a distinction between the vidyās due to the difference in attributes such as universal sovereignty (*sarvaiśvarya*). The phrase "for the sake of non-rebirth" is stated with the intention of the meaning established by the scriptural passage: "Having studied this, the twice-born is released from dwelling in a womb and is liberated."
"Viṣṇu is the self of the blessed Bhava of immeasurable splendor;
therefore, that Maheśvara endured the touch of the bowstring."

By reminding [the reader] of this statement, the phrase "of the one whose body is the corpse of the enemy of the cities" is used to indicate that Rudra’s state of being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of the Blessed Lord is established by many proofs. Because the text "He is to be meditated upon in the midst of space" reveals his status as the inner controller of the Puruṣa, and because his identity with the one residing within the solar orb is revealed, and because that [residing one] is heard in scripture to have lotus-eyes (*puṇḍarīkākṣa*), the intention is that the Blessed Lord alone is established here as the object of meditation; thus, the term "lotus-eyed" is employed.

Since it was understood through the *Ananyapara-Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka* that [the Lord] resides in the center of the heart by virtue of being devoted to the Blessed One, and since this is stated here by the words "He is to be meditated upon in the middle of space," the intention is that it is established that the Blessed One alone is the object of meditation here; with this in mind, it is said: "of the knower who dwells in the middle of the heart-cavity. || 92 ||

The attempt to establish the superiority of another deity over the Lord by means of the scriptural citations and indicative marks (liṅga) in the passages "that which is higher than that" and "that which is within it" has been refuted by demonstrating that those two passages do not have that as their primary intent, in the two verses beginning with "He who is the creator of names and forms" and "Having praised the cause of immortality. Furthermore, in connection with that, the fact that the *Atharvaśiras* and the *Śikhā* Upaniṣads refer to the Lord has been established by demonstrating that they do not have [the aforementioned deities] as their primary intent, through the verses beginning with "That which [is worshipped] by the gods."

Now, having raised that doubt regarding the name (*samākhyā*), [the author] refutes the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) which relies on the name by means of three verses, showing that since the name is sublated by more powerful means of knowledge such as direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and so forth, it does not determine the meaning.

For this is the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa): [the claim] that [the one denoted by the word *īśvara*], whether accompanied by an epithet or without an epithet, is distinct from that which is denoted by the word *puruṣa*, likewise [whether accompanied by an epithet or without an epithet].

[This is] excellence. For the word *puruṣa* is used for the Lord, being common to the individual soul (*jīva*). And when qualified by "greatness," it is used of Him. Furthermore, the words *īśvara* and *maheśvara* are used for Rudra. Now, the term *puruṣa*, being common to the individual soul who is subject to inferiority, when applied to the Lord, would likewise imply inferiority in the Lord as well. However, the term *īśvara*, which distinguishes [the Lord] from all individual souls, makes known a sovereignty that is indeed superior to mere personhood (*puruṣatva*). When qualified by the word "great" (*mahat*), it makes known His greatness. And thus:

It is appropriate that the exaltation of the Blessed Lord Rudra, the Great Lord (Maheśvara), should be superior to that of Puruṣa. He states this prima facie argument as follows: "It has been said by someone: 'The term *īśvara* (Lord) applies to both Śiva and Śrīśa; it occurs many times in connection with those who are great, supreme, eloquent, and liberated.

Since these two terms are explained through their respective scopes of exaltation and disparagement, it is fitting to state the exaltation of Giriśa [Śiva] over Puruṣa, just as one would over Pradhāna and the rest. (Verse 93)

*Mahat* and *paramam* together form *mahatparame*; the neuter gender is used because of the nature of the words themselves, and there is a mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*). *Mahatparame* and those two *vācau* (words) constitute *mahatparamavācau*. Since the focus is on the nature of the words themselves, even though it functions as a feminine qualifier, there is no femininity because of the inherent neuter gender in a *bahuvrīhi* compound with a related term (*bandhu*), just as in the rule *bandhuni bahuvrīhau*. Otherwise, it would have been *sahatī paramā*. This is because, when followed by a word in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) as the latter member, the neuter state does not apply to the abstract state (*bhāva*).

When joined with those two [the words *mahat* and *parama*], or even when not joined with them—meaning, when used alone without being co-uttered (*asamabhivyāhṛta*) with the words *mahat* and *parama* because they reside in the intellect—the terms "Lord" (*īśvara*) and "Person" (*puruṣa*) are used; that is, the words *īśvara* and *puruṣa* occur in the forms of *īśvara*, *maheśvara*, *parameśvara*; and *puruṣa*, *mahāpuruṣa*, *paramapuruṣa*. The suffix *-śas* is used here in the sense of frequent occurrence (*pracura*), relative to the action of existing. They exist—that is, they are employed—in relation to Śiva and Śrīśa (Śiva and Viṣṇu).

The meaning is that [the two terms] become expressive of those [meanings] by virtue of their capacity. Regarding the phrase "by means of words denoting excellence and deficiency" (*utkarṣanikarṣigocarapadaiḥ*): this refers, respectively, to words such as *īśvara*, *maheśvara*, and *parameśvara*, which convey excellence, and words such as *puruṣa*, *mahāpuruṣa*, and *paramapuruṣa*, which convey deficiency. The term "specifically" (*viśeṣeṇa*) indicates that there is no fault even if, in certain instances of usage, they are employed with particular frequency through the specific application of terms like *puruṣa* and *īśvara* to those two [entities] respectively. The word "specifically" (*vi-*) suggests that although there may be occasional usage of terms such as *puruṣa* for *Īśvara* and so forth, no error is incurred.

Between these two—Śiva and Śrī; the locative case is used here in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). There is no substitution of *enad* because the subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*) is not intended. From the "Person" (*pums*), that is, from the Puruṣa mentioned alongside Pradhāna—as in the expression "Pradhāna and Puruṣa"—referring to the Puruṣa denoted by the word "Puruṣa" which is mentioned together with Pradhāna, just as from Pradhāna, which is insentient by nature.

The excellence (*utkarṣa*) of the Blessed One, of Giriśa Rudra, is "fit to be spoken" (*vaktum ucitaḥ*), meaning it is worthy of being expressed. Although the word *giriśa*—derived from the rule *girau ḍaś chandasi* (Pāṇini 3.2.15)—is restricted to the Vedic language (*chandas*), it is stated that because the usage "that fair-haired woman attended upon Giriśa every day" (*giriśam upacacāra pratyahaṃ sā sukeśī*) occurs in classical literature, it must be understood as ending in the possessive suffix *śa*. In this context, words such as *īśvara* possess the quality of being the object of excellence, the capacity to convey excellence, and the power to suggest excellence (*utkarṣa-vyañjakatva*). Conversely, words such as *puruṣa* possess the quality of being the object of inferiority (*nikarṣa-gocaratva*), which consists in their power to suggest inferiority (*nikarṣa-vyañjakatva*).

For lordship (*īśvaratva*) consists of excellence and excludes non-excellence; whereas manhood (*puṃstva*), however, does not consist of inferiority, but rather coexists with inferiority by virtue of its occurrence in one who is not a lord. Thus, because the state of being denoted by a word expressing that [lordship] indicates an excellence or inferiority of the same genus as the excellence or inferiority residing therein, it follows that what is denoted by the word "man" (*puruṣa*) when applied to a living being (*jīva*) is established as having an inferiority relative to the Lord, just like other living beings.

The meaning is as follows: although the term "great minister" (*mahāsaciva*) conveys greatness in relation to other ministers, it nevertheless implies inferiority in comparison to the king denoted by the term "king of kings" (*rājahārāja*); similarly, although that which is expressed by the term "Great Person" (*mahāpuruṣa*) possesses excellence in relation to other persons, it implies inferiority in relation to the Lord (*īśvara*). This was stated by "someone"—meaning it was stated by someone who is unworthy even to have his name mentioned. || 93 ||

In this regard, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: when there is mutual conflict among direct assertion (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth, each preceding factor possesses the quality of sublation by each succeeding factor, consisting in its obstruction of the inferable means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Conflict (*virodha*), moreover, occurs when two means of knowledge exist for a single subsidiary (*śeṣa*) with respect to two principals (*śeṣin*). For example, when by direct assertion the mantra addressed to Indra (*aindrī-mantra*) is a subsidiary to the Gārhapatya fire, while by indicative mark it is a subsidiary to Indra; or, for example, when there are two means of knowledge enjoining two different subsidiaries for a single principal.

Just as in the case of the *gārhapatya* fire, where by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) an *aindrī* mantra is [assigned], yet by indicative power (*liṅga*) it belongs to Agni, so too in subsequent cases a conflict is to be observed. And here, in all instances, because each succeeding factor possesses authority by way of being the basis for the preceding one, the succeeding factor acts as a sublater of the preceding one—consisting in the obstruction of its postulation—by producing a state of lack of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*) in the relationship between the subordinate (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*) through the application of the preceding factor, which has already been established and operates within a different domain.

Thus, when both indicative power (*liṅga*) and name (*samākhyā*) suggest that a portion of the *bhakṣa-mantra* is subsidiary to the act of taking up (*grahaṇa*) and the act of consuming (*bhakṣaṇa*), the name is set aside by the indicative power, and it is therefore subsidiary to the act of taking up. As for the name, which refers merely to a general connection, its application is possible even through a mediated sequence via the acts of taking up and so forth. When there is a conflict between order (*krama*) and name, the mantra "śundhadhvam" and others, which are recited in the section named *pauroḍāśika*, are subsidiary to the preparation of the *sānnāyya* (milk offering) because of their position in the sequence, rather than being subsidiary to the *sānnāyya* itself due to the name.

And likewise, in the case of a single Rudra-form as the principal (*śeṣin*), there arises a conflict between the collection of statements (*vākya*)—which establish his being an effect, his subjection to karma, and so forth—and the designation (*samākhyā*) "Īśvara," because they convey two distinct attributes (*dharma*) belonging to that same principal. Thus, by virtue of the statement, the designation is set aside. This is just as, in the case of the purchase (*parikraya*) and other rites, the designation "Adhvaryava" (indicating the Adhvaryu priest as the agent) is set aside by the statement "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*), which indicates the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) as the agent; and just as [the fire] is indeed the *gārhapatya*...

By the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) indicating the connection with Indra, the indicative power (*liṅga*) that indicates the subsidiary nature of the *āgneyī* [verse] is set aside. To explain: the word *īśvara* is both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍhi*) with respect to Rudra. In that case, the etymological meaning—consisting of the quality of being a ruler (*īśanaśīla*), as indicated by the verbal root *īś* ending in the suffix *varac* according to the rule *stheśabhāsapisakaso varac*—is subordinated to the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) when it refers to Rudra.

From the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by way of identity (*tādātmya*), the cognition of Rudra as one whose nature is to rule arises. In that case, it is impossible to enjoin either the identity of the conventional meaning "Rudra" with the etymological meaning "one whose nature is to rule," or the identity of the etymological meaning "one whose nature is to rule" with the conventional meaning "Rudra," because such a linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) does not exist.

And thus, since the designation (*samākhyā*) cannot otherwise be accounted for as a statement of an established fact, one might postulate a sentence such as "He who is Rudra is of the nature of ruling" (*īśana-śīla*), thereby enjoining lordship (*īśvaratva*) in Rudra. However, at that very moment, the postulation of such a sentence is obstructed by an already established sentence that conveys his being an effect (*kāryatva*) or that conveys his non-lordship; thus, the designation is sublated. Furthermore, [the designation] is sublated because it refers to a lordship dependent upon the Blessed Lord (*bhagavad-āyatta*), as understood from such passages as "Having offered himself, he is the God of gods" (*hutvātmānaṃ devadevaḥ*) and "Then the two paths were shown."

The designation (*samākhyā*) is also applicable [to Rudra]. Therefore, because the designation is sublated by the syntactical connection (*vākya*), the elevation (*utkarṣa*) of Rudra is not established. Furthermore, because it is countered by other designations—such as Viśvarūpa, Nārāyaṇa, Bhikṣu, and Rudra—which pertain to the scope of elevation and depreciation through inversion, the intended elevation and depreciation are not established by the designation alone. Moreover:
"O Govinda, whatever great names you have in the world, those very same are my names; no deliberation need be made on this point."

Thus, because this [designation] is understood as a conventional usage (*saṅketa*) applied to Rudra for names such as "Bhagavat," "Gati," and "Īśvara," the intended meaning is not established by it. How this point is demonstrated by that statement has been set forth by the Mahācāryas in the *Pārāśaryavijaya* and should be investigated there. Furthermore, since we observe that names such as "khadyota" (firefly) and "puṇyajana" (yakṣa) can refer either to a limited application or to the opposite, a similar doubt arises here as well; therefore, the desired conclusion is not established by mere designation.

Thus, regarding the argument that proximity and so forth are established because [the Lord] is denotable by words that denote those [qualities], if the intended meaning of the reason—namely, "being denotable by words that denote those"—is taken as being based solely on the etymological sense (*yogārtha*), then the reason suffers from the fallacy of being unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*). This is because, through such scriptural passages as "I was indeed here before" (*pūrvataṃ vāhamihāsam*) and others, or through the statement "They know the Person as 'I was indeed here before' (*puruṣam... puruṣaṃ viduḥ*)," or the *Padma Purāṇa*'s expansion stating "He is called *Puruṣa* because of his great giving (*bahudāna*"), we understand that the word *puruṣa* has other etymological meanings applied to the Blessed Lord.

Furthermore, if the identity of the basis for the application of the term (*pravṛttinimitta*) is intended, then it would follow as an undesirable consequence that the Lord is denotable by words expressive of the individual soul (*jīva*) by virtue of being the Self (*ātmatva*). If the identity of the basis for the application of the term is intended, then it would follow as an undesirable consequence that the Lord is denotable by words expressive of the individual soul (*jīva*) by virtue of being the Self (*ātmatva*).

Even if a difference in the grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is intended, there would still follow the undesirable consequence of [Rudra] being inferior—like a pillar characterized by height—since the lexicon states: "The word *sthāṇu* denotes a post, a man, and, in three genders, Mahādeva. Furthermore, the reason [adduced for Rudra's superiority] is subject to the fallacy of "missing the time" (*kālātyayāpadeśa*), because it is contradicted by the multitude of authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that establish the Lord’s state as the most excellent. By the same logic, the designations *Indra* and *Mahendra* [would also imply inferiority], based on the root *idi* meaning "supreme sovereignty."

The supremacy of Indra is established by the two words *indra* and *pāramya*, which are derived from recited roots and signify sovereignty and supremacy respectively. However, the weakness of etymological derivation (*samākhyā*) when it contradicts direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and other means of proof applies equally even to Rudra. Furthermore, the harmony of all Vedic texts with respect to the Blessed Lord has been demonstrated through the scriptural accounts of His incarnations and so forth.

He states this established conclusion in two verses: "This is not correct; for since the name [Śiva] has its meaning overridden by more powerful [evidence] such as scriptural statements, it is improper for anyone to assert the superiority of Giriśa on that basis alone, just as in the case of Devendra.

Otherwise, Indra would be the Supreme Lord; however, due to the force of those respective names, the designation [of Śiva as supreme] is indeed sublated by stronger means of knowledge, like the term 'great tree' [applied to a small one]. (94)

This demonstration of superiority and inferiority by means of *samākhyā* (designation) is not sound—that is, not correct. Why? To this he says: "For by designation," and so forth. "For" (*hi*) means because. By "stronger statements and so forth"—that is, by *vākya*, *liṅga*, and so on, which possess the strength of being already established (*klṛptatva*), and by other designations supported by them—the meaning [of the designation] is broken, such that the prior inference of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is destroyed. Thus, by the designation—such as the designation "Lord" (*īśvara*) and so on.

Due to their respective designations—just as in the case of Devendra, by virtue of the titles "Indra" and "Mahendra"—the superiority (utkarṣa), that is, the supremacy, of Giriśa (Rudra) cannot be stated by anyone. Therefore, the meaning is that this [argument] is not correct.

The meaning [of the compound] is that inference is the relationship between the signified and the signifier, because it is observed to be so understood from the object itself; or, the meaning of *bhagnārthayā* is "that whose ultimate purpose has been shattered. Since the genitive case is seen in the object of comparison (*upameya*) in the word *giriśasya*, the suffix *-vat* is applied to the word *devendra* ending in the genitive. Because there is no single common designation for both the standard of comparison and the object of comparison, the phrase "by virtue of their respective designations" is supplied to the standard of comparison.

The phrase "like Indra" (*devendrivat*) is stated to indicate that although Mahādeva possesses superiority over other deities as denoted by the word *mahādeva*, he nonetheless falls into a state of inferiority when compared to the Lord of the Śasins (the Moon), who is designated by the term "Lord of the Gods" (*devendra*). For while his status as *Īśvara* is explicitly stated to have men as its counter-correlates, his status as *Indra* is explicitly stated to have gods as its counter-correlates. This being the case, since even this [inferiority] is set aside by the designations found in the Śrutis and other sources, the meaning is that if Indra’s inferiority is thus negated, then Rudra’s inferiority is all the more so by way of a fortiori (*kaimutya*).

(He expresses the same point even more forcefully with the words "Indra would be," etc. By the statement beginning with "Indra would be," [he means that] otherwise, if superiority and inferiority were established by mere designation alone, then—by virtue of those respective designations—that is, depending on the designations *indra*, *mahendra*, and *devendra*—Indra would be the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), meaning he would be the most excellent of all. The sense is that this is not desired by the opponent. The argument regarding Indra is stated as a counter-objection (*pratibandī*) with the intention of providing an equal rebuttal. Thus he says:

By the words "designation" (*ākhyā*) and so forth, [the author refers] to that—namely, Rudra. "Designation" means names such as Īśvara and the like. The expression "like a great tree" (*mahāvṛkṣavat*) is a *tantra* (elliptical) construction; it consists of two forms ending in the suffix *vat*, derived from bases in the locative and nominative cases respectively.

The syntactical connection is: "in him who is like a great tree, there is a designation like that of a great tree," and so on. It should be understood that in both the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the example (*dārṣṭāntika*), there is sublation by powerful means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), regardless of whether it is direct or indirect.

The meaning is as follows: once the distinctness of the entities (*vastuvailakṣaṇya*) has been established through valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*), their being mentioned together is irrelevant—just as light and darkness [cannot coexist]. Just as in the case of a perception concerning the inferiority of a fruit, a flower, or a shadow, there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the "greatness" (in the form of venerability) denoted by the word "great tree" (*mahāvṛkṣa*) regarding a specific large tree; so too, because of the sublation by stronger means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) such as scriptural statements that indicate the Lord is not the sovereign, the excellence [of the individual soul] is not established by the name (*samākhyā*). || 94 ||
He refutes the reason—consisting in being denotable by the word that expresses it—by means of the two fallacies of "missing the proper time" (kālātyayāpadeśa) and "contradiction" (viruddha).
Is the individual soul (jīva) within the scope of the term "Puruṣa"? Is the Lord of Śrī also within that scope? Would the soul then be Giriśa or Dhruva? Are those two designated as "Sthāṇu"?
Does the title "Teacher" (ācārya) apply to those born from the mouth [of Brahmā]? May he fashion [this] for me.
Does a lion become a frog merely by touching the foot of Hari? || 95 ||

Regarding the statement "the individual soul (jīva) is within the scope of the term 'puruṣa'": because the individual soul is denoted by the word *puruṣa*, would the Lord of Śrī (Śrīśa), who is also within that scope—meaning denoted by it—also be a *jīva*? The word *kim* is used here in a dismissive sense. The meaning is: "The Lord of Śrī cannot be a *jīva*. The intention is that since the excellence of even Śrī—who is the most preeminent according to such passages as "And Śrī shall be the foremost Śrī"—is understood to reside in the Blessed Lord, the reason intended to suggest inferiority [of the Lord] is sublated.

"The two wives [of Viṣṇu] are Hrī and Lakṣmī"; "The one God, generating heaven and earth"; "For this is the subtle Prakṛti"; "Therein the glorious Nārāyaṇa was entreated by me for alms"—by such passages, the title *Śrī* (Glorious One), functioning as a designation (*samākhyā*), serves to remind us of the Lord's status as the supreme cause and His supreme magnanimity. Furthermore, [the name *Puruṣottama* is supported by: "Or rather, they know the Puruṣa as he who existed even before [the world]; or "Or because of his many gifts (*bahu-dāna*), Viṣṇu is indeed the Puruṣa."

It is said: by reminding one of the etymological meaning of the word *puruṣa* as previously stated, the lack of establishment of the aforementioned essential nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*) is also indicated. "Those two"—meaning either Stambha and Rudra, or Śaṅku and Rudra. Regarding the phrase "designated as Sthāṇu": this is because they are understood to be denoted by the word *sthāṇu*, according to the lexicon which states, "Sthāṇu is masculine when referring to Mahādeva; it is feminine when meaning a stake (*śaṅku*), and used for 'fixed' (*sthira*) in three genders. *Giriśa* means Rudra. The meaning is: does he become fixed (*dhruva*), or indeed does he not become a stake (*śaṅku*) or a pillar (*stambha*)?

"The word *dhruva* is masculine when meaning a sacrificial post (*śaṅku*), a banyan tree (*vaṭa*), a wedge (*kīla*), a conjunction (*yoga*), or a star (*tārāntara*); it is neuter when meaning logic (*tarka*) or certainty (*niścita*); and it is used in the three genders when meaning eternal (*nitya*) or immovable (*niścala*). This is the lexicon intended here. And so:

The meaning is as follows: the reason consisting in being denotable by a word expressing that [status] is *viruddha* (contradictory), because it establishes a degradation of Rudra—which is the opposite of the desired excellence. "Sukhabhuvām" refers to the Brāhmaṇas. "Ācāryasaṃśabdanam" means the designation by the term "Teacher. "Mukhabhuvāṃ takṣatvāya" means in order to bring about the status of a carpenter, who is counted among village outcasts (*caṇḍālas*). "Ghaṭeta kim? means "is it fitting?"—the sense is that it is not fitting. The dative case in "takṣatvāya" is used according to the rule "kriyārthopapada... (Pāṇini 2.3.14).

The lion (*kaṇṭhīrava*)—that which is denoted by the word *hari*—does it attain the state of a frog (*maṇḍūkatva*) merely through the contact (*sparśa*) or connection with the word *hari*? It does not. For the lion, who is renowned for his extreme skill in splitting open the rugged temples of female elephants (*karaṭikaraṭa*), how could he become a "well-frog" (*kūpamaṇḍūka*) merely by being designated by that term? The meaning is that the status of a frog consecrated upon the throne of the first example does not arise merely from being denotable by its corresponding word.

In this context, which portion of the following verse is intended? "Yama, Anila, Indra, Candra, Arka, Viṣṇu, Siṃha, Aṃśu, and Vājin; Śuka, Ahi, Kapin, and Bheka—in these [meanings] the word *hari* is masculine; it is also used in the sense of 'tawny' (*kapila*), in which case it is used in three genders. (95)

Regarding the suspicion that sentences which subvert the established designation [of Śiva] might have another intent when supported by other corroborative sentences—just as with words like "space" (*ākāśa*) or "vital breath" (*prāṇa*), which are agreed upon to have inappropriate meanings, so too with specific words like "Śiva" whose inappropriate meanings are determined by such factors as being an effect or being subject to karma—it is logical that these refer to the Blessed Lord who possesses incarnations and other attributes, as established by the *Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka*, through either figurative application (*guṇayoga*) or secondary indication (*aparyavasāna-vṛtti*); thus, they cannot be set aside by other sentences.
Intending to offer the rebuttal that "designation is a supporting factor," he says:
(beginning with *prāṇa*)—"Is the Supreme Brahman not proclaimed by words such as 'Prāṇa' and 'Ākāśa' in the Upaniṣadic sections? Does its status as the Supreme not remain manifest despite that?"

If that supreme nature [of Brahman] is declared by words such as "Śiva" and so forth with respect to Prāṇa and others, then how could it apply to Rudra and the rest, who are created by the Blessed Lord as established by the causal texts? || 97 ||

In the Upaniṣadic portions—in specific sections such as the Chāndogya and others—the Supreme Brahman—that reality which is preeminent in every respect by virtue of its threefold causality and its attendant collection of qualities, and which is endowed with an infinite and unsurpassed greatness both in its essential nature and its attributes—is not celebrated? That is to say, is it not clearly propounded again and again? The meaning is that it is indeed so propounded. This is expressed by means of words such as "prāṇa" (vital breath) and "ākāśa" (ether), which refer to the well-known prāṇas possessing five functions and the elemental ether, etc., as determined by their status as effects and so forth.
Is it not [celebrated]?—the sense being that it certainly is.

And here, either a figurative application (*yogavṛtti*) or a non-terminating application (*aparyavasānavṛtti*) is intended. By the word "mukha," the inclusion of terms such as *avyākṛta* (the unmanifest) and *aja* (the unborn) is intended. Through repetition (*paunaḥpunya*), that is, by the intensive repetition of actions (*kriyāsamabhihāra*), the recurrence of terms such as "prāṇa" is intended in passages like "from prāṇa alone all [beings arise]," "I am prāṇa," "from space alone," "space indeed," "this which is space," and "the small space within this."

By this, it is suggested that even the indicative mark of intention (*tātparyaliṅga*) consisting of repeated practice is refuted by the unfitness of the meaning—which is of the nature of an impossibility that contradicts the indicative mark of intention characterized by logical consistency (*upapatti*). By the phrase "how could it not be so?", it is suggested that this meaning is universally accepted.

To that extent, even without considering the inherent capacity of the meaning, merely by hearing words such as "prāṇa" and "ākāśa" in the Vedāntas within the contexts dealing with the Cause, does there arise a suspicion of supremacy—of pre-eminence—with respect to those things well-known as the fivefold vital breaths (prāṇa) and the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa), which are effects and so forth? Does this suspicion awaken—is it manifested? The meaning is: surely not; for by the certainty that the meaning is otherwise [i.e., refers to the Supreme], the very sprouting of the suspicion of supremacy does not occur. That is the Supreme Brahman.

In the Upaniṣadic portions—such as the Śvetāśvatara and others—the phrase "in the Upaniṣadic portions" (anuṣaktasyopaniṣadbhāgeṣu) takes on a specific sense according to its fitness [with the context]. If it is understood through words such as "Śiva"—that is, if it is signified by terms like Śiva, Rudra, Śambhu, and so forth, either through association with qualities (guṇayoga) or through secondary figurative application (aparyavasānavṛtti).

Since the status of being the cause is established as a quality of the Lord by many Upaniṣads, since words such as "Śiva" are applied to the Lord, since the connection with qualities is required in the contexts dealing with creation, dissolution, and so forth, and since it is necessary to understand that [the Lord] has Śiva and others as His bodies for the sake of meditating upon Him accordingly, it is logical that words like "Śiva" occurring in the causal contexts refer to the Lord; furthermore, the unsuitability of the well-known Rudra and others [for this role] serves as a supporting factor—this he states with the verse beginning "tattatkāraṇa... and so on.

That which is established by the respective causal statements—namely, that which is taught in the *Ananyaparā Mahopaniṣad*, the *Nārāyaṇopaniṣad*, the *Mahānārāyaṇopaniṣad*, the *Subālopaniṣad*, the *Pauṅgirahasya*, and so forth; in those [beings] such as Rudra and others (the word "others" including Indra and the rest), who possess the state of being created by the Lord—their "supremacy" (*paratvam*) means their absolute preeminence. From what? From no cause whatsoever; the meaning is that it is not established by any reason at all.

Therefore, the meaning is that the designation "Lord" (Īśvara) and so forth is not supported by them [the followers of those systems]. This verse also serves as the conclusion of the great section (*mahāprakaraṇa*). The expression "created by the Blessed One" (*bhagavatsṛṣṭya*) is a reference emphasizing the abstract state [of being created]. The syntactical connection is: "If that Brahman is denoted by words such as 'Śiva' and so on, how can there be supremacy among Rudra and the others? [The answer is: because the Blessed One, who is the Supreme Brahman himself, is the one denoted by words such as 'Śiva', whereas Rudra and the others are created by him; therefore [they cannot possess supremacy].

The meaning is that Rudra and the others possess supremacy. Thus, since the designation (samākhyā) is not established as being supported by other scriptural passages (vākya), it is weak; the point is that the desired conclusion cannot be proven by it. || 96 ||

Indeed, for the sake of determining the meaning of the Vedānta texts, the Blessed Lord Bādarāyaṇa has set forth two means: the Brahma-sūtras and the supplementary treatises (upabṛṃhaṇas). Among these, the Brahma-sūtras determine the meaning of the specific Vedic recension one has studied, whereas the supplementary treatises determine the meaning of those recensions one has not studied. As the venerable Bhaṭṭa Sudarśana said: "The logic [of the sūtras] serves to eliminate doubt, misconception, and the like regarding the meaning of the recension one has studied."

The meaning is that "supplementation" (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) serves to make known the meaning of the recited branch [of the Veda] through its harmony with the meaning of the non-recited branches. And therein, by this collection of verses, the determination of the meaning of the currently extant Vedānta passages has been accomplished in accordance with the following sūtras: "And because of the difference in nature, it is not like dreams, etc."; "By this, all [other cases] are explained"; "Desire and so forth [are absent] elsewhere, but present there, on account of the abodes and so forth"; and "Likewise, because of the negation of others."

Now, in order to dispel doubts regarding contradictions in the Upaniṣads and Sūktas that have not been studied, and to demonstrate that this very same meaning is established even in those texts— rather than being contrary to it— the author shows the distinct utility of reasoning (*nyāya*) and the corroborative scriptures (*upabṛṃhaṇa*), and states the natural excellence of the Lord’s supremacy as established by the corroborative scriptures:
"Whatever supreme firmness was proclaimed for the Lotus-eyed One by the Upaniṣads, which have attained refinement through pure logic..."
To conform to other scriptural statements, even the sages headed by Manu clearly support this very point, making it consistent with them.

By those [scriptures] whose refinement—consisting in the endowment with the quality of the capacity for correctly ascertaining the meaning through the removal of mutual contradictions—is attained (*labdhā*) and perfected (*niṣpannā*) by means of faultless reasonings (*viśuddhanayaiḥ*), such as those established in the first chapter on "Harmony" (*samanvaya*) and others, and which are free from defects such as being refuted by counter-arguments (*pratitarka*).

Adornment (*pariṣkṛti*) is decoration, and that is precisely of the form described here. The augment *suṭ* is applied by the rule: "The augment *suṭ* occurs before the root *kṛ* when preceded by *sam* or *pari*, in the sense of adornment. By the *upaniṣads*—meaning those being studied here, such as the *Mahopaniṣad* and others. "Supreme" (*parama*) means being the most excellent, devoid of anything else more excellent. "Of the lotus-eyed one" (*kamaladṛśaḥ*) refers to the Lotus-Eyed Lord (*Puṇḍarīkākṣa*). "Greatness" (*paribraḍhimā*) is the state of being preeminent (*paribṛḍhatva*), meaning the state of being Brahman (*brahmatva*). It was "proclaimed" (*apṛthi*)—that is, made famous. [The root] *prath* means "to become famous. Because it belongs to the *ghaṭādi* group, it is treated as having the marker *mit*; thus, by the rule "the long vowel optionally occurs before *ciṇ* and *ṇamul*," there is an optional lengthening of the vowel.
The [root] *has* takes the affix *ciṇ* in the sense of the object, and there is the elision of the suffix *tal*.

In this context, by the phrase *paramaḥ paribṛḍhimā*, the two statements—"Brahman is all-pervading (*paribṛḍham*)," and "That alone is the supreme Brahman"—are indicated. From the word *paribṛḍha*, the suffix *iman* is added to form the abstract noun, and according to the rule *ra ṛto halādeḥ*, the vowel *ṛ* is replaced by *r*.

By the phrase "the lotus-eyed one," it is indicated that the status of the Supreme Brahman belongs to the Blessed Lord alone; for, through the passages "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," "Brahman is the tail [the support]," and "knowing Brahman," the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*)—who is established as Brahman and resides within another person—is understood to dwell within the solar orb, and from that, it is understood that he possesses lotus-like eyes. Thus, it is shown that the Blessed Lord is rightly the Supreme Brahman.

Thus, this very act—namely, the proclamation of the Lord’s nature as Brahman by means of the Upaniṣads being studied, which are supported by the logic stated in the characteristics such as *samanvaya* (harmonization)—is "action" (*karman*). "Other words" refers to the branches of scripture not being studied; these are the "authoritative sources" (*kartṛyaḥ*). "To conform to" means to follow. "They strive" means they are worthy of doing so. "Thus"—regarding this matter—even the sages headed by Manu "clearly corroborate," meaning they establish it clearly through corroboration (*upabṛṃhaṇa*).
And here, "corroboration" consists in the composition of treatises that set forth the meaning of the entire Veda, having directly realized that meaning through the power of their own yoga.

By the term "headed by Manu" (*manupramukhāḥ*), there is an inclusion of Parāśara, Pārāśarya, Prācetasa, Śuka, Śaunaka, and others. By the mention of "Manu," there is the exclusion of Kapila and others, because the elaborations (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) composed by them do not conform to the Śruti. By the word "also" (*api*), there is the inclusion of the Blessed Lord who is the author of the Pañcarātra. By the word "clearly" (*sphuṭam*), [it refers to the following]:
"These three—Brahmā for creation, Hari for protection, and Rudra for withdrawal—were born directly from Maheśvara, the causal Self."
Nevertheless, out of mutual envy and desiring to surpass one another,
they propitiated their father, the Supreme Lord, through ascetic penance.
In a former kalpa, Brahmā created Nārāyaṇa and Rudra;
in another kalpa, Brahmā, who is identical with the universe, again created Rudra and Viṣṇu.
And likewise, the Lord Viṣṇu created Brahmā;
then Brahmā created Nārāyaṇa, and Bhava again created Brahmā.
Thus, in age after age, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are born from one another, each desiring victory over the other.
With reference to the events at the end of each respective kalpa, the great sages describe their power arising from their mutual interaction.
In some places Brahmā is praised, in some Rudra, and in some Viṣṇu;
yet by this, there is no superiority or inferiority among them whatsoever.
"By means of such passages as, 'The great sages have composed those various [texts] concerning the events of this or that dissolution;

a learned man is not deluded therein,' there is the exclusion of those [passages] which exist in a non-circulating state, which contradict the traditional recitation as being eternal, and which are subjects for suspicion of interpolation. (97)

Thus, the portions of the characteristics of *samanvaya* (reconciliation) and *avirodha* (non-contradiction) that were not yet explained have been explained. Now, regarding the characteristic of *sādhana* (the means), it is stated that the injunction for study intended by the Sūtra—"for one who possesses mere study"—culminates in the grasping of the mass of syllables (*akṣararāśi*). In this regard, the teachers hold that the meaning of the text "The Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied" is: "One should effect the knowledge of the meaning by means of the Veda acquired through study. Others maintain that this [injunction] is a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*) whose purpose is the study of subsidiary rites (*guṇakarma*) which have the knowledge of the meaning as their fruit.

Some [maintain]: the non-mention of the knowledge of meaning as the fruit is a defect common to all three positions. Furthermore, since the capacity to produce the knowledge of meaning is established by perception (*pratyakṣa*), its injunction is impossible; moreover, there is a contradiction with the status of the object of the action (*guṇakarma*) as it appears in the text "The Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo ’dhyetavyaḥ*). Therefore, the aforementioned three meanings are not possible. Rather, its meaning is: "By means of the study of one's own Veda, one should effect the acquisition of that Veda."

Because it is contained within the same word [as the injunction], because it is more proximate to the mental realization of study (*adhyayanabhāvanā*) than the knowledge of meaning, and because it has been established as the result in that context—pervading even the *hum* and other such sounds—the attainment of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyāvāpti*) alone is the object to be realized (*bhāvya*). This consists of the ascertainment of syllables (*akṣarāvadhāraṇa*), which deposits a dense accumulation of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) conducive to the pronunciation of the text itself.

Just as, because the removal of the husks has been observed and because the rice-cake (puroḍāśa) is required for the purpose of the sacrifice, the threshing of rice grains—which are previously unused and distinct from the act of disposal—is held to serve the ritual through the rice-cake, since those husked grains, having been prepared, require a future application.

Thus, since the knowledge of the meaning and the recitation for the *brahmayajña* and so forth possess visible fruits (*dṛṣṭaphala*), they are distinct from the study of the Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana*) performed previously—which was not yet put to use—as a preparatory act (*pratipattikarman*). Therefore, for the Veda already acquired, which stands in need of a subsequent application, a visible utility is sought through the means of knowing the meaning and recitation. And because this is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), reading from manuscripts and the like are excluded. Consequently, it is established that the knowledge of the meaning and so forth arising from the study of the Veda not previously undertaken is not useful for ritual sacrifices. This is the summary of the meaning of the scriptural injunction regarding study according to the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*).

On this point, some raise the following objection: if the knowledge of the meaning does not touch upon the injunction (*vidhi*), it would follow that the *svādhyāya* (Vedic study) has no intended meaning. For in common worldly usage, the intention (*tātparya*) of sentences is understood by uttering words with the aim of communicating a meaning; it is for the sake of conveying that meaning that figurative functions (*lakṣaṇā*) and the like are postulated when the primary sense (*mukhya*) is impossible, but not by mere utterance alone. Therefore, a figurative function is not postulated merely by the utterance of the words "cow," "horse," "man," and "elephant."

When it is understood that the intention (*tātparya*) is that those words are uttered for the purpose of conveying a specific meaning, then, in order to accomplish that, one postulates figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and so forth for the words "cow" and the rest, as in: "this cow is a draft-ox," "the horse is swift," "the man is of disciplined conduct," and "the elephant is large-bodied."

And thus, since the purpose of Vedic sentences is the comprehension of their meaning, if there were no utterance directed toward that end, the intended meaning (tātparya) would not be established; consequently, to ensure its fulfillment, one would face the undesirable consequence of having to abandon the postulation of figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) and other interpretive devices. Therefore, it must necessarily be admitted that even in the Veda, utterance is directed toward the comprehension of meaning. Furthermore, as in the world, in the Veda too there is no utterance prompted by mere worldly desire (rāga) directed toward that end; rather, such utterance must be understood as being prompted solely by an injunction (vidhi). Thus, the contact with the injunction for study (adhyayanavidhi) is indispensable for the knowledge of meaning. Consequently, it is not logical to hold that the injunction for study has the mere apprehension of syllables as its sole purpose.

In this regard, the following is the resolution: while the default status of words as being directed toward meaning—established through worldly linguistic convention—is occasionally set aside in certain worldly sentences due to defects in the speaker, such defects are absent in the case of the non-human (apauruṣeya) [Veda]. Consequently, because the utterance of words intended for the purpose of conveying knowledge is inherently capable and independent of an injunction (*vidhi*), it remains unimpeded even when a mute person writes something down and gives it to another.

Furthermore, since one does not observe the utterance of words with the aim of understanding the meaning when a silent reciter (maunin) intends [the Veda] for the beginning of a verse and so forth, there is no opportunity for the injunction of study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) to touch upon the knowledge of meaning. Moreover, application elsewhere [for other purposes] does not destroy the inherent capacity of a word to convey meaning, just as in the case of the injunction for muttering (*japa-vidhi*).

For injunctions such as, "Having officiated at a sacrifice or received a gift, one should recite the Veda three times without eating," or "Or for three nights, the Sāvitrī," or "One should constantly mutter the Veda itself," do not preclude the Veda’s capacity to convey meaning. This is what [the author] says:

Those who claim that the intention of the injunction for Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya-vidhi*) does not culminate in the direct accomplishment of the meaning of non-human words through their literal sense, but rather results in mere mechanical repetition, should be satisfied by the logic of the injunction for silent recitation (*japa-vidhi*). For it is said that the Word manifests its power regarding objects unobtainable by other means.

The three [interpretations] previously shown by those who propound incorrect meanings regarding the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayanavidhi*) are connected here with the phrase "they say" (*vadanti*). [The injunction] culminates directly in the mastery of the syllables (*akṣarasiddhi*); that is, it culminates in the primary, proximate, and perceptible mastery of the syllables mentioned in its own sentence—namely, in the ascertainment of the syllables through the excellence of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) which are the cause of specific memories that motivate the pronunciation of each respective phoneme, and which reach their final completion (*apavarga*) right there, being devoid of any further contact.

"The purport of the injunction for self-study (*svādhyāyavidhyāśaya*)" means the intention of the prescriptive statement "One's own Veda should be studied. This signifies that the purpose of the injunction for study is the ascertainment of the syllables (*akṣarāvadhāraṇa*). "Innate" (*naisargika*) means natural. "Of the non-human words," namely the Vedic sentences. "Regarding their meanings"—that is, regarding their own denotata in the form of sacrifices, meditations, heaven, liberation, and so forth. "The primary aim" (*aidamparya*) means being directed toward this [the meaning], which is to say, the purport (*tātparya*). "Obstructs" (*vyāhanti*) means it blocks or prevents.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "those who say that [the injunction for recitation] obstructs the apprehension of the Veda’s capacity to convey meaning. Here, because of the necessary correlative relationship between *yat* and *tat*, the word "by them" (*taiḥ*) is to be supplied. By "those who are not you" (*ayusmadbhiḥ*)—that is, by them—it is observed that even when the Veda is applied to recitation according to the principle of the injunction for recitation (*japa-vidhi*), there is no loss of its inherent meaningfulness; therefore, let them be satisfied. The meaning is that one should attain confidence that even when the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) applies the Veda to the acquisition of syllables, there is no loss of its inherent meaningfulness.
The word, in the form of scripture, expands—that is, functions without restraint—regarding an object obtainable through other means, yet not established by any other means of valid cognition.
The word *samam* (equal) is stated to indicate that a specific application (*viniyoga*) elsewhere does not destroy the inherent capacity of a word to convey its own meaning.

Here, by the term *apauruṣeya* (not of human origin), the absence of defects in a speaker who might offer an exception is intended. By the term *naisargika* (inherent), independence from an injunction (*vidhi*) is suggested. Thus, two solutions are indicated. The third solution is the principle of the injunction for silent recitation (*japa-vidhi*). Furthermore, by the word *sākṣāt* (directly), two meanings are intended through a double entendre (*tantra*), based on the lexicographical rule: "the word *sākṣāt* denotes both direct perception and the primary [meaning]. By this, the possibility of conveying a meaning that is remote or not directly expressed is excluded.

By the word "concluded" (*paryavasita*), it is indicated that because the grasping of the syllables is proximate and because it is mentioned in its own sentence, it possesses the status of being the goal (*bhāvyatva*) with ease; however, the status of being the goal does not belong to the knowledge of the meaning—which is remote and not directly expressed by the words—since that would result in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). || 98 ||

The proponent, stating that if the knowledge of meaning were untouched by injunction, it would follow that the *svādhyāya* (Vedic study) lacks the intention to convey meaning, is questioned as follows: Is the injunction for study—"The *svādhyāya* is to be studied"—intended to convey meaning, or not? In the first case, just as the meaningfulness of the sentence "The *svādhyāya* is to be studied" is established by itself even without an injunction aimed at the comprehension of meaning, so too the meaningfulness of other sentences would unavoidably be established by themselves without such an injunction.

In the second case, however, since the obligation to study for the sake of grasping the syllables (*akṣara*) is not established—just as the obligation to study for the sake of understanding the *Atharva* is not established—the meaningfulness of the Vedas remains unopposed. This is what [the author] states: "He who, on account of the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*), explains the Vedic words as not being intent upon their own literal meanings, deserves to be questioned: 'Is it accepted that the injunction has a purpose, or is it purposeless? By this statement, these words would be equal to those [Vedic passages] which are [admittedly] meaningless in the first case; otherwise, how could the injunction suddenly stand as its opponent in the other case? (Verse 99)

Having restated our position—that the injunction for study has as its primary purport the cultivation of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) resulting from the act of studying, which consists in the internalization of the syllables according to the intent of the rule for self-study—he explains [the opponent's view]: "The words of the Śruti"—meaning the Vedic sentences—"would be devoid of purport regarding their own meanings," that is, they would lack intentionality toward their directly expressed senses which are already established by their very nature. He says this [in the phrase] "he declares. The meaning is: he asserts that if the injunction for study were to terminate merely in the grasping of the syllables, it would follow that the Veda has no intended meaning (*avivakṣitārthatva*).

"From the intention" (*āśayāt*) is an ablative used with the elision of the suffix *lyap* (from the root *sthā*). "He" refers to the proponent (*vādī*).
