"The injunction" (*vidhiḥ*) refers to the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhiḥ*). "With meaning" (*sārthaḥ*) means "as having a denotable object. "Is it accepted? (*asthīyate kim*) means "is it admitted by you? Alternatively, "Is it accepted as being meaningless" (*anarthakaḥ*)—meaning "as lacking a denotable object"—is the question regarding the acceptance of the two positions that are about to be refuted. "It is fitting" (*arhati*) means "in my view," implying that he should be questioned in this manner. Among these, [the author first addresses] the first position...

He refutes this with the words beginning with "anena" (by this). Regarding the first point—namely, the meaningfulness of the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayanavidhi*)—the phrase "of these words" refers to those Vedic sentences other than the sentence containing the injunction for study. "Similarity to this statement" means that even in the absence of an injunction for study directed toward the comprehension of meaning, there is a similarity in terms of *dharma* regarding the capacity to convey meaning; for the sentence "One's own Veda is to be studied" conveys meaning by virtue of its inherent meaningfulness, which is established even without an injunction. The word "exists" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied here [to complete the sense].

The instrumental case in the phrase “by the statement beginning with ‘tulyārthaiḥ’” [is used]. He refutes the second [position] with the words “itaratra” and so forth. “Itaratra” means: in the case of the injunction for the study of one’s own Veda (svādhyāyādhyayanavidhi) being devoid of meaning. “Vidhiḥ” means: the injunction for study. “Akasmāt” means: without cause. “Tatpratibhaṭaḥ syāt kim? means: would it be an opponent—that is, would it be a rejector—of the fact that the Veda has meaning as its primary purport? The sense is: it would not. For if the injunction for study were devoid of meaning, then since the necessity of performing the study with the aim of ascertaining the content [of the Veda] would not be established, the fact that the Vedas have meaning as their primary purport would be free from opposition. This is the intended meaning.

Intending this very point, the venerable feet of the Great Teacher (Sureśvara) have graciously stated: "Nor does the fact that the knowledge of the meaning is untouched by injunction entail that the *svādhyāya* has no intended meaning, for this is as logically consistent as the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*). Now, since there is no other injunction prescribing the study of the sentence containing the injunction for study with the aim of merely grasping the syllables, the inherent meaningfulness of that sentence remains unrefuted.

If it is argued that because the injunction for study prescribes the recitation of other sentences with the aim of grasping the syllables, their status as being intent upon meaning would be set aside—this is not so; for the logic of the injunction for *japa* (muttering) has already been stated. This was said by the venerable feet of Meghanādārisūri: "Therefore, even for the injunction of *japa*, the status of the Veda as being intent upon meaning is required in order to establish the comprehension of its own sense.

Nor should it be said that there is a factual contradiction between being intent on *japa* and being intent on meaning, since *japa* consists in the mere utterance of words without purpose; for that [status of being intent on meaning] is possible even from the mere absence of the desire to speak [the meaning] at the time of performance. || 99 ||

The study [of the Veda] is a purificatory act (*saṃskārakarma*); the injunction regarding it is devoted to restrictive rules (*niyama*); teaching is established through the teacher’s own inclination (*rāga*) rather than being prompted by its own injunction; initiation (*upanayana*) is subordinate to study by means of the student; although the injunction for study culminates in the acquisition of the syllables (*akṣaragrahaṇa*), because the Veda is self-evident (*svataḥprāpta*), the engagement in inquiry proceeds from inclination alone toward its meaningfulness (*arthavattā*); even for one who has returned home (*samāvṛtta*), listening [to the Veda] proceeds from inclination; and so too do the duties of the householder.

The established tradition is that there is practice following the words of those who wish one's welfare; and for that [practice], there is listening—both for the sake of ascertaining its basis in valid authority and for the sake of receiving instruction oneself from those who inquire.
On this point, they say: "Even for one who has returned [from his teacher] due to passion, hearing [the scriptures] is not possible;

because he finds no opportunity for hearing that is not obstructed by the performance of household duties, and because there is an obstruction to his practice through tasks such as fetching water and gathering wood for the sake of his teacher. To this, the following is the rebuttal: Since there is a scriptural injunction for the performance of duties stating, "One should acquire wealth through receiving gifts and so forth," provided it does not obstruct the teacher’s own performance of his own duties, an opportunity for hearing is easily available. Furthermore, since the fetching of water and other such tasks are prompted by the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), they cease once that study ceases; therefore, there is no obstruction to practice.

"Even in the absence of fetching water and such tasks, the teacher’s role as a speaker is justified by his desire for other purposes, such as the propagation of the teachings, and by his affection for the disciple. This he expresses in two verses. Therein, restating the objection, he sets forth the solution with the first verse—(beginning with "yat"): "If there were no opportunity for the householder listener in the teacher’s house—who is occupied with the fetching of wood, water, and so forth—in the sequence of those various household duties; or if there were an interval suitable for attending upon the teacher and the like, where would that occasion be?"
Having been asked thus, some experts here resolve it in this manner: || 100 ||

"By some"—that is, by the three types of disputants previously mentioned. This phrase connects with the word "it was said" (*uktam*). "Of one occupied with fetching wood, water, and so forth at the teacher's house"—meaning one who is preoccupied with bringing water, gathering fuel, and other such tasks for the sake of the teacher in every house. "Of a householder" (*gṛhamedhinaḥ*)—meaning a married man. The *dhātupāṭha* states: "the roots *mudh*, *medh*, and *saṃgamana* [are used]," and "*meghṛ* means 'to join'. He is a *gṛhamedhī* because he joins (*saṃgacchate*) with houses, that is, with wives; the meaning is "one who has performed the marriage ceremony."

"Of the listener"—that is, of those qualified for hearing [the teaching]. "In the sequence"—meaning in the proper order and without interruption—of their respective duties, such as the *agnihotra* and the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*). "Opportunity"—meaning time; that is, the time for performing [those duties]. "If it is possible"—meaning if the performance of one's own duty is possible.

The meaning of the objection in the text is as follows: "Where and how could there be an opportunity favorable and conducive to following the teacher—such as fetching wood and water or prostrating—and so forth? It would not exist. Thus, because for a householder there would be the consequence of obstructing the performance of his own duties, and in their absence, the consequence of obstructing service to the teacher, the engagement in inquiry is not tenable. This is what was stated. "In this"—that is, regarding this objection.

"By the virtuous"—by our teachers, such as the author of the Bhāṣya on the Lord’s [Upaniṣads] and others, who follow the heart of the author of the Sūtras and are skilled in establishing the meaning of the Vedas; "thus"—in the manner that will be explained; "is resolved"—a refutation is performed. The verb *samādadhati* is used in the impersonal sense (bhāve lakāraḥ) because its object is not intended to be expressed. || 100 ||
Thus, he states the intended (or alternatively, the opponent's intended) manner of resolution—beginning with "That which one knows," etc.:

"The ritual acts, having found their opportunity through the cessation of the duties of disciples rooted in that [Veda], proceed according to the intention of the injunction for private recitation (*svādhyāya-vidhi*) once one has desisted from the mastery of the mass of Vedic syllables;
and the occasion for the listener and the speaker shall be such that the goal of the listener is accomplished."
Out of affection, desire, and for the sake of wealth and fame, a teacher should cause his disciple to hear [the teachings]. || 101 ||

"Yat" means for which reason. "Svādhyāyavidhyāśayaḥ" refers to the purport of the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayana-vidhi*). In the analysis of the compound *vedaś cāsau akṣararāśiś ca*, it is a *karmadhāraya*. "Tasya siddhau" means in the ascertainment of that [Veda]; "uparataḥ" means having ceased, having come to rest in that very [text] without touching its meaning. The word "bhavati" (it becomes) is to be supplied as the ellipsis here.

By the word *uparata* (ceased), it is understood that even without the explanation provided by the commentator, the meaning itself culminates in that very way; thus, to express a different meaning would indeed be a violation of the scripture (*śruti*). As stated by the venerable Mahācārya: "If one disregards the scripture which makes known its own intended meaning and, for the sake of conveying a desired sense, violates the scripture, then due to such hostility toward the scripture and the resulting succession of misfortunes, there can never be liberation. Therefore—by that reason—the term *virati* (cessation) follows this [meaning].

"Of the listener"—this refers to the householder who is qualified for hearing [the scripture]. "Rites"—refers to the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) and so forth. "Because of the cessation"—meaning because of the cessation resulting from the discontinuation of study, which serves as the cause for the cessation of those duties rooted in that study, namely the duties toward disciples such as fetching water and other necessary tasks. "Having found leisure"—meaning having obtained the time for their performance; this is the reason. The particle *iti* is drawn over here, and it signifies the sense of a reason (*hetvartha*).

And this applies to the case under discussion as well: just as the opportunity for the teacher is established, so too the activity of the listener—consisting of the cessation of study and the performance of duties such as fetching water—is completed by the disciple's withdrawal from those tasks; for this reason, the opportunity for the listener is also established, meaning it is fit for success.

The mention of the word "root" (*mūla*) is intended to show that activities such as fetching water, though prompted by the injunction to study, must necessarily be undertaken for the sake of that study. For even a result can serve as a cause for its own means through the mediation of intention (*saṅkalpa*). Here, by the phrase "as for the reciter... and so forth, the time for hearing is stated as being unobstructed by the performance of one's own duties; and by the phrase "rooted in that... and so forth, the non-obstruction of that [time] through following the teacher is expressed. And here, the first instance of the word "listener" (*śrotuḥ*) connects with the word "action" (*kriyā*); the second, however, refers to the "opportunity" (*avasara*).

Thus, there is no tautology with the phrase "by this. Furthermore, in this context, the opportunity for a householder to hear [the scripture] occurs only if the injunction for study culminates in the mere grasping of the mass of syllables (*akṣararāśi*), and not if it culminates in the knowledge of the meaning. This is because, as long as the performance of duties established by the injunction for study—such as fetching water—continues until their completion, the householder must inevitably encounter either the obstruction to the performance of his own specific duties (such as the five great sacrifices) or the obstruction to serving the teacher. Nor can this undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*) be accepted.

Since it is established in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts that Yudhiṣṭhira and others—who were devoted to the life of a householder—listened to [the teachings] from Bhīṣma and others, the defect you have alleged applies only in that specific case; this is what is implied by the phrase "having ceased from the task of establishing the mass of Vedic syllables."

To the objection, "In the absence of compliance, how could the teacher cause [the student] to hear [the teaching]? he says: "Out of affection," and so forth. The teacher—out of affection, that is, through love for the student; (or out of desire for wealth and fame); that is, through a longing for the money given by the student, or in its absence, through a desire for the renown of supreme generosity resulting from the imparting of knowledge. By this, the notion that teaching is a mandatory duty (*vaidha*) is refuted. He should cause the student to hear; the word "Veda" is to be understood as the ellipsis here.

In this regard, it should be understood that the narration by Āruṇi, Raikva, and Parāśara to Śvetaketu, Jānaśruti, and Maitreya respectively—motivated by affection, the desire for wealth, and the longing for fame—is established by the corroborative texts of the Śruti. Although Parāśara’s narration to Maitreya was prompted by affection, nevertheless, by the statement, "They will speak of me as one who has not undergone exertion through another," his desire for fame is also implied as a motive.

And here, since fame is well known to be rooted in giving, it is said "of wealth and fame" (*vittayaśasoḥ*) to indicate that the imparting of knowledge is the cause of fame. Just as in the verse, "Like maidens toward their beloved, they both tremble and yearn," the genitive case in *vittayaśasoḥ* is used because the sense of being a subordinate factor (*śeṣatva*) is intended. Alternatively, when excellence is intended, the genitive is used either by virtue of the designation "object" (*karman*)—which takes precedence—or as characterized by its connection with a *kṛt*-suffix. Or, as in the expression "giving is equal for a Brahmin," the locative case may be used because the sense of being a recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is intended as a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*).

"One who is indifferent toward the acquisition of honor, fame, and wealth, and who is gracious through supreme compassion regarding questions worthy of inquiry"—this and similar passages should also be considered here. || 101 ||

Thus, the portions to be explained regarding the characteristics of *samanvaya* (reconciliation), *avirodha* (non-contradiction), and *sādhana* (means) have for the most part been explained. Now, he explains the section on the path beginning with light (*arciḥ*) within the characteristic of the fruit (*phala-lakṣaṇa*): (Regarding the verse beginning with "light," etc.

They say that light, day, the bright fortnight, the northern solstice, the year, the wind, the sun, the moon, as well as the one belonging to lightning, Varuṇa, Indra, and Prajāpati, are the conducting deities (*ativāhika*). || 102 ||

*Arciḥ*—the deity presiding over the flame; *ahaḥ*—the deity presiding over the day; *sitapakṣaḥ*—the deity presiding over the bright fortnight. In the compound *arciśca* and so forth, there is a *dvandva* of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*). Those [deities]. *Udagayana*—the northern solstice.

The deity presiding over the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*); *śabda*—the deity presiding over the year; *marut*—the wind deity; *arka*—the sun; *indu*—the moon; *tān*—here also, there is a copulative compound (*dvandva*) of mutual conjunction (*itaretara-yoga*). *Vaidyuta*—the deity presiding over lightning; *varuṇa*—well known; *indra*—well known; *prajāpati*—the creator (*dhātṛ*); *tān*—here also, as before, there is a copulative compound. [These are] the twelve mentioned.

"Of the wise one"—that is, of the liberated one. "The *ātivāhikas* (conveyors)"—those appointed by the Supreme Person for the purpose of *ativahana*, which is to say, for the sake of leading [the soul] to its destination. "They say"—they speak; the word "the authors of the Sūtras" is to be understood as the ellipsis.

In this context, from the words "light" (*arcis*) up to "Prajāpati," both the sequence and the entities of that sequence are intended to be expressed; for [the path] is well-known by the term "light" and so forth. This is established by the Sūtras: "From the year to Vāyu, because of the distinction between the general and the specific"; and "Varuṇa is after lightning, because of their connection. Thus, among the categories beginning with light mentioned in the passages of the *Chāndogya*, *Kauṣītaki*, *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, and other texts, there exist possible sequences consisting of the order of the Śruti, the meaning, the text, the procedure, and the primary division—those [sequences] previously discussed in the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā regarding the meaning of the Śruti, the text, the procedure, and the primary divisions.

Because the identity of the path has also been established through recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) by way of definitive determination; because, by applying the "goat and the sacrificial animal" maxim (*chāgapaśunyāya*) to the words "Vāyu" and "world of the gods," it is determined that they refer to the same object; because the entire host of celestial deities (*vaimānika*) consisting of light is held by the bonds of Vāyu, such that the word "world of the gods" refers to Vāyu himself; and because the term "world of Vāyu" is more appropriately interpreted as a *karmadhāraya* compound—meaning "Vāyu who is the world"—and thus refers to Vāyu as the abode of the gods; therefore, the path beginning with Light (*arcirādi*) is indeed one single path, characterized by the sequence already shown.

This is the intended meaning: by the term "conveyors" (*ātivāhika*), it is meant that these are neither markers of the path nor places of enjoyment; rather, they are specific deities appointed by the Supreme Person for the purpose of conveying the liberated souls. This refers to the conclusion established in the *sūtra* "They are conveyors because of the indicative mark" (*talliṅgāt*). Furthermore, in this context, it should also be understood that the lightning-deity alone acts as the actual guide, while Varuṇa and the others are associated with the act of conveying only in the sense of being supportive facilitators.

And this has been determined by the sūtra: *tataśca vaidyutenaiva* (Brahma-sūtra 4.3.6). Furthermore, the word *ativāhika* used therein ends with the suffix *ṭhak*, which signifies "appointed" (*niyukta*) as prescribed by that very sūtra. In this verse, there is a specific type of Āryā meter called *udgīti*. [The author], desiring to explain it, points out the subject to be explained: "the final section" (*antimādhikaraṇa*). The remainder of the sentence is: "this subject to be explained is now being explained. The "final section" refers to the *Jagadvyāpārādhikaraṇa*, which is the last section at the end of the fourth chapter (*lakṣaṇāntima-pāda*) of the *Śārīraka* (Brahma-sūtra), dedicated to the description of the complete fruit [of liberation].

If "anāvṛttiḥ śabdāt" (non-return [to this world] is known from scripture) constitutes a separate section (*adhikaraṇa*), then that itself is the final section. For in that case, within a series of deliberations concerning its meaning, the non-causality of the lack of independence for the liberated with respect to the deficiency of bliss is established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). This is because the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) and the subsequent (*uttara-pakṣa*) positions are respectively occupied by the views that such lack of independence does and does not cause a deficiency in bliss; thus, the conclusion—that the lack of independence does not cause a deficiency in bliss—is demonstrated there along with its supporting reasons. This is the sense.

The meaning is as follows: although lack of independence (*asvātantrya*) and the possibility of return (*āvṛtti*) are both included [in the state of bondage] in succession, since "lack of independence" is also included therein, one must consider whether its nature as suffering arises from its being a lack of independence, or rather from its conformity with the conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*). Because this too is included, even though the sūtra concerning non-return (*anāvṛtti*) constitutes a separate topic (*adhikaraṇa*), the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*)—that the lack of independence does not result in a deficiency of bliss—is thereby demonstrated. (Regarding the passage beginning with "being a subordinate" [*śeṣatvam*]): Surely, being a subordinate (*śe�ṣatva*) is observed to be suffering; therefore, it is not appropriate for those who are liberated.
Therefore, let it not be so; for the service of Mādhava, which is rooted in the Upaniṣads, remains ever more awake as the most beloved.

Since that [other kind of service] is sublated by the very means of knowledge that apprehends its subject, one might attempt to prove that such service is suffering or that service other than this is unhappy; yet that is already established.

The word "nanu" expresses a doubt. "Subservience" (*śeṣatva*) means lack of independence. According to the method of summary established by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Sudarśana, that for whom the supreme purpose consists solely in the excellence of another is "subordinate" (*śeṣa*), while the other is the "principal" (*śeṣin*); thus, the meaning of subservience is the state of being a cause for the purpose of another, devoid even in the slightest degree of its own purpose. "Suffering has been perceived"—this is seen in the world as something disagreeable to one who is conscious. "That" refers to this subservience. "Therefore"—that is, because of the reason of its nature as suffering.

"In those who are liberated"—that is, in those whose selves are liberated and who are completely freed from all suffering—"it is not fitting"—meaning it is untenable. The sense is: "Is it not [the case] that this is suspected to be untenable?"

The intended inference here is: "That which is subordinate (*śeṣatva*) is of the nature of suffering (*duḥkharūpa*), because it is subordinate, like that which is commonly accepted as such. Furthermore, the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) is intended here: "All that is dependent on another is suffering; service is declared to be the 'dog's way of life' (*śvavṛtti*); therefore, one should avoid it. However, in this case, the reason (*hetu*)—being subordinate—is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because subordination toward a beloved object is observed to be of the nature of happiness (*sukharūpatva*). This is because the fact that being subordinate is of the nature of suffering is contingent upon the identification with the body (*dehātmābhimāna*), which is rooted in karma.

Furthermore, "having a limiting adjunct" (sopādhikatva) means being subordinate to another as determined by something other than the quality of being an object of enjoyment; even though [pleasure] is invariably of the nature of suffering, that [invariable concomitance] does not apply when it is subordinate to the Lord, who possesses both characteristics (liṅga). Moreover, since the fact that subordination to the Lord consists in being of the nature of happiness is established by scripture, there is a fallacy of "mis-timing" (kālātyayāpadeśa). If one attempts to prove that subordination to another is of the nature of suffering, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana). Even if one were to prove that subordination in general is of the nature of suffering, there would be partial contradiction (bādhitatva) and partial proof of the already established.

The general statement that "everything is dependent on another" and so forth is legitimately restricted—according to the principle of the *padāhavanīya* (the fire-pan used for specific purposes)—by hundreds of scriptural statements that reveal the bliss of being a servant of the Blessed Lord. Furthermore, such a restriction is necessary because there is a contradiction with direct perception regarding the aspect of being subordinate to objects of affection. Since being subordinate to one's mother and father is seen to be a form of happiness, it is logical that the subordination to the Blessed Lord—as stated in the verse, "For all people, Mādhava is both father and mother"—is likewise a form of happiness. Moreover, this subordination to mother and father is prescribed by the scriptures; therefore, there is no inconsistency.
Since the determination of human goals conforms to the conceit of a self,
the fact that [the world] is of the nature of suffering is not easily established in its status as a subordinate element.

For when grass and the like are objects of enjoyment for cows and the like, the property of being grass (*tṛṇatva*) and so forth is not the determining factor, because that would entail [the grass] being an object of enjoyment even for tigers and other predators. Nor is it reasonable to say that, in the cognition of grass as an object of enjoyment, the property of being a cow (*gotva*) and so forth—construed through a coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) defined by its own substratum—is the cause; for even at a time when a cow does not recognize its own cowness, it would follow that the grass is still an object of enjoyment for it.

For it is well known that even among those who are human, such as Bharata, Janaka, and others, the cessation of the association with pleasures and other states fixed to humanity occurs simply through the absence of identification with that [humanity]. And it is observed that in another birth, a Brahmin, a *jātismara* (one who remembers past lives), and a particular parrot were said to be prohibited from drinking water and so forth while in the house of a *caṇḍāla*. Therefore, the determination of the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*) conforms precisely to the respective identification with each self.
As it has been said:
"Food is to be eaten by humans, but nectar is for the inhabitants of heaven."
"Dog-like animals, those who eat excrement and grass, and the virtuous whose sole livelihood is service.

In this context, "the virtuous" (*santaḥ*) refers to those who, according to the principle stated in the passage, "If one knows that 'Brahman exists,' then they know him as truly existing," possess the determination of being subordinate (*śeṣatva*) to the Supreme Being (*śeṣin*), which is established by Him. For this very reason, in passages such as "of men" (*manuṣyāṇām*), the meaning obtained is "of those who possess the conceit of being human" (*manuṣyatvādyabhimānavatām*). This has been clearly demonstrated in the *Vedārthasaṅgraha* and its commentary, the *Taddīpikā*. Furthermore, in the *Śrutaprakāśikā*, it is stated: "For all beings, the arrangement of objects of enjoyment and the arrangement of their opposites correspond to their respective self-conceits (*svātmābhimāna*)."

This is likewise observed among human beings, animals, and so forth. Therefore, for the Self whose true nature has manifested as it actually is, its inherent nature is indeed subservience (*śeṣatva*); thus, from the perspective of direct perception, service to the Supreme Person, who is one's own Sovereign (*svaśeṣin*), becomes most beloved. Conversely, the state of being a ruler (*īśitṛtva*) is absolutely undesirable. This has been stated. Nor should it be argued that if even one’s own enjoyment were not a goal, there would be no desire for liberation because the Lord would always accomplish some purpose for Himself through that person; [this is not so] because [the Lord acts] out of the delight of His divine play (*līlā-rasa*).

This is because the bliss of the Lord dependent upon service (*kaiṅkarya*) is of a superior nature. Nor should it be argued that, even so, since bliss could be accomplished by anyone at all, there would not necessarily be a desire for one's own liberation; for there is no contradiction in the Lord’s desire being of the form: "May my supreme purpose, which is my own material cause, be accomplished. Indeed, it is clearly stated in the *Śrutaprakāśikā* that while every conscious being acts solely for its own sake, this rule is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of those endowed with intense affection.

Having intended all this, he said: "Not so, [it is] service to Mādhava. "Not so" means that the previously mentioned objection does not apply. To the question "Why?", he says: "Service to Mādhava," and so forth. "Service to Mādhava" (mādhavadāsyam) means the attendance upon the Lord of Śrī. The suffix *ṣyañ* is applied to the word *dāsa* in the sense of the object (*karman*). "The reality taught in the Upaniṣads" (aupaniṣadaṃ sat) means that which is established by the Upaniṣads. "More dear" (bhūyaḥ priyam) means supremely dear. "It remains awake" (jāgarti) means that it is perceived even through direct sensory experience.

"Therefore"—for the reason stated previously—"the proof of its being suffering"—the inference that the service of the Supreme Person is of the nature of suffering—is "refuted"—its object is sublated—by "the two means of cognition apprehending the subject"—namely, by scripture (*śāstra*) and perception (*pratyakṣa*), which apprehend the very nature of the service as the subject (*dharmin*) standing as the minor term (*pakṣa*) with respect to the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), namely, its nature as suffering. The word "exists" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied here. Or else (*yadvā*)—this refers to an alternative position.

"Servitude other than unto You"—that is, service rendered to one who is not the Supreme Person, distinct from the service of the Supreme Person. "If it were to be established as non-happiness"—meaning, if it were inferred to be of the nature of suffering—then "that"—the fact that everything other than the service of the Supreme Person is of the nature of suffering—is indeed already established; the sense is that it is indeed already known through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Here, the "indication of the lapse of time" (*kālātyayāpadeśa*) and the "proving of what is already established" (*siddhasādhanatva*) are explicitly stated. Furthermore, by the mention of the *Upaniṣad*—which conveys naturalness (*svābhāvikatva*) when no limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) has been stated—the removal of the limiting adjunct consisting in being caused by a condition that brings about the nature of suffering is shown in the subject (*pakṣa*). And by the word "Mādhava," because it conveys the nature of being auspicious in every respect, the removal of being defined by anything other than the qualities of an object of enjoyment is also shown.

By the word "jāgarti" (he remains awake), there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*), because the blissful nature of the servitude (*dāsya*) of the Lord is seen in those residing in the city of Sāketa—such as Yāyajūka, Janaguha, Māruti, Sugrīva, Vibhīṣaṇa, Vidura, Akrūra, and the garland-maker—and others. For it is said of them: "We shall provide shade with these parasols used for the Vājapeya sacrifice."

By such statements as these, it is understood that service to the Lord (bhagavaddāsya) is of the nature of bliss. Furthermore, by the word "moreover" (bhūyas), which denotes unsurpassed excellence, it is indicated that there is an exclusion of the service of those who desire only slight pleasure; thus, the non-invariable concomitance [of the general rule] with respect to that [limited service] is suggested. By the specific injunctions prescribing service to the Lord, such as "Service to Mādhava is the essence of the Upaniṣads," it is implied that the restriction of the general statement—"All is dependent on another"—is logically justified. He is the father and the mother of all the worlds.

The term "Mādhavas" (the virtuous ones) is used to indicate that the service of the Lord, as previously mentioned, is indeed the service of one's mother and father; thus, it possesses both the quality of being beloved and being ordained by the scriptures. Therefore, the sense is that servitude (*dāsya*) is itself the nature of bliss, and thus there is no deficiency in the bliss of the liberated soul. Previously, it was stated that the Lord, accompanied by Lakṣmī, Himself strives for the attainment of His infinite bliss, and that this multitude of His qualities manifests out of His compassion. Here—

The fact that Lakṣmī possesses the status of being a specific means (*upāya*)—characterized by her capacity to awaken the multitude of qualities such as compassion, which are conducive to the attainment of Mādhava—is indicated by the term *lakṣmīsahāya*. Furthermore, the inclusion of Lakṣmī within the category of the "attainable" (*prāpya*) is indicated by the term *mādhava*, because she functions both as the cause of the excellence inherent in service to the Lord and as the one who increases the attainable object itself. By this, it is also indicated that this very point is what is intended by the four chapters (*caturlakṣaṇī*) of the *Śārīraka* [Brahma-sūtras].

For this very reason, the Blessed Lord has indicated in the *Śāstrārthasaṅgraha* that [the suffix] is applied to *brahman* as "Śrīnivāsa. Just as in the case of "the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is established in the tail and so forth," here too, the word "established" (*siddha*) in the phrase "for that is indeed established" serves as an auspicious conclusion to the treatise.

In order to establish the supreme credibility of his own work, the wise Varadāhvaya-maṇḍana— son’s son of the daughter of the preeminent among ascetics (Rāmānuja)— speaking of his own lineage from the tradition of the venerable author of the *Bhāṣya* and his presiding over the auspicious throne for the exposition of the *Śrībhāṣya* as graced by that [preceptor], declares the composition of the *Tattvasāra* solely out of an intense desire to protect the distressed, without any longing for other purposes: "Varadāhvaya-maṇḍana, the wise one,
the grandson of the daughter of the chief of the assembly of ascetics..."
The helmsman of the ocean of the Upanishads has set forth the essence of reality for the welfare of the world.

There is a compound [analysis] as follows: "of the king among ascetics (yati-rāja), the venerable author of the Bhāṣya, who is worshipped by gods (bṛndāraka), serpents (nāga), and great elephants (kuñjara). The nephew (bhāgineya) is the son of the sister; he is Varadaguru, whose lineage is Vatsa. His grandson (pautra) is the son of his son.

The venerable author of the Bhāṣya had two uterine sisters. Of these, the son of one was Vādhūla-Dāśarathi, whose status as a nephew (bhāgineya) is well known. As it has been said: "Is this language easy for others? No; Dāśarathi of the Vādhūla family is the only one."
"Is it not so that [the lineage] has not abandoned its true-born kinsmen?"—thus was it stated by the noble Lakṣmaṇa in the assembly.
But the son of another [lineage] was Vātsya Varadaguru. As he said:
"In the meritorious place called Bhūmika-malā, [there lived] the brother of the noble Rāmānuja."
"From whom both sons named Dāśarathi and Varada were born.

He is his grandson. By this, in accordance with the manner stated in the Śruti—"In his lineage there is no one who does not know Brahman; nor do his descendants ever perish"—the excellence of his knowledge, rooted in his connection with the body of the venerable Commentator (Śaṅkara), who stands at the forefront of those who know Brahman, is intended.

The Vedānta alone is the ocean; it is the milk-ocean because of its similarity [to an ocean] through its being most beloved by the Lord, its vastness, and its being an object of enjoyment. Its "helmsman" (karṇadhāra) is the navigator. In this context, as stated in the phrase "without flaw and capable of reaching the other shore" regarding the Śrībhāṣya, the similarity to a boat is intended to be understood in the same way as the [teaching] it propounds. Therefore, he declares himself to be the helmsman appointed to the auspicious throne of its exposition. According to the lexicon, "karṇadhāra" means a navigator.

"Varada-āhvaya-maṇḍana" means one whose ornament is his name "Varada. By the statement, "He who, by bestowing the nectar of the Bhāṣya, revives even me," the fact that this [work] is named after its subject matter is set aside; for it possesses qualities such as supreme generosity that correspond to the supreme magnanimity residing in the Blessed One, the primary referent of the name "Varada. He is the foremost among the wise (manīṣā).

"For all"—that is, for those who possess mild, middling, or intense wisdom and are thus unfit [for other means]. "For the benefit"—meaning for the sake of accomplishing the faultless human goals through the forms of concise, detailed, or intermediate [teachings] as required. It is also read as *śiṣyahitāya* (for the benefit of disciples); the meaning is clear. Alternatively, *viśvahita* means "beneficial for all," a compound formed according to the rule *caturthī tadartha* ("the fourth case [is compounded] when it denotes the purpose of that").

*Tattvasāram*—a specific work which conveys the most preeminent among the multitude of subjects expounded in the *Śārīraka*, being designated by words expressive of that [preeminence]; *vidadhe*—he composed. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is employed to indicate that the fruit of the action belongs to the agent, based on the intention that benefiting his disciples is equivalent to benefiting himself. The use of the *liṭ* (perfect tense) in the remote past (*parokṣe*) is intended to suggest that even he himself composed the work while under the sway of the bliss derived from partaking of the nectar of the *Bhāṣya*, without any prior conscious deliberation. || 104 ||
Having found its form within the interior of the Meru mountain of the Śrībhāṣya, protected within the firm cage of the words of the Sudarśana [Treatise],
and driven by the force of the fierce wind, it is the sole cause of victory.
May this jeweled necklace, together with its clasp, rest upon you.
I, Vīrarāghavadāsa, the son of the preceptor Nārasiṃha and a vessel for the wealth of noble compassion, have expounded this Essence of Reality.

Thus ends the commentary on the *Tattvasāra* entitled *Ratnasāriṇī*, composed by Vīrarāghavadāsa—the son of the illustrious Narasiṃha Guru, the ornament of the glorious Vādhūla lineage; one who is devoted to serving his teacher’s feet; the offspring of the venerable Vādhūla Veṅkaṭārya; and one who has attained the heart of the pair of Vedāntas through the unfeigned divine grace of the teacher Varada.
